# Balcony solar glossary: the terms, with the numbers behind them

URL: https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-glossary  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

Each of the 38 terms below comes with a plain definition and the figure balco.nyc uses for it, from its calculator, its own PVWatts runs or its reading of the state laws: anti-islanding means an inverter stops within 2 seconds of a blackout, the railing factor for a vertical mount is 0.95, and nine states had signed a plug-in solar law as of 23 September 2026. One figure is new here. By balco.nyc’s arithmetic, an unshaded, south-facing 800 W railing panel in New York City making 604 kWh a year has a capacity factor of 8.6%, about a third of US utility-scale solar’s 24.4%.

## The hardware and the household circuit

The terms that matter describe what happens when a small inverter feeds power into a circuit built to carry it the other way.

**Plug-in solar (balcony solar, Balkonkraftwerk)** · 1,200 W cap in 8 of 9 US laws
A small grid-tied solar system, usually one to four panels on a railing or wall, whose microinverter plugs into a household outlet. Germany calls it a Balkonkraftwerk and caps it at 800 VA; eight of the nine signed US laws cap it at 1,200 W. See [what balcony solar is](https://balco.nyc/what-is-balcony-solar).
**Microinverter** · 96.5% efficient, DC/AC ratio 1.1
A small inverter that turns one or two panels’ direct current into grid-synchronized alternating current. balco.nyc models 96.5% efficiency and 1.1 watts of panel per inverter watt, so little is lost at the inverter’s limit: a vertical south panel in New York reaches 90% of it about 5 hours a year. See [hours near full output](https://balco.nyc/is-plug-in-solar-safe#circuit-arithmetic).
**Anti-islanding** · stop within 2 seconds
Keeping an inverter from energizing wires after the grid fails, which could shock a line worker who believes the line is dead. Under UL 1741 and IEEE 1547 it must stop within 2 seconds of losing the grid, which is also why a plug-in system gives no backup power. Maine’s law asks for 0.2 seconds. See [blackouts and live plugs](https://balco.nyc/is-plug-in-solar-safe#plugs-and-blackouts).
**Backfeed** · 25 A on a 15 A circuit, worst case
Current entering a circuit at an outlet instead of from the breaker panel, so appliances can draw from both while the breaker sees only its share. balco.nyc’s worst case: a 1,200 W inverter on a 15 A circuit lets part of the wire carry 25 A, 67% over its rating, without tripping. See [the circuit arithmetic](https://balco.nyc/is-plug-in-solar-safe#circuit-arithmetic).
**Branch circuit** · 15 A × 120 V = 1,800 W
The wiring from one breaker to its outlets, commonly 15 A (1,800 W at 120 V) or 20 A. A 1,200 W inverter draws 10 A, two-thirds of a 15 A rating. A dedicated circuit removes the backfeed worst case; Maine requires one above 420 W. See [the safety checklist](https://balco.nyc/is-plug-in-solar-safe#checklist).
**GFCI** · 28.6 ms limit; 32.8–36.7 ms under backfeed
A ground-fault circuit interrupter cuts power when current leaks to ground through water or a person; its standard, UL 943, evaluates it for one-way current only. In UL Solutions’ backfeed tests, GFCI breakers took 32.8 to 36.7 milliseconds to clear a simulated body fault, beyond the 28.6 ms limit; GFCI receptacles met it. See [GFCIs and backfeed](https://balco.nyc/is-plug-in-solar-safe#plugs-and-blackouts).

## Standards and certification

Three documents and one federal definition decide what “certified” means for a plug-in system, and a listing to one says nothing about the others.

**UL 1741** · edition 3, 2021
The US safety standard for inverters and other grid-interconnection equipment, used with IEEE 1547; edition 3 is dated 28 September 2021. A microinverter listed to it was evaluated alone, not with panels, cord or circuit. Connecticut’s is the only signed plug-in law naming it. See [the certification vocabulary](https://balco.nyc/ul-3700-plug-in-solar-certification#vocabulary).
**IEEE 1547** · 2018 edition
The IEEE standard for connecting distributed generators to the grid: how they respond to voltage and frequency, and how they avoid islanding. The 2018 edition replaced the 2003 original. It governs grid behavior, not shock or fire safety; Vermont’s law names IEEE 1547-2018. See [how the documents differ](https://balco.nyc/ul-3700-plug-in-solar-certification#vocabulary).
**UL 3700** · outline, edition 1, 11 Dec 2025
UL’s Outline of Investigation for Interactive Plug-In PV Equipment and Systems, the first US safety document for a plug-in system as a whole: an outline, not a consensus standard. As of 23 September 2026 no complete system is listed to it; a few microinverters claim certification. Only Maine’s and Vermont’s laws require a system listing. See [UL 3700 explained](https://balco.nyc/ul-3700-plug-in-solar-certification).
**NRTL and “listed”** · 29 CFR 1910.7
A nationally recognized testing laboratory, recognized by OSHA under 29 CFR 1910.7 to test, list and label products independently of their makers; UL LLC, CSA Group and Intertek are among them. “Listed” means named in such a lab’s list. Every signed plug-in law accepts labs other than UL, except Colorado’s 2027 sales rule. See [how to check a listing](https://balco.nyc/ul-3700-plug-in-solar-certification#check-a-listing).

## The law and permission

Most plug-in laws settle whether the utility gets a say, not whether anyone else does. These are summaries, not legal advice; details vary by state and utility.

**Plug-in solar law** · 9 states signed, 5 in force
A state statute letting a small plug-in system connect without utility approval, under a wattage cap and a certification rule. balco.nyc’s check of every legislature on 23 September 2026 counts nine signed laws, five in force (Utah, Maine, Colorado, Maryland and Vermont), covering 5.2% of US residents. New York’s [SUNNY Act](https://balco.nyc/sunny-act) (S8512C / A9111C) has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature; it grants no right to install. See [every law compared](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-laws-compared).
**Interconnection** · waived by all 9 signed laws
The utility’s approval process for a generator running in parallel with the grid: application, agreement, sometimes fees. All nine signed laws bar the utility from requiring approval, fees or extra equipment, and eight expressly exempt the device from interconnection review. Some still require notice. See [exempt versus a right to install](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-laws-compared#exempt-vs-right).
**Right to install** · 4 of 9 laws; Vermont’s in force
A clause stopping a landlord, association or town from prohibiting a compliant device, usually allowing “reasonable” limits; it is separate from the interconnection exemption. Four signed laws limit landlords (Vermont, Virginia, New Jersey and Colorado); as of 23 September 2026 only Vermont’s protection is in force. See [what renters can do](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-renters).
**Solar-access law** · 1 of 10 statutes clearly covers a railing
An older kind of statute voiding association rules against solar, written for the roof of a house the owner owns. balco.nyc read ten against a condo or co-op railing panel: one clearly covers it (Vermont’s), two are unclear, seven do not. New York’s, Real Property Law §342, covers only rooftops. See [condo, co-op and HOA rules](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-condo-hoa).
**Common element (condo)** · 3 of 9 laws curb association bans
The parts of a condominium owned by all unit owners together. A balcony and its railing are commonly a limited common element: reserved for one unit, controlled by the association. Three signed laws curb association bans (New Jersey, Vermont and, from 2027, Colorado); Virginia’s expressly preserves them. See [why access laws stop at the balcony](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-condo-hoa#why-it-stops).
**Alteration agreement (co-op)** · facade inspections every 5 years
A co-op’s proprietary lease typically requires the board’s written consent for alterations, usually given as an alteration agreement setting conditions for the work. Boards have a reason for caution: New York City buildings over six stories must have their facades, railings and attached equipment included, examined every five years. See [co-ops and condos in NYC](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-condo-hoa#new-york-co-ops).

## The energy model

balco.nyc’s estimate is PVWatts output for the panel’s tilt and direction, times a railing factor, times a shade factor, month by month.

**Kilowatt (kW) and kilowatt-hour (kWh)** · 800 W makes 604 kWh a year (NYC)
A kilowatt is a rate of power; a kilowatt-hour is energy, one kilowatt for one hour, and what the utility bills. balco.nyc’s PVWatts run puts an unshaded, south-facing 800 W railing panel in New York City at 604 kWh a year, 8.8% of an average New York household’s use. See [output by state and direction](https://balco.nyc/800w-balcony-solar-output).
**Capacity factor** · 8.6% for a vertical NYC panel
Energy produced divided by what the system would make at full rated power all year. By balco.nyc’s arithmetic, 604 kWh ÷ (0.8 kW × 8,760 h) = 8.6% in New York City, 14.1% tilted to 35°, and a median 9.4% for a vertical south panel across all 51 state runs. The EIA reports 24.4% for US utility-scale solar in 2025. See [why a vertical panel differs](https://balco.nyc/what-is-pvwatts#seasons).
**PVWatts** · V8; defaults overstate a railing by 72%
The free hourly solar model from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR, formerly NREL), which balco.nyc runs for every estimate. At its rooftop defaults it overstates a vertical, south-facing 800 W panel in New York City by about 72% (1,037 kWh against 604), mostly through the 20° default tilt. See [what PVWatts gets wrong](https://balco.nyc/what-is-pvwatts).
**TMY and NSRDB** · 8,760 hours
A typical meteorological year is 8,760 hours of weather chosen to represent a multi-year period. PVWatts V8 uses TMY files from the National Solar Radiation Database (NSRDB), NLR’s satellite-derived record of direct and diffuse sunlight, on a 4 km grid. Any real year will differ. See [how accurate PVWatts is](https://balco.nyc/what-is-pvwatts#what-pvwatts-is).
**Tilt** · 35° makes 64% more than vertical (NYC)
The panel’s angle from horizontal; a railing panel hangs at 90°. balco.nyc models 35°, 60°, 70° and 90°. In New York, tilting a south-facing panel from vertical to 35° raises output from 604 to 988 kWh a year, because a vertical panel sees only half the sky and meets the summer sun at a glancing angle. See [railing versus roof](https://balco.nyc/800w-balcony-solar-output#vertical-vs-roof).
**Azimuth** · north makes 72% less than south (NYC)
The compass direction a panel faces, in degrees clockwise from true north: 90° east, 180° south. In balco.nyc’s New York runs a vertical panel facing east makes 26% less than one facing south, west 30% less and north 72% less. Manhattan’s street grid runs about 29° off true north. See [east, west and north](https://balco.nyc/800w-balcony-solar-output#direction).
**Railing factor** · 0.95 for a vertical mount
balco.nyc’s multiplier for light the railing, brackets and slab above take off a panel’s lower edge, which PVWatts cannot see; an assumption, not a measurement. It is 0.95 at 90°, 0.97 at 70°, 0.98 at 60° and 0.99 at 35°, turning New York’s 635.7 kWh PVWatts result into 604. See [where it enters the chain](https://balco.nyc/calculate-balcony-solar-output#steps-2-3-shade).
**Soiling** · 3–7% a month, 5% on average
Light lost to dust, pollen and grime on the glass. PVWatts’ default 14% losses include 2% for it; balco.nyc models soiling separately, month by month, from 3% in winter to 7% in pollen season, 5% on average, and keeps 14% for wiring and other losses. See [the methodology](https://balco.nyc/methodology).
**Beam and diffuse light** · 60/40 split
Beam light comes straight from the sun and casts shadows; diffuse light is scattered by air and cloud and comes from the whole sky. balco.nyc’s shade model splits light 60% beam and 40% diffuse, in line with the Northeast’s diffuse share of about 35–42%, which is why a north-facing panel does not produce zero. See [diffuse light](https://balco.nyc/balcony-sunlight#diffuse-light).
**Horizon profile** · 360 one-degree bins
The skyline seen from the balcony: the highest obstruction angle in each direction. balco.nyc builds it in 360 one-degree bins, in New York City from every building within 200 m, elsewhere from your description of what stands opposite. When the sun is below the profile, there is no beam light. See [how the shade step works](https://balco.nyc/calculate-balcony-solar-output#steps-2-3-shade).
**Shade factor** · 1.00 open; 0.38 on a low NYC floor
The share of the light PVWatts assumed that reaches the balcony. It prices obstruction only, so an open view scores 1.00 in any direction; monthly values are floored at 0.10. A third-floor New York balcony facing a six-to-ten-story building 20 m away scores an effective 0.38, cutting 604 kWh a year to 227. See [the worked examples](https://balco.nyc/calculate-balcony-solar-output#worked-examples).

## Money

Savings are kilowatt-hours times the price of a kilowatt-hour you no longer buy; most disagreements between calculators come down to which price.

**Self-consumption** · 60% at a 150 W baseload (NYC)
The share of output used in the home as it is produced; with exports unpaid, only that share saves money. balco.nyc’s hourly New York run finds an apartment drawing a steady 150 W uses about 60% of an 800 W panel’s 604 kWh, saving $124 a year rather than $205. See [how much an apartment uses](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-net-metering#how-much-you-use).
**Marginal rate vs average price** · 34¢ (Con Edison) vs 27.96¢ (NY average)
The marginal rate is what one kWh more or less costs, excluding fixed charges; the average price divides the whole bill, fixed charges included, by kWh. Solar saves at the margin. balco.nyc uses Con Edison’s 34¢ in New York City and EIA state averages elsewhere; New York State’s, 27.96¢, blends in lower-priced utilities outside the city. See [what a kWh costs](https://balco.nyc/electricity-rate).
**Price to compare** · supply only, about 13–18¢
The utility’s supply-only price per kWh, published for comparing independent suppliers (ESCOs in New York). Reported Con Edison figures for 2026 run about 13–18¢: right for choosing a supplier, too low for valuing solar you use, which also avoids delivery charges, surcharges and tax. See [supply-only rates](https://balco.nyc/electricity-rate#supply-only).
**Fixed customer charge** · $20 a month set aside (NYC)
A charge billed every month regardless of use, for costs such as billing and meter reading. Solar cannot reduce it, so balco.nyc subtracts $20 from a New York City bill before converting it to kWh. Elsewhere the EIA average spreads fixed charges over every kWh, which can overstate savings. See [why it is left out](https://balco.nyc/electricity-rate#fixed-charge).
**Payback (nominal)** · 5.5 years in NYC; 9.9 in the median state
Years until cumulative savings equal the kit’s cost. balco.nyc’s figure compounds rate escalation and degradation with no discount rate, so it is nominal. On a $1,200 kit an unshaded south-facing railing pays back in 5.5 years in New York City (5.8 simple) and 9.9 in the median state’s largest city. See [payback in every state](https://balco.nyc/is-balcony-solar-worth-it).
**Degradation** · 0.5% a year; 88.7% left in year 25
The slow loss of a panel’s output with age. A review by NREL researchers of more than 11,000 measured rates found a median of 0.5–0.6% a year for crystalline silicon. balco.nyc uses 0.5% for mid-tier equipment, leaving 88.7% of the original output in year 25. See [the methodology](https://balco.nyc/methodology).
**Escalation** · 3% a year by default
The assumed yearly rise in electricity prices, which raises the value of future kWh. balco.nyc defaults to 3%, with 2% and 4% presets. By its arithmetic, the unshaded New York City panel’s 25-year nominal savings are $7,000 at 3%, $6,165 at 2% and $7,976 at 4%. See [reading the 25-year number](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-cost#reading-the-25-year-number).

## The grid and emissions

What happens to power the apartment does not use, and what the power it does use displaces.

**Net metering** · no signed plug-in law pays for exports
Billing that credits electricity sent to the grid against electricity bought; it normally comes with the paperwork plug-in laws waive. balco.nyc’s reading of the nine signed laws finds none requiring payment for plug-in exports, and at least five expressly excluding the devices from net metering. See [surplus power](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-net-metering).
**Export compensation** · none; 240 kWh a year given away (NYC)
Payment or credit for surplus power leaving through the meter. balco.nyc assumes none unless a law or tariff provides it; New York’s SUNNY Act bill says exports “shall be uncompensated”. In the site’s hourly New York run, an apartment drawing a steady 150 W gives away 240 kWh a year of an 800 W panel’s output. See [surplus is given away](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-net-metering#given-away).
**eGRID subregion** · 27 regions; NYC’s rate is 3.6× upstate’s
One of 27 grid regions in the EPA’s eGRID database, each with its own plant mix and emission rates; balco.nyc finds an address’s subregion from its ZIP code. New York City and Westchester (NYCW), 98% gas-fired, emit 864.5 lb of CO₂ per MWh, 3.6 times upstate New York’s 242.1. See [CO₂ in the calculation](https://balco.nyc/calculate-balcony-solar-output#steps-4-6-value).
**CO₂ output emission rate** · 0.864 lb per kWh (NYC)
Pounds of CO₂ per unit of electricity generated in a subregion, averaged over all its plants. balco.nyc uses eGRID2023’s total output rate: 604 kWh × 0.864 lb is about 522 lb a year in New York City. The non-baseload rate, 976.9 lb/MWh in NYCW, would give a larger figure. See [the methodology](https://balco.nyc/methodology).

## Common questions

**What is a microinverter in balcony solar?**

A microinverter is the small inverter that turns a solar panel’s direct current into alternating current synchronized to the grid, so the power can flow into a home’s circuits through a plug. US plug-in laws cap its AC output, most often at 1,200 W.

**What is anti-islanding?**

Anti-islanding is the inverter function that stops a solar system from energizing wires after the grid goes down, which could shock a utility worker. Under UL 1741 and IEEE 1547 an inverter must stop within 2 seconds of losing the grid, which is also why a plug-in panel gives no power in a blackout.

**What does kWh mean for a solar panel?**

A kilowatt-hour is energy: one kilowatt for one hour, the unit a utility bills. A panel’s watt rating says how fast it can produce; its annual kWh says how much it does. balco.nyc puts an unshaded, south-facing 800 W railing panel in New York City at 604 kWh a year.

**Are balcony solar and plug-in solar the same thing?**

Yes. Both describe a small solar system whose microinverter plugs into a household outlet and feeds the home’s circuits; the German name is Balkonkraftwerk. Germany caps these devices at 800 VA of inverter output, and eight of the nine signed US state laws cap them at 1,200 W.

**What is the capacity factor of a balcony solar panel?**

By balco.nyc’s arithmetic, an unshaded south-facing 800 W railing panel in New York City has a capacity factor of 8.6%, and the median across the largest city in every state and DC is 9.4%, against 24.4% for US utility-scale solar in 2025. Shade lowers a balcony’s figure further.

**Is UL 3700 a standard?**

Not a consensus standard. UL 3700 is UL LLC’s Outline of Investigation for Interactive Plug-In PV Equipment and Systems, edition 1, dated 11 December 2025. As of 23 September 2026 no complete plug-in system is listed to it, though a few microinverters claim certification as components.

# The balcony solar kWh formula: estimate output by hand

URL: https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-kwh-formula  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

For a panel on a balcony railing, multiply its watts by your state’s vertical-south yield (0.67 to 1.08 kWh per watt a year), a direction factor (0.74 for east, 0.29 for north), 0.95 for the railing and a shade factor. Tested against balco.nyc’s PVWatts runs for the largest city in every state, that formula lands within 3.5% of the full simulation in the median case. The familiar rooftop formula, kW × peak sun hours × 365 × performance ratio, overstates a south-facing railing by about 60% and an east- or west-facing one more than twofold.

## The rooftop formula, and why it overstates a railing

The formula that circulates for estimating solar output by hand is **kWh a year = system kW × peak sun hours × 365 × performance ratio**. A peak sun hour is one kilowatt-hour of sunlight per square meter, so a place receiving 4.5 kWh/m² a day has 4.5 peak sun hours. The performance ratio covers inverter, wiring, heat and dirt losses; consumer guides quote 0.75 to 0.85, and the original PVWatts used an overall derate of 0.77.

On a roof, the formula works. balco.nyc took NREL’s latitude-tilt solar resource for the largest city in each state (the Solar Resource API, which returns no data for Anchorage, so 50 places) and set the formula against its own PVWatts runs for an 800 W panel tilted 35° to the south. With a performance ratio of 0.75 the formula came within **2.4%** of PVWatts in the median city; at 0.80 it ran 6.6% high.

On a railing, it does not. In Chicago NREL gives 4.50 peak sun hours at latitude tilt, so 0.8 kW × 4.50 × 365 × 0.75 = **986 kWh**. PVWatts puts the same panel on a 35° south roof at 1,010 kWh: close. Hung vertically on a south-facing railing, with the 5% railing loss the site applies to every vertical estimate, it makes **616 kWh**. The formula is 60% high. Across the 50 places the median overstatement for a south-facing railing is **61%**, and it grows as the railing turns away from south: the formula gives about 2.2 times the real output facing east or west, and about 5.5 times facing north. It has no term for direction at all.

The arithmetic is fine; the input is wrong. A peak-sun-hour figure describes sunlight on a horizontal or latitude-tilted surface, and many published tables do not say which. A railing panel is neither. It faces the horizon, so the high summer sun strikes it at a glancing angle; it sees half of the sky’s diffuse light, where a 35° panel sees about nine-tenths; and more of its direct light arrives at steep angles, where the glass reflects it away, a loss PVWatts models explicitly. In balco.nyc’s runs a vertical south panel, after the railing loss, makes a median **63%** of what the same panel makes at 35°, from 44% in Honolulu to 75% in Anchorage. Using horizontal peak sun hours instead does not rescue the formula: at the same 0.75 performance ratio it still overstates a south railing by a median 39%.

## A formula built for a railing

balco.nyc’s balcony formula keeps the shape of the rooftop one, but every input describes a vertical panel:

> **kWh a year ≈ W × Ystate × Fdir × (1 − 0.05) × Sshade**

| Term | What it is | Typical value | Where it comes from |
|---|---|---|---|
| W | The panels’ rated power in watts | 400 or 800 | The label |
| Ystate | kWh a year per watt from a vertical, south-facing panel with an open view, before the railing loss | 0.67 to 1.08; median 0.87 | balco.nyc’s PVWatts run for the state’s largest city (section 3) |
| Fdir | Output in your direction as a fraction of south | 1.00 S, 0.93–0.96 SE/SW, 0.73–0.74 E/W, 0.29 N | Median across 51 cities (section 4) |
| 1 − 0.05 | Railing loss: the rail, brackets and the slab above clip the panel’s lower edge | 0.95 | The factor the calculator applies to every vertical panel (methodology) |
| Sshade | The share of that light the buildings opposite let through | 1.00 for an open view; 0.18–0.94 in a street canyon | balco.nyc’s street-canyon model (section 5) |

A worked example: an 800 W system on an east-facing 10th-floor balcony in Chicago, looking across the street at a building of six to ten stories. That building is lower than the balcony, so nothing is blocked and S is 1.00.

**800 × 0.81 × 0.74 × 0.95 × 1.00 ≈ 456 kWh a year.**

PVWatts, run for an east-facing vertical panel in Chicago and given the same railing loss, says 444 kWh. The hand calculation is 2.5% high. Now move the same system to a south-facing 2nd-floor balcony, 20 meters from that same building. Direction improves, to 1.00; shade collapses, to 0.31:

**800 × 0.81 × 1.00 × 0.95 × 0.31 ≈ 191 kWh a year.**

The better-facing balcony makes less than half as much. In a city, your floor and what stands opposite usually move the answer more than the compass does.

## Ystate: the number that depends on where you live

Y is the input that depends on where you live. balco.nyc ran NREL’s PVWatts V8 for an 800 W vertical south-facing panel at the largest city in every state and DC, with the calculator’s own parameters, and divided the annual output by 800. Half the states fall between 0.81 and 0.94 kWh per watt a year. A selection:

| Largest city | Ystate (kWh per W a year, before railing loss) | 800 W, vertical south, open view, after railing loss |
|---|---|---|
| Albuquerque | 1.08 | 819 kWh |
| Denver | 1.06 | 805 kWh |
| Phoenix | 1.02 | 778 kWh |
| Minneapolis | 0.96 | 730 kWh |
| Los Angeles | 0.95 | 720 kWh |
| Boston | 0.89 | 673 kWh |
| Median of 51 | 0.87 | 658 kWh |
| Chicago | 0.81 | 616 kWh |
| Jacksonville | 0.80 | 612 kWh |
| New York City | 0.79 | 604 kWh |
| Houston | 0.76 | 576 kWh |
| Seattle | 0.69 | 524 kWh |
| Honolulu | 0.67 | 510 kWh |

Every state is on [the state pages](https://balco.nyc/states), which carry the same runs. The order is not the order of a rooftop sunshine map, and that is the second reason the rooftop formula misleads. Ranked by what a 35° roof panel produces, Minneapolis is 31st of the 51 cities; ranked by what a vertical railing produces, it is 8th. Jacksonville falls from 13th to 40th, Houston from 24th to 47th, and Honolulu from 9th to last. A wall-mounted panel likes a low sun, which strikes it nearly square on in a northern winter, while near the tropics the sun spends much of the year high overhead and passes over the panel’s face. Across the 51 cities, the ratio of vertical to 35° output rises steadily with latitude (a correlation of 0.90).

Each Y comes from one city. The runs do not measure variation inside a state, which in a large or mountainous state can be substantial; the [calculator](https://balco.nyc/) runs PVWatts for your exact address.

## Fdir: which way the railing faces

F is output in a given direction divided by output facing south, from the same PVWatts runs. The medians across the 51 cities, and how far individual cities stray from them:

| Railing faces | Fdir (median) | Middle half of cities | Full range |
|---|---|---|---|
| South | 1.00 | — | — |
| South-west | 0.96 | 0.93–0.98 | 0.91 (Billings) to 1.13 (Honolulu) |
| South-east | 0.93 | 0.92–0.96 | 0.87 (Anchorage) to 1.11 (Honolulu) |
| East | 0.74 | 0.72–0.79 | 0.61 (Anchorage) to 1.07 (Honolulu) |
| West | 0.73 | 0.70–0.77 | 0.66 (Billings) to 1.05 (Honolulu) |
| North-east | 0.46 | 0.44–0.49 | 0.41 (Anchorage) to 0.73 (Honolulu) |
| North-west | 0.44 | 0.42–0.47 | 0.39 (Denver) to 0.70 (Honolulu) |
| North | 0.29 | 0.29–0.32 | 0.25 (Albuquerque) to 0.42 (Honolulu) |

The pairs are close enough to share a number (about 0.95, 0.74 and 0.45); pairing them moves the test results in section 6 by a few tenths of a point. The medians also sit close to the fixed factors in the calculator’s New York fallback model (0.92, 0.72, 0.45, 0.32), which were set independently.

The factors drift with latitude in the same way Y does. Near the Gulf, where the summer sun is high, a south wall loses more and east and west lose less: east is 0.88 of south in Houston and New Orleans and 0.86 in Jacksonville, well above the 0.74 median. In Honolulu the order inverts, and east and west both out-produce south. In Anchorage east is only 0.61. If you are in Hawaii, skip the direction factor and use [the Hawaii page](https://balco.nyc/states/hawaii), which has the run for each direction.

## Sshade: what stands across the street

With an open view (a park, water, or buildings lower than your floor) S is 1.00, at every orientation, because PVWatts has already priced direction. Otherwise S depends on how tall the obstruction is, how far away, and how high you are.

balco.nyc’s street-canyon model treats the building opposite as a continuous wall parallel to your facade and traces the sun against it through the year. These figures come from the calculator’s own code, run for a south-facing balcony in Chicago (41.88°N), 20 meters across a street, with a balcony height of (floor − 1) × 3.05 m + 1.0 m:

| Across the street (20 m away) | 2nd floor | 5th floor | 10th floor |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nothing, an open view | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| 1 to 2 floors, or trees (7 m) | 0.94 | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| 3 to 5 floors (13 m) | 0.75 | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| 6 to 10 floors (25 m) | 0.31 | 0.58 | 1.00 |
| 11 floors or more (43 m) | 0.18 | 0.24 | 0.47 |

These are the factors as the calculator applies them: monthly, to monthly output, here weighted by Chicago’s vertical-south PVWatts months. The model’s one-line annual summary, weighted by New York’s monthly sunshine, reads higher under heavy shade: 0.40 rather than 0.31 on the 2nd floor opposite six to ten stories, 0.63 rather than 0.58 on the 5th, 0.55 rather than 0.47 on the 10th opposite a tower. The gap is seasonal. A south railing does its best work in winter (in Chicago, about 62 kWh in January against 33 in June after the railing loss), exactly when the low sun sits behind the building opposite. Use the lower figures.

Three cautions. An east- or west-facing balcony loses more to the same building, because its direct sun arrives low: 0.64 rather than 0.75 on the 2nd floor opposite three to five stories. The same street blocks more sun further north, less further south. And a continuous wall has no gaps, so it errs toward too much shade. What it cannot see at all (a tree, an air-conditioner, the slab overhead) is covered in [how much sun a balcony gets](https://balco.nyc/balcony-sunlight).

## How wrong the formula is

balco.nyc tested each version against the PVWatts run it tries to predict, both with the 5% railing loss applied. The state-yield test leaves out south, since Y is built from the south run and would score zero by construction: seven directions in 51 places, 357 predictions. The national-yield test keeps all eight directions (408), and the rooftop tests use a south railing in the 50 places with NREL sun-hour data, or all 51 for the calibrated version.

| Version | Median error | 1 prediction in 10 is off by more than | Worst case |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rooftop formula, NREL peak sun hours, performance ratio 0.75, south railing | +61% | +88% | +157% (Honolulu) |
| Rooftop formula calibrated exactly to each city’s 35° roof, south railing | +61% | +82% | +132% (Honolulu) |
| Balcony formula with one national Y (0.87), all 8 directions | 5.5% | 19% | +50% (Anchorage, east) |
| Balcony formula with each state’s Y, 7 non-south directions | 3.5% | 12% | −37% (Honolulu, north-east) |
| The same, leaving out Honolulu | 3.4% | 10% | +22% (Anchorage, east) |

The rooftop formula overstated every railing it was tested on. Even calibrated perfectly to each city’s own roof, with peak sun hours times performance ratio taken straight from the 35° PVWatts run, it is 61% high. That isolates the cost of going vertical: no choice of derate fixes it.

The balcony formula with state yields lands within 10% of PVWatts in 87% of cases. Its large misses cluster where section 4 says they will. Every Honolulu direction is under-predicted, by 15% to 37%; the Gulf-state cities (Houston, New Orleans, Jackson and Jacksonville) are under-predicted in most directions away from south, by up to 21%; and Anchorage facing east is over-predicted by 22%. Those five states and Alaska account for 28 of the 46 predictions that miss by more than 10%. Using one national Y instead roughly doubles the share of predictions off by more than 10%, from one in eight to one in four; for a south railing it overstates Seattle and Portland, Oregon, by 25% and understates Albuquerque by 20%. That is what location is worth.

These are errors against a model, not a meter. PVWatts has its own uncertainty, and balco.nyc’s stated accuracy for its fullest New York estimates is a modeled band of about 15%, not a field-validated one. A hand result is no better than PVWatts; round it to the nearest 25 kWh.

## What a hand formula cannot see

Five multiplications cannot carry everything a year of simulation does:

- **The seasons.** One annual number hides that a south railing is winter-heavy and an east or west one summer-heavy, which matters on a seasonal rate.

- **The interactions.** The terms are multiplied as if independent; in fact shade depends on direction and season, and direction factors on latitude.

- **Your street.** Y is one city per state; S assumes one uniform building opposite.

- **Money and permission.** kWh is not savings: value it at [your marginal rate](https://balco.nyc/electricity-rate), remembering that the state averages used outside New York City include fixed charges. Whether you may install a plug-in system varies by state and building; nothing here is legal advice.

Used for what it is, the formula answers the first question well: is this a 600 kWh balcony or a 200 kWh one? For a figure to act on, the [calculator](https://balco.nyc/) runs PVWatts for your exact address, applies shade month by month, and in New York City uses the real buildings around you.

## Common questions

**What is the formula for balcony solar panel output?**

balco.nyc's hand formula for a railing-mounted panel is: kWh a year ≈ watts × Y × F × 0.95 × S. Y is the vertical-south yield for your state (0.67 to 1.08 kWh per watt a year across the largest city in each state, median 0.87), F is the direction factor (1.00 south, about 0.95 south-east or south-west, 0.74 east or west, 0.29 north), 0.95 is the railing loss and S is the shade factor (1.00 for an open view). Tested against PVWatts in all 51 places, it came within 3.5% in the median case.

**Can I use peak sun hours to estimate a balcony panel's output?**

Not directly. Peak sun hour figures describe sunlight on a horizontal or latitude-tilted surface, and a vertical railing panel receives much less. Using NREL's latitude-tilt figures and a 0.75 performance ratio, the standard formula (kW × peak sun hours × 365 × performance ratio) overstated a south-facing railing by a median 61% in balco.nyc's comparison across 50 states, and an east- or west-facing one by more than double.

**How much does an 800 W balcony solar system produce a year?**

Mounted vertically on a south-facing railing with an open view, balco.nyc's PVWatts runs put it at 510 to 819 kWh a year after a 5% railing loss, from Honolulu to Albuquerque, with a median of about 658 kWh across the largest city in each state. Facing east or west, multiply by about 0.74; facing north, by about 0.29; then multiply by a shade factor if taller buildings stand opposite.

**Why does a vertical solar panel produce less than a tilted one?**

A vertical panel faces the horizon, so the high summer sun strikes it at a glancing angle, it sees only half of the sky's diffuse light, and more of its direct light arrives at steep angles where the glass reflects it. Across the largest city in each state, a vertical south-facing panel with a 5% railing loss produced a median 63% of what the same panel tilted at 35 degrees produced, from 44% in Honolulu to 75% in Anchorage.

**Does an east- or west-facing balcony work for solar?**

It produces about three-quarters of what a south-facing one does: a median factor of 0.74 for east and 0.73 for west across the largest city in every state, in balco.nyc's PVWatts runs. Near the tropics east and west do relatively better, because the sun spends much of the year high overhead: in Houston and New Orleans east is about 0.88 of south, and in Honolulu east and west both out-produce south.

**How accurate is a hand calculation of balcony solar output?**

Accurate enough to tell a 600 kWh balcony from a 200 kWh one. Against PVWatts, balco.nyc's balcony formula errs by 3.5% in the median case and by more than 10% about one time in eight, mostly in Hawaii, Alaska and the Gulf states. PVWatts is itself a model rather than a meter, so a hand result is best rounded to the nearest 25 kWh.

## Sources

- [NREL — PVWatts V8 API documentation](https://developer.nlr.gov/docs/solar/pvwatts/v8/): the model behind every run on this page: NSRDB typical-year weather, tilt and azimuth inputs (180° = south), and ac_annual / ac_monthly as annual and monthly AC output in kWh.
- [NREL — Solar Resource Data API documentation](https://developer.nlr.gov/docs/solar/solar-resource-v1/): the latitude-tilt and horizontal daily solar resource (kWh/m²/day, i.e. peak sun hours) used for the rooftop-formula test; the API returned no data for Anchorage.
- [NREL — PVWatts Version 5 Manual (Dobos, 2014)](https://pvwatts.nlr.gov/downloads/pvwattsv5.pdf): the Perez plane-of-array model, the angle-of-incidence reflection correction, the 14% default system losses, and the 0.77 overall derate of the original PVWatts.
- [U.S. DOE OSTI — Performance Parameters for Grid-Connected PV Systems (Marion et al., 2005)](https://www.osti.gov/biblio/15016389): performance ratio and reference yield as the standard parameters relating PV output to the solar resource.
- [SolarReviews — Peak sun hours explained](https://www.solarreviews.com/blog/peak-sun-hours-explained): the definition of a peak sun hour as an hour at 1,000 W/m², and an example of a state table that does not say which surface it describes.
- [NREL — PVWatts Calculator](https://pvwatts.nlr.gov/): where any figure on this page can be re-run for a specific address, tilt and azimuth.
- [U.S. Census Bureau — Vintage 2025 subcounty population estimates](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/popest/datasets/2020-2025/cities/totals/sub-est2025.csv): the source for the largest city in each state, which is the reference point for every state run.

# What the US plug-in solar laws actually say, provision by provision

URL: https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-laws-compared  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

Nine US states have signed plug-in solar laws, and five are in force today: Utah, Maine, Colorado, Maryland and Vermont. All nine stop the utility from requiring its approval and eight cap a device at 1,200 W, but only four limit what a landlord, association or town can do, and the certification wording differs enough that a kit can qualify in one state and not the next. balco.nyc’s compilation of the legislature pages, weighted by Census population, puts 5.2% of US residents under a law in force today, and 29.5% if every signed law and the New York and California bills take effect.

## The count on 23 September 2026

balco.nyc checked plug-in solar legislation in all 50 states and the District of Columbia on 23 September 2026, from each legislature’s own bill pages and enacted text rather than third-party trackers, which disagree with the primary sources on several effective dates. (Trackers list Maryland’s as taking effect on signing or on 1 October; the act and the state’s fiscal note both say 1 July 2026.) The result:

| Status | Count | Where | Share of US residents |
|---|---|---|---|
| In force | 5 | Utah, Maine, Colorado, Maryland, Vermont | 5.2% |
| Signed, not yet in force | 4 | Connecticut (1 Oct 2026), Virginia and New Hampshire (1 Jan 2027), New Jersey (1 Mar 2027) | 6.9% |
| Passed, awaiting a governor | 2 | New York, California | 17.4% |
| Bill pending | 7 | District of Columbia, Illinois, Massachusetts, Michigan, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania | 19.6% |
| Bill died, 2025–26 | 18 | Alaska, Arizona, Delaware, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Indiana, Iowa, Minnesota, Missouri, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Oregon, Rhode Island, South Carolina, Washington, West Virginia, Wyoming | 21.7% |
| No bill found | 15 | Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, North Dakota, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Wisconsin | 29.3% |

The shares are balco.nyc’s arithmetic: each jurisdiction’s July 2025 Census Bureau population estimate, summed by status, over the 341.8 million total for the 50 states and DC (rounded). Read cumulatively, **5.2% of US residents** live where a plug-in law is in force today, 12.1% will once New Jersey’s starts on 1 March 2027, and 29.5% would if New York and California enact theirs. Sources for every state are on [the states page](https://balco.nyc/states).

> **No law is not the same as a ban.** Before its act passed, Maryland’s legislative analysts noted that balcony solar was not prohibited there, but that utilities “frequently require customers to enter into interconnection agreements” first. That is broadly the position in the 42 jurisdictions without a signed law. A plug-in law takes the device out of that process.

## “Exempt from interconnection” is not a right to install

Every plug-in law can answer two separate questions. Most answer only the first.

**The utility question** is whether you need your power company’s permission. A device that feeds power into your wiring while the grid is live is, in utility rules, a small generator, which normally needs an interconnection application and agreement before it runs. All nine signed laws bar the utility from requiring its approval, charging a fee or demanding extra equipment; eight expressly free the device from interconnection agreements or review, and Colorado gets there by listing what the utility may not demand. That is “exempt from interconnection”, and it is the whole of what Utah, Maine, Maryland, Connecticut and New Hampshire do.

**The property question** is whether anyone else can stop you: a landlord, a lease, a condominium declaration, a homeowners’ association, a town’s zoning. An interconnection exemption does not touch any of it. A *right to install* is a separate clause that makes some of those prohibitions unenforceable, usually while allowing “reasonable” limits on size and placement. Only Vermont, Virginia, New Jersey and Colorado have one.

Two points get lost in between. **Notice is not approval**: Maryland and Virginia require notice to the utility before installing, Maine within 30 days above 420 W, and none lets the utility refuse a compliant device. And **codes still apply**: Connecticut says its exemption does not reach the building and fire codes or “any local ordinance or regulation”, and Colorado and New Jersey require installation to meet the fire, electrical or construction codes.

## The utility side, law by law

The first matrix is what each enacted text says about the device and the utility, quoting the statute where the wording matters. “Not addressed” means we read the provision and it is silent; “unclear” means it says something that does not settle the point. NRTL is a nationally recognized testing laboratory; NEC the National Electrical Code. The two bills awaiting a governor are in italics; they are not law.

| Law | In force | Size cap, as worded | Certification wording | Utility notice | Net metering and exports |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| UtahHB 340 | 7 May 2025 | 1,200 W “maximum power output”; AC or DC not stated | “Certified by Underwriters Laboratories or an equivalent” NRTL; NEC | None | “Not subject to” net metering |
| MaineLD 1730 | 29 Jul 2026 | 1,200 W AC inverter output per address; above 420 W, licensed electrician and dedicated circuit | “In accordance with UL 3700”, a comparable NRTL standard, or configured per the NEC | Within 30 days, above 420 W only | “May not be used for net energy billing” |
| ColoradoHB26-1007 | 12 Aug 2026; property rules 1 Jan 2027 | 1,920 W “to the electric grid”; one system per address | “Labeled and listed” by an NRTL; from 2027, over 391 W must be “UL labeled and listed” to be sold | Utility may ask for presence and size | Not addressed |
| MarylandHB 1532 | 1 Jul 2026 | 1,200 W supplied back to the building; one per meter | “Certified by Underwriters Laboratory or an equivalent” NRTL | Before installing, with a safety and capacity certification | Outside net metering; no renewable energy credits |
| VermontAct 149 | 1 Jul 2026 | 1,200 W combined inverter capacity per meter; smart meter required | “Complies with UL 3700” or an equivalent certification; IEEE 1547 | None | Ineligible; exports “shall not be compensated” |
| ConnecticutPA 26-127 | 1 Oct 2026 | 1,200 W “maximum power output”; one per meter | UL or an equivalent NRTL, “and meets” UL 1741; IEEE 1547; NEC | None | Must warn that excess is “charged to the customer as usage” without a net-metering meter |
| VirginiaHB 395 / SB 250 | 1 Jan 2027 | 1,200 W per customer or multifamily unit | An NRTL (29 CFR 1910.7) or equivalent; NEC | State form before installing; utility has 15 days to query it | Outside net metering |
| New HampshireSB 540 | 1 Jan 2027 | 1,200 W AC inverter output; one per metered customer | An NRTL, to “nationally recognized safety standards” (none named) | Optional, after installation | Unclear: no credit provided |
| New JerseyS2368 / A4836 | 1 Mar 2027 | 1,200 W combined per address or dwelling unit | “In accordance with” UL 3700 or “a comparable standard”, by an NRTL | None | Outside net-metering requirements; credit not addressed |
| New YorkSUNNY Act (bill) | 90 days after enactment | 1,200 W AC inverter nameplate, to the grid | NRTL listing “as a complete plug-in photovoltaic system” | Within 30 days | “Uncompensated” unless the owner opts in |
| CaliforniaSB 868 (bill) | 1 Jan 2027 if enacted; exemption ends 2030 | 1,200 W aggregated AC per dwelling | “Certified as a plug-in photovoltaic system” by UL or an NRTL | Utility may require online registration | Not addressed |

The caps do not all measure the same thing. Maine, Vermont, New Hampshire and California’s bill cap inverter AC output, so panel wattage behind a smaller inverter does not count; Maryland, Colorado and New York’s bill cap what is supplied back to the building or grid; Utah, Connecticut and New Jersey say only “maximum power output”. Several also limit the number of devices: one per meter in Maryland, Connecticut and New Hampshire, one system per address in Colorado.

## The property side: landlords, associations and towns

The second matrix is where the laws genuinely diverge. Five of the nine say nothing about who else may stop you; four do, each in its own way.

| Law | Landlord and tenant | HOA, condo and co-op | Local government |
|---|---|---|---|
| Utah | Not addressed | Not addressed | Not addressed |
| Maine | No right; on a structure you do not own you must protect it, meet building, fire and zoning codes, and restore it | Not addressed | Not addressed |
| Colorado | From 2027, no “unreasonable” prohibition; the owner may set reasonable limits, including prior notice | From 2027, unreasonable covenants are void; may install on a limited common element such as a balcony | Fire and local building codes apply; the 2027 bar binds any “person”, which includes governments (our reading) |
| Maryland | Not addressed | Not addressed | Not addressed in §7-321 |
| Vermont | 10 days’ notice; the landlord may set reasonable restrictions; silence lets the tenant proceed | Covenants may not prohibit, including on condo, co-op and apartment patio railings | Zoning bylaws may not regulate them |
| Connecticut | Not addressed | Not addressed | Local ordinances and codes still apply |
| Virginia | Landlords with more than four units may not prohibit on the tenant’s exterior; reasonable limits; 7 days’ notice | Not overridden: association, condo and co-op instruments preserved | May not prohibit on residential structures; height, setback and historic rules apply |
| New Hampshire | Not addressed | Not addressed | Not addressed |
| New Jersey | May not bar tenants who pay their own electric bill, including on a balcony or patio; reasonable limits; 14 days’ notice | May not enforce bans on exterior placement; reasonable limits allowed | May not prohibit, or require a permit, fee or approval |
| New York (bill) | Not addressed | Not addressed | Not addressed |
| California (bill) | Not addressed | Not addressed | Not addressed |

The four rights are not one right. Vermont’s turns on notice: silence from the landlord lets the tenant proceed. Virginia’s covers only tenants of landlords with more than four units, and leaves condominium and association documents intact. New Jersey’s covers tenants who pay their own electric bill and also binds associations and towns. Colorado’s bars “unreasonable” prohibitions from 1 January 2027; our reading that it reaches towns rests on state law defining a “person” to include governmental subdivisions.

On balco.nyc’s population arithmetic those four states hold **7.3%** of US residents, but three of the four rights are not yet operative. The only one in force today is Vermont’s, covering about 0.2%. What this means in practice is covered in [balcony solar for renters](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-renters) and [condos, co-ops and HOAs](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-condo-hoa).

## Why a kit that qualifies in one state may not qualify in the next

Each law protects only a device that meets its own definition, and the definitions differ most in the certification clause:

- **Certified by a lab, standard unnamed:** Utah, Maryland, Virginia and Colorado. None says certified *to what*, or whether listings of the separate components count.

- **A component standard, or a description of one:** Connecticut adds UL 1741, the inverter standard; New Hampshire asks for “nationally recognized safety standards” without naming one.

- **UL 3700 or something comparable:** Maine, Vermont and New Jersey. Maine and New Jersey identify UL 3700 by its title, an “Outline of Investigation”, and Maine also accepts a system configured to the electrical code.

- **Certified as a complete system:** New York’s bill and California’s.

The spread matters because, as of September 2026, no complete plug-in system has been certified to UL 3700; the components (panels, microinverters) carry their own listings. A kit sold with a UL 1741-listed microinverter and listed panels may therefore satisfy the unnamed-standard wording of Utah or Maryland, while in Vermont the question becomes what counts as an “equivalent certification”, and under New York’s or California’s bill whether any complete-system listing exists for it at all. The statutes do not answer those questions and we cannot either. The standard itself is covered in [what UL 3700 is, and is not](https://balco.nyc/ul-3700-plug-in-solar-certification), and the hazards these clauses target in [is plug-in solar safe?](https://balco.nyc/is-plug-in-solar-safe)

Certification is not the only trap. A device sized to Colorado’s 1,920 W cap falls outside every other state’s definition. An 800 W kit that meets Utah’s definition with no installer requirement needs, in Maine, a licensed electrician and a dedicated circuit. Vermont allows devices only on smart-metered services. And a second unit behind the same meter in Connecticut or Maryland takes you outside the law even if each unit qualifies.

## The patterns: 1,200 W, 391 W, and exports nobody pays for

**1,200 W is the default.** Of the 36 jurisdictions where balco.nyc found a plug-in bill in 2025–26, 34 wrote in a wattage figure, and 30 of those chose 1,200 W, including eight of the nine signed laws and both bills now with a governor. The exceptions: Colorado’s 1,920 W, also proposed by [New Mexico](https://balco.nyc/states/new-mexico)’s SB 157 before it died; [Delaware](https://balco.nyc/states/delaware)’s 800 W bill; and Illinois. Utah’s 2025 law, the first, is visibly the template: Connecticut, Virginia and New Jersey reuse its definition almost word for word, down to “intended primarily to offset part of the customer’s electricity consumption”.

**391 W is the other number.** Colorado, Maryland and Virginia exempt devices at or below 391 W from code or listing provisions that would require rewiring; New Jersey sets that line at 400 W, and Maine’s unconditional tier stops at 420 W. None of the texts explains 391, and we could not trace its origin. [Illinois’](https://balco.nyc/states/illinois) SB 3104, as amended in committee in March 2026, would make it a ceiling: it prohibits any system above 391 W until the National Electrical Code adopts a standard for them, about a third of what every signed law allows. It cleared committee 9–4, was sent back to the Assignments committee on 22 May 2026, and has not moved since.

**Exports are almost never paid for.** Five of the nine signed laws expressly take the device out of net metering or deny it any export credit (Utah, Maine, Maryland, Vermont, Virginia); New Jersey exempts it from net-metering program requirements without saying whether exports are paid; Connecticut requires a warning that exports are billed as usage; and none provides another credit. Vermont says exports “shall not be compensated”; Connecticut goes further, requiring a warning that excess generation is charged as usage unless the meter allows net metering. Colorado is silent, and New Hampshire shields the utility from “compensation or charges” without saying more. The one bill in balco.nyc’s data that would have credited exports, [Oregon](https://balco.nyc/states/oregon)’s HB 4080, died in March 2026. See [why surplus earns nothing](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-net-metering).

**Who is bound varies by utility.** The statutes bind utilities under different labels (“electrical corporation”, “electric company”, “electric distribution company”, “electric public utility”, “provider of retail electric service”), each defined by its own state’s law. California’s bill names local publicly owned utilities outright; most others leave it to those definitions, which we have not resolved state by state. If you buy power from a municipal utility or a cooperative, ask it whether the law applies.

## The two bills on a governor’s desk, and checking your own state

[New York](https://balco.nyc/states/new-york)’s SUNNY Act (S8512C / A9111C) has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature. The final version cleared both on 28 May 2026; as of 23 September the Assembly’s record shows no delivery to the Governor, so her decision clock has not started. If signed, it takes effect on the 90th day. It would exempt devices of up to 1,200 W AC from interconnection and net metering, leave exports uncompensated unless the owner opts into an agreement, require notice within 30 days, and require listing as a complete system. It grants no right to install: renters, co-op shareholders and condo owners would still need permission. [The SUNNY Act in detail](https://balco.nyc/sunny-act).

[California](https://balco.nyc/states/california)’s SB 868 was presented to Governor Newsom on 31 August 2026. Under the state constitution he has until 30 September to act, or it becomes law without his signature; if enacted, it takes effect on 1 January 2027. It binds local publicly owned utilities as well as investor-owned ones, and is silent on exports, landlords and associations. It is the only text here with an end date: the exemption is repealed on 1 January 2030, the day a ban begins on selling plug-in devices that do not meet its code and certification conditions.

For any state, check five things against the enacted text before relying on a summary, including this one: the effective date; how the cap is measured; the certification wording, against your device’s paperwork; whether and when the utility must be told; and whether the law mentions your landlord, association or town — if it does not, their rules still apply. This page summarizes statutes as written. It is not legal advice, and a utility, court or building department may read a clause differently.

## Common questions

**Which states allow plug-in or balcony solar?**

As of 23 September 2026, nine states have signed plug-in solar laws. Five are in force: Utah, Maine, Colorado, Maryland and Vermont. Connecticut's takes effect on 1 October 2026, Virginia's and New Hampshire's on 1 January 2027, and New Jersey's on 1 March 2027. New York's SUNNY Act and California's SB 868 have passed both chambers and await their governors. Elsewhere a plug-in system is not necessarily banned, but the utility's ordinary interconnection rules for generators apply.

**Which states give renters a right to install balcony solar?**

Four signed laws limit a landlord's power to say no, each differently. Vermont lets a tenant proceed if the landlord does not answer a 10-day notice; Virginia bars landlords with more than four units from prohibiting devices on the exterior of the tenant's premises; New Jersey protects tenants who pay their own electric bill; Colorado bars unreasonable prohibitions. Only Vermont's is in force today: Colorado's and Virginia's start on 1 January 2027 and New Jersey's on 1 March 2027. Utah, Maine, Maryland, Connecticut and New Hampshire give tenants no such right, and neither would New York's SUNNY Act.

**Is 1,200 watts the limit in every state?**

Nearly. Eight of the nine signed plug-in solar laws cap devices at 1,200 W, and 30 of the 34 jurisdictions whose 2025-26 plug-in bills set a wattage figure chose 1,200 W. Colorado allows 1,920 W supplied to the grid. Maine allows up to 420 W with no conditions and up to 1,200 W only if a licensed electrician installs each system on a dedicated circuit and the utility is notified. The caps are also measured differently: some count inverter AC output, some the power supplied back to the building or grid, and some just say maximum power output.

**Do plug-in solar laws pay you for electricity sent to the grid?**

Almost never. Five of the nine signed laws take plug-in devices out of net metering or deny them export credit, and none provides another credit; Vermont's says exported power shall not be compensated, New Jersey's exempts the devices from net-metering program requirements without saying whether exports are paid, and Connecticut's requires a warning that excess generation will be charged as usage unless the meter allows net metering. New York's SUNNY Act would leave exports uncompensated unless the owner opts into an agreement. Plan on the value coming only from electricity you use yourself.

**What does 'exempt from interconnection' mean for plug-in solar?**

It means the utility cannot make you apply, sign an interconnection agreement, pay a fee or add equipment before using a compliant device, as it can for a rooftop array. It says nothing about whether a landlord, condo board, homeowners' association or town can stop you; that takes a separate right-to-install clause, which only four of the nine signed plug-in laws (Vermont, Virginia, New Jersey and Colorado) contain.

**If a plug-in solar kit is legal in one state, is it legal in another?**

Not necessarily. Each law protects only devices that meet its own definition, and the certification wording differs: Utah and Maryland ask for certification by UL or an equivalent lab without naming a standard, Maine, Vermont and New Jersey name UL 3700 or a comparable standard, and New York's and California's bills require certification as a complete plug-in system. As of September 2026 no complete plug-in system has been certified to UL 3700. Wattage caps, per-meter device limits and Vermont's smart-meter requirement also differ.

**Is balcony solar legal in New York or California yet?**

Not yet in either. New York's SUNNY Act has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature; it had not been delivered to her as of 23 September 2026 and would take effect 90 days after becoming law. California's SB 868 was presented to Governor Newsom on 31 August 2026; he has until 30 September 2026 to act, it becomes law without his signature if he does not, and it would take effect on 1 January 2027.
