# Balcony solar claims, checked: nine numbers traced to their source

URL: https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-myths  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

Of nine claims widely repeated about balcony solar, one holds up roughly as stated, two are best cases presented as typical, and six are wrong or out of date. balco.nyc’s PVWatts runs for the largest city in every state and DC put an unshaded, south-facing 800 W railing system at a median 6.4% of the average home’s electricity (4.2% to 11.9%), not 15–25%, and at a median payback of 9.9 years on a $1,200 kit, with no state under four. The claim that survives is the unexpected one: a north-facing railing really does produce about 70% less than a south-facing one.

## The nine claims and their verdicts

Each claim below is stated as it usually circulates, traced as far back as we could take it, and checked against balco.nyc’s own data: NREL’s PVWatts V8 run with the calculator’s settings for an 800 W system at the **largest city in each of the 50 states and DC**; the EIA’s state prices and household consumption; and every state’s plug-in solar law, researched from legislature pages and checked on 23 September 2026.

|  | The claim | Where it comes from | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | An 800 W kit covers 15–25% of your electricity | Solar.com’s 2026 guide, among others; no derivation given | A ceiling. A south-facing railing panel covers a median 6.4% of the state-average home. No state reaches 15% |
| 2 | A north-facing balcony produces 75% less | Earliest we found: a 2024 newsletter. It matches a PVGIS run for a vertical panel in Berlin | Roughly right for an unshaded vertical panel: 58% to 75% less in US cities, median 71% |
| 3 | You need four hours of direct sun a day | Could not be traced | No threshold exists. A north-facing railing gets essentially no direct sun from October to March and still produces a median 70 kWh |
| 4 | It pays for itself in two years | Bright Saver, for a kit bought at cost in a high-rate state | A special case. A $1,200 kit on a south railing takes 4.8 to 13.9 years, median 9.9 |
| 5 | You get the 30% federal tax credit | IRC §25D, which was real through 2025 | Out of date. It ended for expenditures after 31 December 2025 |
| 6 | It keeps your lights on in a blackout | Could not be traced | False. The inverter must shut off within 2 seconds of an outage |
| 7 | Any outlet will do | Sellers’ shorthand for “it has a plug” | False. It needs a weather-rated outdoor outlet on a circuit with room for it |
| 8 | It is legal in every state | Seller copy | False. 5 states have a law in effect and 4 more have signed one |
| 9 | It sells your surplus back to the grid | Carried over from rooftop net metering | False under the signed laws. Six rule it out, three are silent, none provides a credit |

That is one claim that holds up roughly as stated (2), two best cases presented as typical (1 and 4), and six that are wrong or out of date. Every output figure on this page applies the site’s railing-obstruction factor — 0.95 for a vertical panel, 0.99 at 35° — and none includes shade from neighboring buildings, so each is the *unobstructed best case* for its city. Paybacks use the calculator’s own loop: 0.5% a year panel degradation, prices rising 3% a year, and every kilowatt-hour used at home at the state’s EIA average price.

## Output: 15–25%, 75% less, four hours of sun

### 1. “An 800 W kit covers 15–25% of your electricity”

Solar.com’s 2026 guide says a standard 800 W kit can often cover 15% to 25% of a typical apartment’s monthly electricity. It shows no working, and we found none elsewhere. balco.nyc’s runs give this:

| 800 W, facing south, unshaded | kWh a year (median city) | Share of the state’s average home | Share of an average large-building apartment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vertical, on a railing | 658 | 4.2% to 11.9%, median 6.4% | 8.4% to 13.4%, median 10.8% |
| Tilted to 35° | 1,053 | 7.3% to 21.3%, median 10.3% | 11.7% to 22.6%, median 17.3% |

Against the average home in its own state (EIA, 2024: a median of about 10,600 kWh a year), no state’s railing panel reaches 15%. Thirteen stay under 5%, most of them Southern states where homes use the most electricity; only California, Maine and New Mexico pass 10%. A fairer test of an apartment claim is an apartment: the EIA’s 2020 Residential Energy Consumption Survey puts households in buildings of five or more units at 20.8 million Btu of electricity, about **6,100 kWh a year**. A railing panel still tops out at 13.4% of that. The 15–25% only appears when the panel is tilted to 35°, sits in full sun and serves a smaller-than-average user — then 48 of the 51 land between 15% and 23%, and none reaches 25%. It is a ceiling, not an expectation. In New York City, balco.nyc’s 3D shade model puts real balconies at 400–900 kWh, 6% to 13% of the state-average home.

### 2. “A north-facing balcony produces 75% less”

The earliest instance of this figure we have found is a February 2024 newsletter post that states it, together with “30% less” for east and west, without showing the calculation; its listed sources include the European Commission’s PVGIS tool, run for Berlin. We reran PVGIS for Berlin ourselves with an 800 W vertical panel: **612 kWh facing south, 154 facing north — 74.8% less**. East and west averaged 419 kWh, 31.5% less. Both numbers match, so a Berlin PVGIS run is the likely origin, though we cannot confirm the author used exactly that.

The surprise is that it roughly survives the trip to America. balco.nyc’s PVWatts runs put a vertical north-facing railing **58% to 75% below** a south-facing one, with a median of 71%; 28 of the 51 cities lose 70% or more. The biggest losses are in the clear-skied Southwest — Albuquerque 75%, Las Vegas 75%, Phoenix 74% — because there the south side has the most direct sun to win. The smallest is Honolulu, 58%, where the midsummer sun passes north of overhead. So the verdict is roughly right, for an unobstructed vertical panel. What it leaves out is everything but the compass: in a street canyon a high-floor north balcony can out-produce a boxed-in south one, which is [why balco.nyc models the block rather than the direction](https://balco.nyc/balcony-sunlight).

### 3. “You need four hours of direct sun a day”

The threshold circulates as four hours, four to five, or six to eight, and one guide we read gave two different figures on one page. We could not trace any version to a study or a standard. A panel has no threshold: it produces whatever the light allows, continuously. The cleanest test is a north-facing railing. Between the September and March equinoxes the sun rises and sets south of due east and west everywhere in the United States, so a north-facing vertical panel gets essentially *no* direct sun for half the year — zero hours, not four. balco.nyc’s runs still give it a median **70 kWh from October to March**, all of it from diffuse and reflected light, about 35% of its annual output. Small, and no reason on its own to buy, but proof that output fades with the light rather than switching off at a line. The useful question is how many kilowatt-hours, which [our guide to balcony sunlight](https://balco.nyc/balcony-sunlight) works through.

## Money: the two-year payback and the tax credit

### 4. “It pays for itself in two years”

The most specific source we found is Bright Saver, a nonprofit that sells kits at cost. It says that in a sunny, high-rate state such as California or New York, a kit bought at its at-cost price typically pays back in about two years. Its price is the first condition: 360 W for $414.17 to members, about $1.15 a watt, against $1.50 a watt for balco.nyc’s $1,200 mid-range assumption for 800 W. Rerun on balco.nyc’s assumptions, a $1,200 kit on an unshaded south-facing railing pays back as follows:

| Payback on a $1,200 kit | States (of 51) | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Under 2 years | 0 | — |
| Under 4 years | 0 | — |
| 4 to 5 years | 1 | California (Los Angeles), 4.8 |
| 5 to 8 years | 12 | Hawaii 5.2, Massachusetts 5.5, New York 6.6 |
| 8 to 10 years | 15 | Pennsylvania 8.1, Colorado 8.3, Illinois 9.4 |
| 10 years or more | 23 | Florida 11.2, Texas 11.5, Louisiana 13.1; Washington (Seattle) slowest at 13.9 |

The median is **9.9 years**. The arithmetic for the fastest state: 720 kWh a year in Los Angeles at California’s average 32.89¢ is $237 in year one, and rising prices bring $1,200 back in 4.8 years. Even the $850 budget kit gets under five years in only eight states, all high-price ones: California, Hawaii and six in the Northeast. Two years does reproduce, but only when three conditions line up. Take Bright Saver’s 360 W price, tilt the panel to 35° instead of hanging it on a railing, and put it in Los Angeles: about 579 kWh (the 800 W run scaled to 360 W), $190 a year, **2.1 years**, or 2.3 counting the $29 membership. Hang the same panel on a railing and it is 3.8 years. At balco.nyc’s budget price, a tilted 800 W system beats two years in two states, Hawaii and California. A $1,200 kit on a railing does it nowhere. These figures are generous (section 6); the [cost and payback guide](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-cost) works the same arithmetic for New York City.

### 5. “You get the 30% federal tax credit”

This one was true. The residential clean energy credit under IRC §25D paid 30% of the cost of solar electric property installed from 2022 through 2025, and pages written in that period still say so. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (P.L. 119-21, signed 4 July 2025) ended it: the IRS says the credit is not allowed for any expenditure made after 31 December 2025, and that an expenditure counts as made when installation is complete. A kit installed in 2026 earns no federal credit, even one paid for in 2025. balco.nyc’s payback figures net out no credit. The details are in [our tax credit guide](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-tax-credit).

## Hardware: blackouts and outlets

### 6. “It keeps your lights on in a blackout”

It does the opposite, by design. Grid-connected inverters are built to IEEE Std 1547-2018 and tested under UL 1741. The standard requires them to detect an outage — an “unintentional island” — and stop energizing the line **within 2 seconds**, then wait, by default, five minutes after the grid returns before starting again. The reason is safety: a line crew must be able to treat a dead line as dead. State plug-in laws write the same rule in. Utah requires a feature that stops the device energizing the building during an outage; Maine requires inverters that shut off 0.2 seconds after power is disrupted. We could not trace the belief to any source. Our guess is that it comes from portable “solar generators”, battery units that do run appliances in an outage because they connect to nothing. Backup power from a balcony means a battery system, a separate product and a separate decision.

### 7. “Any outlet will do”

A plug-in kit does end in an ordinary plug. That is true of the plug, not of every outlet, and three things narrow it:

- **It has to be outdoors and rated for it.** An outlet on a balcony needs to be one rated and covered for a wet location, and many balconies have none. Adding one is work for a licensed electrician, and in an apartment building usually needs the building’s approval too; [the installation guide](https://balco.nyc/install-balcony-solar) lists what to check.

- **The circuit behind it matters.** A standard breaker does not see current that a plug-in panel injects into the circuit, so household load plus solar output can exceed what the wiring was designed for without tripping anything. Protection against overloads is one of the things UL Solutions’ certification program for plug-in systems tests for.

- **Some laws specify the outlet.** Maine lets a household run up to 420 W without an electrician, but anything larger, up to 1,200 W, must be installed by a licensed electrician on a dedicated circuit with a single outlet.

None of this is electrical advice: which outlet and circuit suit a given home is a question for an electrician.

## Law: every state, and selling power back

### 8. “It is legal in every state”

We saw this in the footer of one kit seller’s website in August 2026, on a page whose own article counted ten states with laws. balco.nyc has now reviewed all 50 states and DC from their legislatures’ bill pages. As of 23 September 2026:

| Status | Count | States |
|---|---|---|
| Law in effect | 5 | Colorado, Maine, Maryland, Utah, Vermont |
| Signed, not yet in effect | 4 | Connecticut (1 Oct 2026), New Hampshire (1 Jan 2027), Virginia (1 Jan 2027), New Jersey (1 Mar 2027) |
| Passed, awaiting signature | 2 | California (SB 868), New York (SUNNY Act) |
| Bill pending | 7 | DC, Illinois, Massachusetts, Michigan, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania |
| Bill failed or vetoed | 18 | Alaska, Arizona, Delaware, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Indiana, Iowa, Minnesota, Missouri, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Oregon, Rhode Island, South Carolina, Washington, West Virginia, Wyoming |
| No plug-in law found | 15 | Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, North Dakota, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Wisconsin |

Where there is no law, plug-in solar is not banned as such, but the utility’s interconnection rules apply, and those usually require approval before anything feeds power into a home circuit. New York’s SUNNY Act has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature; it would grant no right to install. California’s SB 868 was presented to Governor Newsom on 31 August 2026. Even where a law is in effect, most do not stop a landlord or a condo board from saying no: four of the nine signed laws (Colorado, New Jersey, Vermont, Virginia) limit that power in different ways, and the other five give no right to install. This is not legal advice; [every state’s bills, dates and limits](https://balco.nyc/states) are listed with their sources, and [the SUNNY Act page](https://balco.nyc/sunny-act) covers New York.

### 9. “It sells your surplus back to the grid”

Rooftop solar usually earns credit for exported power under net metering, and the assumption carries over. For plug-in systems it mostly does not. Of the nine signed laws, **six rule it out**: Utah and Maryland exempt the devices from net-metering rules, Maine bars them from net energy billing, Virginia excludes them from its definition of an eligible customer-generator, and Vermont says exported generation shall not be compensated. Connecticut goes further: its law requires a warning that surplus is charged to the customer as usage unless the meter allows net metering. Colorado, New Hampshire and New Jersey are silent. New York’s bill would leave exports uncompensated unless the owner signs a separate agreement, and California’s is silent. None provides a credit. balco.nyc therefore assumes surplus earns nothing in every state, which is why the share of output used at home — the fridge, the router, whatever runs in daylight — matters as much as the output itself.

## What these numbers leave out

The figures behind the nine verdicts are generous in some ways and blunt in others. Five limits are worth knowing before quoting them:

- **One city per state.** Each state is represented by its largest city. Buffalo is not New York City, and Flagstaff is not Phoenix. The [state pages](https://balco.nyc/states) name the city behind every number.

- **No shade.** Every output figure assumes nothing blocks the sky. In New York City balco.nyc’s 3D model finds roughly a threefold spread between the best and worst realistic balconies, mostly from the buildings opposite.

- **Average prices.** The EIA’s state averages divide total revenue by total sales, so they include fixed monthly charges a panel cannot touch. That overstates the value of a kilowatt-hour you avoid buying. In New York City the calculator uses Con Edison’s marginal rate of 34¢ instead, and anywhere else the per-kWh rate from your own bill is the better input.

- **Everything used at home.** Savings and paybacks assume every kilowatt-hour displaces one you would have bought. Surplus earns nothing (claim 9), so a home that exports part of its output saves less.

- **Modeled, not metered.** These are PVWatts simulations over a typical weather year, not measurements from installed systems.

The pattern across the nine claims is consistent: the numbers that travel furthest describe a tilted, unshaded panel serving a light user in a high-price state, then get repeated as if they described a railing panel anywhere. For one balcony rather than 51 cities, [run your own address](https://balco.nyc/); the [methodology](https://balco.nyc/methodology) sets out every assumption used here.

## Common questions

**Is balcony solar a scam?**

No. A plug-in panel does generate electricity and cut a bill, but the most repeated numbers oversell it. balco.nyc's PVWatts runs for the largest city in every state put an unshaded, south-facing 800 W railing system at a median 658 kWh a year: about 6.4% of the average home's use, worth about $109 a year at the state's average price. It saves money slowly: balco.nyc's model finds no state where a $1,200 kit on a south-facing railing pays back in under four years.

**Does balcony solar really save money?**

Yes, but slowly in most states. On balco.nyc's $1,200 mid-range kit price, an unshaded south-facing 800 W railing system pays back in 4.8 years in California, the fastest, and 13.9 years in Washington, the slowest, with a median of 9.9 years across the 50 states and DC. Those figures assume every kWh is used at home and prices rise 3% a year; shade or unused surplus makes them longer.

**How much of my electricity will an 800 W balcony kit cover?**

For a south-facing railing panel, usually 4% to 12% of an average home's use, with a median of 6.4%, according to balco.nyc's PVWatts runs for the largest city in every state. The often-quoted 15-25% needs a panel tilted to about 35 degrees, no shading, and an apartment with below-average consumption.

**Does a north-facing balcony really produce 75% less?**

Close, for an unshaded vertical panel. balco.nyc's PVWatts runs put a north-facing railing 58% to 75% below a south-facing one across US cities, with a median of 71%, and the 75% figure matches a PVGIS calculation for a vertical panel in Berlin. In a dense city, the buildings opposite often matter more than the compass direction.

**Does balcony solar work during a power outage?**

No. Grid-connected inverters must detect an outage and stop energizing the line within 2 seconds under IEEE Std 1547-2018, and plug-in laws such as Utah's and Maine's require the same, so that line crews are not put at risk. Power during a blackout needs a battery system, which is a separate product.

**Is plug-in solar legal in every state?**

No. As of 23 September 2026, balco.nyc's review of all 50 states and DC finds a plug-in solar law in effect in 5 states (Colorado, Maine, Maryland, Utah, Vermont), signed but not yet in effect in 4 (Connecticut, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Virginia), and passed and awaiting signature in 2 (California, New York). Elsewhere the utility's interconnection rules apply, which usually means approval is required. This is not legal advice.

**Can I sell surplus balcony solar power back to the utility?**

Generally no. Six of the nine signed plug-in solar laws exclude these devices from net metering or deny any export credit, and the other three are silent; none provides a credit. Connecticut's law requires a warning that surplus is charged to the customer as usage unless the meter allows net metering.

**Can I still claim the 30% federal solar tax credit on a balcony kit?**

Not for a kit installed now. The residential clean energy credit under IRC section 25D ended for expenditures made after 31 December 2025 under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, and the IRS treats an expenditure as made when installation is complete, so a kit installed in 2026 earns no federal credit.

## Sources

- [NLR — PVWatts V8 API documentation](https://developer.nlr.gov/docs/solar/pvwatts/v8/): the hourly production model behind balco.nyc’s 800 W runs for the largest city in every state and DC (retrieved 23 September 2026).
- [EIA — Form EIA-861M monthly sales and revenue by state](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/data/eia861m/xls/sales_revenue.xlsx): state average residential prices over the twelve months to June 2026, used for savings and payback; averages that include fixed charges.
- [EIA — 2024 average monthly bill, residential (Table 5A)](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/sales_revenue_price/pdf/table_5A.pdf): average household consumption by state, the denominator for the coverage figures.
- [EIA — 2020 Residential Energy Consumption Survey, Table CE2.1](https://www.eia.gov/consumption/residential/data/2020/c&e/pdf/ce2.1.pdf): 20.8 million Btu (about 6,100 kWh) of electricity a year for apartments in buildings of five or more units, against 36.1 million Btu for all homes.
- [Solar.com — 2026 guide to balcony and plug-in solar](https://www.solar.com/learn/guide-to-balcony-plug-in-solar/): an instance of the claim that an 800 W kit covers 15–25% of an apartment’s electricity, cited in order to check it.
- [’tings — Balcony solar: tiny panels, big promises (February 2024)](https://tings.substack.com/p/balcony-solar-tiny-panels-big-promises): the earliest instance we found of the 75%-less north-facing figure, with 30% less for east and west, and its listing of a PVGIS run for Berlin among its sources.
- [European Commission Joint Research Centre — PVGIS](https://re.jrc.ec.europa.eu/pvg_tools/en/): the tool balco.nyc reran for an 800 W vertical panel in Berlin: 612 kWh facing south, 154 facing north, 425 east and 413 west.
- [Bright Saver — Is plug-in solar worth it?](https://www.brightsaver.org/post/is-plug-in-solar-worth-it): the two-year payback claim, for a kit bought at cost in a high-rate state such as California or New York. Its member price of $414.17 for 360 W plus a $29 annual membership is as recorded in balco.nyc’s cost guide in September 2026.
- [IRS — FAQs for modification of sections 25C, 25D and others under Public Law 119-21](https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/faqs-for-modification-of-sections-25c-25d-25e-30c-30d-45l-45w-and-179d-under-public-law-119-21-139-stat-72-july-4-2025-commonly-known-as-the-one-big-beautiful-bill-obbb): that the §25D credit is not allowed for expenditures made after 31 December 2025, and that an expenditure is made when installation is complete.
- [IRS — Residential Clean Energy Credit](https://www.irs.gov/credits-deductions/residential-clean-energy-credit): that the credit equaled 30% of the cost of qualified property installed from 2022 through 31 December 2025.
- [NLR — A primer on the unintentional islanding protection requirement in IEEE Std 1547-2018 (2022)](https://docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy22osti/77782.pdf): that a DER must detect an island and cease to energize within 2 seconds, the five-minute default return-to-service delay, and UL 1741 testing.
- [Utah Legislature — H.B. 340 (2025), enrolled copy](https://le.utah.gov/Session/2025/bills/enrolled/HB0340.pdf): the required feature preventing a device from energizing the building during an outage, and the exemption from net metering program requirements.
- [Maine Legislature — Public Law 2026, chapter 644 (LD 1730)](https://legislature.maine.gov/legis/bills/getPDF.asp?paper=SP0676&item=5&snum=132): inverters that shut off after 0.2 seconds, a licensed electrician and a dedicated single-outlet circuit above 420 W, and no net energy billing.
- [Vermont Legislature — Act 149 (S.202) as enacted](https://legislature.vermont.gov/Documents/2026/Docs/ACTS/ACT149/ACT149%20As%20Enacted.pdf): that plug-in devices are not eligible for net metering and their exports shall not be compensated.
- [Connecticut General Assembly — Public Act 26-127](https://www.cga.ct.gov/2026/ACT/PA/PDF/2026PA-00127-R00HB-05340-PA.PDF): the required warning that surplus generation is charged to the customer as usage unless the meter allows net metering.
- [Virginia Acts of Assembly, 2026, Chapter 1052 (HB 395)](https://lis.blob.core.windows.net/files/1225204.PDF): the exclusion of small portable solar generation devices from the definition of an eligible customer-generator and from net energy metering provisions.
- [Maryland General Assembly — 2026 Laws, Chapter 353 (HB 1532)](https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/2026RS/Chapters_noln/CH_353_hb1532e.pdf): that a portable solar energy generating system is not subject to the net metering sections, §§7-306 and 7-306.1.
- [New York State Senate — S8512C (SUNNY Act)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/S8512/amendment/C): passage on 28 May 2026, and that exported energy would be uncompensated unless the customer enters a separate agreement.
- [California Legislature — SB 868 status](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB868): enrolled and presented to the Governor on 31 August 2026.
- [UL Solutions — testing and certification framework for plug-in solar (January 2026)](https://www.ul.com/news/ul-solutions-debuts-testing-and-certification-framework-safer-plug-solar-across-united-states): that the program requires features that protect against overloads and prevent current flowing in the wrong direction.
- [pv magazine — How to design a UL-certified balcony solar kit in the United States](https://www.pv-magazine.com/2026/02/02/how-to-design-a-ul-certified-balcony-solar-kit-in-the-united-states/): that plug-in systems can inject current standard breakers do not detect, so household load plus solar can exceed a circuit’s limit.

---

# Do you get paid for balcony solar power you don’t use?

URL: https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-net-metering  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

Almost certainly not. None of the nine state plug-in solar laws signed so far requires a utility to pay for power a balcony system sends back to the grid, five of them expressly shut these devices out of net metering, and New York’s SUNNY Act says exports “shall be uncompensated.” So the number that matters is how much you use yourself: balco.nyc’s hourly PVWatts run for an 800 W south-facing railing in New York City finds that an apartment drawing a steady 150 W uses about 60% of the output and gives the other 240 kWh a year away.

## Surplus power is given away, not sold

A plug-in panel’s power goes first to whatever the apartment is drawing at that moment: the fridge, the router, a laptop charger. Only when the panel produces more than the apartment uses does anything flow back out through the meter to the neighbors. That outflow is the surplus.

The arrangement that pays for exports is net metering, under which the kilowatt-hours you send out are credited against the ones you buy. Net metering normally comes with an interconnection application and utility approval — exactly the paperwork plug-in laws exempt these devices from. The trade the states have made is consistent: no application, no fee, no credit. This is not legal advice, and it varies by state and utility, but the safe planning assumption is that surplus earns **nothing**.

That makes one number decisive: the share of the panel’s output you use at the moment it is produced. balco.nyc’s calculator, like most, assumes that share is 100% and values every kWh at Con Edison’s all-in marginal rate of 34¢. That is a ceiling. To see how far below it a real apartment sits, balco.nyc ran NREL’s PVWatts V8 hour by hour for an 800 W system on a vertical, south-facing railing in New York City, with the calculator’s own parameters. The hourly run reproduces the 635.7 kWh a year in the site’s state data exactly; less the 5% railing loss the site applies to vertical panels (a factor of 0.95), that is about **604 kWh**. Set hour by hour against an apartment drawing a steady 150 W, 364 kWh of it is used at home and **240 kWh** leaves through the meter. At 34¢ that is a saving of about $124 a year, not the $205 the 100% assumption gives.

## What each plug-in law says about exported power

Nine states have signed plug-in solar laws, and bills in New York and California have passed their legislatures. balco.nyc read each in the legislature’s own text. Five expressly shut plug-in devices out of net metering, three say nothing about paying for exports, and Connecticut requires a warning that exports may be billed. None requires a utility to pay for them.

| State | Law | Status (23 Sep 2026) | What it says about exports |
|---|---|---|---|
| Utah | HB 340 (2025) | In force since 7 May 2025 | “Not subject to the net metering program requirements”; residential net metering now starts above 1,200 W. Unpaid. |
| Maryland | HB 1532, ch. 353 | In force since 1 July 2026 | Not subject to §7-306, the state’s net-metering statute, or §7-306.1. Unpaid. |
| Vermont | Act 149 (S.202) | In force since 1 July 2026 | “Shall not be eligible for net metering”; exports “shall not be compensated.” Smart meter required. Unpaid. |
| Maine | LD 1730, ch. 644 | In force since 29 July 2026 | “May not be used for net energy billing.” Unpaid. |
| Colorado | HB26-1007 | In force since 12 August 2026 | Silent: bars utility approval and fees, says nothing about credit. Assume unpaid. |
| Connecticut | Public Act 26-127, sec. 9 | From 1 October 2026 | Device must warn that excess generation is “charged to the customer as usage” unless the customer has a net-metering meter. Unpaid, possibly billed. |
| Virginia | HB 395 / SB 250 | From 1 January 2027 | Excluded from the definition of an eligible customer-generator for net metering. Unpaid. |
| New Hampshire | SB 540, ch. 262 | From 1 January 2027 | Exempt from interconnection review; no provision pays for exports. Assume unpaid. |
| New Jersey | P.L.2026, c.82 | From 1 March 2027 | Exempt from interconnection and metering requirements; silent on payment. Assume unpaid. |
| New York | SUNNY Act, S8512C / A9111C | Passed both chambers; awaits the Governor's signature | Exports “shall be uncompensated” unless the customer voluntarily enters a net-metering or other compensation agreement. Unpaid. |
| California | SB 868 | On the Governor’s desk; he has until 30 September 2026 to act | Silent. Assume unpaid. |

Silence is not a credit: where a law says nothing, balco.nyc assumes no payment unless a utility publishes a tariff for plug-in devices. New York’s bill leaves one door open: an owner may voluntarily enter an interconnection or net-metering agreement, and exports stay unpaid unless they do. Getting paid, in other words, means doing the paperwork the bill otherwise waives. Size limits, certification and the right to install are in the [side-by-side comparison of the laws](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-laws-compared), and New York in detail on [the SUNNY Act page](https://balco.nyc/sunny-act).

## Does the meter spin backwards?

“Spinning backwards” is the old picture of net metering: while you export, the meter subtracts, and you are billed for the difference. Whether anything like that happens with a plug-in panel depends on the meter, not the law. The Maryland Public Service Commission’s balcony-solar guidance describes what a meter that cannot track exports may do: treat the surplus as zero consumption, or add it to your consumption in error, depending on the meter type. That gives three possibilities.

- **Not counted.** The surplus vanishes from the bill in both directions. This is the outcome balco.nyc’s figures assume: you lose its value and nothing more.

- **Counted as usage.** A meter that registers power flowing either way as consumption bills you at the full retail rate for electricity you gave away. Connecticut’s law requires every device to carry a warning saying exactly this. In the New York example above, the 240 kWh exported would be billed at about $82 a year, cutting a $124 saving to about **$42**.

- **Netted.** A meter set up for net metering does subtract exports. That is the only version of “spinning backwards” that pays you, and under these laws it comes with a net-metering arrangement, not with the plug.

Utilities are beginning to say which applies. Potomac Edison, a FirstEnergy utility in Maryland, states that its standard service meter has no separate register to track energy a customer feeds back to its system. Vermont’s law allows plug-in devices only on smart-metered service. In New York City, Con Edison describes a net meter for customers enrolled in net metering; what an ordinary meter records when power flows out is worth asking Con Edison before the SUNNY Act, which awaits the Governor's signature, takes effect. The practical step is the same everywhere: ask your utility, in writing, how your meter records power flowing out of the apartment.

## How much of the output an apartment actually uses

The share you use depends on how much the panel produces in each hour and how much the apartment draws in that hour. The second has a hard lower limit. Every home has a floor it never drops below: the fridge, the router, standby electronics, smoke alarms. NRDC’s 2015 study of smart-meter data from 70,000 northern California homes found that floor, the lowest hourly level, averaged **218 W**; the one multifamily home in its ten-home audit, occupied by a couple it described as unusually energy-conscious, idled at 92 W. A smaller apartment will usually sit below the study average, so 100 to 300 W brackets most floors.

balco.nyc set the hourly New York output against a constant load at each of those levels. A constant floor is what an apartment draws with nobody home, so these shares hold even for an apartment empty all day; daytime cooking, working or laundry raises them.

| Apartment’s steady draw | 400 W system (302 kWh/yr) | 800 W system (604 kWh/yr) | 1,200 W system (906 kWh/yr) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100 W | 72% | 46% | 34% |
| 150 W | 87% | 60% | 46% |
| 200 W | 95% | 72% | 56% |
| 300 W | ~100% | 87% | 72% |

Share of annual output used at home: New York City, vertical south-facing railing, PVWatts V8 hourly, 0.95 railing factor, no shading. For an 800 W railing, most apartments will use between about 60% and 90% of the output; a small, efficient apartment that is empty in the daytime can use less than half. Hourly averages flatter these figures slightly, since passing cloud and a cycling fridge make supply and demand miss each other within the hour; real loads sitting above the floor for much of the day push the other way.

The surplus is seasonal, and not in the direction most people expect. A vertical south-facing panel meets the low winter sun almost head-on, so in New York it produces most in winter: 69 kWh in January against 30 kWh in June, with midday peaks near 690 W. Against a 150 W floor only 43% of January’s output is used at home; in June, 96%. The kilowatt-hours given away are winter ones, which in New York are the cheaper ones, since Con Edison’s delivery charges are higher from June through September (see [what a kWh costs](https://balco.nyc/electricity-rate)).

**Why a 400 W system uses more of its output than a 1,200 W one.** The apartment’s load does not grow when you add panels. Every extra panel produces in the same midday hours as the first, when the floor is already covered, so most of its output is surplus. At a 150 W floor, going from 400 to 800 W adds 302 kWh a year of output but only 102 kWh used at home; going from 800 to 1,200 W adds another 302 kWh of output and only **49 kWh** used, about $17 a year at 34¢. The table has a simple symmetry that shows why: a 400 W system against a 150 W floor behaves exactly like an 800 W system against 300 W. What matters is the ratio of system size to what the apartment draws.

## What self-consumption does to payback

Because surplus earns nothing, savings scale directly with the share you use, and payback stretches with it. The table runs the calculator’s own payback loop — a 3% annual rise in the electricity price, 0.5% yearly panel degradation, no discounting — for an unshaded 800 W south-facing railing in each state’s largest city, on the $1,200 mid-range kit, at three self-consumption levels.

| State (city) | Output | Price used | 100% used | 80% used | 60% used |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| New York (NYC) | 604 kWh | 34¢ Con Edison marginal | $205/yr · 5.5 yrs | $164/yr · 6.8 yrs | $123/yr · 8.8 yrs |
| Illinois (Chicago) | 616 kWh | 18.54¢ EIA average | $114/yr · 9.4 yrs | $91/yr · 11.5 yrs | $69/yr · 14.7 yrs |
| California (Los Angeles) | 720 kWh | 32.89¢ EIA average | $237/yr · 4.8 yrs | $190/yr · 6.0 yrs | $142/yr · 7.8 yrs |

First-year saving and nominal payback; output is PVWatts V8 for each city less the 0.95 railing factor. The Illinois and California prices are EIA averages for the 12 months to June 2026, which include fixed monthly charges and so overstate what an avoided kWh is worth. Illinois has no plug-in law (its bill stalled in 2026) and California’s awaits the Governor; they show a cheap-power state and a sunny, expensive one.

At 60% self-consumption, payback is about 1.6 times the 100% figure in all three. In New York, 60% is what the hourly run gives an empty apartment with a 150 W floor, so the 5.5-year headline becomes 8.8. In Illinois it becomes 14.7 years, well over half the 25-year span the calculator models. The self-consumption shares are computed for New York’s sun; Chicago and Los Angeles will differ somewhat at the same floor, but the direction is the same. [Whether balcony solar is worth it](https://balco.nyc/is-balcony-solar-worth-it) sets out the 100% figures for every state.

## Batteries, timers and system size

A battery stores midday surplus for the evening, so its value is capped by how much surplus there is. balco.nyc ran the same hourly New York data with a 2 kWh battery (1.92 kWh usable, 90% round-trip efficiency) that captures each day’s surplus up to its capacity and releases all of it in the evening — a generous setup that ignores the battery’s own standby draw. The last column applies the calculator’s 3% annual price rise.

| Apartment’s steady draw | kWh shifted a year | Worth at 34¢ | Price at which it pays back in 10 years |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100 W | 262 | $89 | about $1,020 |
| 150 W | 201 | $68 | about $780 |
| 200 W | 149 | $51 | about $580 |
| 300 W | 72 | $24 | about $280 |

The more you already use, the less a battery has to work with; at balcony scale the ceiling is tens of dollars a year. Modeling in Germany points the same way: the nonprofit balkon.solar, using HTW Berlin’s plug-in solar simulator with a vertical west-facing array and no pay for exports, found a 2 kWh battery stretched payback from 5–6 years to about 13 for small households with small arrays, improving to about 8 only with larger arrays and higher consumption.

The cheaper ways to use more of the output cost nothing. Put the dishwasher, the washing machine or a laptop charger on a timer for the middle of the day, especially from October to March, when a south-facing railing has the most to give. And weigh size by the marginal panel rather than the average one: in the empty-apartment case above, each step up in size buys less than the one before it.

## Common questions

**Do you get paid for balcony solar power you don't use?**

Not under any US plug-in solar law signed as of September 2026. Utah, Maine, Maryland, Vermont and Virginia expressly exclude plug-in devices from net metering, Colorado, New Hampshire and New Jersey say nothing about payment, and Connecticut requires a warning that exports may be billed as usage. New York's SUNNY Act, which has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature, says exports are uncompensated unless the owner voluntarily signs a net-metering or other compensation agreement.

**Does my electric meter spin backwards with a plug-in solar panel?**

Only if it is set up for net metering, which plug-in solar laws do not provide by default. On a meter that cannot track exports, the Maryland Public Service Commission says the surplus may be treated as zero consumption or erroneously added to consumption, depending on the meter type. Ask your utility how your meter records power flowing out before plugging a panel in.

**Can a balcony solar panel make my electric bill go up?**

It can on a meter that counts exported power as consumption, which is why Connecticut's plug-in law requires every device to warn that excess generation will be charged as usage unless the customer has a net-metering meter. In balco.nyc's New York example, an 800 W railing in an apartment drawing a steady 150 W exports about 240 kWh a year; billed at Con Edison's 34-cent rate, that would cut a $124 annual saving to about $42.

**How much of a balcony solar system's output does an apartment use?**

It depends on what the apartment draws while the sun is up. balco.nyc's hourly PVWatts model of an 800 W south-facing railing in New York City finds that an apartment drawing a steady 150 W uses about 60% of the output, one drawing 100 W about 46%, and one drawing 300 W about 87%. Those shares assume nobody is home in the daytime; daytime activity raises them.

**Why does a smaller balcony solar system use more of its output?**

Because the apartment's load stays the same while each added panel produces in the same midday hours as the first. In balco.nyc's New York model with a 150 W floor, a 400 W system uses 87% of its output, an 800 W system 60% and a 1,200 W system 46%. The step from 800 to 1,200 W adds about 302 kWh a year of output but only 49 kWh used at home.

**Is a battery worth adding to balcony solar?**

Rarely at balcony scale. In balco.nyc's hourly New York model, a 2 kWh battery on an 800 W railing is worth about $24 to $89 a year at Con Edison's 34-cent rate, depending on how much the apartment already uses, so it would have to cost roughly $280 to $1,020 to pay for itself in 10 years. The more electricity the household already uses in daylight, the less surplus the battery has to store.

# Vertical or tilted: what angle should a balcony solar panel be?

URL: https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-panel-angle  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

On output, tilted wins everywhere: balco.nyc’s PVWatts runs for the largest city in every state find that leaning a south-facing 800 W panel back from vertical adds a median 29% at 70°, 42% at 60° and 59% at 35°, worth about $33, $48 and $69 a year at each state’s average price. A 60° bracket captures about 70% of the 35° gain while projecting about 40% less. The catch is timing: most of the extra arrives at summer middays, when a small apartment already has surplus it gives away, and behind a building across the street tilting matters more, not less.

## What each angle adds, and why latitude sets it

balco.nyc asked PVWatts V8, the production model now run by the National Laboratory of the Rockies (formerly NREL), what an 800 W south-facing system makes at four angles in the largest city of every state and DC, with the calculator’s own parameters. Angles are measured from horizontal, as PVWatts measures them: 90° hangs flat against a railing, 70° leans 20° back, 60° leans 30° back and 35° is roughly a roof pitch. Every result is multiplied by the site’s railing factor, exactly as the calculator does: 0.95 at 90°, 0.97 at 70°, 0.98 at 60° and 0.99 at 35°, because the railing and its hardware clip the lower edge of an upright panel more than a leaning one. The national medians are on [the 800 W output page](https://balco.nyc/800w-balcony-solar-output); this page is about how the gain varies and what it is worth.

| Latitude | Cities | Vertical (kWh/yr) | Lean to 70° | 60° | 35° |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Honolulu, 21°N | 1 | 510 | +50% (+257) | +79% (+403) | +129% (+659) |
| 29–33°N | 5 | 605 | +37% (+225) | +55% (+333) | +81% (+495) |
| 33–37°N | 11 | 654 | +34% (+213) | +48% (+314) | +69% (+461) |
| 37–41°N | 14 | 660 | +29% (+189) | +42% (+277) | +59% (+394) |
| 41–44°N | 13 | 692 | +26% (+172) | +37% (+252) | +51% (+358) |
| 44–48°N | 6 | 679 | +23% (+155) | +34% (+228) | +46% (+313) |
| Anchorage, 61°N | 1 | 535 | +16% (+85) | +24% (+130) | +33% (+178) |

Medians within each band, unshaded, after the railing factor; kWh a year added in brackets. Fitted across the 49 cities between 29° and 48°N, the gain from a 35° tilt falls by about **2.2 percentage points for every degree of latitude**, 1.4 at 60° and 0.9 at 70°. Latitude alone accounts for about four-fifths of the variation (R² = 0.79). Much of the rest tracks how sunny a city’s winter is compared with its summer. The cities furthest below the line, 5 to 10 points under it, are Manchester (New Hampshire), Cheyenne, Sioux Falls, Omaha and Minneapolis, where a vertical panel already makes 1.7 to 2.1 times as much from December to February as from June to August (1.5 to 1.6 in Chicago, Detroit and Milwaukee). Seattle and Portland, Oregon, sit 16 to 18 points above it, because their cloudy winters give a railing little to work with.

**Most of the gain comes from the first 30° of lean.** In every city, 60° captures between 61% and 74% of what 35° adds (median 71%), and 70° between 39% and 51%.

## Winter is a draw; summer decides it

The low winter sun already strikes an upright panel nearly square on, so leaning it back does comparatively little from November to February. The gain arrives when the sun is high. Three cities at different latitudes show the shape, in kWh from an unshaded 800 W panel after the railing factor:

| City | Dec–Feb: 90° / 60° / 35° | Jun–Aug: 90° / 60° / 35° | Share of the 35° gain made Apr–Sep | Best month, vertical / 35° |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houston, 29.8°N | 184 / 225 / 226 | 81 / 191 / 275 | 73% | November / March |
| New York City, 40.7°N | 191 / 216 / 205 | 104 / 213 / 283 | 83% | January / July |
| Minneapolis, 45.0°N | 226 / 230 / 209 | 132 / 241 / 307 | 95% | March / July |

In winter the three angles sit within 10% to 23% of one another in these cities, and in Minneapolis the vertical panel beats 35° outright in December, January and February. Across all 51 cities, a vertical panel out-produces a 35° one over those three months in 16, and 60° is the best of the four angles for them in 48; only Honolulu, Houston and New Orleans favor 35°. In summer the order reverses completely: in New York a 35° panel makes **2.7 times** what a vertical one does from June to August. Across the 51 cities, a median 84% of the 35° gain is made from April to September.

That makes an adjustable bracket less useful than it sounds. Picking the best of the four angles every month, rather than leaving the panel at 35°, adds a median **1.5%** a year in balco.nyc’s runs, and 2.7% at most (Sioux Falls). The angle is worth choosing once, carefully, and then leaving alone.

## What the angle is worth, and why less of it reaches your bill

At each state’s average residential price, which balco.nyc computes from EIA sales and revenue for the 12 months to June 2026, tilting from vertical is worth a median **$33 a year at 70°, $48 at 60° and $69 at 35°**. Those averages include fixed monthly charges, so they can overstate what an avoided kWh saves. Where power is expensive, the same kWh are worth several times more:

| State (city, price) | 70° | 60° | 35° | Payback on a $1,200 kit: 90° → 60° → 35° |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hawaii (Honolulu, 42.75¢) | $110 | $172 | $282 | 5.2 → 3.0 → 2.4 yrs |
| California (Los Angeles, 32.89¢) | $91 | $131 | $186 | 4.8 → 3.2 → 2.8 yrs |
| New York City (Con Edison, 34¢ marginal) | $62 | $91 | $131 | 5.5 → 3.9 → 3.5 yrs |
| Median of 51 cities (each column separately) | $33 | $48 | $69 | 9.9 → 7.2 → 6.5 yrs |
| Texas (Houston, 15.90¢) | $34 | $51 | $78 | 11.5 → 7.7 → 6.6 yrs |
| Washington (Seattle, 14.02¢) | $21 | $31 | $44 | 13.9 → 10.2 → 9.2 yrs |
| North Dakota (Fargo, 12.30¢) | $19 | $28 | $38 | 12.1 → 9.5 → 8.8 yrs |

Payback uses the calculator’s loop (prices up 3% a year, output down 0.5%) and excludes whatever the bracket costs. balco.nyc could not find a neutral published price range for tilting brackets, only sellers’ listings, so none is quoted here. The test is simple: a bracket earns its cost back within five years only if it costs less than five years of its gain, about $250 for a 60° bracket in the median state.

All of these figures assume every extra kWh is used at home, and the extra arrives at the wrong time for that. A tilted panel’s gain comes mostly at summer middays, when an apartment’s steady load is already covered and the surplus goes to the grid, usually for nothing (see [whether you get paid for surplus](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-net-metering)). balco.nyc ran PVWatts hour by hour in New York City at each angle and set the output against a constant household draw, the same method as that page:

| Apartment’s steady draw | 60°: extra kWh used (of 269) | Worth at 34¢ | 35°: extra kWh used (of 384) | Worth at 34¢ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100 W | 34 (13%) | $11 | 54 (14%) | $18 |
| 150 W | 59 (22%) | $20 | 91 (24%) | $31 |
| 300 W | 158 (59%) | $54 | 223 (58%) | $76 |
| Everything used | 269 (100%) | $91 | 384 (100%) | $131 |

An apartment idling at 150 W uses about a quarter of what tilting adds. A constant draw is the empty-apartment case: someone home in the daytime, or an air conditioner running on summer afternoons, raises the share, and in a state or utility that credits exports the full figure applies. But for a small household, much of what leaning all the way to 35° adds is surplus.

## Behind a building, tilting matters more, not less

A building across the street takes the low winter sun a vertical panel depends on. To see what that does to the choice of angle, balco.nyc ran its own shade code for a third-floor, south-facing balcony facing a six-to-ten-story building 20 m away, the case worked on [the calculation page](https://balco.nyc/calculate-balcony-solar-output). Straight out, the wall rises 41.8° above the balcony. The code computed a shade factor for each month at each angle, and each was applied to the PVWatts run for that angle. In New York City:

| Angle | Open view (kWh/yr) | Behind the building | Share kept | Gain over vertical, open | Gain over vertical, behind the building |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 90° | 604 | 227 | 38% | — | — |
| 70° | 787 | 389 | 49% | +30% | +72% |
| 60° | 872 | 475 | 54% | +44% | +110% |
| 35° | 988 | 651 | 66% | +64% | +187% |

Across all 51 cities the median gain behind the building is +69% at 70°, +105% at 60° and +178% at 35°, against +29%, +42% and +59% in the open. In kilowatt-hours the picture is closer: 35° adds more behind the building than in the open in 50 of the 51 cities (a median 449 kWh against 390), while 60° and 70° add slightly less (266 against 279, and 175 against 190). Obstruction, in short, makes tilting matter much more in proportion, and about as much or more in kilowatt-hours.

Two things drive it, roughly equally. The building removes winter sun: in New York the vertical panel’s October-to-February output falls from 304 kWh to 32, while the high summer sun that a leaning panel gains from clears the roofline from March to September. And a leaning panel faces more of the sky overhead, which the wall does not reach: it leaves 33% of a vertical panel’s sky view open, 53% at 60° and 68% at 35°. Blocking only the direct sun, tilting to 35° gains 102% in New York; cutting only the diffuse sky light, 93%.

This is a simplified model: a continuous wall, a fixed split of direct and diffuse light, and a floor of 0.10 on each monthly factor, which if anything flatters the vertical panel in winter. Its largest blind spot is the balcony above. A slab overhead, or a recessed balcony, takes away exactly the high sky and high summer sun a tilted panel gains from, most of all if the panel sits back from the edge. Treat the direction of this result as sound and its size as an upper bound, and see [does my balcony get enough sun?](https://balco.nyc/balcony-sunlight) for how obstruction works.

## What limits the angle in practice

The model does not decide the angle; the balcony and the building usually do. Four things set the limit.

- **Depth.** For every meter of panel length, a 70° lean needs 0.34 m of depth, 60° needs 0.50 m and 35° needs 0.82 m, the cosine of the angle. The panel either leans into the balcony, taking floor space, or out beyond the railing over whatever is below. Check your panel’s length and multiply.

- **Egress.** New York City’s Fire Code requires every required means of egress to be “continuously maintained free from obstructions,” and fire escapes and access to them likewise (sections 1027.3 and 1027.7). A panel on a bracket must not narrow a path to a door, window or fire escape used for escape.

- **Wind.** New York City’s Building Code requires wind loads to be determined under ASCE 7, the national structural loads standard (section 1609.1.1). In it, velocity pressure, the starting point for any wind load, rises with the square of the wind speed and with height above ground. A panel held out on a bracket adds leverage: the further it sits from the clamp, the harder the same gust twists the clamp and the railing. Guards are designed to resist 50 lb per linear foot and a 200 lb point load, and their balusters and infill 50 lb (section 1607.8.1); a panel adds its own wind load, through a clamp, on top. Anything that projects should be checked by an engineer.

- **The building’s rules.** In New York City, the facade inspection rule for buildings over six stories treats railings, guard rails and “any equipment attached to or protruding from the facade” as appurtenances the owner’s inspector must examine, and classes a guard whose parts are not positively secured against movement as unsafe. A bracket that projects is something the building has to inspect, and a reasonable board may refuse it where it would accept a panel clamped flat inside the railing.

Ask for the specific angle, the projection, the weight and the secondary tether when you seek permission; [how to install balcony solar](https://balco.nyc/install-balcony-solar) covers the rest, and [condo and co-op rules](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-condo-hoa) and [renters’ rights](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-renters) cover who can say no. Nothing here is legal advice, and rules vary by state, city and building.

## How to choose an angle

Put together, the runs point to a short set of rules:

- **If only vertical is allowed, it is not a bad answer.** An upright south panel makes about 63% of what the same panel makes at 35° in the median city, and gives up little in winter, when the angle matters least.

- **For a small household that gives surplus away, 60° to 70° captures most of the usable gain.** 70° gets about half of the 35° gain with 42% of its depth, and 60° about 70% with 61% of the depth; at a steady 150 W draw, 35° adds only $11 a year more of used power than 60° in New York.

- **Leaning all the way to 35° pays where the extra is used or credited:** a large daytime load, summer air conditioning, a high price, or an export credit.

- **Behind a building on a low floor, tilting helps most**, provided the panel sees open sky overhead rather than the balcony above.

The [calculator](https://balco.nyc/) takes 90°, 70°, 60° or 35° for any US address, with shade from what stands opposite, and [the methodology](https://balco.nyc/methodology) documents every constant used here.

## Common questions

**What is the best angle for a balcony solar panel?**

For output alone, as close to 35 degrees as your balcony and building allow: in balco.nyc's PVWatts runs for the largest city in every state, a south-facing panel leaned back to 35 degrees makes a median 59% more than a vertical one, and 60 degrees makes 42% more. In practice 60 to 70 degrees captures about half to three-quarters of that gain with far less projection, and much of the extra from leaning further back arrives at summer middays, when a small apartment may give it away as unpaid surplus.

**How much more does a tilted balcony solar panel produce than a vertical one?**

It depends mostly on latitude. In balco.nyc's runs, tilting a south-facing panel from vertical to 35 degrees adds about 81% between 29 and 33 degrees north, 59% between 37 and 41 degrees, and 46% between 44 and 48 degrees; 60 degrees adds 55%, 42% and 34%. The gain falls about 2.2 percentage points per degree of latitude for 35 degrees, and cities whose winters are sunny relative to their summers gain less than their latitude predicts.

**Are vertical solar panels efficient?**

Less productive over a year, but not in winter. A vertical south-facing panel makes a median of about 63% of what the same panel makes at 35 degrees across balco.nyc's 51 city runs, and most of the shortfall comes from April to September. From December to February, vertical, 60-degree and 35-degree panels are within 20% of each other in 46 of the 51 cities, and in 16 a vertical panel out-produces a 35-degree one over those three months.

**Is a tilting bracket worth the money?**

At state average prices, tilting from vertical to 60 degrees is worth a median $48 a year and to 35 degrees $69, if every extra kWh is used at home. Hourly modeling for New York City shows an apartment drawing a steady 150 W uses only about a quarter of the extra, because it arrives at summer middays. A bracket is worth buying only if it costs less than a few years of the gain you will actually use.

**Does tilting a balcony panel help if a building across the street blocks the sun?**

Yes, more than in the open, in balco.nyc's shade model. For a third-floor south balcony facing a six-to-ten-story building 20 m away in New York City, tilting from vertical to 35 degrees raises modeled output from 227 to 651 kWh a year, a 187% gain against 64% with an open view. The model does not include a balcony slab above, which would take away some of the overhead sky a tilted panel relies on.

**Is it allowed to tilt a solar panel out beyond my balcony railing?**

That depends on your building, city and state, and this is not legal advice. A projecting bracket adds wind load and leverage at the clamp and the railing, can hang over a sidewalk, and must never obstruct a means of egress or fire escape. In New York City, facade inspection rules for buildings over six stories cover equipment attached to or protruding from the facade, so landlords and boards have reason to ask for an engineer's review.

## Sources

- [PVWatts Calculator](https://pvwatts.nlr.gov/): the public interface to the same model, for reproducing any figure at your own address and angle.
- [U.S. Department of Energy — Energy Department Renames NREL “National Lab of the Rockies”](https://www.energy.gov/cmei/articles/energy-department-renames-nrel-national-lab-rockies): the renaming of NREL, which now hosts PVWatts at nlr.gov.
- [U.S. Census Bureau — Vintage 2025 subcounty population estimates (SUB-EST2025)](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/popest/datasets/2020-2025/cities/totals/sub-est2025.csv): the largest city in each state and DC, which sets the 51 reference points.
- [EIA — Form EIA-861M monthly sales and revenue by state](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/data/eia861m/): the residential revenue and sales from which balco.nyc computes each state’s average price for the 12 months to June 2026.
- [Con Edison — historical average full-service electric rates](https://www.coned.com/-/media/files/coned/documents/save-energy-money/using-private-generation/historical-average-full-service-electric-rates.pdf): the NYC SC-1 residential rate (33.83¢/kWh in 2025) that the 34¢ marginal rate starts from.
- [Sandia PV Performance Modeling Collaborative — Isotropic sky diffuse model](https://pvpmc.sandia.gov/modeling-guide/1-weather-design-inputs/plane-of-array-poa-irradiance/calculating-poa-irradiance/poa-sky-diffuse/isotropic-sky-diffuse-model/): the (1 + cos tilt)/2 sky view factor: a tilted panel sees more of the sky dome than a vertical one.

- [NYC Department of Buildings — 1 RCNY §103-04, Periodic Inspection of Exterior Walls and Appurtenances](https://www.nyc.gov/assets/buildings/rules/1_RCNY_103-04.pdf): the definition of appurtenances, including railings and any equipment attached to or protruding from the facade; the over-six-stories scope; and the requirement that guards be positively secured.
- [NYC Fire Code 2022, Chapter 10 — Means of Egress](https://up.codes/viewer/new_york_city/nyc-fire-code-2022/chapter/10/means-of-egress): sections 1027.3 and 1027.7: means of egress and fire escapes continuously maintained free from obstructions.

# Can renters install balcony solar?

URL: https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-renters  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

Usually only with the landlord’s permission. As of 23 September 2026, four states — Vermont, Virginia, New Jersey and Colorado — have signed laws that limit a landlord’s power to refuse, and only Vermont’s protection is in force; the other three start in January or March 2027. balco.nyc’s count of Census data puts 3.3 million renter households, 7.2% of the US total, in those four states, and 76,431 (0.17%) in the one where the protection works today. New York’s SUNNY Act has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature, and it grants no right to install.

## The short answer, and the four exceptions

A plug-in kit hangs on a railing the landlord owns and plugs into wiring the landlord owns, so in most of the country the lease and the landlord decide. A law that makes plug-in solar *legal* is not one that makes it your *right*: five of the nine signed US plug-in laws stop the utility from demanding approval and give tenants nothing.

balco.nyc read the enacted text of every law in its [state tracker](https://balco.nyc/states). Four limit a landlord’s power to refuse: [Vermont](https://balco.nyc/states/vermont) (in force since 1 July 2026; after 10 days’ notice with no answer, the tenant may proceed), [Virginia](https://balco.nyc/states/virginia) (from 1 January 2027; landlords who own more than four rental units), [New Jersey](https://balco.nyc/states/new-jersey) (from 1 March 2027; tenants who pay their own electric bill) and [Colorado](https://balco.nyc/states/colorado) (from 1 January 2027; no person may “unreasonably prohibit” a device). All four still let the landlord impose reasonable restrictions.

balco.nyc’s count from the Census Bureau’s 2024 American Community Survey puts **3,334,151 renter households** in those four states, 7.2% of the 46.1 million in the United States. Until the 2027 start dates, the protected group is Vermont’s 76,431 renter households: **0.17% of American renters**. New York alone has 3,575,503 renter households, more than the four states combined, and its [SUNNY Act](https://balco.nyc/sunny-act) would give none of them a right to install. Everyone else needs permission.

> **Not legal advice.** This page summarizes statutes and bills as of 23 September 2026. Your lease, your state’s law and any association rules decide your case, and a law that is signed but not yet in effect protects nobody.

## Every tenant provision, compared

balco.nyc’s compilation of every US plug-in solar law or 2026 bill that addresses tenants, from the legislatures’ own pages, as of 23 September 2026. Quoted words are statutory or bill text. The rest of each law (caps, certification, utility notice) is in [the provision-by-provision comparison](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-laws-compared).

| State | Law or bill | Status | Who it protects, and how | What the landlord keeps |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vermont | Act 149 (S.202) | In force 1 Jul 2026 | All tenants, for a device that meets the Act (UL 3700 or equivalent, 1,200 W per meter). 10 days’ notice; “If the landlord does not respond within 10 days, the tenant may proceed with installation.” | “Any reasonable restrictions,” including making the tenant pay a licensed electrician for any electrical work. No electrical work without the landlord’s permission. |
| Virginia | HB 395 / SB 250 (Chs. 1052, 998) | Signed 22 Apr 2026; effective 1 Jan 2027 | “No landlord who owns more than four rental dwelling units” (or more than a 10% interest in more than four) “shall prohibit a tenant from installing” a device “on the exterior of the tenant’s premises.” 7 days’ notice with documentation. Not units on a ratio utility billing system. | Reasonable restrictions on “size, place, and manner of placement”; may bar devices elsewhere on the premises. The tenant is responsible for any damage. |
| New Jersey | P.L.2026, c.82 (S2368 / A4836) | Signed 1 Sep 2026; effective 1 Mar 2027 | Tenants who pay their own electric bill, within their leased premises including a balcony or patio. 14 days’ written notice with documentation.* | Reasonable restrictions on the device’s physical dimensions, placement and manner of placement; no blanket ban.* |
| Colorado | HB26-1007 (C.R.S. 40-2-140) | In force 12 Aug 2026; tenant clause from 1 Jan 2027 | “A person shall not directly or indirectly unreasonably prohibit” a device. The Act does not mention landlords or tenants. | “Reasonable restrictions,” including prior notice and limits aimed at fire or electrical overload, damage, and the device’s location. |
| Illinois | SB 3104 (House: HB 4524) | Pending; re-referred to Assignments 22 May 2026 | Landlords could not enforce a lease that “unreasonably restricts or prohibits” a system.* | As amended, the bill bars systems over 391 W until the National Electrical Code has a standard for them. |
| North Carolina | HB 1129 | Pending; in House Rules since 30 Apr 2026 | Tenants of landlords who own more than four rental dwellings. 7 days’ notice. | Size and placement limits only “if required to prevent” blocked egress or “unreasonable property damage.” |
| Oregon | HB 4080 | Died in committee, March 2026 | Would have limited restrictions by landlords, HOAs and condo associations.* | — |
| Washington | SSB 6050 | Died in Senate Rules, 2026 | A landlord could not require its approval, or any fee, before a tenant used a device. | — |
| South Carolina | H 4579 | Died in committee, 2026 | A lease or rental agreement “must not prohibit or have the effect of prohibiting” a balcony solar panel. | — |

* New Jersey’s row is summarized from the Governor’s signing announcement, published legal summaries and balco.nyc’s state tracker; the Illinois and Oregon rows are from the legislatures’ official bill digests, not the bill text.

**Laws with nothing for tenants.** [Utah](https://balco.nyc/states/utah), [Maryland](https://balco.nyc/states/maryland), [Connecticut](https://balco.nyc/states/connecticut), [New Hampshire](https://balco.nyc/states/new-hampshire) and [Maine](https://balco.nyc/states/maine) have signed plug-in laws with no tenant right; Maine’s only requires anyone installing on a structure they do not own to protect it and restore it on removal, a duty rather than a right. The same silence runs through [New York](https://balco.nyc/states/new-york)’s SUNNY Act, which has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature; [California](https://balco.nyc/states/california)’s SB 868, awaiting the Governor’s decision; and pending bills in [Massachusetts](https://balco.nyc/states/massachusetts), [Michigan](https://balco.nyc/states/michigan), [Pennsylvania](https://balco.nyc/states/pennsylvania) and the [District of Columbia](https://balco.nyc/states/district-of-columbia). Tracker summaries saying the Massachusetts and Pennsylvania bills protect tenants describe provisions balco.nyc could not find in either text.

## How many renters the laws reach

A law’s reach is a head count, so balco.nyc made one: renter-occupied homes (households) by state from the Census Bureau’s 2024 American Community Survey 1-year estimates, table **B25003** (Tenure). That is the newest 1-year release; on 4 August 2026 the Bureau said the 2025 release date “is being determined.” Two laws cover only some tenants, so each gets a narrower estimate:

- **Virginia** turns on how many units the landlord owns, which no Census table records. The nearest proxy is renters in buildings of five or more units (table **B25032**): 555,373, or 49.0% of the state’s renters.

- **New Jersey** turns on paying your own electric bill. The published tables do not split electricity billing by tenure, but **B25069** records renters who pay extra for at least one utility: 1,152,187, against 126,937 who pay for none. The first figure is a ceiling.

| State | Renter households (B25003) | Narrower estimate | What the narrower figure counts | Protection starts |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vermont | 76,431 | 76,431 | All tenants | 1 Jul 2026 |
| Colorado | 844,547 | 844,547 | All tenants | 1 Jan 2027 |
| Virginia | 1,134,049 | 555,373 | Renters in buildings of 5+ units (B25032) | 1 Jan 2027 |
| New Jersey | 1,279,124 | 1,152,187 | Renters paying for at least one utility (B25069) | 1 Mar 2027 |
| Four states | 3,334,151 | 2,628,538 |  |  |
| Share of US renter households (46,101,640) | 7.2% | 5.7% |  |  |

The arithmetic: 76,431 + 844,547 + 1,134,049 + 1,279,124 = 3,334,151, and 3,334,151 ÷ 46,101,640 = 7.2%; the narrower column sums to 2,628,538, or 5.7%. The Census margin of error on the four-state total is about ±25,000 at 90% confidence. For scale, New York has 3,575,503 renter households (45.7% of its households), and the five states with a plug-in law but no tenant clause hold 1,939,324 renter households for whom plugging in is, or will shortly be, legal and the landlord still decides.

The same data qualifies a figure in New Jersey’s signing announcement, where an advocate says the law benefits “roughly 40 percent of New Jerseyans who rent or live in apartments.” That counts people and includes apartment owners, who fall under the law’s association provisions, not its tenant clause. By households, the ACS puts renters at 36.1% of the state’s total (1,279,124 of 3,543,944), and the tenant clause reaches at most 32.5% (1,152,187).

What these numbers are not: they count households, not balconies. The ACS does not ask whether a home has a balcony, a patio or an outdoor outlet, so the renters who could actually use these protections are fewer than every figure above, by an amount nobody has measured. The Virginia proxy is loose both ways: it includes condo units rented out by small owners, who are not covered, and units on ratio utility billing, which the law excludes; it misses houses owned by large landlords, who are covered.

## What “can’t prohibit” still allows

None of the four laws hands the balcony to the tenant. Read closely, they replace a landlord’s veto with a landlord’s conditions:

- **Reasonable restrictions survive everywhere.** Virginia names “size, place, and manner of placement” and lets the landlord bar devices anywhere but the exterior of the tenant’s premises; Colorado lists notice, fire and overload risk, damage and location. What is reasonable has not been tested in any of the four states.

- **Notice comes first.** Seven days in Virginia, with documentation that the device qualifies and where it will go; ten in Vermont; fourteen, in writing, in New Jersey. The laws protect a tenant who gives notice before installing.

- **Wiring stays the landlord’s.** Vermont says a landlord “shall not be compelled to perform or pay for electrical work”; Virginia requires express written approval for anything that alters wiring or panels. If your balcony has no outdoor outlet, none of these laws gets you one.

- **Damage is the tenant’s.** Virginia makes the tenant responsible for any damage the device causes.

- **Only a qualifying device is protected.** Vermont covers devices certified to UL 3700 “or an equivalent certification.” No complete plug-in system is certified to UL 3700 as of September 2026 (components are), so a Vermont tenant’s protection depends on whether a kit’s listing counts as equivalent, which the Act does not settle. New Jersey also accepts a comparable standard; Virginia and Colorado ask for certification or listing by a nationally recognized testing laboratory.

- **Surplus power earns nothing.** Vermont says exports “shall not be compensated,” Virginia excludes the devices from net metering, and New Jersey and Colorado are silent. Assume what you do not use is given away.

- **Association rules may still bind.** Virginia’s law does not override condominium or HOA documents, so a tenant in a rented condo can be protected against the landlord and still refused by the association; New Jersey’s and Colorado’s bind associations too. See [condos, co-ops and HOAs](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-condo-hoa).

## Asking your landlord: a checklist and a letter

In most states the request is the whole process; in the four above it doubles as the statutory notice. A specific written request is easier to approve than a general one. Do the physical checks first with [the installation guide](https://balco.nyc/install-balcony-solar); if the landlord’s worry is fire or shock, [the safety evidence](https://balco.nyc/is-plug-in-solar-safe) is summarized separately. Include:

- **The device:** make, model, panel count, maximum AC output, and the certification exactly as the listing states it, including the anti-islanding feature each of the four laws requires.

- **Size and weight** of the panels with brackets.

- **Mounting without drilling:** clamps or hooks inside the railing, nothing fixed to the facade, secured against wind.

- **The outlet:** which existing outdoor outlet, whether it is GFCI-protected and covered, no extension cord, and no new wiring without written approval.

- **Insurance:** your renters policy’s liability limit, and acceptance of responsibility for damage.

- **Removal** at move-out, or on short notice for building work, with the railing restored.

- **The law, if one applies:** the statute and the notice period.

> **A neutral template.** Dear [landlord or managing agent], I would like to install a small plug-in solar system on the balcony of [unit]. The details are below, and I am happy to discuss any conditions. *Device:* [make and model], [number] panels, [watts] maximum AC output, listed to [standard] by [laboratory]. It switches off automatically if grid power is lost. Specification sheet attached. *Size and mounting:* [dimensions], [total weight]. It clamps to the inside of the railing; nothing is drilled into or fixed to the building. *Power:* it plugs into the existing outdoor outlet at [location]. No extension cord and no change to the wiring. *Insurance:* my renters policy with [insurer] carries [amount] of liability coverage, and I will be responsible for any damage the system causes. *Removal:* I will remove it and restore the railing when I move out, or within [number] days if you need access for building work. [If a state law applies: I am giving this notice under [statute], [number] days before installation on [date].] I would be grateful for your written approval, or for any conditions you would attach.

The template is a starting point, not legal advice. Where a statute applies, match its wording: Virginia’s notice, for example, must include documentation that the device meets the law’s definition and identify the proposed location.

## If the answer is no

Outside the four states, a refusal usually stands until the lease changes. A no to a vague request is sometimes a yes to a specific one: a smaller system, a floor stand instead of a railing mount, proof of insurance, a firm removal commitment. Lease renewal is a natural moment to ask again.

Where one of the four laws covers you, the landlord can restrict but not refuse, and a dispute over what is “reasonable” goes through the ordinary landlord-tenant channels. In [New York](https://balco.nyc/states/new-york) the SUNNY Act has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature, and nothing in it limits a landlord’s answer: [renters will need permission after it is signed, as they do now](https://balco.nyc/sunny-act).

Before asking at all, check it is worth asking. Output depends mostly on how much sky the balcony sees, which is [a kilowatt-hour number, not a yes or no](https://balco.nyc/balcony-sunlight); the [calculator](https://balco.nyc/) gives it for any US address, and a shaded balcony may not pay back in the time you expect to stay.

## Common questions

**Can my landlord stop me from installing balcony solar?**

In most US states, yes: a plug-in kit attaches to a railing and outlet the landlord owns, so the lease and the landlord decide. As of September 2026 four states have signed laws limiting that power. Vermont's protection is in force; Virginia's and Colorado's start on 1 January 2027 and New Jersey's on 1 March 2027. Even there, the landlord may impose reasonable restrictions.

**Which states give renters a right to install plug-in solar?**

Vermont (in force since 1 July 2026, 10 days' notice), Virginia (from 1 January 2027, tenants of landlords owning more than four rental units, excluding ratio-utility-billed units), New Jersey (from 1 March 2027, tenants who pay their own electric bill, 14 days' written notice) and Colorado (from 1 January 2027, no unreasonable prohibition). Tenant bills in Illinois and North Carolina are pending but stalled.

**Does New York's SUNNY Act let renters install balcony solar?**

No. The SUNNY Act (S8512C / A9111C) has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature, and it contains no landlord or tenant provision. A New York renter would still need the landlord's permission after it is signed.

**How many renters do state balcony solar tenant protections cover?**

balco.nyc's count from the Census Bureau's 2024 American Community Survey (table B25003) puts 3,334,151 renter households, 7.2% of the US total, in Vermont, Virginia, New Jersey and Colorado; about 2.6 million (5.7%) narrowed to the tenants each law covers. Until 2027 only Vermont's 76,431, or 0.17%, are protected.

**Does my landlord have to add an outdoor outlet for balcony solar?**

No. None of the four state laws with tenant provisions requires a landlord to add wiring. Vermont's says a landlord shall not be compelled to perform or pay for electrical work, and Virginia's requires the landlord's express written approval for anything that alters wiring or electrical panels.

**What should a balcony solar request to a landlord include?**

The device's make, model, AC wattage and certification; its size and weight; how it mounts without drilling; which existing outdoor outlet it uses, with no extension cord; your renters insurance and acceptance of responsibility for damage; removal and restoration at move-out; and, where a state tenant law applies, the statute and notice period.
