# 400, 800 or 1,200 watts: what size balcony solar system makes sense?

URL: https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-system-size  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

For most apartments, 400 or 800 W: the third 400 W, which takes a system to 1,200 W, repays its cost within about 12 years only where the home draws some 300 W all day. balco.nyc’s hourly PVWatts model of a south-facing New York City railing prices each extra 400 W separately: in an apartment drawing a steady 150 W, the first 400 W saves about $89 a year and repays its $600 in 6.3 years, the second saves $35 and takes 14.5, and the third saves $17 and does not repay its cost within the 25 years the calculator models. Size to what your home draws while the sun is up, not to the legal cap.

## Each extra 400 W is worth less than the one before

If you use every kilowatt-hour, size does not change payback: output and kit cost both scale with watts, so in New York City an unshaded south-facing railing of 400, 800 or 1,600 W pays back in the same 5.5 years at Con Edison’s 34¢ marginal rate. balco.nyc’s calculator makes that assumption. It fails for output the apartment is not drawing at that moment, which flows to the grid and, under every signed state plug-in law, earns nothing.

So balco.nyc priced each 400 W step separately. It ran [PVWatts V8](https://balco.nyc/what-is-pvwatts), from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (formerly NREL), hour by hour for a vertical, south-facing New York City railing with the calculator’s parameters (reproducing the site’s 635.7 kWh a year for 800 W), scaled the 8,760 hours to each size, applied the 0.95 railing factor, and set every hour against an apartment drawing a steady 100 to 300 W. Each step adds 302 kWh a year of output. How much of it gets used:

| Apartment’s steady draw | First 400 W | Second (to 800 W) | Third (to 1,200 W) | Fourth (to 1,600 W) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100 W | 216 kWh · $74 | 59 kWh · $20 | 31 kWh · $10 | 21 kWh · $7 |
| 150 W | 262 kWh · $89 | 102 kWh · $35 | 49 kWh · $17 | 33 kWh · $11 |
| 200 W | 287 kWh · $98 | 146 kWh · $50 | 73 kWh · $25 | 46 kWh · $15 |
| 300 W | 302 kWh · $103 | 222 kWh · $76 | 125 kWh · $43 | 80 kWh · $27 |

Electricity used at home that each step adds per year, and its value at 34¢: New York City, vertical south-facing railing, no shading, no daytime use above the steady draw.

The draws bracket real homes. NRDC’s 2015 smart-meter study defined idle load as a home’s lowest hourly level: 218 W on average across 70,000 northern California homes, with a quarter of a Bay Area subsample below 119 W, half above 185 W and a quarter above 282 W. The one audited apartment idled at 92 W. At a 150 W floor the third 400 W adds **49 kWh** of use and sends 84% of its output to the grid, unpaid (see [whether you get paid for surplus](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-net-metering)).

## What the extra 400 W costs, and when it pays for itself

balco.nyc’s kit costs scale in a straight line, so the $1,200 mid-range figure for 800 W makes each 400 W step **$600**. The table runs each step through the calculator’s payback loop (3% annual price rise, 0.5% yearly degradation, nominal dollars, 25 years), then gives the price at which the step would pay back in 10 years.

| Apartment’s steady draw | First 400 W | Second | Third | Fourth |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100 W | 7.5 yrs · $824 | 22.6 yrs · $225 | Over 25 · $117 | Over 25 · $79 |
| 150 W | 6.3 yrs · $997 | 14.5 yrs · $390 | Over 25 · $187 | Over 25 · $125 |
| 200 W | 5.8 yrs · $1,092 | 10.7 yrs · $555 | 19.2 yrs · $277 | Over 25 · $173 |
| 300 W | 5.5 yrs · $1,148 | 7.3 yrs · $846 | 12.2 yrs · $476 | 17.9 yrs · $303 |

Payback on the step’s $600 · the most the step could cost and still pay back in 10 years. New York City, south-facing railing, 34¢.

A whole-system payback hides this. At a 150 W floor a 1,200 W system pays back its $1,800 in 11.3 years, which looks tolerable, but that averages a 6.3-year first step, a 14.5-year second and a third that returns $568 over 25 years on its $600. Averages flatter the last panel.

Lifetime totals pull the other way. Any step that pays back inside 25 years raises the nominal 25-year total net of hardware, so the total peaks at a larger size: 800 W for a 150 W floor ($3,023, against $2,991 at 1,200 W), 1,200 W for 200 W, 1,600 W for 300 W. But the steps that get there take 14.5 to 19 years to break even, count a dollar in year 25 as one today, and assume the hardware lasts. A ceiling, not an expectation. The straight-line cost is an assumption too: a panel that shares an inverter may cost less than $600, which is what the second figure in each cell is for.

## A west-facing railing can carry more watts

Surplus comes from the midday peak, so a lower peak leaves room for more panel. balco.nyc ran the same hourly model for a west-facing railing (reproducing the site’s 443.6 kWh for 800 W). Each 400 W makes 211 kWh a year against 302, and 800 W peaks at 563 W instead of 691 W. At a 150 W floor:

| Step | South: kWh used added (of 302) | South: payback on $600 | West: kWh used added (of 211) | West: payback on $600 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| First 400 W | 262 | 6.3 yrs | 196 | 8.2 yrs |
| Second | 102 | 14.5 yrs | 94 | 15.5 yrs |
| Third | 49 | Over 25 | 64 | 21.3 yrs |
| Fourth | 33 | Over 25 | 49 | Over 25 |

The west railing saves less overall, but beyond 800 W its next panel is worth more. Its output also leans toward summer, 53 kWh in July against 19 in December for 800 W before the railing loss, when air conditioners run; a constant floor ignores that, so for an air-conditioned west-facing apartment these figures are conservative. A south railing is the reverse, producing most in winter (see [why a south railing is a winter panel](https://balco.nyc/800w-balcony-solar-output)). An east railing makes a similar annual total to the west one, but balco.nyc did not run it hourly, and a building across the street, which also trims the peak, is not in these runs.

## What the laws allow: 1,200 W in most states, 420 W and 1,920 W at the edges

Eight of the nine signed state plug-in laws cap a device at 1,200 W, as do New York’s SUNNY Act, which has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature, and California’s SB 868, with the Governor as of 23 September 2026 (his deadline is 30 September). The caps are written as output: New York’s and California’s bills, Vermont and Maine say inverter or AC outright; Utah, Connecticut and Virginia say only “maximum power output.” The calculator’s sizes are panel watts, and at its DC-to-AC ratio of 1.1 their inverters are about 364, 727, 1,091 and 1,455 W. From balco.nyc’s reading of the legislature texts (not legal advice):

| Where | Cap as written | 400 W | 800 W | 1,200 W | 1,600 W |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Utah, Maryland, Vermont, Connecticut, Virginia, New Hampshire, New Jersey | 1,200 W | Within | Within | Within | Over |
| New York (bill) | 1,200 W aggregate AC inverter nameplate | Within | Within | Within | Over |
| California (bill) | 1,200 W AC per dwelling | Within | Within | Within | Over |
| Maine | 420 W AC per service address; up to 1,200 W with conditions | Within the 420 W tier | Licensed electrician, dedicated single-outlet circuit, utility notice | Same conditions | Over |
| Colorado | 1,920 W to the grid, one system per address | Within | Within | Within | Within |

For an apartment the cap rarely binds: the rule in section 6 reaches 1,200 W only at a 300 W floor. Maine prices the second step explicitly: 400 to 800 W needs a licensed electrician and a dedicated circuit on top of $600 of hardware, for a step worth about $35 a year in the New York example at a 150 W floor. Colorado’s 1,920 W allows 1,600 W of panel, but Colorado’s EIA average residential price is 16.45¢ (12 months to June 2026), under half of 34¢, and Denver’s stronger sun (805 kWh from an 800 W south railing, against New York’s 604) probably means more surplus at the same floor, though balco.nyc did not run Denver hourly.

400 W also sits at a second line. Colorado, Maryland and Virginia exempt devices of 391 W or less from code or listing provisions that would require rewiring, New Jersey’s line is 400 W, and from 1 January 2027 Colorado bars selling devices over 391 W that are not UL labeled and listed. Whether a product falls under a line depends on how each law measures output. Where a cap counts inverter output, more panel behind a capped inverter is a question of wording; it barely changes self-consumption, since clipping removes only output far above any apartment’s floor. [Every law side by side](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-laws-compared) has the rest.

## The circuit is the other ceiling

Size also sets how much current the inverter adds to a household circuit. balco.nyc’s [safety guide](https://balco.nyc/is-plug-in-solar-safe) works through the worst case: at 120 V a 400, 800 or 1,200 W inverter adds 3.3, 6.7 or 10 A, and on a shared 15 A circuit, loads beyond the inverter’s outlet can pull that plus the breaker’s 15 A through part of the wire — 18.3, 21.7 or 25 A — without tripping it. If the gap between the 80% continuous-load convention and the breaker’s rating is the only slack, it is 3 A on a 15 A circuit, about 360 W.

In the hourly run, a 400 W south railing peaked at 345 W (2.9 A) and never exceeded 360 W; 800 W did for 455 hours a year, 1,200 W for 944 and 1,600 W for 1,329. Hourly averages smooth over brief peaks and the worst case is set by the inverter’s rating, so read these as exposure, not a safety margin. Maine’s 420 W tier, about 3.5 A, is the one cap near that slack; above it Maine requires a dedicated single-outlet circuit, which removes the worst case at any size. This is not electrical advice: whether a circuit can host a system is a question for a licensed electrician.

## The sizing rule: about 400 W of panel per 100 W of floor

At New York City’s price, **allow about 400 W of panel for every 100 W your home draws when nothing is in use**, round down to a 400 W step, and stop at your state’s cap. In balco.nyc’s runs, every step inside that line repaid its $600 in 12.2 years or less (13.7 on the west railing), and every step beyond it took 14.5 years or more, or never repaid.

| Floor | Size by the rule | Its last 400 W pays back in | The next 400 W would take |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100 W | 400 W | 7.5 years | 22.6 years |
| 150 W | 400 W | 6.3 years | 14.5 years |
| 200 W | 800 W | 10.7 years | 19.2 years |
| 300 W | 1,200 W | 12.2 years | 17.9 years |

South-facing railing, New York City, 34¢, $600 per 400 W, the calculator’s payback loop.

**Finding your floor.** Con Edison says its smart meters let customers see electric use in 15-minute increments; the lowest level that recurs overnight and while you are out is your floor, close to how NRDC measured it. Without that, NRDC’s idle load was 31% to 36% of annual use in its two climate zones and 29% in the audited apartment, so a third of your average draw is a rough guide: monthly kWh divided by 2.2, in watts. At 350 kWh a month that is about 160 W, which the rule puts at 400 W.

**Adjusting it.** If someone is home drawing power through the day, size to that daytime draw: a steady 200 W while the sun is up justifies 800 W whatever the overnight floor. Where power is cheaper, shrink the rule. At the US average of 17.9¢ (EIA, 12 months to June 2026), the same runs put the first 400 W at 9.9 to 13.3 years and the second under 20 only with a floor of 200 W or more: roughly halve the rule, which for most apartments means one 400 W step. The sun here is New York’s; other cities will differ in the numbers more than the direction. balco.nyc’s [calculator](https://balco.nyc/) offers all four sizes but assumes every kWh is used, so treat its larger sizes as ceilings.

## Common questions

**Is 800 W or 1,200 W balcony solar better?**

For most apartments, 800 W or less. In balco.nyc's hourly New York City model, going from 800 to 1,200 W adds about 302 kWh a year of output, but a home drawing a steady 150 W uses only 49 kWh of it, about $17 a year at Con Edison's 34-cent rate, which does not repay the step's $600 within 25 years. The extra 400 W pays back in about 12 years only where the home draws a steady 300 W.

**What size balcony solar system do I need?**

A rough rule from balco.nyc's hourly model of New York City: about 400 W of panel for every 100 W your home draws when nothing is in use, rounded down to a 400 W step and capped by your state's limit. That gives 400 W for a floor of 100 to 150 W, 800 W for 200 W and 1,200 W for 300 W. Where electricity costs about half New York City's 34 cents, roughly halve it.

**Is a 400 W balcony solar system worth it?**

It is usually the best value per dollar, because a home can use nearly all of 400 W as it is produced. balco.nyc's hourly New York City model puts payback on $600 of hardware at 5.5 to 7.5 years for homes drawing a steady 100 to 300 W at Con Edison's 34-cent rate, and about 10 to 13 years at the US average price of 17.9 cents.

**How many solar panels should I put on my balcony?**

For most apartments, 400 to 800 W: one or two panels, if each is rated about 400 W. In balco.nyc's hourly New York City model, a home drawing a steady 150 W uses 262 kWh a year from the first 400 W, 102 from the second and 49 from the third, because every panel peaks at the same midday hours. A third panel pays back within about 12 years only where the home draws 300 W around the clock.

**Can I install more than 1,200 W of balcony solar?**

In most states with a plug-in law, not as a plug-in device: eight of the nine signed laws cap a device at 1,200 W, and New York's SUNNY Act, which has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature, uses the same figure. Colorado allows 1,920 W. Several laws count inverter output rather than panel watts, so check the wording; this is not legal advice.

**Why doesn't a bigger balcony solar system save proportionally more?**

Because a home's load does not grow when panels are added, and power not used the moment it is produced goes to the grid, usually unpaid. In balco.nyc's New York City model with a steady 150 W draw, going from 400 to 1,200 W triples output but raises the electricity used at home by only 58%, from 262 to 413 kWh a year.

- [Maryland General Assembly — Chapter 353 of 2026 (HB 1532), PUA §7-321](https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/2026RS/Chapters_noln/CH_353_hb1532e.pdf): no more than 1,200 W back to the building’s electric system; systems of 391 W or less exempt from listing provisions that would require alterations to wiring.
- [Connecticut General Assembly — Public Act 26-127, sec. 9](https://www.cga.ct.gov/2026/ACT/PA/PDF/2026PA-00127-R00HB-05340-PA.PDF): a maximum power output of not more than 1,200 W; effective 1 October 2026.
- [Virginia Acts of Assembly — Chapter 1052 (HB 395)](https://lis.blob.core.windows.net/files/1225204.PDF): a maximum power output of not more than 1,200 W per dwelling unit; devices of 391 W or less exempt from listing provisions that would require alterations to wiring.
- [Office of the Governor of New Jersey — Garden State Balcony Solar Act signed, 1 September 2026](https://www.nj.gov/governor/news/2026/approved/20260901a.shtml): plug-in solar devices of up to 1,200 W.
- [EIA — Form EIA-861M monthly sales and revenue](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/data/eia861m/): the data behind balco.nyc’s US average (17.9¢) and Colorado (16.45¢) residential prices: revenue over sales for the 12 months to June 2026, averages that include fixed charges.

---

# Is there a tax credit for balcony solar in 2026?

URL: https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-tax-credit  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

No. The 30% federal Residential Clean Energy Credit (IRC §25D) does not cover anything installed in 2026: the One Big Beautiful Bill Act ended it for expenditures made after 31 December 2025, and the IRS counts an expenditure as made when installation is completed, not when you pay. On a $1,200 mid-range kit the credit would have been worth $360. balco.nyc’s PVWatts runs for the largest city in every state put the median payback at 9.9 years at full price against 7.1 years at $840, so losing the credit adds a median 2.7 years.

## No federal credit in 2026, and what it would have been worth

The credit solar sellers used to quote was the Residential Clean Energy Credit in section 25D of the Internal Revenue Code: 30% of the cost of qualified solar electric property, with no dollar cap. Section 70506 of Public Law 119-21, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act signed on 4 July 2025, rewrote its termination clause so that the credit “shall not apply with respect to any expenditures made after December 31, 2025.” The same act ended the separate home-improvement credit in section 25C. There is no replacement federal credit for a household buying solar in 2026, plug-in or rooftop.

To put a number on what went away, balco.nyc reran its state-by-state payback with the credit restored. The method is the one behind the [state pages](https://balco.nyc/states): an 800 W kit on an unshaded south-facing railing in each state’s largest city, NREL PVWatts V8 output multiplied by the 0.95 railing factor for a vertical panel, valued at the state’s EIA average residential price for the 12 months to June 2026, with output falling 0.5% a year and prices rising 3% a year. The only thing that changes is the price: $1,200 for a mid-range kit, or $840 after a 30% credit.

| State (reference city) | Output, kWh/yr | Average price | Payback at $1,200 | Payback at $840 | Credit was worth |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Maine (Portland) | 692 | 28.99¢ | 5.6 years | 4.0 years | 1.6 years |
| New York (New York City) | 604 | 27.96¢ | 6.6 years | 4.7 years | 1.9 years |
| Maryland (Baltimore) | 673 | 20.75¢ | 7.9 years | 5.7 years | 2.2 years |
| Colorado (Denver) | 805 | 16.45¢ | 8.3 years | 6.0 years | 2.3 years |
| Utah (Salt Lake City) | 724 | 13.36¢ | 10.9 years | 8.0 years | 3.0 years |
| Median, 50 states and DC | — | — | 9.9 years | 7.1 years | 2.7 years |

Three things follow from the full 51-row run. The credit was worth most, in years, where electricity is cheapest: 1.6 years in Maine, 3.0 in Utah, and 3.7 in Washington, which has the longest payback of the 51. With the credit, the mid-range kit would pay back inside ten years in 50 of the 51; at full price, 28 do. And a 30% price cut shortens payback by a little less than 30% — a median 28% — because the years it removes are the late ones, when rising prices make each year’s saving larger. Differences in the table are computed before rounding.

Every figure here is a ceiling, not an expectation. It assumes an unshaded railing and that every kilowatt-hour is used in the home, since the model treats surplus power as earning nothing, which is how most of the new plug-in laws work. The EIA figures are averages that include fixed monthly charges a panel does not reduce, which flatters the value of each kWh. New York’s row uses the state average, not the 34¢ Con Edison marginal rate balco.nyc uses for [New York City addresses](https://balco.nyc/electricity-rate).

## When an expenditure counted as “made”

The cut-off is not the day you paid. Section 25D(e)(8)(A) has long said that an expenditure is treated as made “when the original installation of the item is completed.” In its August 2025 questions and answers on the new law (Fact Sheet 2025-05, question 7), the IRS applied that rule to the termination directly: paying on or before 31 December 2025 does not preserve the credit if installation is completed afterwards.

For a plug-in kit the consequence is plain. A kit bought in December 2025 but mounted and switched on in January 2026 is outside the credit on the IRS’s reading. The IRS has not said what “installation completed” means for a device you clamp to a railing and plug in yourself. The natural reading is the day it was mounted and running, but we could not find the point addressed anywhere.

The IRS’s own credit page words the cut-off differently — the credit “is not available for any property placed in service after December 31, 2025” — and tells filers to claim it for the year the property “is installed, not merely purchased.” Both formulations point the same way, and the statute’s test, the one the IRS applied in its FAQ, is completed installation.

What survives is narrow. A system installed in 2025 is claimed on the 2025 return, and the IRS says a taxpayer who missed it can generally amend within three years of filing or two years of paying the tax, whichever is later. Unused credit carries forward to later years. All of that assumes a plug-in kit was eligible in the first place, which is the question in section 4. None of this is tax advice; a preparer can tell you how it applies to your return.

## Why “30% off with the federal tax credit” is now wrong

Kit listings, comparison pages and articles written before the summer of 2025 often advertise a plug-in kit as “30% off with the federal tax credit,” or print a net price with the credit already subtracted. Many are still online and still turn up in search. For any kit installed in 2026 the claim is wrong for the simplest reason: the credit no longer exists for new installations. Web pages are rarely rewritten when a tax law changes, and a price with 30% taken off is the most flattering number a seller can show.

The claim was loose even while the credit existed. Section 25D was never a discount at checkout. It was a nonrefundable credit claimed on IRS Form 5695 when you filed, limited to the tax you owed that year, with any excess carried forward. A household with little federal income tax got little or nothing in the year it installed the kit. And no seller could promise eligibility: that was between the taxpayer and the IRS, and for plug-in kits the IRS never addressed it.

The practical rule for 2026: compare kits on the sticker price. If a page shows a price “after tax credit,” divide it by 0.7 to recover the real one — an $840 net price is a $1,200 kit. balco.nyc’s own [cost and payback figures](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-cost) are gross, with no federal credit netted out.

## Did 25D ever clearly cover a plug-in kit?

Plausibly, but nobody with authority said so. The statutory definition is broad: a qualified solar electric property expenditure is one “for property which uses solar energy to generate electricity for use in a dwelling unit” in the United States that the taxpayer uses as a residence (§25D(d)(2)). Nothing in it sets a minimum size or requires a roof, a licensed installer, net metering or the utility’s approval. The IRS’s FAQ adds that the taxpayer may rent the home, which is unusual for a tax break on equipment and mattered for apartment dwellers. For solar, the home did not have to be a main residence either; a second home the taxpayer lived in part-time counted.

What was never settled is how a device built to be moved fits a credit organized around installation. The timing rule keys to “original installation,” the IRS told filers to claim the year the property was installed, and several of the new state laws define plug-in devices as moveable or portable. We found no IRS ruling, FAQ, form instruction or publication that addresses plug-in or portable solar. One edge is clear: a battery bundled with a kit counted as battery storage technology only if its capacity was at least 3 kWh.

There was also a practical wrinkle. On balco.nyc’s state research, Utah was the only state with a plug-in solar law in force during 2025; everywhere else, connecting a kit meant going through the utility’s interconnection rules. The tax code did not make the credit depend on that, but a claim could have rested on an installation the utility had not approved. The honest summary is eligible on the text, untested in practice, and moot for anything installed from 2026.

## State tax breaks in the plug-in states

We checked every state with a plug-in solar law in force or signed — Utah, Maine, Colorado, Maryland, Vermont, Connecticut, Virginia, New Hampshire and New Jersey — plus New York, whose SUNNY Act has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature. None has a state income-tax credit or rebate that plainly covers a self-installed plug-in kit. Five exempt solar equipment from sales tax in wording a kit plausibly fits, though none of the guidance we found mentions plug-in systems.

| State | What exists | Does it fit a plug-in kit? |
|---|---|---|
| New York | Solar energy system equipment credit, 25% up to $5,000 (Tax Law §606(g-1)). State sales-tax exemption for residential solar equipment; New York City charges no local tax on it. | Credit: probably not. The IT-255 instructions require a net-metering contract (or compliance with the utility’s net-metering schedule) and a connection to the utility’s system; the SUNNY Act would exempt plug-in devices from net metering. Sales tax: plausibly, if a kit counts as equipment “installed in a residence”. Claimed with Form ST-121. |
| New Jersey | Sales-tax exemption for solar energy devices that provide electrical power (N.J.S.A. 54:32B-8.33) | Plausibly. Claimed with Form ST-4. |
| Connecticut | Sales-tax exemption for solar electricity generating systems, defined as systems that convert sunlight directly into electricity, including modules, inverters and mounting hardware | Plausibly. Claimed with Form CERT-140. |
| Maryland | Sales-tax exemption for solar energy equipment that generates electricity “to be used in a structure or supplied to the electric grid” (Tax-General §11-230). Maryland Solar Access Program rebate of $750 per kW DC. | Exemption: plausibly. Rebate: no. It is for income-qualified homeowners, requires a participating contractor and pays after interconnection. |
| Colorado | Sales-tax exemption for components that produce alternating-current electricity from a renewable source, including solar modules and inverters | Plausibly, but only for state and some special-district taxes. Most city and county taxes still apply unless adopted locally, and home-rule cities set their own. |
| Vermont | Renewable-energy equipment is generally taxable; the home exemptions cover off-grid systems and solar water heating | No. A plug-in device is grid-connected and cannot be net metered. |
| Utah | Renewable Energy Systems Tax Credit | No. Residential solar installed in 2024 or later is not eligible. |
| New Hampshire | Residential Renewable Electrical Generation Rebate | No. The program is permanently closed. |
| Maine, Virginia | We found no state credit, rebate or sales-tax exemption that applies | We could not confirm that none exists. |

An exemption is worth the sales tax you would otherwise pay. New York City is the largest case: residential solar equipment is exempt from the 4% state tax and the 0.375% Metropolitan Commuter Transportation District tax, and the city’s own rate on it is zero, so a qualifying $1,200 kit would avoid the full 8.875% combined rate, or **$106.50**. That is under a third of the $360 the federal credit used to be worth, and it depends on a retailer accepting an exemption certificate for a product the rules never contemplated. Ask before you pay: the exemption is normally claimed by giving the seller a certificate at the time of sale. In New York the question is also premature, since until the SUNNY Act is signed and takes effect the utility’s approval is still required to connect a kit.

This is not legal or tax advice. Sales-tax treatment can turn on facts the published guidance does not address, local rates vary, and we found no state agency that has ruled on a plug-in kit. For what each state’s law allows, see [how the state laws compare](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-laws-compared) or the individual [state pages](https://balco.nyc/states); for whether a kit is worth buying at full price, see [is balcony solar worth it](https://balco.nyc/is-balcony-solar-worth-it).

## Common questions

**Is there a federal tax credit for balcony solar in 2026?**

No. The 30% Residential Clean Energy Credit under section 25D of the Internal Revenue Code was ended by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (Public Law 119-21, signed 4 July 2025) for expenditures made after 31 December 2025. There is no replacement federal credit for household solar, plug-in or rooftop.

**I paid for a balcony solar kit in December 2025 but set it up in January 2026. Can I claim the 30% credit?**

Not on the IRS's reading. Section 25D treats an expenditure as made when the original installation is completed, and the IRS's August 2025 FAQ says that paying on or before 31 December 2025 does not preserve the credit if installation was completed afterwards.

**Did the 30% federal credit ever cover plug-in balcony solar?**

Plausibly, but it was never confirmed. The statute covers property that uses solar energy to generate electricity for use in a home the taxpayer lives in, including a rented one, with no minimum size or interconnection requirement. But the credit is organized around installation, and the IRS never issued guidance on plug-in or portable systems. The question is moot for anything installed from 2026.

**How much longer does balcony solar take to pay back without the tax credit?**

balco.nyc's model of an 800 W kit on a south-facing railing in each state's largest city puts the median payback on a $1,200 kit at 9.9 years, against 7.1 years at the $840 it would have cost after a 30% credit: about 2.7 years longer. The gap ranges from 1.4 years in California to 3.7 years in Washington, and every figure is a ceiling that assumes no shade and full self-consumption.

**Does New York's solar tax credit apply to a plug-in balcony system?**

Probably not. New York's solar energy system equipment credit (25% up to $5,000) requires, for systems that make electricity, a net-metering contract with the utility or compliance with its net-metering schedule, and a connection to the utility's system. The SUNNY Act, which has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature, would exempt plug-in devices from net metering. We could not confirm how the two would interact.

**Is a balcony solar kit exempt from sales tax?**

In some states, plausibly. New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, Maryland and Colorado exempt solar equipment from sales tax in wording a plug-in kit appears to fit, though no guidance we found mentions plug-in systems, and Colorado's exemption covers only state and some special-district taxes. Vermont's does not fit a grid-connected plug-in device. The exemption is normally claimed with a certificate at the time of sale.

**Are there state rebates for balcony solar?**

None that we found for a self-installed plug-in kit in the states with plug-in laws. Maryland's Solar Access Program requires a participating contractor and interconnection, New Hampshire's residential solar rebate is permanently closed, and Utah's residential solar credit ended for systems installed in 2024 or later.

# Balcony solar in winter: what a railing panel makes, month by month

URL: https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-winter  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

Yes, balcony solar works in winter, and a panel hung on a south-facing railing usually makes more then than in summer. balco.nyc’s PVWatts runs for the largest city in every state put an unshaded 800 W vertical south panel at a median 31% of its year from December to February, about 64 kWh in December alone, against 21% for the same panel tilted to a rooftop 35°. Two things undo it: a railing facing east, west or north, which follows the summer like a roof, and a building across the street, which on a third floor in New York takes about 90% of the winter.

## Only a south-facing railing is a winter panel

A vertical south railing makes more from December to February than from June to August in 48 of the 51 cities balco.nyc modeled ([what an 800 W system produces](https://balco.nyc/800w-balcony-solar-output)). That is one direction. For the rest, balco.nyc took its PVWatts V8 runs for the largest city in every state and DC, applied the site’s railing factor to each (0.95 vertical, 0.98 at 60°, 0.99 at 35°) and measured how much of each panel’s year falls in winter. Spread evenly, December through February would carry 24.7%.

| 800 W panel, unshaded | Share of year, Dec–Feb | Share of year, Oct–Mar | Dec–Feb ÷ Jun–Aug | Most often the best month | Most often the worst month |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| South, vertical | 31.2% | 61.7% | 1.84 | January (15 cities) | June (48) |
| South-east or south-west, vertical | 24.5% | 51.2% | 0.98 / 1.08 | March (22 / 19) | December or June |
| East or west, vertical | 17.3% | 39.3% | 0.56 / 0.53 | July (26 / 22) | December (43 / 36) |
| North, vertical | 16.0% | 35.1% | 0.45 | June (43) | December (24) or November (23) |
| South, 60° bracket | 24.6% | 51.5% | 1.03 | March (21) | December or June (21 each) |
| South, 35° | 20.7% | 45.1% | 0.74 | July (19) | December (41) |

Shares and ratios are medians of the 51 cities; paired rows give each direction’s figure. **Only a railing facing close to due south leans toward winter.** Turn it 45° to the south-east or south-west and the year spreads almost evenly, 24.5% in December–February, usually peaking in March. East, west and north railings are summer panels, as seasonal as a roof or more so: in none of the 51 cities does one make more in winter than in summer. A north railing’s winter output is nearly all diffuse light, since between the equinoxes the sun rises and sets south of due east and west ([does my balcony get enough sun?](https://balco.nyc/balcony-sunlight)).

In December a south railing draws level with a roof-angle panel: the median unshaded railing makes **64 kWh**, about 2.1 kWh a day, and the same panel at 35° makes 65. The railing wins December outright in 24 cities, all at or north of Louisville’s 38°N. Tilting pays in summer, the subject of [what angle a balcony panel should be](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-panel-angle).

## Month by month in six cities

Six cities from 30° to 61°N show how latitude and weather bend the shape. balco.nyc’s PVWatts output for an unshaded 800 W vertical south railing, in kWh, after the 0.95 railing factor:

| kWh, south railing | Jacksonville | Phoenix | New York City | Chicago | Seattle | Anchorage |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jan | 79 | 95 | 69 | 61 | 36 | 14 |
| Feb | 62 | 84 | 66 | 66 | 42 | 32 |
| Mar | 62 | 76 | 62 | 59 | 48 | 76 |
| Apr | 40 | 53 | 45 | 49 | 50 | 67 |
| May | 28 | 35 | 36 | 36 | 45 | 64 |
| Jun | 23 | 25 | 30 | 33 | 37 | 57 |
| Jul | 25 | 28 | 34 | 38 | 42 | 54 |
| Aug | 34 | 41 | 39 | 46 | 56 | 58 |
| Sep | 47 | 63 | 53 | 57 | 56 | 52 |
| Oct | 66 | 86 | 59 | 61 | 48 | 35 |
| Nov | 76 | 95 | 55 | 57 | 32 | 16 |
| Dec | 71 | 99 | 55 | 52 | 30 | 9 |
| Year | 612 | 778 | 604 | 616 | 524 | 535 |

Four of the six peak between December and February and bottom out in June: Phoenix in December, at 99 kWh, Jacksonville and New York in January, Chicago in February. Seattle and Anchorage are the exceptions. Seattle’s winter weather leaves September its best month, narrowly, and December its worst; in Anchorage the December sun barely clears the horizon and March is best. Per day, December gives 3.2 kWh in Phoenix, 2.3 in Jacksonville, 1.8 in New York, 1.7 in Chicago, 1.0 in Seattle and 0.3 in Anchorage.

Direction reshapes the year again. Winter (December–February) against summer (June–August) output, in kWh, for the same six cities:

| Winter / summer kWh | South, vertical | East, vertical | West, vertical | North, vertical | South at 35° |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jacksonville | 213 / 81 | 92 / 157 | 91 / 128 | 31 / 70 | 258 / 266 |
| Phoenix | 278 / 94 | 118 / 173 | 106 / 184 | 32 / 71 | 314 / 332 |
| New York City | 191 / 104 | 76 / 142 | 68 / 143 | 23 / 61 | 205 / 283 |
| Chicago | 180 / 117 | 76 / 151 | 71 / 158 | 33 / 63 | 183 / 309 |
| Seattle | 108 / 135 | 40 / 141 | 39 / 165 | 15 / 63 | 113 / 300 |
| Anchorage | 55 / 170 | 14 / 130 | 16 / 160 | 7 / 78 | 50 / 273 |

In New York the south railing makes 191 kWh over the winter months, two and a half times an east railing and eight times a north one; in summer the east railing out-produces it, 142 to 104. The 35° panel is nearly flat across the seasons in Jacksonville and Phoenix and summer-heavy everywhere else.

## Short days, low sun, and why most winter figures describe a roof

Winter days are short, and the U.S. Naval Observatory’s rise and set times for the 2026 solstices put numbers on it. The noon sun’s height is 90° minus the latitude, minus or plus the sun’s 23.44° declination:

| City | Daylight, 21 Dec | Daylight, 21 Jun | Noon sun, 21 Dec | Noon sun, 21 Jun |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jacksonville | 10h 12m | 14h 07m | 36° | 83° |
| Phoenix | 9h 57m | 14h 22m | 33° | 80° |
| New York City | 9h 15m | 15h 06m | 26° | 73° |
| Chicago | 9h 08m | 15h 13m | 25° | 72° |
| Seattle | 8h 25m | 15h 59m | 19° | 66° |
| Anchorage | 5h 27m | 19h 23m | 5° | 52° |

A rooftop panel faces most of the sky, so a long day and a high sun are simply more energy, and the familiar line that panels make about half as much in winter describes roofs fairly. The Energy Information Administration estimates monthly output from the country’s small-scale solar, systems under 1 MW sited mostly on homes and businesses: in 2025 December was **59% of June**, and January, February and December together made 18% of the year (capacity grows through the year, flattering December slightly). balco.nyc’s 35° runs agree: December is a median 69% of June.

A vertical railing turns the same inputs around. In New York the sun is up 39% fewer hours on 21 December than on 21 June, yet the unshaded south railing makes 55.5 kWh in December against 30.3 in June, 1.8 times as much. The low sun, 26° up at noon, meets the upright panel nearly square on; the June sun at 73° passes over it at a glancing angle (the cosine arithmetic is on [the 800 W output page](https://balco.nyc/800w-balcony-solar-output)). Geometry beats day length except where the day nearly disappears: Anchorage’s 5 hours 27 minutes, with the sun 5° up at noon, leave a south railing 9 kWh for all of December. When a page says solar panels make less in winter, check what it describes. It is usually a roof.

## Cold helps a little, and the figures already include it

Solar cells convert light more efficiently when they are cold. The Department of Energy puts the turning point at 77°F, or 25°C, the cell temperature panels are rated at, and the PVWatts manual models the effect as a straight line: DC power is multiplied by 1 + γ × (cell temperature − 25°C). PVWatts’ module-type page gives the coefficient γ as −0.37% per °C for a standard module, −0.32% for thin film and −0.35% for the premium module balco.nyc models.

What counts is the cell, not the air, and a sunlit cell runs warmer than the air around it. PVWatts computes an hourly cell temperature (for an open rack it assumes an installed nominal operating temperature of 45°C), and its API returns it. balco.nyc pulled those hours for the unshaded vertical south panel in three cities and averaged them, weighting each hour by the sunlight reaching the panel:

| Vertical south panel | January air | January cells | Effect on output | July air | July cells | Effect on output |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| New York City | 0.5°C | 10.5°C | +5.1% | 26.8°C | 32.1°C | −2.5% |
| Chicago | −3.1°C | 5.5°C | +6.8% | 23.7°C | 29.1°C | −1.5% |
| Phoenix | 18.7°C | 35.4°C | −3.6% | 39.8°C | 44.2°C | −6.7% |

In New York, January’s cells at 10.5°C give 1 − 0.0035 × (10.5 − 25) = 1.051, about 5% more per unit of light than the rating; July’s 32.1°C costs 2.5%. The gap between the two months is about 8% in both New York and Chicago. In Phoenix even January’s cells average above the rating point, so heat still costs 3.6% in January, against 6.7% in July.

So the cold bonus is real but in single digits, small beside the near-doubling geometry gives a south railing in winter. And it is already inside every PVWatts figure here and in the [calculator](https://balco.nyc/), which applies no separate temperature adjustment. Do not add it on top.

## Snow: a vertical face gives it little to hold

Snow is the winter loss the cold-is-good story leaves out, and on roofs it is not small. Modeling fixed panels at 20° and at latitude tilt, the National Laboratory of the Rockies (then NREL) put average annual snow losses at **0% to 16%** across the continental US, and near 40% at one Alaska site, heaviest from the Northeast through the Great Lakes and Midwest to the northern Rockies.

A railing panel should fare much better, though we found no published measurement of one. The Department of Energy’s winter guidance says vertical installations are less likely than tilted ones to collect snow or ice, and more likely to shed what sticks. The snow model NLR uses, from Marion and colleagues, treats sliding as the main way snow leaves a panel and ties its speed to tilt: in an hour bright and warm enough, 1.97 × sin(tilt) tenths of the panel’s height is uncovered, about 20% of a vertical panel against 11% at 35°. Take that as a direction, not a number: the model was built for tilts of 10° to 45° and ignores melting and snow frozen to the glass.

Two balcony details cut the other way. Snow drifting onto the balcony floor can bury a panel’s lower edge: in Sandia National Laboratories’ Vermont tests, snow piled beneath the modules stopped further sliding for five days, and module frames held snow back. balco.nyc’s runs allow 1% for snow within their 14% losses and hold ground reflectance at 0.20, so they neither charge for a buried panel nor credit the light snowy ground reflects onto a panel that faces half the ground (early PVWatts raised reflectance to 0.6 whenever snow lay on the ground). In snowy cities, read the winter months as approximate in both directions.

## The building across the street takes the winter first

Every figure so far assumes an open view, and the low sun that suits a railing is the easiest to block. balco.nyc ran its own shade code at New York’s latitude for a south-facing third-floor balcony, 7.1 m up, facing a six-to-ten-story building (25 m) across a 20 m street. This is the calculator’s described-surroundings model, a continuous wall; for a New York address the live calculator uses real building footprints. Straight out, the wall rises 41.8°. On the 15th of each month from October to February the sun never climbs that high, so the panel gets no direct sun and its monthly shade factor falls to 0.10–0.12, against 0.54 in June and 0.73 in March. (The model floors each factor at 0.10; unfloored, December and January would be 0.097 and 0.099.) The full monthly working is on [how to calculate your balcony’s output](https://balco.nyc/calculate-balcony-solar-output).

The effect on the seasons is total. The panel keeps **10% of its December–February output**, 20 kWh of 191, but 58% of June–August’s, and of everything the building takes over the year, 72% goes between October and February. The winter panel becomes a summer one: its best month is March, at 45 kWh, and December is its worst, at 5.5.

Height brings the winter back, and quickly. The same wall and street, floor by floor, with the balcony’s height taken as (floor − 1) × 3.05 m + 1 m:

| Floor | Balcony height | Dec–Feb kWh | Share of open-view winter | Year kWh | Best month |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2nd | 4.1 m | 19 | 10% | 211 | March |
| 3rd | 7.1 m | 20 | 10% | 227 | March |
| 4th | 10.2 m | 31 | 16% | 284 | March |
| 5th | 13.2 m | 67 | 35% | 349 | March |
| 6th | 16.3 m | 135 | 71% | 463 | February |
| 7th | 19.3 m | 167 | 87% | 524 | January |
| 8th | 22.4 m | 181 | 95% | 569 | January |
| 9th, above the roofline | 25.4 m | 191 | 100% | 604 | January |

Distance does the same work: with the building 40 m away the third floor keeps 69% of its open-view winter, and at 80 m 91%; a three-to-five-story building (13 m) across the same street leaves it 87%. The code samples the 15th of each month, so the switch from a dark February to a sunlit March is sharper here than on a real balcony, where it takes a few weeks.

## What the winter kilowatt-hours are worth

Priced at each state’s EIA average residential rate for the 12 months to June 2026 — an average that includes fixed charges, so it can overstate what a saved kWh is worth — an unshaded south railing’s December–February output is worth a median **$33** across the 51 cities, from $15 in Anchorage to $88 in Honolulu. In New York City, where balco.nyc uses Con Edison’s marginal rate instead ([why](https://balco.nyc/electricity-rate)), the arithmetic is 191 kWh × $0.34 = $65 for the winter quarter.

| Unshaded 800 W south railing | Dec–Feb kWh | Price (¢/kWh) | Worth, Dec–Feb | Worth, full year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jacksonville | 213 | 15.40 (Florida avg.) | $33 | $94 |
| Phoenix | 278 | 15.40 (Arizona avg.) | $43 | $120 |
| New York City | 191 | 34 (Con Edison marginal) | $65 | $205 |
| New York City | 191 | 27.96 (New York avg.) | $53 | $169 |
| Chicago | 180 | 18.54 (Illinois avg.) | $33 | $114 |
| Seattle | 108 | 14.02 (Washington avg.) | $15 | $73 |
| Anchorage | 55 | 26.74 (Alaska avg.) | $15 | $143 |

At a flat price the winter quarter is worth exactly its share of the kWh, about 31% of the year for a south railing. Three things change that. A seasonal tariff does: where summer power costs more, as it does under Con Edison’s delivery charges from June through September ([what a kWh costs](https://balco.nyc/electricity-rate)), a winter-heavy panel’s kWh are worth a little less than the average suggests. Surplus does: a south railing’s highest midday output comes in the colder months — in New York’s hourly run it tops out near 730 W in January and March, against about 200 W in June — and any of it your home is not using is assumed to earn nothing unless a state law or utility credits it ([net metering and self-consumption](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-net-metering) covers how much that is). And shade does, most of all: the shaded third-floor balcony in section 6 makes 20 kWh from December to February, about $7 at Con Edison’s rate.

Which of these describes your balcony depends on its direction and what stands opposite, which is what the [calculator](https://balco.nyc/) runs for any US address. Whether the whole year pays back a kit is on [whether balcony solar is worth it](https://balco.nyc/is-balcony-solar-worth-it).

## Common questions

**Do balcony solar panels work in winter?**

Yes. In balco.nyc's PVWatts runs for the largest city in every state, an unshaded 800 W panel hung vertically on a south-facing railing makes a median 31% of its annual output from December to February, against about 25% if output were spread evenly, and more in those months than from June to August in 48 of the 51 cities, because the low winter sun strikes an upright panel nearly head-on. East-, west- and north-facing railings, and any balcony with a taller building close across the street, make much less in winter.

**Do solar panels produce more in winter or summer?**

A rooftop panel produces more in summer: EIA estimates put 2025 December output from US small-scale solar at 59% of June's. A vertical south-facing balcony panel is the reverse. In 48 of the 51 cities balco.nyc modeled it makes more from December to February than from June to August, a median 1.84 times as much. Railings facing east, west or north follow the summer like a roof.

**How much does an 800 W balcony solar panel produce in December?**

Unshaded and hung vertically facing south, a median 64 kWh in December across the largest city in every state, about 2 kWh a day, in balco.nyc's PVWatts runs: 99 kWh in Phoenix, 55 in New York City, 52 in Chicago, 30 in Seattle and 9 in Anchorage. Facing east or west the median is about 23 to 25 kWh, and facing north about 9.

**Does cold weather make solar panels more efficient?**

Yes, but only by a few percent. PVWatts lowers output by 0.35% for each degree Celsius a premium module's cells run above 25°C and raises it by the same amount below. For a vertical south panel in New York, sunlit cells average about 10.5°C in January and 32°C in July, worth roughly 5% more and 2.5% less than the rating. PVWatts-based estimates already include this, so it should not be added again.

**What happens to a balcony solar panel when it snows?**

A vertical panel gives snow little to rest on. The Department of Energy says vertical installations are less likely than tilted ones to accumulate snow or ice and more likely to shed it, and the snow model NLR uses makes sliding faster as tilt increases. That model was built for tilts of 10 to 45 degrees, and balco.nyc found no published measurement of snow losses on a balcony railing. Snow drifting onto the balcony floor can still cover a panel's lower edge.

**Why does my balcony panel make so little in winter?**

Usually because of what stands opposite. The winter sun is low, so a building across the street blocks it first. In balco.nyc's shade model, a south-facing third-floor balcony in New York facing a six-to-ten-story building 20 meters away keeps only about 10% of its unshaded December-to-February output, and its best month moves to March. The same balcony on the 7th floor keeps 87%.

## Sources

- [National Laboratory of the Rockies — PVWatts V8 API documentation](https://developer.nlr.gov/docs/solar/pvwatts/v8/): the model behind balco.nyc’s runs, its monthly output, and the hourly ambient and module temperature outputs (tamb, tcell) used for the cold-weather table.
- [PVWatts — Module type help](https://pvwatts.nlr.gov/docs/en/help_module_type.php): temperature coefficients of −0.37%/°C (standard), −0.35%/°C (premium) and −0.32%/°C (thin film).
- [Dobos, PVWatts Version 5 Manual (NREL, 2014)](https://pvwatts.nlr.gov/downloads/pvwattsv5.pdf): DC power scaled by 1 + γ(Tcell − 25°C), the Fuentes cell-temperature model, the premium module’s −0.35%/°C, and that PVWatts V1 raised albedo to 0.6 when snow lay on the ground.
- [PVWatts — Array type help](https://pvwatts.nlr.gov/docs/en/help_system_array_type.php): the installed nominal operating cell temperature of 45°C assumed for an open rack.
- [U.S. Department of Energy, FEMP — Solar Photovoltaic Hardening for Resilience: Winter Weather](https://www.energy.gov/cmei/femp/solar-photovoltaic-hardening-resilience-winter-weather): that modules lose voltage above 77°F, and that vertical installations are less likely to accumulate snow or ice and more likely to shed it.
- [Ryberg and Freeman — Integration, Validation, and Application of a PV Snow Coverage Model in SAM (NREL/TP-6A20-68705, 2017)](https://docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy17osti/68705.pdf): the Marion snow model’s sliding term of 1.97 × sin(tilt) tenths of row height per hour, its design range of 10–45° tilt, that it ignores melting and frozen snow, and national fixed-tilt snow losses of 0–16% (near 40% at one Alaska site).
- [Riley et al. (Sandia National Laboratories) — Differences in Snow Shedding in Photovoltaic Systems with Framed and Frameless Modules](https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1640734): Vermont measurements in which snow accumulating beneath the modules prevented sliding for five days, and frames impeded shedding.
- [U.S. Naval Observatory — Sun and Moon rise/set times for one day](https://aa.usno.navy.mil/data/RS_OneDay): sunrise and sunset on 21 December and 21 June 2026 for the six cities, from which the day lengths are computed.
- [PVEducation — Elevation angle](https://www.pveducation.org/pvcdrom/properties-of-sunlight/elevation-angle): the noon sun elevation as 90° minus latitude plus the solar declination, behind the solstice noon angles.
- [EIA — Electric Power Monthly, Table 1.1.A: Net generation from renewable sources](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/monthly/epm_table_grapher.php?t=epmt_1_01_a): estimated small-scale solar generation by month; 2025 December (5,569 thousand MWh) was 59% of June (9,423), and December–February 18% of the year.
- [EIA — Electricity data now include estimated small-scale solar PV capacity and generation (2015)](https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=23972): that small-scale means under 1 MW, usually at the customer’s site, and that its output is higher in summer and lower in winter.
- [EIA — Form EIA-861M monthly sales and revenue](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/data/eia861m/): the state average residential prices for the 12 months to June 2026 used to value winter output (balco.nyc’s data/state-energy.json).

---

# Does my balcony get enough sun for solar?

URL: https://balco.nyc/balcony-sunlight  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-04

There is no threshold: the honest answer is a kilowatt-hour number, not a yes or no. In a dense city what sets it is mostly how much sky your balcony can see past the building opposite, and how high up you are — which way it faces matters less than the rules of thumb suggest. A typical 800 W New York system produces 400 to 900 kWh a year, and a high-floor south balcony makes roughly three times what a low-floor north one does.

## “Enough sun” is a number, not a threshold

The standard answer to this question is a rule of thumb: three to four hours of direct sunlight a day and you are fine. It is a reasonable rule and it comes from somewhere sensible — it is roughly the line between a balcony that will grow herbs and one that will not. But it treats the question as a gate you either pass or fail, and that is not how a solar system behaves. A panel does not switch on at four hours. It produces a continuously varying amount all year, and the useful output of that arithmetic is a single figure: annual kilowatt-hours.

That figure is what everything downstream depends on. In New York the number to multiply it by is Con Edison’s all-in marginal rate of about **$0.34 per kilowatt-hour** — supply, delivery and surcharges together, which is [the correct rate for electricity you generate and consume yourself](https://balco.nyc/electricity-rate). A typical 800 W system on an NYC balcony lands somewhere between **400 and 900 kWh a year**, so the annual saving runs from roughly $136 to roughly $306. On a $1,200 mid-range kit that is the difference between a [payback of under four years and one of over eight](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-cost). Both of those balconies get “enough” sun in the sense that the panels work. Only one of them is a good idea.

This is also where a widely repeated figure needs qualifying. You will often read that an 800 W kit covers 15–25% of an apartment’s electricity. That is a nameplate-ideal number with no shading derate applied. Against the EIA’s New York average household consumption of about 6,850 kWh a year, the real 400–900 kWh band works out at **6% to 13%** — and the lower end of that is not a rounding error, it is what a shaded low-floor balcony actually delivers. The 15–25% figure describes a well-sited system belonging to a light consumer. It is a ceiling, not an expectation.

> **One number, not a verdict.** If someone answers “does my balcony get enough sun” with yes or no, they have skipped the only part of the answer that changes what you should do.

## The four things that decide it, in order

Most solar guidance is written for a detached house, where orientation is the first question because it is very nearly the only one. In a dense city the ranking inverts. Here is the order that actually matters for an NYC balcony:

|  | Variable | What it really is | Why it ranks here |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Obstruction | The height of the building across the street relative to yours, and how far away it stands | It sets the floor of the sky you can see. On a low floor in a narrow canyon it can remove the entire middle of the day for months at a time — a bigger swing than every other variable combined. You cannot change it, and it is the one nobody asks about. |
| 2 | Floor height | How far above the street the panel sits | Every storey you climb drops the skyline. The same balcony, facing the same way, is a materially different proposition on the 3rd floor and the 12th. Published research on vertical facade PV finds incident energy distributed non-uniformly along the height of the wall for exactly this reason. |
| 3 | Orientation | The compass direction the railing faces | Real, predictable and correctly priced by any decent model — but it only prices sun you can actually see. Orientation decides how you use an open sky; obstruction decides whether you have one. |
| 4 | Tilt | Flat against the railing (vertical, 90°) or angled out on a bracket | The only variable you get to choose, and the one most often taken away by the railing design or the building’s rules. balco.nyc models four mount angles — 35°, 60°, 70° and vertical — because the gap between them is worth knowing before you argue with a board. |

This ordering is why one particular claim deserves care. You will find it stated as a constant, across many pages, that a north-facing balcony produces **75% less** than a south-facing one. We could not trace that figure to a primary source; it appears without attribution and gets copied forward. The deeper problem is not the number, it is the framing. It presents azimuth as if it were the whole answer, on a page written for someone whose real constraint is the twelve-storey building forty feet away.

In a city the two effects compete, and obstruction usually wins. **An unobstructed high-floor north balcony can out-produce a south-facing balcony boxed in by a taller building across a narrow street.** balco.nyc’s own modelling puts roughly **3×** between the best and worst realistic NYC cases — a high-floor south balcony against a low-floor north one — and that spread is the *combination* of all four variables, not orientation working alone. Attribute the whole gap to which way you face and you will mis-rank two apartments in the same building.

One local wrinkle before you take the listing at its word: most of Manhattan’s grid is rotated about **29° east of true north**, aligned to the axis of the island rather than to the compass. What a broker calls a north-facing apartment is usually facing north-north-east. That rotation is large enough to change the answer, which is why the calculator asks for an address rather than a direction.

## A street canyon is not a suburban lot

The geometry is worth making concrete, because once you see it the rest of the page follows. A panel receives direct sunlight when the sun is above the skyline in that direction. In the suburbs the skyline is a fence and a maple tree, so it sits a few degrees above the horizon and the sun clears it for most of the day. The sun’s path is the story. In a street canyon the skyline is a wall, it can sit thirty or forty degrees up, and the sun’s path is just the thing that does or does not cross it.

Take a standard Manhattan side street. The Commissioners’ Plan of 1811 set cross streets at **60 feet** (about 18 m) building face to building face, and avenues at 100 feet. Put a six-storey building — roughly 18 m — directly opposite, and ask how high the sun has to climb before it reaches your railing:

| Your floor | Panel height above street | Sun must be above | Clears the 21 Dec noon sun (26°)? | Clears the equinox noon sun (49°)? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2nd | 4 m | 37° | No | Yes |
| 4th | 10 m | 24° | Barely | Yes |
| 6th | 16 m | 6° | Yes | Yes |
| 8th and up | 22 m+ | Clear | Yes | Yes |

Nothing about that table depends on which way the balcony faces. A second-floor apartment on that street has no direct midday sun for weeks around the winter solstice whether it is south-facing or not, because the sun never gets high enough to clear the parapet opposite. Six floors up, on the same facade, the obstruction has essentially vanished. That is the whole argument for putting address and height ahead of azimuth.

Two things make the real city messier than the table, both in the same direction. Buildings are rarely a uniform wall — a setback, a gap at the corner, a lower neighbour mid-block can open a wedge of sky that changes a balcony’s year. And the obstruction that matters is not only the one across the street: the wing of your own building, the tower on the diagonal, and the balcony slab immediately above you all take a bite. This is why a real answer needs a model of the actual surrounding block rather than a street width and a rule.

## Diffuse light, and why a north balcony is not zero

Sunlight arrives in two forms. **Beam** (or direct) radiation travels in a straight line from the disc of the sun, and it is what casts a shadow. **Diffuse** radiation has been scattered by the atmosphere and by cloud, and it arrives from the whole dome of the sky at once. Panels convert both. Almost every intuition people have about balconies concerns only the first.

The split matters more than the vocabulary suggests. In the northeastern United States roughly **40% of annual global horizontal irradiance is diffuse**, which is the figure balco.nyc’s shadow model uses for its beam/diffuse constants (see [the methodology](https://balco.nyc/methodology)). On a clear day the diffuse share is small; on an overcast day it is essentially everything, and under a fully overcast sky *surface orientation stops being a significant variable at all*. Roughly two-fifths of the year’s energy, then, does not care which way your railing points. It cares how much sky your railing can see.

That is the honest case for a north-facing balcony, and it is a real one. A vertical panel sees half the sky dome no matter which direction it faces. Diffuse light is not free of the city — the building opposite blocks its share of that half-dome exactly as it blocks the beam — but what it takes away is set by obstruction, not by compass direction. A north balcony’s output is not a fraction of a south balcony’s because of some efficiency penalty; it is lower because it has given up most of its beam.

Most, but not all. The sun rises north of due east between the equinoxes: at the June solstice in New York it comes up at an azimuth of about **58°** and sets at about **302°**. A true-north-facing wall therefore has the sun in front of it for around seven hours of a fifteen-hour midsummer day. The catch is that all of those hours are at a glancing angle with the sun low in the sky, so the beam they deliver is modest. And from the September equinox to the March equinox, a true-north vertical panel receives **essentially no direct sunlight at all** — the sun rises and sets south of the east–west line for the entire winter half of the year. Everything it produces in those six months is diffuse.

Here the Manhattan grid rotation earns its keep again. A balcony facing 29° rather than 0° meets the summer morning sun much closer to head-on, and still catches a couple of hours of direct sun around the equinoxes, when a true-north wall catches none. A “north-facing” NYC apartment and a true-north-facing one are not the same object.

## Winter, honestly

Winter is where the two halves of this page collide, and where the standard reassurance is most misleading. The reassurance goes: photovoltaic cells are *more* efficient when cold, so winter is not the problem you think. The first clause is true. Cell efficiency does improve below the 25°C rating temperature, which is why the same panel makes slightly more per unit of sunlight in February than in July. The second clause does not follow from it, and the gap between them is most of the winter story.

What actually costs you output in a New York winter is three things, none of them temperature:

- **Short days.** About **9 hours 15 minutes** of daylight on 21 December, against 15 hours 6 minutes at the June solstice. Roughly 40% fewer hours to work with, before anything else happens.

- **Low sun.** At 40.7°N the sun reaches only about **26°** above the horizon at solar noon on the winter solstice (25.9°, from latitude and the 23.44° solar declination). At the June solstice it reaches 73°.

- **Inter-building shading.** Long shadows down the canyon, all day, at the exact time of year they are hardest to escape.

That third point is the one that gets left out, and it is not an independent penalty — it is caused by the second. Low sun elevation is precisely the condition under which street-canyon shading is worst, because the sun spends the whole day below the parapet opposite instead of above it. Look back at the table in section 3: the second-floor balcony needs the sun above 37° and December offers 26°. A cell-efficiency bonus of a few percent does not touch a balcony that is in shadow from breakfast to dusk.

There is a genuine and rarely mentioned consolation, though, and it applies specifically to balcony systems. A *vertical* panel likes a low sun. A south-facing vertical panel meets the December noon sun almost square on — within about 26° of perpendicular — while in June that same panel watches the noon sun pass 73° overhead and catches very little of it. In pure incidence-angle terms, winter is the season a railing-mounted panel is built for. The reason December is still the worst month in New York is not the panel’s geometry. It is the building across the street.

None of which means winter output is zero. It means winter is the trough, that the depth of the trough is set by your skyline rather than by the thermometer, and that a model which does not simulate your specific block cannot tell you how deep it is.

## Getting the number for your actual address

The usual advice at this point is to go and look: stand on the balcony, note when the sun arrives and leaves, and repeat across the seasons. It is honest advice and it is not wrong — but it asks for a year of your attention to produce an observation, and an observation is still not a kilowatt-hour figure. The winter answer, which is the one that decides whether your worst months are workable, cannot be had before December. A shadow model answers the same question in seconds, because the geometry is entirely known in advance.

That is what balco.nyc does. For any NYC address it assembles three things:

- **The buildings.** NYC PLUTO records and building-footprint data give the heights and shapes of every neighbouring structure **within 200 m**, which are assembled into a 3D scene around your balcony.

- **The sun.** Sun positions are traced against that scene through the year to produce monthly shade factors — how much of the light your balcony would otherwise receive is actually blocked, beam and diffuse separately.

- **The weather.** NREL’s **PVWatts V8** runs an **8,760-hour** simulation over a typical meteorological year for your location, with the panel’s real tilt and azimuth, which is where orientation gets priced properly rather than by rule of thumb.

Stated accuracy is **±15%** on annual production, or ±20% when the client-side fallback is used. That is a *modelled* band and we are explicit about the distinction: it comes from the uncertainty in the inputs and the method, not from comparing predictions against meters. **No metered NYC balcony installation has been compared against this model**, for the straightforward reason that plug-in solar is not yet legal here and so there are very few of them to compare against. The full derivation is on [the methodology page](https://balco.nyc/methodology).

> **Worth knowing before you shop.** Plug-in solar is not yet legal in New York. The SUNNY Act passed both chambers of the Legislature and is awaiting the Governor’s signature; it has not been signed. [What the Act does and does not change](https://balco.nyc/sunny-act) — including that it grants no right to install, so renters and co-op residents still need permission.

## What the model cannot see

A shadow model built from building footprints resolves buildings. Everything smaller than a building is invisible to it, and on a balcony some of those things are two metres from the panel. The honest list:

- **Micro-shading.** A window air-conditioner projecting from the unit above. A street tree at the corner in full leaf from May to October. Your own parapet, or the underside of the balcony slab overhead, which on a deep-set balcony can shade a vertical panel for much of the day. A satellite dish, a laundry rack, a neighbour’s planter. None of these appear in PLUTO.

- **Exactly where the panel goes.** The model assumes the balcony’s facade direction. If you mount at an angle to the railing, hang the panel on the return wall, or shift it to the shadier end to keep the view, your result moves off the modelled figure.

- **Facade detail.** Setbacks, bay windows, cornices and the geometry of your own building’s wings are represented at footprint resolution, which is coarser than the things immediately around a single balcony.

- **Validation against reality.** Stated again because it belongs in this list: the ±15% is modelled, not measured.

This is where a few minutes of your own observation genuinely helps, and it is a different task from watching your balcony for a year. The model has already handled the part that takes a year — the sun’s path, the seasons, the surrounding block. What it needs from you is the part it cannot see: stand at the railing on one clear morning and look for anything within a few metres that casts a shadow onto the spot where the panel would sit. If there is nothing, take the modelled number as it stands. If there is something, treat it as a haircut on that number rather than as a reason to start over.

Then run the address. If you have not read [what a plug-in system actually is](https://balco.nyc/what-is-balcony-solar) or [what one costs in New York](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-cost), those are the two pages that turn a kilowatt-hour figure into a decision.

## Common questions

**How many hours of direct sun does a balcony need for solar to be worth it?**

There is no hour threshold that makes solar work or not work — panels produce continuously, so the meaningful output is annual kilowatt-hours rather than a pass/fail. The common "three to four hours" rule comes from gardening advice and gives no method for finding out whether a given balcony clears it. In NYC, a typical 800 W system produces 400–900 kWh a year, worth roughly $136 to $306 at Con Edison's $0.34/kWh marginal rate.

**Do balcony solar panels work in winter in New York?**

Yes, but less. The real winter losses are short days (about 9h15m of daylight on 21 December against 15h06m in June), a sun that reaches only about 26 degrees above the horizon at solar noon, and inter-building shading — which is worst precisely when the sun is lowest. Cold weather does slightly improve cell efficiency, but that is the smallest term in the equation and it does not compensate for a balcony sitting in the shadow of the building opposite all day.

**Is a north-facing balcony worth solar panels?**

Sometimes, and more often than the widely repeated "75% less" figure implies — a claim we could not trace to any primary source. About 40% of the year's light in the Northeast is diffuse and reaches a north-facing panel regardless of orientation, and from late September to late March a north-facing wall gets no direct sun at all, so diffuse is most of what it lives on. In a dense city an unobstructed high-floor north balcony can out-produce a south-facing one boxed in by a taller building across a narrow street.

**Does my floor number really change the answer that much?**

Considerably, and often more than orientation does. With a six-storey building directly across a standard 60-foot Manhattan side street, a 2nd-floor balcony needs the sun above 37 degrees to see it at all — which never happens in December — while a 6th-floor balcony on the same facade needs only 6 degrees. Same building, same direction, very different year.

**Can I just watch my balcony to work out how much sun it gets?**

You can, but it takes a year to do properly and still returns hours rather than kilowatt-hours. The sun's path is known in advance and the surrounding buildings are in public data, so a shadow model answers the seasonal question immediately. Direct observation is best reserved for the things a model genuinely cannot see: a window AC unit above you, a corner tree, a deep parapet.

**Will an 800 W kit really cover 15–25% of my electricity?**

Usually not in New York. That figure is a nameplate-ideal one quoted with no shading derate applied. Against the EIA's New York average household consumption of about 6,850 kWh a year, the realistic 400–900 kWh NYC production band works out at roughly 6–13%, and a shaded low-floor balcony sits at the bottom of it.

- [ScienceDirect — diffuse irradiance](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/engineering/diffuse-irradiance): definition of diffuse radiation and its distribution across the sky dome.
