---

# Balcony solar or community solar: which saves a renter more?

URL: https://balco.nyc/balcony-vs-community-solar  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

For an average household that pays its own electric bill, community solar usually saves more, and it costs nothing to start. balco.nyc compared the two in New York, New Jersey, Illinois, Massachusetts and Minnesota: a subscription discounted 10% to 20% saves about $117 to $415 in the first year, while an unshaded south-facing 800 W balcony panel saves $114 to $204 after a $1,200 purchase, and $44 to $79 with a taller building across the street. The balcony comes out ahead mainly where no subscription is available, or for someone who would rather own a panel than sign a contract.

## The answer in five states

balco.nyc put the two side by side in five states with established community solar programs: New York, Massachusetts and Minnesota, three of the four largest markets in the country, plus New Jersey and Illinois. The household uses the state’s average amount of electricity, from the U.S. Energy Information Administration: 570 to 712 kWh a month. The balcony is an 800 W panel hung vertically on a south-facing railing in the state’s largest city, first with an open view, then on the 3rd floor with a building of 6 to 10 floors across a 20 m street.

| State (average use) | Community solar, year one | Balcony, open view, year one | Balcony, building opposite, year one | Balcony payback on a $1,200 kit: open / shaded | After ten years: community vs open balcony, net of the kit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| New York (571 kWh/mo) | $192 | $169 | $63 | 6.6 / 15.7 yrs | $2,197 vs $690 |
| New Jersey (662) | $379 | $153 | $57 | 7.3 / 17.1 yrs | $4,339 vs $513 |
| Illinois (693) | $130 | $114 | $44 | 9.4 / 21.0 yrs | $1,487 vs $79 |
| Massachusetts (570) | $415 | $204 | $79 | 5.5 / 13.1 yrs | $4,762 vs $1,089 |
| Minnesota (712) | $117 | $118 | $46 | 9.2 / 20.3 yrs | $1,345 vs $120 |

balco.nyc’s computation. **Community solar** = average use × 12 × what a kWh of credit is worth × the discount. New York: 571 × 12 = 6,854 kWh × 28.0¢ = $1,916 of credit, and 10% of that is $192. Credits are valued at the EIA average price in New York, New Jersey and Massachusetts (a ceiling; see section 3), at ComEd’s 10.4¢ supply price in Illinois and at 85% of the average price in Minnesota; discounts are 10%, 20%, 15%, 20% and 10%. **Balcony** = balco.nyc’s PVWatts output for the largest city after the 0.95 railing factor (604, 643, 616, 673 and 730 kWh a year) × the EIA average price (28.0¢, 23.8¢, 18.5¢, 30.4¢, 16.2¢). New York: 604 × 28.0¢ = $169. The shaded case runs the calculator’s street-canyon model, which keeps 37% to 39% of the output. Paybacks and ten-year totals use the calculator’s loop (prices up 3% a year, panels down 0.5% a year, nominal dollars) and assume the subscription and its discount last all ten years.

In New Jersey and Massachusetts, where new projects must now guarantee a 20% discount, a subscription saves two to two and a half times what an open south-facing balcony panel does in the first year. In New York at 10% it is ahead by $23; at the 5% minimum for net-crediting projects, it saves $96, about half what the balcony does. In Illinois and Minnesota the first year is roughly even. Then count the kit. A subscription costs nothing to start, while the panel spends 5.5 to 9.4 years earning back $1,200, so after ten years community solar is ahead in all five states, by $1,200 to $3,800. Put a building across the street and the balcony saves $44 to $79 a year and takes 13 to 21 years to pay back.

The balcony figures are generous in one respect: they assume every kWh the panel makes is used at home, which [depends on what is running in daylight](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-net-metering). Community solar credits do not depend on when you use power.

## What community solar is, and where you can get it

Community solar is a share of a solar farm you never see: the U.S. Department of Energy defines it as a solar project whose benefits flow to multiple customers. In most programs you subscribe to part of an off-site array’s output, the utility turns your share of each month’s production into a credit on your bill, and you pay the project’s owner a subscription fee. New York’s Public Service Commission describes that fee as fixed or variable but generally designed to be less than the credits. The gap between the two is your saving.

For a renter, what matters is what is missing. Nothing is installed, so there is no landlord to ask, no outlet to find and no shade from the building across the street: the panels are in a field somewhere in your utility’s territory. What you need is an electricity account in your own name. If power is included in your rent you cannot subscribe, and a balcony panel would lower your landlord’s bill, not yours.

Where it exists: as of February 2025, 24 states and the District of Columbia had policies that enable community solar, according to the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR, formerly NREL), which tracks the market; 20 of them include provisions for low- and moderate-income households. Installed capacity passed 11 GW by June 2025, and about 75% of it is in four states: Florida, New York, Massachusetts and Minnesota. Florida’s capacity comes mainly from utility-run programs in a state without enabling legislation. Those work differently and are left out here.

A state policy does not guarantee a place, and most programs have capacity caps. In Illinois, subscriptions are offered only in ComEd and Ameren territory. Minnesota’s newer program can approve no more than 100 MW a year through 2026 and 80 MW a year from 2027 to 2030. New Jersey opened a 3,000 MW round on 6 March 2026, with registrations accepted until 31 December 2029 or until it fills, and at least 51% reserved for low- and moderate-income subscribers.

## What the discount is a discount on

The advertised percentage is a discount on the value of the credits, not on your whole bill. What you save depends on what a kWh of credit is worth as much as on the discount, and both differ by state:

| State and program | What a kWh of credit is worth | Minimum saving required | Used in section 1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| New York: Community Distributed Generation | The project’s tariff compensation (the “Value Stack”, or an older volumetric rate), not your retail rate | 5% for projects on net crediting, where the fee and credits share one utility bill; no set minimum otherwise | 10% (NYSERDA: often 5–20%) |
| New Jersey: Community Solar Energy Program | The pre-tax retail rate for supply and delivery, minus non-bypassable charges such as the Societal Benefits Charge, for up to 20 years | 20% (25% for low- and moderate-income) for projects registered from 6 March 2026, for the life of the subscription | 20% |
| Illinois: Illinois Shines | Your energy supply rate. ComEd’s Price to Compare from 1 June 2026 is 10.4¢ (8.68¢ supply, 1.72¢ transmission), against an average price of 18.5¢ | None in Illinois Shines, though a seller may not promise savings the contract does not guarantee. Illinois Solar for All, for income-eligible households, sets a minimum | 15% (Citizens Utility Board: most offers 10–20%) |
| Massachusetts: SMART 3.0 community shared solar | Bill credits from net metering or SMART’s alternative on-bill credit | 20% (40% for low-income) under the rules effective 12 September 2025; projects under earlier SMART rules are not covered | 20% |
| Minnesota: community solar gardens | Gardens since 2024: 85% of the average retail rate for residential subscribers who are not low- or moderate-income (100% for those who are). Older Xcel gardens: Xcel’s value-of-solar rate | The subscription may not cost more than the credit; for low- and moderate-income subscribers, no more than 90% of it | 10%, an illustration |

Illinois is where the credit matters most. It covers the supply side of the bill, and ComEd’s 10.4¢ is 56% of the state’s average price. A 15% discount on it is worth 1.6¢ per kWh; the same 15% on a Massachusetts credit near 30¢ would be worth almost three times as much. If a ComEd credit excludes the transmission charge, the Illinois saving is a sixth lower: $108 rather than $130.

In New York, New Jersey and Massachusetts, the EIA average price overstates the credit somewhat, because it includes fixed monthly charges and, in New Jersey, surcharges the credit does not cover. The balcony side uses the same average, so both are a little high and the comparison between them holds. Minnesota’s law caps the subscription price rather than setting a discount, and balco.nyc found no published typical figure; 10% is there so the row can be compared.

## Contracts, cancellation and moving

A balcony panel is a purchase. A subscription is a contract, and the terms vary more than the discounts do. What the five programs require or advise:

- **New York.** NYSERDA advises checking for cancellation fees and for the notice needed to leave without penalty, which it says is often 30 to 90 days. Some projects let you move a subscription to a new address; not all do.

- **New Jersey.** The guaranteed discount applies for as long as the subscription runs, and the credit’s value is tied to retail rates for up to 20 years.

- **Illinois.** Illinois Shines requires a standard disclosure form before you subscribe, and subscriptions must be portable or transferable. It does not ban termination fees, and the Citizens Utility Board tells subscribers to expect one and to ask about it first. Illinois Solar for All subscribers can cancel at any time on 30 days’ notice.

- **Massachusetts.** Every SMART 3.0 subscriber signs a state-designed disclosure form, which the project files with its application.

- **Minnesota.** For gardens under the 2023 law, the subscriber organization may not check a residential subscriber’s credit or charge an exit fee, the subscription is transferable and portable within the utility’s Minnesota territory, and the utility must offer a single bill. The Department of Commerce warns that contract terms can vary greatly.

Two risks are easy to miss. The value of a credit can change after you sign: Minnesota regulators ordered subscribers in Xcel’s oldest gardens moved to the lower value-of-solar rate from 1 April 2025, with 3¢ a kWh added for residential subscribers. And billing can go wrong. In February 2026 the Citizens Utility Board reported that Ameren customers on budget billing did not see their community solar savings until the budget amount was recalculated.

The Department of Energy’s list of consumer-protection best practices is a useful yardstick for any offer: at least 20% household savings, no exit, termination or sign-up fees, and a plain-language disclosure before you sign. An offer that misses one is not necessarily bad, but know which clause you are accepting.

## Where the balcony wins

The balcony has real advantages, and sometimes they decide it:

- **Low use, open railing.** A subscription’s saving grows with your bill; a balcony panel’s does not, as long as you use what it makes. In the first year an unshaded south panel beats the subscription in section 1 for households using less than about 270 kWh a month in New Jersey, 280 in Massachusetts, 500 in New York (1,000 at a 5% discount), 610 in Illinois and 715 in Minnesota. The averages include houses, so check your own bills. Count the kit, though, and over ten years the balcony is ahead only below 40 to 180 kWh a month, depending on the state.

- **Ownership, no contract.** No credit check, no fee schedule, nothing to cancel, and it moves with you to the next apartment, including across a utility or state line, where a subscription stops.

- **No program, or no room in one.** In the 26 states without a state community solar policy, the choice may be a utility’s own program or nothing. There, and where projects in your utility area are full, the comparison is a balcony panel against no solar at all.

- **A higher rate.** In New York City, at Con Edison’s 34¢ marginal rate, the same open south panel saves $205 a year and pays back a $1,200 kit in 5.5 years. balco.nyc did not model the value-stack credit a Con Edison subscriber would receive.

It also carries a hurdle a subscription does not: none of these five states has a plug-in solar law in force as of 23 September 2026. New York’s SUNNY Act has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature. New Jersey’s law takes effect on 1 March 2027 and is the only one of the five that limits a landlord’s power to refuse, for tenants who pay their own electric bill. Illinois and Massachusetts have bills pending, and Minnesota’s died when the session ended in May. Without a law in force, the utility’s interconnection rules apply, and until New Jersey’s law starts, a renter in any of the five needs the landlord’s yes ([what renters can and cannot do](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-renters)). This summarizes state law and is not legal advice; [the laws compared](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-laws-compared) has the detail.

## Doing both, and choosing

The two are not either-or. A balcony panel cuts the kWh you buy at the full rate; a subscription sized to what you still buy then earns its discount on the rest. The only overlap is the discount the subscription would have earned on the balcony’s kWh, which in balco.nyc’s figures is $10 to $41 a year. With an open south railing, doing both saves $344 in the first year in New York, $501 in New Jersey, $234 in Illinois, $579 in Massachusetts and $225 in Minnesota. Size the subscription after the panel is up, and check how your program treats credits that exceed your bill.

| Your situation | The better bet on these numbers | Why |
|---|---|---|
| You pay your own electric bill and a project in your utility area has room | Community solar | No upfront cost; 8% to 20% off an average bill in these five states |
| Low floor, a taller building across the street | Community solar | The balcony saves $44 to $79 a year and takes 13 to 21 years to pay back |
| Open south railing, low electricity use | Close; the balcony only if it is allowed | It can out-save a subscription in the first years; over a decade it wins only below about 40 to 180 kWh a month |
| No community solar where you live | The balcony, where the law and the landlord allow it | The alternative is no solar |
| You move often, or will not sign a long contract | The balcony | It goes with you; a subscription ends at the utility’s boundary |
| Electricity is included in your rent | Neither pays you | You have no bill to credit and no bill to cut |
| Both are open to you | Both | The overlap costs $10 to $41 a year |

For your own balcony, [the calculator](https://balco.nyc/) gives the kWh figure for any US address, including what stands across the street. See also [balcony vs rooftop solar](https://balco.nyc/balcony-vs-rooftop-solar) and [payback in every state](https://balco.nyc/is-balcony-solar-worth-it).

## Common questions

**Does community solar save more than balcony solar?**

For an average household that pays its own electric bill, usually yes. balco.nyc's comparison for New York, New Jersey, Illinois, Massachusetts and Minnesota puts a community solar subscription discounted 10% to 20% at $117 to $415 in the first year, with nothing to buy. An unshaded south-facing 800 W balcony panel saves $114 to $204 a year at state average prices after a $1,200 purchase, and $44 to $79 with a taller building across the street. After ten years, net of the kit, community solar is ahead in all five states.

**Is community solar worth it for renters?**

Where a project in your utility area has room and the electricity account is in your name, it is one of the few solar options a renter can take without the landlord: there is nothing to install. Savings depend on the program. New Jersey and Massachusetts require new projects to discount credits by at least 20%, New York requires 5% for projects on consolidated billing, Minnesota only requires that the subscription not cost more than the credit, and Illinois sets no minimum. Read the cancellation terms before signing.

**What discount does community solar give?**

The discount applies to the value of the bill credits, not the whole bill. As of September 2026: at least 20% (25% for low- and moderate-income subscribers) for New Jersey projects registered from 6 March 2026; at least 20% (40% for low-income) under Massachusetts' SMART 3.0 rules; at least 5% for New York projects on net crediting; no required minimum in Illinois, where the Citizens Utility Board says most offers are 10% to 20%. In Illinois the credit is worth only the supply part of the bill, about 10.4 cents a kWh in ComEd territory.

**Do I need my landlord's permission for community solar?**

No. A community solar subscription attaches to your utility account and the panels are on an off-site solar farm, so nothing is installed at your home. You do need to pay your own electric bill; if electricity is included in your rent, there is no bill for the credits to reduce.

**Can I have community solar and a balcony panel at the same time?**

Yes. The balcony panel cuts the electricity you buy at the full rate, and a subscription sized to what you still buy earns its discount on the rest. The only overlap is the discount you would have earned on the balcony's output, which balco.nyc puts at $10 to $41 a year in New York, New Jersey, Illinois, Massachusetts and Minnesota. Size the subscription after the panel is up.

**Can I cancel a community solar subscription?**

It depends on the contract and the state. NYSERDA says New York projects often require 30 to 90 days' notice to leave without penalty; Illinois does not ban termination fees but requires subscriptions to be portable or transferable; Minnesota bans exit fees for residential subscribers in gardens under its 2023 law. Moving out of your utility's territory generally ends a subscription, while a balcony kit goes with you.

**Where is community solar available?**

According to the National Laboratory of the Rockies (formerly NREL), 24 states and the District of Columbia had policies enabling community solar as of February 2025, and about 75% of installed capacity is in Florida, New York, Massachusetts and Minnesota. Florida's is mainly utility-run programs. Even in a state with a policy, availability depends on your utility and on whether projects have room.

- [NLR — Sharing the Sun: Community Solar Deployment and Subscriptions (as of June 2024)](https://docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy25osti/91361.pdf): Florida, Texas and Georgia driving capacity in states without enabling legislation; utility-led programs in Florida; program caps.
- [U.S. Department of Energy — Community Solar Basics](https://www.energy.gov/cmei/systems/community-solar-basics): the federal definition, how subscriptions and bill credits work, suitability for renters, and the consumer-protection best practices (at least 20% household savings, no exit or sign-up fees, plain-language disclosure).
- [New York Department of Public Service — PSC improves billing and crediting for Community Distributed Generation (17 July 2025)](https://dps.ny.gov/news/psc-improves-utility-billing-and-crediting-processes-community-distributed-generation): how CDG works: credits on the utility bill, a subscription fee generally designed to be less than the credits, and net crediting adopted in 2019.
- [National Grid — Community Distributed Generation Net Crediting Manual, v3.0 (filed with the NY PSC, 31 Dec 2025)](https://documents.dps.ny.gov/public/Common/ViewDoc.aspx?DocRefId=%7B90DF749B-0000-CE28-BA4A-780CBC52090A%7D): CDG savings rates “shall not be less than 5 percent” under net crediting (Case 19-M-0463, 12 December 2019); net crediting is opt-in; Value Stack and volumetric compensation.
- [NYSERDA — Community Solar: Choosing a Project](https://www.nyserda.ny.gov/All-Programs/NY-Sun/Community-Solar/Choosing-a-Project): discounts often 5–20%; cancellation notice often 30–90 days; transfer on moving possible in some cases.
- [New Jersey Board of Public Utilities — 3,000 MW Community Solar Energy Program expansion (5 March 2026)](https://www.nj.gov/bpu/newsroom/2026/approved/20260305.html): the 3,000 MW round, registrations through 31 December 2029, at least 51% of capacity for low- and moderate-income subscribers, and at least a 25% discount for them.
- [New Jersey’s Clean Energy Program — Community Solar Energy Program (CSEP)](https://cleanenergy.nj.gov/programs/solar/community-solar-energy-program-csep): guaranteed bill credit discount of at least 20% (25% for LMI) for registrations from 6 March 2026, for the duration of the subscription.
- [New Jersey’s Clean Energy Program — Community solar bill credits](https://cleanenergy.nj.gov/support/category/community-solar-bill-credits): credits valued at the retail rate for supply and delivery, not applied to non-bypassable charges, for up to 20 years.
- [Illinois Power Agency — Power Hour: Net Metering (29 April 2022)](https://ipa.illinois.gov/content/dam/soi/en/web/ipa/documents/ipapowerhour3onnetmetering42922.pdf): community solar subscribers are net metered at the subscriber’s energy supply rate (220 ILCS 5/16-107.5(l)); subscriptions only in ComEd and Ameren territory.
- [Illinois Power Agency — Exploring Illinois Shines and Illinois Solar for All (fact sheet, June 2023)](https://ipa.illinois.gov/content/dam/soi/en/web/ipa/documents/ipa-il-shines-ilsfa-101-factsheet-web-post_6-23-23.pdf): Illinois Shines sellers may not claim guaranteed savings without a binding guarantee in the contract; Illinois Solar for All requires no upfront cost and a minimum saving, and lets community solar subscribers cancel at any time on 30 days’ notice.
- [Plug In Illinois (Illinois Commerce Commission) — ComEd Price to Compare](https://plugin.illinois.gov/understanding-the-price-to-compare/price-to-compare-comed.html): 10.399¢/kWh from 1 June 2026: 8.677¢ electric supply plus 1.722¢ transmission.
- [Illinois Shines — Exploring Community Solar](https://illinoisshines.com/exploring-community-solar/): required disclosure form before subscribing; subscriptions must be portable or transferable; questions to ask about contract term and early-exit fees.
- [Citizens Utility Board — Community Solar in Illinois](https://www.citizensutilityboard.org/community-solar-illinois/): expected savings of 10–20% on the electricity from a subscription, and the likelihood of a termination fee.
- [Citizens Utility Board — Q&A: community solar billing (13 February 2026)](https://www.citizensutilityboard.org/blog/2026/02/13/cub-qa-community-solar-billing/): dual and consolidated billing, most discounts 10–20% (higher for income-eligible projects), and the Ameren budget-billing problem.
- [Minnesota Statutes § 216B.1641 — Community solar garden](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/216B.1641): credit at 85% of the average retail rate for non-LMI residential subscribers; subscription no more than the credit (90% for LMI); no credit checks or residential exit fees; portability within the utility’s territory; consolidated billing.
- [Minnesota House Research — Changes to Xcel Energy’s Community Solar Garden Program: 2023–2024 (December 2024)](https://www.house.mn.gov/hrd/pubs/solarchng24.pdf): the 2023 law applying to gardens approved from 2024, the 100 MW and 80 MW annual caps, and the 1 April 2025 move of the oldest gardens to the value-of-solar rate with a 3¢ residential adder.
- [Minnesota Department of Commerce — Community Solar Gardens](https://mn.gov/commerce/energy/consumer/energy-programs/community-solar-gardens.jsp): which program a garden falls under, suitability for renters, and the warning that contract terms can vary greatly.
- [Massachusetts DOER — 225 CMR 28.00, SMART Program 3.0 (effective 12 September 2025)](https://www.mass.gov/doc/225-cmr-28-solar-massachusetts-renewable-target-smart-program-30/download): community shared solar must discount allocated bill credits by at least 20% for residential subscribers and 40% for low-income subscribers, and file a signed disclosure form for each subscriber.
- [U.S. EIA — Form EIA-861M monthly sales and revenue by state](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/data/eia861m/): state average residential prices, revenue divided by sales over the twelve months to June 2026, so they include fixed charges.
- [U.S. EIA — 2024 average monthly bill, residential (Table 5A)](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/sales_revenue_price/xls/table_5A.xlsx): average monthly household use: 571 kWh (NY), 662 (NJ), 693 (IL), 570 (MA), 712 (MN).
- [NLR — PVWatts V8 API documentation](https://developer.nlr.gov/docs/solar/pvwatts/v8/): the production model behind the balcony figures, run for each state’s largest city with the calculator’s parameters.

---

# Balcony solar vs rooftop solar: what a kWh costs from each

URL: https://balco.nyc/balcony-vs-rooftop-solar  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

Per kilowatt-hour, an unshaded balcony railing is the cheaper of the two. balco.nyc’s PVWatts runs for the five largest US cities put a $1,200 800 W kit on a south-facing railing at 6.5 to 8.9¢ per kWh over 25 years, against 8.9 to 12.3¢ for a typical 7.7 kW rooftop system at Berkeley Lab’s 2025 median price of $3.6 a watt. But the roof makes 16 to 18 times as much electricity, worth up to $1,600–$4,100 a year against the railing’s $90–$240, if you have a roof: only 7.8% of New York City households own a detached house.

## What a kWh costs from each, city by city

The fair way to compare a small system with a large one is cost per kilowatt-hour: the up-front price divided by every kWh the system makes. balco.nyc worked it out for the five largest US cities with the site’s own PVWatts runs and the calculator’s assumptions: 25 years, output falling 0.5% a year, nominal dollars with no discounting, and no upkeep costs on either side. On those terms a system makes 23.56 times its first year’s output.

- **Balcony:** an 800 W kit at the site’s three hardware-only prices, $850, $1,200 and $1,600. Output is PVWatts V8, from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (formerly NREL), for a vertical railing facing south, multiplied by 0.95 for the railing and mounting hardware; for a south-facing bracket at 35°, by 0.99.

- **Roof:** a 7.7 kW system, the median size of US residential systems installed in 2025 in Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory’s latest Tracking the Sun data update (August 2026). It is priced at that update’s median for 2025 installations, **$3.6 per watt** in 2025 dollars, or $27,720: the price before incentives for systems their owners bought, without a battery. Cash buyers paid a median $3.0; loan buyers $4.5, which can include loan fees. Output is the same city’s 35° south-facing run scaled from 0.8 to 7.7 kW, with no railing factor. We use 35° as a proxy for a pitched roof; a separate run at 20° came within 3% in all five cities.

| City | Railing, $850 kit | Railing, $1,200 kit | Railing, $1,600 kit | 35° bracket, $1,200 kit | Roof, cash ($3.0/W) | Roof, median ($3.6/W) | Roof, loan ($4.5/W) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| New York City | 6.0¢ | 8.4¢ | 11.2¢ | 5.2¢ | 10.2¢ | 12.3¢ | 15.3¢ |
| Los Angeles | 5.0¢ | 7.1¢ | 9.4¢ | 4.0¢ | 7.8¢ | 9.4¢ | 11.8¢ |
| Chicago | 5.9¢ | 8.3¢ | 11.0¢ | 5.1¢ | 10.1¢ | 12.1¢ | 15.1¢ |
| Houston | 6.3¢ | 8.9¢ | 11.8¢ | 4.8¢ | 9.5¢ | 11.4¢ | 14.2¢ |
| Phoenix | 4.6¢ | 6.5¢ | 8.7¢ | 3.8¢ | 7.4¢ | 8.9¢ | 11.2¢ |

Cents per kWh over 25 years. balco.nyc’s computation: price divided by 25 years of unshaded PVWatts V8 output for each city, declining 0.5% a year. No discounting, maintenance or incentives.

On an open, south-facing railing, the mid-range kit makes a kWh for 22% to 32% less than the median roof in all five cities. The premium kit roughly ties the roof: level in Los Angeles, 0.4¢ dearer in Houston, slightly cheaper elsewhere. A 35° bracket at the same price, where a building allows one, undercuts every roof price in the table.

The reason is price per watt, not sunshine. In these five cities a railing makes only 54% to 61% as much per watt as the roof, because a vertical panel meets the high summer sun at a glancing angle ([why a railing makes less than a roof](https://balco.nyc/800w-balcony-solar-output)). But the mid-range kit costs $1.50 a watt and the roof $3.6. The kit is hardware you carry home. The roof price also pays for labor, permits, interconnection, sales, financing fees and the installer’s margin; Berkeley Lab puts these soft costs, with hardware other than panels and inverters, at about 80% of the installed price.

A check on the roof’s output: PVWatts run with its standard roof-mounted settings gives 4% to 6% more than the scaled figures, mostly because the site’s runs allow 3% to 7% a month for urban grime (with the same allowance, the New York gap is under 2%). If anything, the table leans slightly against the roof.

## What each saves in a year

Cost per kWh measures value for money. It says nothing about scale, and on scale the roof wins by more than an order of magnitude. A 7.7 kW roof makes 16 to 18 times what an 800 W railing makes in these cities, so it saves 16 to 18 times as much:

| City (price per kWh used) | Railing, kWh/yr | Railing saves | Roof, kWh/yr | Roof saves, at most | Roof output vs. an average household’s use |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| New York City (34¢, Con Edison marginal) | 604 | $205 | 9,606 | $3,266 | 140% |
| Los Angeles (32.89¢) | 720 | $237 | 12,503 | $4,112 | 207% |
| Chicago (18.54¢) | 616 | $114 | 9,725 | $1,803 | 117% |
| Houston (15.90¢) | 576 | $92 | 10,355 | $1,646 | 79% |
| Phoenix (15.40¢) | 778 | $120 | 13,177 | $2,029 | 102% |

First year, unshaded, every kWh valued at the price shown. Outside New York City the prices are EIA state averages for the 12 months to June 2026; they include fixed monthly charges, which solar cannot reduce, so they overstate what an avoided kWh is worth. Household use is EIA’s 2024 state average (New York State’s for New York City).

Both savings columns are ceilings, for mirror-image reasons. The railing figure assumes you use every kWh as it is made, because under most plug-in laws power sent back to the grid earns nothing. The roof figure assumes every kWh is worth the retail price, which holds only if the house uses it all or net metering credits exports at retail. The last column shows where that is a stretch: in Los Angeles a median-sized roof makes about twice what an average California household uses, and California’s median system is the smallest of any state in Berkeley Lab’s data. State averages include apartments, so a house may use more than this column assumes, but any surplus is worth only what the utility’s export rules pay.

Even so, the gap is not close. A balcony kit is a small, cheap source of cheap electricity; a roof is a large, expensive source of slightly dearer electricity, and it takes a far bigger bite out of the bill.

## What changes the answer

Section 1 compares two best cases: an open, south-facing railing and a south-facing roof, each getting full value for every kWh. Real installations fall short of both, by different amounts.

- **Power you do not use.** A kWh the apartment does not need at that moment is given away, so each kWh that does replace a purchase costs more. At 60% used, the mid-range kit costs 10.9 to 14.8¢ per useful kWh, more than the median roof in all five cities; at 80% it is 8.2 to 11.1¢, still less. balco.nyc’s hourly model puts a New York apartment with a steady 150 W draw at 60% ([how much of the output an apartment uses](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-net-metering)). The roof’s figure depends just as much on how its exports are credited.

- **Shade.** In balco.nyc’s shade model, a 3rd-floor south balcony facing a 6-to-10-floor building across a 20 m street keeps only 38% to 43% of its output ([the building across the street](https://balco.nyc/is-balcony-solar-worth-it)). That puts the mid-range kit at 17 to 22¢ per kWh in New York City, Los Angeles, Chicago and Houston, dearer than any roof in the table. Roofs get shaded too, but people install on a roof because it gets sun; a balcony comes with the apartment.

- **Which way the roof faces.** Across Berkeley Lab’s data about half of panels (53% in 2024) face within 45° of south, 22% face west and most of the rest east. East- and west-facing roofs make less than the table shows, so the roof column is a ceiling too.

- **Upkeep and lifetime.** The National Laboratory of the Rockies’ Annual Technology Baseline allows $29.83 per kW a year for a home system’s operation and maintenance, covering insurance, cleaning, component failures and administration. That adds about a fifth to the roof’s figures (12.3¢ becomes 14.8¢ in New York City). The same baseline assumes a 30-year life, which cuts them by about 16%. Together, upkeep over 30 years leaves the roof about 5% above the table. We found no comparable benchmark for a railing kit.

- **Tax credits.** The federal residential clean energy credit (IRC 25D) now helps neither. It ended for expenditures made after 31 December 2025, and an expenditure counts as made when installation is completed. On the median roof it was worth $8,316; on a mid-range kit $360, and whether a plug-in kit ever qualified was never settled ([what ended and when](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-tax-credit)). Some state incentives survive, and they favor the roof: New York’s 25% solar credit, capped at $5,000, requires a net-metering contract or schedule, and the SUNNY Act would exempt plug-in systems from net metering.

- **Costs outside the kit.** The kit prices cover hardware only. If your balcony has no outdoor outlet, adding one is an electrician’s job, and that bill belongs on the kit’s side.

## Who can install which

For most households the choice is made before any arithmetic. A roof system needs a roof you control. In Berkeley Lab’s data, 93% of residential systems installed in 2025 went on single-family detached homes. The National Laboratory of the Rockies, then NREL, estimated in 2024 that 42% of US households cannot host solar on their own property, because they rent, live in a multifamily building or have an unsuitable roof.

balco.nyc counted the households rooftop solar is built for, those that own the detached house they live in, in the Census Bureau’s 2024 American Community Survey (table B25032):

| Place | Households that own a detached house | Households that rent |
|---|---|---|
| United States | 53.6% | 34.7% |
| New York City | 7.8% | 67.3% |
| Los Angeles | 27.2% | 64.1% |
| Chicago | 23.0% | 53.5% |
| Houston | 34.5% | 59.1% |
| Phoenix | 49.3% | 42.4% |

Share of occupied homes, ACS 2024 1-year estimates, table B25032; each city is the city proper. The margin of error on each share is at most about 1.3 percentage points.

In New York City fewer than one household in twelve owns a detached house. For most of the rest a roof is not an option at any price per kWh, and the useful comparisons are a balcony kit against nothing, or [against community solar](https://balco.nyc/balcony-vs-community-solar). The balcony is not automatic either. Renters generally need the landlord’s permission, and only four states have laws limiting a landlord’s power to refuse ([can renters install balcony solar?](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-renters)). Condo boards, co-op boards and HOAs have [their own say](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-condo-hoa).

## Permits, the utility and net metering

A rooftop system is a building project. It needs a building or electrical permit, an inspection, and the utility’s approval before it may be switched on. The permit is usually the quick part: in Berkeley Lab’s permit records, the median solar-only home system in 2025 got its permit 6 days after applying, and 80% within 25 days. The utility step is separate; in New York, grid-connected generators go through the state’s Standardized Interconnection Requirements. The installer usually handles all of it, and the cost is inside the $3.6 a watt.

Once connected, a roof usually gets net metering or a successor tariff, which credits the power it sends to the grid. New York’s Public Service Law requires utilities to offer net metering for residential solar up to 25 kW. In California, customers of the three large investor-owned utilities who applied from 15 April 2023 are on a net billing tariff, whose export credit is, in the state commission’s words, “usually lower than the retail rate.” Rules vary by state and utility, and they decide how much of the roof’s savings column survives.

A plug-in kit, where a state law allows one, skips the process and gives up the credit. New York’s SUNNY Act, which has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature, would exempt devices up to 1,200 W from interconnection and net-metering requirements and says exported energy “shall be uncompensated” unless the owner signs a net-metering agreement. Utah’s law already exempts them. Where no such law applies, the utility’s interconnection rules do, which usually means approval before connecting anything that feeds power into a home circuit. As of 23 September 2026 none of the five cities here has a plug-in law in force: California’s SB 868 was presented to the Governor on 31 August and he has until 30 September to act, Illinois’s bill has stalled, Arizona’s died and Texas has none ([every state law compared](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-laws-compared)). Several laws, New York’s among them, also require the complete system to be listed, and [no complete plug-in system is yet certified to UL 3700](https://balco.nyc/ul-3700-plug-in-solar-certification). This summarizes state rules and is not legal advice.

## How long each lasts, and what happens when you move

The panels are the same technology. The Department of Energy puts the average working life of a solar panel at 25 to 35 years as of 2025, and the Annual Technology Baseline models a home rooftop system over 30. balco.nyc uses 25 years for both sides, which is conservative for the roof. For a railing kit there is little track record: the first US plug-in law took effect in 2025, and we know of no long-term US field data on how railing mounts, outdoor cables and plug-in microinverters hold up.

What matters more is moving. A kit comes with you and can keep saving in the next home if it has a usable balcony, though every figure here assumes 25 years in one place. A roof system stays with the house, so its cost per kWh depends on staying long enough, or on a buyer paying for it.

> **The short version.** If you own a house with a sunny roof, a rooftop system saves far more money, roughly $1,600 to $4,100 a year in these cities against $90 to $240 for a railing, at a slightly higher cost per kWh. If you do not, the roof was never on the table, and a well-sited balcony produces electricity as cheaply as any roof does. [The calculator](https://balco.nyc/) gives the kWh figure for your own address, direction and shade.

## Common questions

**Is balcony solar as good as rooftop solar?**

Per kilowatt-hour, a well-sited balcony kit is at least as good: balco.nyc's PVWatts runs for the five largest US cities put a $1,200 800 W kit on an unshaded, south-facing railing at 6.5 to 8.9 cents per kWh over 25 years, against 8.9 to 12.3 cents for a typical 7.7 kW rooftop system at Berkeley Lab's 2025 median price of $3.6 per watt. In total output it is not close: the roof makes 16 to 18 times as much electricity. Shade, or using only part of the kit's output, can erase its cost advantage.

**How much more does rooftop solar save than balcony solar?**

About 16 to 18 times as much, because a median 7.7 kW roof makes 16 to 18 times the output of an 800 W railing. In balco.nyc's first-year figures for five large US cities, a roof saves at most about $1,600 to $4,100 a year and an unshaded south-facing railing about $90 to $240. In New York City the figures are $3,266 and $205. The roof figure assumes every kWh is worth the retail price, which needs net metering at retail for any surplus.

**Why is a balcony kit cheaper per kWh than a rooftop system?**

Because of installation costs, not sunshine. In balco.nyc's PVWatts runs, a vertical railing makes only 54% to 61% as much electricity per watt as a south-facing roof in New York City, Los Angeles, Chicago, Houston and Phoenix, but a mid-range 800 W kit costs about $1.50 per watt in hardware against a median installed price of $3.6 per watt for rooftop systems in 2025. Berkeley Lab puts soft costs such as labor, permitting, interconnection and sales, together with non-module hardware, at about 80% of a residential system's installed price.

**Can renters or apartment dwellers get rooftop solar?**

Rarely. The National Laboratory of the Rockies (formerly NREL) estimated in 2024 that 42% of US households cannot host solar on their own property, and 93% of residential systems installed in 2025 went on single-family detached homes. In New York City only 7.8% of households own a detached house, according to balco.nyc's count from the 2024 American Community Survey. The usual alternatives are a balcony kit, where the law and the landlord allow it, or community solar.

**Does balcony solar need a permit or utility approval like a rooftop system?**

A rooftop system needs a local permit, an inspection and the utility's interconnection approval before it runs, and it usually gets net metering. In states with a plug-in solar law, small balcony systems are generally exempt from interconnection and get no payment for exported power; New York's SUNNY Act, which has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature, would work this way. Where no such law is in force, the utility's interconnection rules apply. This varies by state and utility and is not legal advice.

**Is there still a federal tax credit for rooftop solar?**

No. The 30% residential clean energy credit (IRC 25D) ended for expenditures made after 31 December 2025, and an expenditure counts as made when installation is completed. On a median 7.7 kW rooftop system at $3.6 per watt it would have been worth about $8,316. Some state incentives remain for rooftop systems; New York's 25% solar credit, capped at $5,000, requires a net-metering contract or schedule, which plug-in systems would not have.

# How to calculate balcony solar output and savings for any US address

URL: https://balco.nyc/calculate-balcony-solar-output  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

Take NREL’s PVWatts output for your location, tilt and direction. Multiply it by 0.95 for the railing and by a month-by-month shade factor for whatever stands opposite, then value each kWh at the price you actually stop paying. Worked through that chain with balco.nyc’s own PVWatts runs, an 800 W south-facing panel on a vertical railing makes 778 kWh a year in Phoenix, 616 in Chicago and 604 in New York City with an open view, and 328, 239 and 227 kWh on a third floor facing a six-to-ten-story building across a 20 m street. Shade changes the kWh more than the city does, and the price of a kWh decides the payback.

## The chain in one line, and what it gives for three cities

Every balcony solar estimate, including the one [the balco.nyc calculator](https://balco.nyc/) gives you, is a few multiplications and one loop:

- **kWh a year** = the sum over twelve months of (PVWatts monthly output × railing factor × that month’s shade factor)

- **Savings a year** = kWh × the price of a kWh you no longer buy

- **Payback** = years until cumulative savings reach the kit cost, with the price rising 3% and output falling 0.5% a year

- **CO₂ avoided** = kWh × your grid region’s emission rate

That is six steps, each with a number and a source, set out below so you can run the chain by hand or check another calculator against it. To show what it does, balco.nyc ran it for an 800 W system on a vertical, south-facing railing in three cities with very different sun and prices, using the site’s own PVWatts runs for each state’s largest city and its own shade code:

- **With an open view** the panel makes about **778 kWh a year in Phoenix, 616 in Chicago and 604 in New York City**. On a railing, Phoenix’s desert sun buys only 29% more than New York’s, against 37% more at a roof-style 35° tilt, because a vertical panel meets the high summer sun at a glancing angle.

- **From a third floor facing a six-to-ten-story building across a 20 m street**, the same panel loses 58% to 62% of that: **328, 239 and 227 kWh**. What stands opposite matters more than which city you are in.

- **Price matters more than sun.** At Con Edison’s 34¢ marginal rate the open New York panel saves $205 a year. At Arizona’s 15.4¢ average the Phoenix panel makes 29% more electricity and saves $120.

These are modeled figures for one reference point per city, not measurements. The full table is in section 5.

## Step 1: the sun and the panel’s geometry (PVWatts V8)

The first number is the one everything else multiplies: what the panel would make at this spot, tilt and direction with nothing in the way. balco.nyc gets it from NREL’s **PVWatts V8**, the Department of Energy’s reference production model, which simulates every hour of a typical meteorological year (TMY) drawn from the satellite-derived National Solar Radiation Database. The calculator sends these inputs:

| PVWatts input | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| system_capacity | 0.8 kW | Two 400 W panels (the calculator allows 0.4–1.6 kW) |
| tilt | 90° | Hung flat on a railing; 70°, 60° and 35° model angled brackets |
| azimuth | 180° | Due south (0 north, 90 east, 270 west) |
| module_type | 1 (premium) | PVWatts’s higher-efficiency crystalline module |
| array_type | 0 (fixed, open rack) | Air moves behind a railing panel, so it runs cooler than a roof-flush one |
| losses | 14% | PVWatts’s default total, which balco.nyc reads as wiring, mismatch, connections, nameplate and availability |
| soiling | 3, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 7, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3% by month | balco.nyc’s urban dust profile, heaviest in summer |
| dc_ac_ratio / inv_eff | 1.1 / 96.5% | A microinverter matched to one or two modules |
| albedo | 0.20 | A concrete balcony floor |

One caveat: PVWatts’s own manual builds its 14% default partly from 2% soiling and 3% shading, and balco.nyc applies soiling and shading again separately. Any overlap pushes the estimate down, not up.

For an 800 W vertical south panel PVWatts returns **819.4 kWh a year in Phoenix, 648.8 in Chicago and 635.7 in New York City**, before any railing loss. Tilted to 35° the same panel would make 1,369, 1,010 and 998 kWh, so a vertical railing keeps only **60% to 64%** of a rooftop-style figure. That ratio explains most inflated balcony estimates: they quote a tilted panel’s output for one that will hang straight down.

The monthly shape matters too. A vertical south panel is a winter machine: it meets the low winter sun almost head-on. In Phoenix it peaks at 104.7 kWh in December and bottoms out at 26.5 in June; in New York it runs from 73.0 in January to 31.9 in June. Winter is also when buildings opposite do the most damage. And a TMY is a typical year, not a forecast; any real year will differ.

## Steps 2 and 3: the railing, and the building across the street

**Step 2, the railing.** The railing, the mounting hardware and the slab above clip a rail-mounted panel’s lower edge, and PVWatts cannot see them. balco.nyc multiplies by **0.95 for a vertical panel** (0.97 at 70°, 0.98 at 60°, 0.99 at 35°). It is the site’s own assumption, not a measurement, and it applies to every estimate. Open-view output is therefore 819.4 × 0.95 = **778 kWh** in Phoenix, 616 in Chicago and 604 in New York.

**Step 3, the buildings opposite.** PVWatts assumes an open horizon, so the shade model answers one question: of the light PVWatts assumed, how much reaches this balcony? It starts from a horizon profile, the highest obstruction angle in each of 360 compass directions. In New York City the profile comes from real building footprints and heights within 200 m. Elsewhere it comes from your description, modeled as a continuous wall parallel to your facade:

> β(φ) = atan( (H − h) × cos φ / D ), with h = (floor − 1) × 3.05 m + 1.0 m

H is the height of the building opposite, h your balcony’s height, D the distance and φ the angle away from straight out. In the worked examples a third floor gives h = 7.1 m, “6 to 10 floors” is H = 25 m, and “across a street” is D = 20 m. Straight out, the wall rises to atan(17.9 / 20) = **41.8°** (32.3° at 45° either side). The winter-solstice noon sun reaches only about 33° in Phoenix, 25° in Chicago and 26° in New York. It clears 41.8° at noon only from about early March to early October in Chicago and New York, and early February to early November in Phoenix.

The shade factor comes from a sweep: on the 15th of each month, every 10 minutes from sunrise to sunset, light is split into beam (0.60) and diffuse (0.40). Beam counts only when the sun is above the horizon profile in its direction. Diffuse counts in proportion to the sky the panel can still see, which this wall cuts to 33%:

> shade factor = Σ received / Σ assumed, where received = beam × (sun visible) + diffuse × sky openness, and assumed = beam + diffuse

Hours with the sun behind the facade add almost nothing to either sum, since PVWatts has already priced orientation, so **an open view returns 1.00 at every orientation**, north included. Behind this wall New York’s factor is 0.73 in March, 0.54 in June and 0.72 in September. From October through February it falls to 0.10–0.12, with the sun below the wall all day. Three of those months sit at or just above the model’s floor of 0.10.

Apply the factors month by month, never as one annual average, because the shade is worst when a vertical panel produces most. In Phoenix the panel makes 373 kWh from November to February with an open view and 74 behind this wall: two-thirds of the year’s loss in four months. Multiplying by the plain average of Phoenix’s twelve factors (0.46) would overstate its shaded output by 10%. The month-by-month result is equivalent to 0.42 in Phoenix, 0.39 in Chicago and 0.38 in New York.

## Steps 4 to 6: the price of a kWh, payback and carbon

**Step 4, what a kWh is worth.** balco.nyc assumes every kWh is used at home, replacing one you would have bought. Over a year the volume is small: 604 kWh is under 9% of the average New York household’s 6,854 kWh. But self-consumption is decided hour by hour. When the panel makes more than the apartment is drawing, the surplus goes to the grid and is assumed to earn nothing unless your state or utility credits it, so the savings figure is a ceiling, not an expectation. Whether you may connect a panel at all varies by state and utility (see [the state pages](https://balco.nyc/states)). None of this is legal advice.

The right price is the *marginal* one: what one fewer kWh takes off your bill, meaning supply, delivery, surcharges and tax but not the fixed monthly charge. In New York City balco.nyc knows the tariff, so it uses **Con Edison’s 34¢/kWh** all-in marginal rate. That starts from Con Edison’s own SC-1 bill history (33.83¢ in 2025) and is [carried into 2026 here](https://balco.nyc/electricity-rate). Elsewhere it uses the state’s average residential price, which balco.nyc computes from EIA revenue and sales over the 12 months to June 2026: **15.40¢ in Arizona, 18.54¢ in Illinois, 27.96¢ in New York**. An average spreads fixed charges over every kWh, so it can overstate what an avoided kWh saves, and on tiered or time-of-use tariffs it can miss either way. It also blends utilities: New York’s statewide figure sits about six cents below Con Edison’s marginal rate. The best number is your own: a recent bill’s total minus fixed charges, divided by kWh billed. Enter it under Adjust assumptions, or as rate in a link.

**Step 5, payback.** The cost basis is balco.nyc’s mid-tier planning figure of $1,200 for 800 W ($850 budget, $1,600 premium), hardware only, with no electrical work. No federal credit is netted out: the residential clean energy credit (IRC 25D) ended with 2025. Simple payback is cost over first-year savings. The calculator’s figure comes from a loop, in nominal dollars with no discounting:

- Year 1 savings = kWh × price.

- Each later year, output falls 0.5% (degradation) and the price rises 3% (the default; 2% and 4% are presets).

- Add each year to a running total until it reaches the kit cost, then interpolate within that year.

For the open New York panel, year 1 saves 603.9 × $0.34 = $205.33. The next four years save $210.43, $215.66, $221.02 and $226.51, for $1,078.96 after five. Year 6 adds $232.14, and $1,200 is reached 52% of the way through it: **5.5 years**, against 5.8 simple.

**Step 6, carbon.** CO₂ avoided = kWh × the EPA eGRID2023 total output emission rate for the address’s grid subregion: 0.704 lb per kWh for WECC Southwest (Phoenix), 0.911 for RFC West (Chicago) and 0.864 for NYC/Westchester. eGRID’s non-baseload rates are higher in all three, so this is the conservative choice. Grid mix is why the Chicago panel avoids slightly more CO₂ than the Phoenix one (562 against 548 lb a year) while making 21% fewer kWh.

## Worked examples: Phoenix, Chicago and New York City

The whole chain side by side, for an 800 W vertical south panel at the $1,200 mid-tier cost, open and then from a third floor facing a six-to-ten-story building 20 m away. The shade step is balco.nyc’s own code run at each city’s latitude. In New York City the live calculator would use real footprints rather than a described wall; the wall is used here so the three cities are compared on equal terms. New York appears at Con Edison’s marginal rate, which the calculator uses, and at the EIA state average for comparison.

| Step | Phoenix, AZ | Chicago, IL | New York City | NYC at EIA state average |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. PVWatts, 90° south (kWh/yr) | 819.4 | 648.8 | 635.7 | 635.7 |
| 2. × 0.95 railing = open view (kWh) | 778 | 616 | 604 | 604 |
| 3. Shade factor, applied monthly (effective) | 0.42 | 0.39 | 0.38 | 0.38 |
| Shaded output (kWh) | 328 | 239 | 227 | 227 |
| 4. Price of a kWh | 15.40¢ (EIA avg) | 18.54¢ (EIA avg) | 34¢ (Con Ed marginal) | 27.96¢ (EIA avg) |
| Year-1 savings, open / shaded | $120 / $50 | $114 / $44 | $205 / $77 | $169 / $63 |
| 5. Payback, open (loop / simple) | 9.0 / 10.0 yrs | 9.4 / 10.5 yrs | 5.5 / 5.8 yrs | 6.6 / 7.1 yrs |
| Payback, shaded (loop / simple) | 18.9 / 23.8 yrs | 21.0 / 27.1 yrs | 13.3 / 15.6 yrs | 15.7 / 18.9 yrs |
| 25-year savings, open / shaded (nominal) | $4,087 / $1,720 | $3,896 / $1,512 | $7,000 / $2,629 | $5,757 / $2,162 |
| 6. CO₂ avoided, open / shaded (lb/yr) | 548 / 231 | 562 / 218 | 522 / 196 | 522 / 196 |

The shaded New York case month by month (PVWatts output × 0.95 × shade factor), so the sum can be checked:

| Month | PVWatts (kWh) | Shade factor | Result (kWh) | Month | PVWatts (kWh) | Shade factor | Result (kWh) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jan | 73.0 | 0.100 | 6.9 | Jul | 36.2 | 0.558 | 19.2 |
| Feb | 69.2 | 0.109 | 7.2 | Aug | 41.2 | 0.635 | 24.9 |
| Mar | 64.9 | 0.735 | 45.3 | Sep | 55.7 | 0.716 | 37.9 |
| Apr | 47.6 | 0.669 | 30.2 | Oct | 61.6 | 0.116 | 6.8 |
| May | 37.8 | 0.586 | 21.0 | Nov | 58.2 | 0.102 | 5.6 |
| Jun | 31.9 | 0.536 | 16.3 | Dec | 58.4 | 0.100 | 5.5 |

The total is **226.8 kWh**. Three things follow:

- **New York pays back fastest while making the fewest kWh**: 5.5 years open against Phoenix’s 9.0, and 13.3 shaded against 18.9. Price does that, not sun.

- **The choice of rate is worth a year.** The same New York panel pays back in 5.5 years at Con Edison’s marginal rate and 6.6 at the state average. A calculator that does not say which it used has hidden a result-changing input.

- **Heavy shade in a cheap-power state can eat most of a panel’s life.** Chicago’s shaded case needs 21 years on the loop. That argues for running your own address, not for giving up: a higher floor, a lower building or a wider street changes the answer quickly.

## The five numbers to check in any balcony solar calculator

A trustworthy balcony calculator shows five things. If any is missing, you cannot tell whether its answer is generous, cautious or wrong:

- **Annual kWh, with the tilt and direction behind it.** balco.nyc’s runs put an open 800 W vertical south panel at about 600–780 kWh across three very different cities. Near 1,000 kWh for a railing panel in the Northeast is probably a 35° rooftop number.

- **The electricity rate, and whether it is marginal.** Supply-only, average and all-in marginal rates answer different questions, and move the same New York panel’s payback by a year or more.

- **The shading method.** None, a flat percentage, or a horizon from real or described buildings, ideally applied by month. “No shading” on a low city floor is a best case, not an estimate.

- **The self-consumption assumption.** Whether every kWh is assumed to be used at home, and what surplus earns. Unless your state or utility credits exports, it earns nothing.

- **The cost basis.** Which kit price, whether wiring is included, and whether a tax credit was subtracted. The federal 25D credit ended with 2025.

balco.nyc states each of these with its estimates, and [the methodology](https://balco.nyc/methodology) documents every constant used above. To run your own address, start at [the calculator](https://balco.nyc/). To share an estimate, or have an assistant hand you one, use a prefilled link:

> https://balco.nyc/?address=STREET+ADDRESS,+CITY,+STATE&floor=3&facing=south&across=tall&distance=street

facing takes the eight compass points; across takes none, low, mid, tall or tower; distance takes alley, street, wide or far. Optional tilt, watts, bill and rate (cents per kWh from your bill) also work. Outside New York City, a link with address, floor, facing and across runs at once; in the city you still pin your balcony on the 3D model, because real buildings replace the description. State figures are on the [Arizona](https://balco.nyc/states/arizona), [Illinois](https://balco.nyc/states/illinois) and [New York](https://balco.nyc/states/new-york) pages, and [does my balcony get enough sun?](https://balco.nyc/balcony-sunlight) and [what balcony solar costs](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-cost) go deeper on shade and kit prices.

## Common questions

**How much electricity will an 800 W balcony solar panel produce in a year?**

It depends mostly on tilt and shade. balco.nyc's PVWatts runs put an 800 W south-facing panel hung vertically on a railing at about 778 kWh a year in Phoenix, 616 in Chicago and 604 in New York City with an open view, after a 5% railing loss. From a third floor facing a six-to-ten-story building across a 20 m street, the same panel makes about 328, 239 and 227 kWh.

**How do I calculate balcony solar output by hand?**

Take PVWatts' monthly output for your location, tilt and direction, multiply each month by 0.95 for a vertical railing mount and by that month's shade factor for the buildings opposite, and add the twelve months. PVWatts is NREL's free production model. The shade factor is the share of beam and diffuse light that still reaches the panel, and it equals 1.00 for an open view.

**Why are balcony solar estimates lower than rooftop solar estimates?**

Because a railing panel usually hangs vertically. In balco.nyc's PVWatts runs for Phoenix, Chicago and New York City, a vertical south-facing panel makes 60% to 64% of what the same panel tilted to 35 degrees would make, before any shading or railing loss. An estimate near 1,000 kWh a year for an 800 W railing panel in the Northeast is probably a tilted-panel figure.

**What electricity rate should I use to calculate balcony solar savings?**

Use the marginal rate: what one fewer kWh takes off your bill, including supply, delivery, surcharges and tax but excluding fixed monthly charges. To get it, subtract the fixed charges from a recent bill and divide by the kWh billed. In New York City balco.nyc uses Con Edison's all-in marginal rate of 34 cents; elsewhere it uses the EIA state average, which includes fixed charges and can overstate the value of an avoided kWh.

**How much does a building across the street reduce balcony solar output?**

It can more than halve it. In balco.nyc's model, a third-floor south-facing balcony facing a six-to-ten-story building 20 m away loses 58% to 62% of its annual output in Phoenix, Chicago and New York City. Most of the loss comes in winter, when the sun stays below the building opposite all day, and that is also when a vertical panel would produce the most.

**How is balcony solar payback calculated?**

Divide the kit cost by the first year's savings for a simple payback, or run a year-by-year loop in which output falls 0.5% and the electricity price rises 3% each year until cumulative savings reach the kit cost. For an unshaded 800 W vertical south panel in New York City at a $1,200 kit cost and Con Edison's 34-cent rate, balco.nyc gets 5.5 years on the loop and 5.8 years simple.

## Sources

- [NLR (formerly NREL) — PVWatts V8 API](https://developer.nlr.gov/docs/solar/pvwatts/v8/): the request parameters used in step 1 (module_type, array_type 0 “Fixed – Open Rack”, tilt, azimuth, losses, dc_ac_ratio, inv_eff, albedo, the 12-value monthly soiling array) and the ac_monthly and ac_annual outputs.
- [Dobos, PVWatts Version 5 Manual (NREL, 2014)](https://pvwatts.nlr.gov/downloads/pvwattsv5.pdf): the 14% default total system loss, and its components (including 2% soiling and 3% shading), behind the caveat in step 1.
- [NLR — National Solar Radiation Database (NSRDB) data](https://developer.nlr.gov/docs/solar/nsrdb/): the satellite-derived irradiance, with typical meteorological year products, that PVWatts simulates from.
- [EIA — Form EIA-861M monthly sales and revenue by state](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/data/eia861m/): the residential revenue and sales from which balco.nyc computes the 12-month state averages to June 2026: 15.40¢ Arizona, 18.54¢ Illinois, 27.96¢ New York.
- [EIA — 2024 Average Monthly Bill, Residential (Table 5A)](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/sales_revenue_price/pdf/table_5A.pdf): average New York household consumption of 571 kWh a month (about 6,854 a year), used for the self-consumption comparison in step 4.
- [Con Edison — historical average full-service electric rates](https://www.coned.com/-/media/files/coned/documents/save-energy-money/using-private-generation/historical-average-full-service-electric-rates.pdf): the NYC SC-1 residential rate of 33.83¢/kWh in 2025 that the 34¢ marginal rate starts from.
- [EPA — eGRID2023 Summary Tables (revision 2, June 2025)](https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2025-06/summary_tables_rev2.pdf): subregion total output CO₂ rates of 703.7 (WECC Southwest), 911.4 (RFC West) and 864.5 lb/MWh (NYC/Westchester), and the higher non-baseload rates.
- [IRS — Residential Clean Energy Credit](https://www.irs.gov/credits-deductions/residential-clean-energy-credit): that the credit is not available for property placed in service after December 31, 2025, so none is netted out of the cost basis.
