# Con Edison and plug-in solar: what applies today, and after the SUNNY Act

URL: https://balco.nyc/con-edison-plug-in-solar  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

Today Con Edison treats a plug-in panel like any other generator: its tariff allows no second source of power in a home outside its net-metering and standby rules, and New York’s Standardized Interconnection Requirements set the process, which for 50 kW or less means an online application and a certified inverter but no fee. If the SUNNY Act, which has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature, becomes law, a compliant device of up to 1,200 W needs only a notice to Con Edison within 30 days of installation. balco.nyc’s month-by-month model puts what an unshaded 800 W south-facing railing saves an SC-1 customer at about $205 a year if every kWh is used ($209 with the summer delivery tier), or $124 in an apartment drawing a steady 150 W, which gives 240 kWh a year to the grid uncredited.

## Today: a generator, whatever its size

Con Edison’s electric tariff, PSC No. 10, starts from a blunt rule. General Rule 8.1, “Segregated Service”, says no other source of electric energy may be introduced in connection with a customer’s equipment except under a short list of provisions: Rider R (net metering and the Value Stack), emergency generators wired so they cannot run in parallel with the grid, a few demand-response cases, and Standby Service. Every interconnection of generating equipment must comply with Rider R or the Standby Service rules. There is no exception for small equipment.

The interconnection itself is governed by the New York State Standardized Interconnection Requirements (SIR), the Public Service Commission’s rulebook for generators and batteries of 5 MW or less that run in parallel with a utility’s distribution system. The current edition took effect on 9 February 2026. It has no minimum size. The only systems it leaves out are those “neither designed to operate, nor operating, in parallel” with the grid, and a plug-in microinverter is designed to do exactly that: it synchronizes with the voltage at the outlet and pushes current into it. Con Edison’s own solar guide puts it from the utility’s side: solar of 5 MW or less is subject to the SIR.

So under the rules in force on 23 September 2026, a balcony panel feeding a Con Edison customer’s outlet without an approved interconnection is operating outside the tariff. This page is not legal advice. The useful questions are what the lawful route involves and what New York’s pending bill would change.

## What the SIR asks of a system under 50 kW

The SIR splits projects at 50 kW AC. Below that line is the expedited process nearly all home solar uses; Con Edison’s 2022 solar guide put about 98% of its solar jobs in it. An 800 W railing would take the same path as a rooftop array.

| Step | What the SIR and Con Edison require | Clock |
|---|---|---|
| Apply | Online only: the SIR requires electronic submission through an interconnection portal, which at Con Edison is PowerClerk’s Small DG portal for 50 kW AC or less. Con Edison asks for the 14-digit account and 7-digit meter numbers. | — |
| Fee | None at 50 kW or less. Con Edison charges $750 above that. | — |
| Package | Application form; a signed copy of the standard interconnection contract; a single-line drawing showing the inverter’s protection settings; the inverter’s UL 1741 certificate and data sheet; the manufacturer’s verification test procedure. | — |
| Equipment | Inverter tested by an OSHA-recognized laboratory to the current UL 1741, including Supplement SB, with the settings in Con Edison’s technical requirements. | — |
| Review | Con Edison decides whether the application is complete and approved. | 10 business days; 10 more after missing information arrives, which the applicant has 30 business days to send |
| Install | Once installed, an inverter system may be connected for no more than two hours, only to check that it works; regular operation starts after the verification test. | — |
| Test | For single-phase inverters of 25 kW or less: cut the grid supply, confirm the inverter disconnects and stays off for at least five minutes after power returns, keep a log, and repeat every four years. | Owner certifies within 5 business days of testing |
| Acceptance | A formal acceptance letter; Con Edison also orders a net meter. | 5 business days |

Two things make the route harder, or dearer, in New York City than the table suggests.

**The network.** SIR Exception 3 says systems of 50 kW or less in underground secondary network areas may need more information and review, and that “in some cases, interconnection may not be allowed or approved.” Con Edison’s guide says network grids are used extensively throughout Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens and the Bronx. For many apartment dwellers the small-system path comes with an extra review.

**The monthly charge.** Net-metered residential solar interconnected since 1 January 2022 pays a Customer Benefit Contribution on panel capacity. Con Edison’s 2026 statement sets it at **$1.29 per kW DC a month** for SC-1 solar on Phase One net metering: about $12 a year for 800 W of panels.

None of this was written with a plug-in device in mind. balco.nyc found nothing in Con Edison’s distributed-generation pages or solar guide that addresses plug-in or balcony systems. Whether an outlet connection belongs on a single-line drawing at all is a wiring question, covered on [the safety page](https://balco.nyc/is-plug-in-solar-safe).

## What the SUNNY Act would change

The SUNNY Act (S8512C / A9111C) adds a subdivision on “portable solar generation devices” to section 66-j of the Public Service Law. balco.nyc read the text that passed, on the Assembly’s bill page. It covers a device of up to 1,200 W of continuous AC inverter output that plugs into a standard outlet, is listed by an accredited laboratory “as a complete plug-in photovoltaic system”, and stops energizing the building during an outage. The bill has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature.

|  | Today: tariff and SIR | If the SUNNY Act takes effect |
|---|---|---|
| Approval | An accepted application and a passed verification test before regular operation | Con Edison may not require approval before installing or using the device |
| Paperwork | Application, drawing, signed contract, test certification | A notice within 30 days of installing: name and contact details, service address and account number, make and model, rated size |
| Fees | No application fee; $1.29/kW DC a month if net metered | No “fee or charge related to the device or for feeding energy back into the utility electric grid” |
| Equipment | Net meter, and possibly more in network areas | No “additional controls or equipment beyond what is integrated into the device” |
| Certification | Inverter to UL 1741 SB | The whole system listed as a complete plug-in system, which no complete system is yet |
| Exports | Credited under net metering (Rider R) | “Shall be uncompensated” unless the owner voluntarily enters a net-metering or other compensation agreement |

Two clocks follow a signature. The Act takes effect on the 90th day after it becomes law, and every electric utility then has 30 days to post a “simple notification form” on its website, so Con Edison’s form would be due about 120 days after signing. An owner would then have 30 days from installing to file it. The bill has not yet been delivered to the Governor, so neither clock has started; [the SUNNY Act page](https://balco.nyc/sunny-act) tracks its status.

The Act keeps the SIR route open for anyone who wants credit for exports. For an 800 W railing the prize is small. The 240 kWh a year that balco.nyc’s model has an empty 150 W apartment exporting would be worth at most about $82 at 34¢; less the $12 contribution, roughly $70 a year, before the paperwork and any network review. Nor does the Act give anyone a right to hang a panel. Permission is a separate question for [co-op and condo boards](https://balco.nyc/nyc-coop-condo-board-balcony-solar), [landlords and NYCHA](https://balco.nyc/nyc-rent-stabilized-nycha-balcony-solar), [landmarked facades](https://balco.nyc/nyc-landmarks-balcony-solar) and [fire escapes](https://balco.nyc/nyc-fire-escape-facade-rules).

## What a Con Edison smart meter does with exported power

Con Edison began installing smart meters in 2017, more than 4.8 million gas and electric meters in what it called the largest capital project in its history, and it shows customers their electric use in 15-minute increments. On paper the meters can also see power leaving an apartment. Con Edison’s 2015 smart-meter business plan, filed with the Public Service Commission, lists the Commission’s minimum requirement that “AMI systems must provide net metering”, and its own specification called for meters that support net metering, remote configuration and downloadable firmware. The plan also counted as a saving that smart meters would end the need for a separate meter at solar sites.

What is not published is how an ordinary residential meter, on an account not enrolled in net metering, is configured to treat power flowing out. It could ignore it, net it against use, or add it to use. The tariff says bills are based on “the registration of the Company-owned meters”, so the configuration decides the bill. balco.nyc found no Con Edison or Commission document that says which applies to an SC-1 account without net metering. Ask Con Edison in writing how the meter on your account registers power flowing out, and how it would be billed, before plugging anything in.

Other states show why the answer matters. The Maryland Public Service Commission warns that a meter unable to track exports may treat them as zero or add them to consumption in error, depending on the meter, and Connecticut’s law requires every device to warn that surplus generation will be “charged to the customer as usage” without a net-metering meter. New York’s bill is worded differently: it bars “any fee or charge” for feeding energy back into the grid, which on its face would rule out billing exports as usage. How the Commission and Con Edison would implement that is not yet known. If exports were billed as usage, the 150 W example in the next section would fall from about $124 to about $42 a year. The three possible meter outcomes are set out on [the surplus-power page](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-net-metering).

## Month by month: what an 800 W railing saves on SC-1

Con Edison’s standard residential rate, SC-1 Rate I, has one seasonal feature. From 1 February 2026 (Leaf 388, Case 25-E-0072) the energy delivery charge is 16.402¢/kWh in every month, except that from June through September each kWh above the first 250 in the month costs 18.858¢. The customer charge of $21.00 a month does not change with use, and a panel cannot reduce it. Supply and the other per-kWh adjustments are set separately, most of them monthly, and this table does not try to forecast them.

A panel’s kWh come off the top of the bill. In a summer month where the apartment still uses more than 250 kWh after the panel, every solar kWh avoids the upper tier: 2.456¢ more, about 2.6¢ with the 4.5% city sales tax. balco.nyc added that to the flat 34¢ [marginal rate](https://balco.nyc/electricity-rate) for June to September. That slightly overstates the summer figure, since the annual 34¢ already averages in some upper-tier kWh; below 250 kWh a month there is no summer premium at all. Output is balco.nyc’s PVWatts V8 run for New York City, 800 W on an unshaded vertical south-facing railing, times the 0.95 railing factor. The split at a steady 150 W draw comes from the same run, hour by hour, as on [the surplus-power page](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-net-metering).

| Month | Output (kWh) | Value per kWh | Saved if all used | Used at 150 W (kWh) | Exported, uncredited (kWh) | Saved at 150 W |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| January | 69 | 34¢ | $23.58 | 30 | 40 | $10.07 |
| February | 66 | 34¢ | $22.35 | 30 | 36 | $10.24 |
| March | 62 | 34¢ | $20.96 | 33 | 29 | $11.10 |
| April | 45 | 34¢ | $15.37 | 32 | 13 | $10.79 |
| May | 36 | 34¢ | $12.21 | 31 | 5 | $10.62 |
| June | 30 | 36.6¢ | $11.08 | 29 | 1 | $10.59 |
| July | 34 | 36.6¢ | $12.58 | 32 | 3 | $11.65 |
| August | 39 | 36.6¢ | $14.31 | 31 | 8 | $11.49 |
| September | 53 | 36.6¢ | $19.35 | 34 | 19 | $12.39 |
| October | 59 | 34¢ | $19.90 | 31 | 27 | $10.68 |
| November | 55 | 34¢ | $18.80 | 26 | 30 | $8.70 |
| December | 55 | 34¢ | $18.86 | 26 | 30 | $8.76 |
| Year | 604 | — | $209 | 364 | 240 | $127 |

Monthly kWh are rounded, so they do not sum exactly. At a flat 34¢ all year the totals would be $205 and $124.

- **The summer tier is worth about $4 a year to this railing** ($209 against $205). A vertical south-facing panel makes only 26% of its output from June to September, when the high sun strikes it at a glancing angle.

- **Winter does the work, and the giving away.** October to March produces 61% of the output and 80% of the exports. In January the railing makes 69 kWh and, against a 150 W draw, sends 40 of them to the grid for nothing.

- **This is a best case.** Shade from the building opposite, or a railing facing east or west, cuts every column; [output by direction](https://balco.nyc/800w-balcony-solar-output) has the other orientations, and [the calculator](https://balco.nyc/) models your own block.

## Common questions

**Does Con Edison allow plug-in solar today?**

Only through the same process as any other generator. Con Edison's tariff (General Rule 8.1) bars any other source of electricity in a customer's installation except under its net-metering, standby or emergency-generator provisions, and interconnection follows New York's Standardized Interconnection Requirements. For systems of 50 kW or less that means an online application, a UL 1741 SB-certified inverter, a signed contract and a verification test, with no application fee. Con Edison publishes no separate route for plug-in devices.

**Will I have to tell Con Edison about a balcony solar panel under the SUNNY Act?**

Yes, but only tell, not ask. If the SUNNY Act, which has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature, becomes law, the owner must notify the utility within 30 days of installing a device, using a simple web form each utility must post within 30 days of the law taking effect. The form may ask only for name and contact details, service address and account number, the device's make and model, and its rated size. Con Edison could not require approval, fees or extra equipment.

**Is there a fee to connect small solar to Con Edison?**

There is no application fee for systems of 50 kW AC or less under New York's Standardized Interconnection Requirements; Con Edison charges $750 above that. Net-metered residential solar interconnected since 1 January 2022 does pay a monthly Customer Benefit Contribution, $1.29 per kW DC a month on SC-1 in 2026, about $12 a year for 800 W of panels. The SUNNY Act would bar any fee or charge related to a compliant plug-in device.

**Does a Con Edison smart meter record power a balcony panel sends to the grid?**

Con Edison's smart meters were specified to support net metering, which implies they can measure power in both directions, and Con Edison shows electric use in 15-minute increments. What Con Edison has not published is how an ordinary, non-net-metered residential meter is configured to treat exports: ignored, netted, or counted as usage. Ask Con Edison in writing before plugging a panel in.

**How much does an 800 W balcony panel save a Con Edison customer?**

In balco.nyc's model, an unshaded, vertical south-facing 800 W railing in New York City produces about 604 kWh a year, worth about $205 at Con Edison's 34-cent marginal rate if every kWh is used at home, or $209 counting the June-to-September delivery tier. In an apartment drawing a steady 150 W with nobody home, about 364 kWh is used and the saving falls to about $127, or $124 at the flat rate; the other 240 kWh go to the grid uncredited.

**Does Con Edison charge more for electricity in summer?**

On standard residential SC-1 service, yes for kWh above the first 250 in a month. From 1 February 2026 the energy delivery charge is 16.402 cents per kWh all year, but from June through September each kWh above 250 in the month costs 18.858 cents. The supply charge also changes monthly. For a south-facing balcony panel the summer tier is worth only about $4 a year, because a vertical south panel produces most in winter.

## Sources

# What does a kilowatt-hour actually cost in NYC?

URL: https://balco.nyc/electricity-rate  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-04

In New York City, a kWh you don’t buy from Con Edison is worth about 34 cents. That is the all-in marginal rate — supply, delivery, surcharges and the 4.5% city sales tax — from Con Edison’s published SC-1 residential bill history (33.83¢/kWh in 2025) plus the 3.5% delivery increase approved on 22 January 2026. Lower figures near 13–18¢ are supply only: correct for comparing suppliers, too low for valuing solar you consume yourself.

## There is no single “Con Edison rate”

People asking “what does electricity cost in New York City?” are usually asking one of three different questions, and each has a different correct answer.

- **What does the energy itself cost?** Con Edison’s Market Supply Charge, also published as the Price to Compare. Reported figures for 2026 run roughly **13.4¢ to 17.8¢/kWh** — it resets monthly with wholesale prices.

- **What does the average customer pay per kWh?** Total bill divided by kWh, including the fixed monthly charge. Higher than the supply rate, and it moves with how much you use.

- **What does one more — or one fewer — kWh cost me?** The all-in *marginal* rate: supply plus delivery plus surcharges, grossed up for tax, excluding anything fixed. Con Edison’s own bill history puts this at **33.83¢/kWh** for a New York City SC-1 residential customer in 2025.

balco.nyc uses **$0.34/kWh**. Not because the other figures are wrong, but because the third question is the one a balcony solar panel answers. Every kWh a panel produces and you consume is a kWh you do not buy, at the margin, at whatever the margin costs.

## What is actually in 34 cents

Con Edison’s residential bill separates into a supply half and a delivery half, plus surcharges and tax on top. The table uses a New York City residential customer at **350 kWh a month**.

| Component | Approximate value | Scales with usage? | In the 34¢? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Supply — Market Supply Charge, merchant function charge, Clean Energy Standard surcharge | 13.4–17.8¢/kWh, resets monthly | Yes | Yes |
| Delivery — energy delivery charge plus riders and adjustment clauses | Remainder, roughly 14–19¢/kWh | Yes | Yes |
| Basic service charge (fixed) | A fixed monthly amount, reported around $16–20 | No | No |
| NYC sales tax at 4.5% — residential energy is exempt from the 4% state tax | Applied to the charges above | Yes | Yes |
| All-in variable rate (SC-1, NYC, 2025) | 33.83¢/kWh | — | → modelled as $0.34 |

The delivery row is derived by subtraction, not quoted from a tariff sheet: it is what remains once the reported supply rate is taken out of the reported all-in rate. It is shown as a range because the supply side moves every month. The point of the table is the shape, not the third decimal place — *delivery and surcharges are roughly as large as the energy itself*, which is why supply-only figures understate the value of a self-consumed kWh by more than half.

## Why the fixed monthly charge is deliberately left out

Con Edison charges a basic service charge that you pay whether you use 50 kWh or 500. A balcony solar panel does not reduce it. Nothing reduces it except closing the account.

So it does not belong in a rate used to value generation. At 350 kWh a month a fixed charge in the region of $16–20 works out to roughly 5¢/kWh, and including it would inflate the apparent savings from every kWh a panel produces by about that much — a number the customer would never actually see.

> **The rule: value avoided consumption at the marginal rate, not the average rate.** An average rate that spreads a fixed charge across kWh answers “what did I pay per unit last month?” A marginal rate answers “what changes if I use one unit less?” Only the second question is the one solar answers.

This cuts the other way too, and it is worth being explicit about it: excluding the fixed charge makes balco.nyc’s savings figures *smaller* than an average-rate calculation would produce. It is the conservative choice, not the flattering one.

## Supply-only rates are correct — for a different question

Con Edison publishes a Price to Compare precisely so customers can evaluate offers from independent energy suppliers (ESCOs). An ESCO can only sell you the supply component; delivery stays with Con Edison regardless. Comparing an ESCO’s 15¢ offer against a 34¢ all-in rate would be a category error, and the Price to Compare exists to prevent exactly that.

A calculator quoting 17.8¢, or 13.4¢, is not making a mistake about arithmetic. It is answering the ESCO-shopping question. If you are choosing a supplier, that is the number you want, and this page is not an argument against it.

But a panel on your balcony does not compete with a supplier. It sits behind your meter and reduces the metered kWh flowing into your apartment. Every layer of the bill charged per metered kWh — delivery, riders, surcharges, sales tax — falls away with it. That is why self-consumption is valued at the full stack.

New York’s [SUNNY Act](https://balco.nyc/sunny-act) makes this structural rather than incidental: it exempts plug-in solar from interconnection and net-metering requirements, which means there is no export credit at all. Production you don’t consume is worth nothing; production you do consume is worth the full marginal retail rate. There is no middle tier.

## Where $0.34 comes from, and how it is kept current

The starting point is Con Edison’s published average full-service rate for New York City SC-1 residential customers, which covers delivery, commodity and riders and is grossed up for state and local tax, with the fixed customer charge billed separately. That series reads **29.52¢ (2023) → 33.45¢ (2024) → 33.83¢ (2025)**, and 33.83¢ has continued to be reported as the effective rate through mid-2026.

On **22 January 2026** the New York Public Service Commission adopted a three-year Joint Proposal in cases 25-E-0072 and 25-G-0073, raising electric *delivery* charges 3.5% in 2026, 3.2% in 2027 and 3.1% in 2028 — about 2.8% on a total residential bill in year one. Applying that to 33.83¢ gives roughly 34.8¢.

So the defensible band for 2026 runs from about 33.8¢ to about 34.8¢. **balco.nyc uses $0.34**, near the bottom of that band. Rounding down by most of a cent is intentional: on a question where the modeller has an incentive to be generous, the tie should go against the model.

Last reviewed **31 August 2026**. The figure is re-checked each January against Con Edison’s published bill history and the standing rate-case settlement, since the settlement fixes the delivery escalation path through the end of 2028 and removes most of the guesswork from the intervening years.

## What a single number costs you in accuracy

$0.34/kWh is a modelling simplification, and it is worth saying plainly what it papers over.

- **Season.** Con Edison’s residential delivery charges are tiered and materially higher from June through September, above 250 kWh a month. This is the largest single distortion — and it runs in solar’s favour, because peak summer rates coincide with peak summer production. An annual average *understates* the value of a summer kWh.

- **Rate plan.** Time-of-use and standard SC-1 customers face different per-kWh structures. Across plans, reported Con Edison residential rates span roughly 22¢ to 38¢/kWh.

- **Supplier.** If you buy supply from an ESCO, your supply component is whatever your contract says. Your delivery, surcharges and tax are unchanged.

- **Service territory.** Con Edison serves New York City and Westchester on different rate schedules. balco.nyc models the five boroughs.

- **Month-to-month supply.** The supply half resets monthly with wholesale prices. A single annual figure is a smoothing, not a forecast.

Realistically, a household could sit anywhere from the high 20s to the high 30s. If you want the number that applies to you rather than to the median New Yorker, take a recent bill, subtract the basic service charge from the total, and divide by the kWh billed. That is your marginal rate.

## Why this matters more in New York than almost anywhere else

The US average residential electricity price was reported at about **18.3¢/kWh in September 2026**, and New York State averaged **29.5¢**, among the highest in the nation. Con Edison’s New York City residential rate sits above even that, at roughly **1.8 times the national average** — close to double, though not quite.

This is the whole reason balcony solar pencils out in New York City despite mediocre sun. A panel in Phoenix produces considerably more kWh per year than the same panel on a Brooklyn balcony. But each of those Arizona kWh displaces electricity worth well under 20¢, while each New York kWh displaces electricity worth about 34¢. Rate, not irradiance, is doing most of the work.

It also means the choice of rate is the single most consequential input in any NYC balcony solar model. The gap between a supply-only 17.8¢ and an all-in 34¢ is a factor of nearly two on every payback period, every lifetime-savings figure, every break-even date. Which is why it is worth stating exactly which question a given number answers. The [cost and payback page](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-cost) shows what that does to the arithmetic.

On escalation, balco.nyc assumes **3% a year** by default, with 2% and 4% presets, and reports results in nominal dollars. That default is anchored to the settlement’s own path — 3.5%, 3.2%, 3.1% on delivery through 2028 — rather than to recent history, which has run hotter: the SC-1 average rose from 29.52¢ to 33.83¢ between 2023 and 2025, about 7% a year compounded. If anything, 3% is the cautious assumption.

## Common questions

**Why do different solar calculators show different Con Edison rates?**

Because they are answering different questions, usually without saying which. A figure near 13 to 18 cents is the supply-only Price to Compare, which is the right basis for comparing energy suppliers; a figure near 34 cents is the all-in marginal rate including delivery, surcharges and tax, which is the right basis for valuing electricity you generate and consume yourself. Figures in the low-to-mid 20s are generally consistent with an older data vintage — Con Edison's own SC-1 average was 29.52 cents as recently as 2023.

**What is the actual all-in cost of a kWh in New York City?**

Con Edison's published average full-service rate for a New York City SC-1 residential customer was 33.83 cents per kWh in 2025, covering delivery, commodity and riders and grossed up for state and local tax. The 3.5% delivery increase approved on 22 January 2026 puts 2026 somewhere around 34 to 35 cents. balco.nyc models $0.34 per kWh, deliberately at the lower end of that band.

**Why doesn't the 34 cent figure include the monthly customer charge?**

Because the basic service charge does not change when you use less electricity. Solar reduces your metered kWh, not your fixed charges, so including it would credit a panel with savings you would never actually receive. Excluding it makes balco.nyc's estimates smaller, not larger.

**Should I use 34 cents if I buy my electricity from an ESCO?**

Not exactly. Your delivery charges, surcharges and sales tax are identical, but your supply component is set by your contract rather than by Con Edison's Market Supply Charge. Take a recent bill, subtract the fixed basic service charge from the total, divide by kWh billed, and use that figure instead.

**Does a balcony solar panel earn credit for power I don't use?**

No. Under New York's SUNNY Act, plug-in solar is exempt from interconnection and net-metering requirements, which also means there is no export compensation — surplus generation is simply given to the grid for nothing. This is why the self-consumption fraction matters so much, and why the value of the kWh you do consume is the full marginal retail rate rather than any wholesale or credit rate.

**How much does the rate vary across New York City households?**

Reported Con Edison residential rates span roughly 22 to 38 cents per kWh depending on rate plan, and delivery charges are tiered and materially higher from June through September. A single annual number is a simplification worth several cents in either direction — though the summer skew works in solar's favour, since peak production coincides with peak rates.

## Sources

- [Con Edison — historical average full-service electric rates](https://www.coned.com/-/media/files/coned/documents/save-energy-money/using-private-generation/historical-average-full-service-electric-rates.pdf): the published SC-1 series behind 33.83¢ (2025), 33.45¢ (2024) and 29.52¢ (2023).
- [Con Edison electric rate case summary, January 2026](https://dps.ny.gov/system/files/documents/2026/01/con-edison-electric-rate-case-summary.pdf): the New York DPS summary of the approved 2026–2028 electric rate plan.
- [Con Ed bills are going up as regulators approve a rate hike](https://gothamist.com/news/con-ed-bills-are-going-up-as-regulators-approve-a-rate-hike): the Public Service Commission approving the increase in January 2026.
- [About Con Edison's rates](https://www.coned.com/en/accounts-billing/your-bill/about-con-edisons-rates): the supply, delivery and surcharge structure, and the Price to Compare.
- [EIA — electricity sales, revenue and average price](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/sales_revenue_price/): the primary source for US and state average residential prices.
- [New York utility tax exemptions](https://www.salesandusetax.com/new-york-sales-tax-exemption-utilities): residential energy is exempt from the 4% state sales tax, leaving the 4.5% city tax.

# How to find what a kWh really costs you, from your electric bill

URL: https://balco.nyc/find-your-electricity-rate  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

What a kWh really costs you is the sum of every charge on your bill that is billed per kilowatt-hour — supply, delivery, riders and surcharges, plus the taxes on them — with the fixed monthly charge left out. That marginal rate is what each kWh a balcony panel replaces is worth. Working from the published tariffs of five large utilities, balco.nyc found it runs from 13.3¢ at Florida Power & Light to 37.5¢ at PG&E for a south-facing railing’s output, and that the EIA state average, the calculator’s default outside New York City, misses it by between 12% too low and 16% too high.

## Average, marginal and the price to compare

There are at least three ways to put a price on a kilowatt-hour, and they answer different questions.

- **Average price:** the whole bill divided by the kWh on it. It includes the fixed monthly charge, so it rises as your usage falls. The EIA state figures balco.nyc’s calculator uses outside New York City are this kind: every utility’s residential revenue in the state, which EIA’s instructions say includes customer charges, surcharges and franchise fees, divided by kWh sold over the twelve months to June 2026.

- **Price to compare:** the supply part only (generation and, in some states, transmission), published so you can compare offers from retail suppliers. ComEd’s is 10.399¢ for June to September 2026 and PECO’s is 11.759¢ for June to November 2026. By balco.nyc’s computation below, those are 61% and 53% of what a kWh actually costs those customers.

- **Marginal price:** what one kWh more, or one fewer, changes on the bill. That is every charge billed per kWh, plus the taxes on them, and nothing that is fixed.

A balcony panel only changes the third. It reduces the kWh you draw from the grid, not the customer charge, which you pay whether you use 50 kWh or 5,000.

> **The rule:** value solar you use yourself at the marginal price. The average spreads a fixed charge you cannot avoid over every kWh; the price to compare leaves out delivery, which you still avoid.

New York City, where balco.nyc uses Con Edison’s all-in marginal rate of about 34¢, has [its own page](https://balco.nyc/electricity-rate). This one is for everywhere else.

## How to work out your marginal rate from one bill

You need one recent bill that lists each charge with its rate. Then:

- **Find every charge billed per kWh**: lines shown as “kWh × rate”. Supply or generation, fuel, transmission, distribution or delivery, and riders with names like conservation, environmental, storm protection or energy efficiency. Add up their rates.

- **Leave out anything fixed**: the customer, basic service, base services or meter charge, and any minimum-bill top-up. Leave out one-off credits too, such as Florida Power & Light’s one-month storm refund in September 2026 or California’s Climate Credit, a flat $36.18 per PG&E household.

- **Keep per-kWh credits that recur.** ComEd’s carbon-free resource adjustment is billed per kWh and was a credit in every month of ComEd’s filings from June 2025 to January 2026, so it belongs in the sum with a minus sign.

- **Check for tiers.** If the rate changes with how much you use, your marginal price is the rate for the block your last kWh lands in, not the first block.

- **Add the taxes that scale with usage**: taxes charged per kWh, and percentage taxes and fees (gross receipts, franchise, sales tax) applied to the per-kWh total.

Florida Power & Light’s own sample bill for a 1,000 kWh customer in September 2026 shows how it works. The per-kWh lines are base energy $78.65, fuel $28.93, storm protection $9.95, environmental $3.45, conservation $1.48, capacity $0.52 and a transition credit of −$0.40: $122.58, or 12.26¢ a kWh. Gross receipts tax and the regulatory fee add 2.65%, which gives **12.58¢**. The $10.52 base charge and the $7.97 storm refund are left out. The bill’s own total, divided by 1,000, is 12.85¢; in a month without the refund it would be 13.66¢. Neither is what a kWh costs.

The shortcut on [the NYC page](https://balco.nyc/electricity-rate), total minus the fixed charge divided by kWh, gives the right answer only when every kWh is priced the same. FPL’s is not: above 1,000 kWh a month its energy and fuel charges each rise by 1¢, and the marginal price becomes 14.64¢.

## Five utilities, worked from their tariffs

balco.nyc read the current residential tariff of five large utilities in five states, taken from the utility’s own tariff sheets or the state commission, and added every per-kWh component for a typical customer. The rates are those on bills in September 2026 unless the table says otherwise. PG&E says it moved residential customers to time-of-use plans in 2020, so its row uses E-TOU-C, the plan with a 4–9 p.m. peak.

| Utility and tariff | Fixed charge | Per-kWh components, ¢ | All-in marginal |
|---|---|---|---|
| PG&E (California), E-TOU-C, PG&E supply, off-peak, usage above baseline; total rates effective 1 June 2026 | $24.13/month base services charge ($0.79343 a day) | October–May: generation, net of a 1.01 power charge indifference credit, 10.03 + transmission 5.10 + distribution with over-baseline adjustment 20.00 + public purpose, wildfire and other charges 1.62 + state surcharge 0.03. June–September: generation 9.47, distribution 23.74 | 36.8¢ Oct–May; 40.0¢ Jun–Sep |
| ComEd (Illinois), apartment without electric heat, ComEd supply, Chicago; September 2026 bills | $16.50/month (customer 11.51, metering 3.82, low-income discount recovery 1.17) | Supply 8.68 + purchased electricity adjustment −0.09 + transmission 1.72 + distribution 4.79 + distribution tax charge 0.13 + riders 0.82 (efficiency, renewable energy, zero-emission, energy transition, coal-to-solar, environmental) + franchise cost 0.17 + Illinois excise tax 0.33 + Chicago electricity use tax 0.61 | 17.2¢ before the monthly carbon-free credit |
| Florida Power & Light, RS-1; rates in force January–August 2026 and again from 1 October | $10.52/month base charge | First 1,000 kWh: base energy 7.87 + fuel 2.89 + clauses 1.50 (conservation, capacity, environmental, storm protection, less the transition credit), then 2.65% gross receipts tax and regulatory fee. Above 1,000 kWh: base energy 8.87, fuel 3.89 | 12.6¢ to 1,000 kWh; 14.6¢ above |
| Georgia Power, R-31; bills from June 2026 | $0.4603 a day, about $14.00/month, before riders | October–May: base energy 8.21 + environmental and efficiency riders (14.22% of base) 1.17 + fuel 3.86, then 3.08% franchise fee inside city limits. June–September above 1,000 kWh: base energy 15.08 + riders 2.14 + fuel 3.81 | 13.6¢ Oct–May; 21.7¢ Jun–Sep above 1,000 kWh (14.3¢ and 21.1¢ in the lower summer blocks) |
| PECO (Pennsylvania), Rate R, PECO default supply; distribution tariff effective 1 April 2026, supply 1 June 2026 | $11.29/month | Distribution 10.28 (universal service, efficiency, transmission and nuclear riders included; two small percentage adjustments) + generation 10.79 + transmission 0.97. No sales tax; gross receipts tax is already inside the rates | 22.0¢ all year |

balco.nyc’s computation from each utility’s published tariff (sources below). Components are rounded to two decimals; the totals are computed from the unrounded rates.

Three things stand out. None of the fixed charges, from $10.52 to $24.13 a month, moves when you use less. At PG&E, FPL and Georgia Power the price of a kWh changes with the season, with how much you use, or both; ComEd’s summer and winter supply prices differ only slightly, and PECO’s changes each June and December. And supply is only a little over half the price: at ComEd and PECO, delivery, riders and taxes add another 6.9¢ and 10.3¢ to every kWh.

What the computation leaves out:

- **ComEd’s carbon-free resource adjustment** is reset monthly: a 2.38¢ credit in January 2026 in ComEd’s filing, roughly a penny in June 2026 according to the Citizens Utility Board. We found no published September value, so the table stops before it; subtract what your bill shows. The purchased electricity adjustment, also monthly, is included at the Illinois Commerce Commission’s September figure, −0.087¢.

- **Local taxes that vary by city**: California’s utility users taxes, Florida’s franchise fees and municipal utility taxes, and Georgia’s sales tax, which the Georgia Public Service Commission’s bill calculator leaves you to enter. Where they apply, your rate is higher than the table.

- **Other supply**: customers of a community choice aggregator or a retail supplier pay their provider’s price instead of the utility’s generation charge.

- **ComEd’s franchise cost** uses ComEd’s system-average 3.538%; Chicago’s may differ. Single-family homes pay a higher distribution charge, 6.23¢, for a marginal rate of 18.7¢.

## How far off the state average is, and which way

What matters is the rate on the kWh a panel actually replaces. A panel hung vertically on a south-facing railing faces the low winter sun almost head-on: in balco.nyc’s PVWatts runs for the largest city in every state, it makes a median of **75% of its output from October to May**, from 58% in Anchorage to 82% in Honolulu. Where a tariff is seasonal, balco.nyc weighted it by the railing’s month-by-month output, after the site’s 0.95 railing factor: the Los Angeles run for PG&E, the nearest in the site’s data, with 78% of output from October to May, and Atlanta for Georgia Power, 77%. For FPL’s 1,000 kWh threshold, EIA’s monthly data show the average Florida home used more than 1,000 kWh in six of the twelve months to June 2026, May to October; the Jacksonville railing makes 36% of its output in those months.

| Utility | Marginal rate, weighted to a south railing’s output | EIA state average, 12 months to June 2026 | State average against the marginal rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| PG&E | 37.5¢ | California 32.9¢ | 4.6¢ too low (−12%) |
| PECO | 22.0¢ | Pennsylvania 20.5¢ | 1.6¢ too low (−7%) |
| Georgia Power | 15.5¢ | Georgia 15.0¢ | 0.5¢ too low (−3%) |
| ComEd (apartment) | 17.2¢ before the monthly credit | Illinois 18.5¢ | 1.4¢ too high (+8%) |
| Florida Power & Light | 13.3¢ | Florida 15.4¢ | 2.1¢ too high (+16%) |

balco.nyc’s computation. State averages are the EIA figures the calculator uses; they include fixed charges and every utility in the state.

The state average is not biased in one direction: too low for three utilities, too high for two. Each gap has a traceable cause.

- **Fixed charges push the average up.** A ComEd apartment customer at Illinois’s average of 693 kWh a month pays about 19.6¢ a kWh on average against 17.2¢ at the margin; at 300 kWh the average is 22.9¢. With ComEd’s carbon-free credit subtracted, the state average overstates the apartment’s rate further still.

- **Tiers can push the average down.** At Florida’s average of 1,104 kWh, an FPL bill averages 13.8¢, below the 14.6¢ marginal rate. But a south railing makes most of its power in winter, when the typical Florida home stays under 1,000 kWh and the marginal rate is 12.6¢. The Florida average also includes franchise fees, which the table leaves out, and every other utility in the state.

- **A state average mixes utilities.** California’s blends PG&E with every other utility in the state and with customers on discounted low-income rates. PG&E customers on its standard tiered plan, E-1, pay 40.7¢ above baseline, higher still.

- **The average is behind.** PECO’s price to compare rose from 11.024¢ to 11.759¢ on 1 June 2026, after the EIA window closed. At the old price the marginal rate would be 21.3¢, still 0.8¢ above the state average.

- **Seasons can cancel out.** Georgia Power’s summer kWh cost up to 21.7¢, its winter kWh 13.6¢, and the railing’s winter-heavy output lands close to the state average.

The error passes straight into the result: first-year savings are output times rate, so a rate 12% too low understates them by 12%. Price already explains most of the difference in [payback between states](https://balco.nyc/is-balcony-solar-worth-it); it deserves the five minutes this takes.

## Tiers, seasons and time of use: which kWh a railing replaces

**Tiers.** A panel takes kWh off the top of your monthly usage, not the bottom. Where the price rises with usage (FPL above 1,000 kWh, Georgia Power in summer, PG&E above baseline), the panel saves the top block’s price in months you reach it and the lower price in months you do not. If you never leave the first block, the first block is your marginal rate: a small PG&E user within baseline saves 32.6¢ on the E-1 plan, not 40.7¢.

**Seasons.** Georgia Power charges 13.6¢ a kWh from October to May and up to 21.7¢ in summer. Because a south railing makes 77% of its Atlanta output in the cheap season, its kWh are worth 15.5¢ on average. East- and west-facing railings make 60% to 62% of their Atlanta output from October to May, so their kWh are worth more, 16.7¢ to 16.9¢, though they make about a fifth less power. [How output splits between winter and summer](https://balco.nyc/800w-balcony-solar-output) is set out by state and direction.

**Time of use.** PG&E’s E-TOU-C plan charges its peak price from 4 to 9 p.m. every day. A south-facing railing makes most of its output around midday, so it replaces off-peak kWh, 36.8¢ to 40.0¢, rather than peak kWh at up to 52.3¢. PECO’s optional time-of-use supply price puts the peak earlier: from June to November 2026 it is 32.404¢ from 2 to 6 p.m. on weekdays and 9.336¢ at most other hours. On that plan, each kWh from a west-facing railing’s afternoon output is worth more than one from a south railing at midday.

All of this applies only to kWh you use at home. Power the panel sends back to the grid is almost always unpaid, so the share you use yourself matters as much as the rate: [how much of a panel’s output an apartment uses](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-net-metering).

## Which number to type into the calculator

On the calculator’s results page, open **Adjust assumptions** and find the box labeled **Electricity rate (¢/kWh)**. Left blank, it uses Con Edison’s 34¢ marginal rate in New York City and, everywhere else, your state’s EIA average, which includes fixed charges and every utility in the state. Savings are output multiplied by this number, so replace the default with your own.

- **One price all year:** type the sum from your bill, as in the steps above.

- **Seasonal or tiered prices:** weight them by when the panel produces. For a south railing, three-quarters winter (October to May) and one-quarter summer is within five points of balco.nyc’s runs in 45 of 51 cities; use the rate of the block your usage actually reaches.

- **Time of use:** use the off-peak rate for a south railing. For an east- or west-facing railing, check how much of your plan’s peak window falls in its sunny hours.

- **Retail supplier or community choice:** use your contract’s supply price in place of the utility’s generation charge, plus the utility’s delivery charges, riders and taxes, which you pay regardless.

Then [run the calculator](https://balco.nyc/) with it. The number will not stay put: ComEd’s supply price resets on 1 October, PECO’s on 1 December, and fuel and rider charges move through the year. The calculator’s rate escalation setting (3% a year by default) covers the long run; the figure you type should be today’s.

## Common questions

**How do I find the cost per kWh on my electric bill?**

Add up the rates of every charge billed per kilowatt-hour: supply or generation, fuel, transmission, distribution or delivery, and the per-kWh riders and surcharges. Then add the taxes and fees that scale with usage. Leave out the fixed monthly customer or meter charge and any one-off credits. If the price changes with usage, use the rate for the block your last kWh falls in.

**What is the difference between my average and my marginal electricity rate?**

The average rate is your whole bill divided by the kWh on it, so it includes the fixed monthly charge and rises as your usage falls. The marginal rate is what one kWh more or less changes on the bill. For a ComEd apartment customer in Chicago using 693 kWh a month, balco.nyc computed an average of about 19.6 cents against a marginal rate of 17.2 cents in September 2026, before ComEd's monthly carbon-free credit.

**Is the price to compare my electricity rate?**

No. The price to compare covers supply only, so you can judge offers from retail suppliers. You also pay delivery charges, riders and taxes on every kWh. In balco.nyc's September 2026 computation, ComEd's price to compare of 10.399 cents was 61% of the all-in marginal rate, and PECO's 11.759 cents was 53%.

**Should I use my state's average electricity price to estimate solar savings?**

Only as a starting point. balco.nyc compared EIA state averages with the marginal rate of five large utilities, worked from their published tariffs and weighted to a south-facing railing's output. The average ranged from 12% too low (PG&E, California) to 16% too high (Florida Power & Light), so savings based on it were off by the same proportions.

**Which rate should I use if my utility has tiers or time-of-use pricing?**

Use the rate for the kWh the panel replaces. Under tiers, that is the top block you reach in the months the panel produces; a south-facing railing makes about three-quarters of its output from October to May. Under time-of-use pricing, a south railing replaces mostly midday kWh, so the off-peak rate usually applies unless the peak window starts in the early afternoon.

**Does a balcony solar panel lower the fixed charge on my bill?**

No. Customer, meter and base services charges are the same whether you use 50 kWh or 5,000, so solar cannot reduce them. That is why a solar kWh is worth the marginal rate, which leaves the fixed charge out, and why using an average rate that includes it overstates savings for most small households.

# What Germany's balcony solar boom tells the US, in registry data

URL: https://balco.nyc/germany-balcony-solar  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

Germany’s official register listed 1,512,855 plug-in solar systems in operation on 23 September 2026, about 37 for every 1,000 households. balco.nyc’s compilation of that register shows the boom has leveled off, with about 450,000 registrations in each of 2024 and 2025 and 2026 running 11% behind, while the systems themselves grew: panels on a new system average about 1,390 W this year, against 775 W in 2023. At Germany’s rate the US would have about 4.9 million, but the wiring, prices and law it would take to get there differ in ways that matter.

## The count: 1.5 million, and no longer growing

Germany keeps the record the United States lacks. German law requires every plug-in solar system, down to a single panel on a railing, to be entered in the *Marktstammdatenregister* (MaStR, “market master data register”), run by the *Bundesnetzagentur* (BNetzA, the Federal Network Agency). The register has its own category for *steckerfertige Solaranlagen*, “plug-in solar systems”, which it glosses as the so-called *Balkonkraftwerk*, or “balcony power plant”.

balco.nyc queried the register’s public unit search on 23 September 2026 and compiled the category by the date each system started running and the date it was registered. Capacity is not totaled in the public search, so we summed it by counting systems in narrow size bands, which pins the totals to within about 1%; the few entries above the legal limits are included as entered. The result, rounded:

| Started running | Systems | Inverter capacity | Panel capacity | Average inverter | Average panels |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2022 and earlier | 83,454 | 48 MW | 57 MW | 570 W | 685 W |
| 2023 | 287,558 | 172 MW | 222 MW | 600 W | 775 W |
| 2024 | 446,315 | 316 MW | 439 MW | 710 W | 985 W |
| 2025 | 437,901 | 332 MW | 541 MW | 755 W | 1,235 W |
| 2026, to 22 Sep | 314,853 | 241 MW | 438 MW | 765 W | 1,390 W |
| In operation now | 1,512,855 | 1,071 MW | 1,647 MW | 710 W | 1,090 W |

The yearly rows include systems since taken out of service. Of 1,598,054 entries in the category, 1,512,855 are marked in operation, 51,637 permanently decommissioned, 5,589 temporarily shut down and 27,973 still planned. Counting only systems still running, by the year they were registered, gives 431,688 for 2024 and 434,505 for 2025, close to the “about 435,000” and “about 430,000” the BNetzA announced each January.

Those two years are the story: growth stopped. Registration dates avoid the lag between switching a system on and entering it, so they give the cleanest trend. From January through August, owners registered 338,366 systems in 2024, 344,486 in 2025 and 307,391 in 2026, **11% fewer than a year earlier**. By capacity the fleet is still small beside the country’s rooftops: the systems now running that started before 2026 carry roughly 1.2 GW of panels, about 1% of the 117 GW of solar the BNetzA counted in Germany at the end of 2025.

## What the 2024 rules changed

The rule changes usually summarized as “Germany legalized balcony solar in 2024” were several steps, and it helps to date each one. balco.nyc checked each against the statute or the regulator’s own announcement:

| In force | Change | Source |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Apr 2024 | Registering a balcony system in the MaStR takes five facts about the device instead of about 20, and the BNetzA passes the entry to the local grid operator itself. | BNetzA announcement, 28 Mar 2024 |
| 16 May 2024 | The Solarpaket I (“solar package I”) amends the Renewable Energy Sources Act (EEG). A Steckersolargerät (“plug-in solar device”) of up to 2 kW of panels and 800 VA of inverter output in total, behind a household’s meter and giving its surplus to the grid without payment (unentgeltliche Abnahme), may be connected; the grid operator may not demand any notice beyond the register entry. EEG § 8(5a) | Law of 8 May 2024, BGBl. 2024 I Nr. 151 |
| 16 May 2024 | Such a device may run on whatever meter is already installed, even an older one without a reverse lock, and that meter’s readings are presumed correct until the meter operator fits a two-way meter (Zweirichtungszähler), which it must do promptly once the register entry is passed on for checking. EEG § 10a | Same law |
| 16 May 2024 | The 600 VA limit for simplified connection in the grid-connection rule VDE-AR-N 4105 falls away. | VDE FNN |
| 17 Oct 2024 | Tenants and condominium owners gain a claim to permission (section 4). | Law of 10 Oct 2024, BGBl. 2024 I Nr. 306 |
| Dec 2025 (scheduled) | First product standard, DIN VDE V 0126-95: 800 VA; up to 960 W of panels on an ordinary household plug, up to 2,000 W with a special energy plug. | VDE / DKE |

Two points get lost in translation. The 800 VA figure defines which devices get the simplified route; a larger system is not banned, but it goes through the ordinary connection process with the grid operator. And the surplus is given away by default, as under the signed US laws, none of which pays for exports; the BNetzA notes that an owner may instead claim the regular feed-in payment, but the simplified route in § 8(5a) applies only to devices whose surplus is unpaid. The safety side of the German rules, including the plug requirements, is covered in [is plug-in solar safe?](https://balco.nyc/is-plug-in-solar-safe) This is a summary of statutes, not legal advice.

## What the register shows the rules did: bigger systems, not more of them

If the 2024 rules had a clear effect in the register, it is on size rather than numbers. balco.nyc’s count of new systems by the inverter and panel capacity their owners entered:

| Started running | 600 W inverter | 800 W inverter | Panels over 960 W | Panels at 2,000 W |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2023 | 81.6% | 8.0% | 7.8% | 0.5% |
| 1 Jan – 15 May 2024 | 52.5% | 36.9% | 21.9% | 2.0% |
| 16 May – 31 Dec 2024 | 17.2% | 72.3% | 30.3% | 4.2% |
| 2025 | 6.5% | 84.9% | 51.2% | 20.4% |
| 2026, to 22 Sep | 3.8% | 88.7% | 65.9% | 34.3% |

The inverter switch was under way before the law took effect. The share of new entries listing 800 W rose from 3% in January 2023 to 37% in April 2024, then jumped to 57% in May 2024, the month the new limit applied, and 67% in June. The register records what owners typed in; it cannot show whether an earlier 800 W unit was set to deliver only 600.

Panels grew more steadily and further. In 2026, 2,000 W is the most common panel size entered, and the average new system carries about 1,390 W of panels behind a 765 W inverter, a ratio of 1.8. The inverter clips the midday peak, and the extra panel raises output in the mornings, evenings, winter and shade. Two-thirds of 2026 systems have more than the 960 W the product standard allows on an ordinary plug; the register does not record plug type, so it cannot say how many use a special plug or were bought before the standard.

The count moved less clearly. Registrations from January to May 2024 were 48% above the same months of 2023; from June to December 2024, after the new limits, they were 68% higher. Then, from June to December 2025, they fell 12% below the same months of 2024. The acceleration coincides with the rules, but also with the April registration change and the summer season, and we cannot separate them. Nor is there a visible step after the tenant right arrived in October 2024: 2025 finished 1% below 2024.

## The tenant right: BGB § 554, and the condo rule beside it

Since 17 October 2024, section 554 of the German Civil Code (*Bürgerliches Gesetzbuch*, BGB) has read, in our translation: “The tenant may demand that the landlord permit structural alterations of the rented property that serve use by people with disabilities, the charging of electric vehicles, protection against burglary or **the generation of electricity by plug-in solar devices**.” The last clause was added by a law of 10 October 2024, which took effect the day after its publication on 16 October.

It is a right to permission, not a right to install without asking. The claim does not exist where the alteration “cannot reasonably be expected” of the landlord, even weighing the tenant’s interests; the tenant may offer an extra security deposit; and any lease term that takes the right away is void. The same law added plug-in solar to the alterations every condominium owner can demand under § 20(2) of the Condominium Act (WEG), which must be “appropriate”, with the owners’ association deciding by resolution how the work is done.

A tenant right reaches more people in Germany than it would in the US. Fewer than 42% of German households live in a home they own (Destatis, 2022). In the US, 34.7% of households rent: 46.1 million of 132.7 million in the Census Bureau’s 2024 American Community Survey.

The US equivalent is thin. Of the nine signed state plug-in laws, four give tenants or owners some right to install, and only Vermont’s is in force; New York’s SUNNY Act has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature, and grants no such right. The details are in [the US laws compared](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-laws-compared), [balcony solar for renters](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-renters) and [condos, co-ops and HOAs](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-condo-hoa). The German register cannot tell us what the right achieved, because it does not record whether an owner rents. This is not legal advice in either country.

## Per household, and the systems nobody registered

Destatis, the federal statistics office, counted 41,126,000 households in Germany in 2025 (first results). On that base, balco.nyc’s compilation gives **36.8 registered systems in operation per 1,000 households**, one for every 27 households. Using systems still running today, by the date they were registered, the rate has climbed like this:

| Date | Registered and still running | Per 1,000 households |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Jan 2023 | 63,751 | 1.6 |
| 1 Jan 2024 | 321,510 | 7.8 |
| 1 Jan 2025 | 753,198 | 18.3 |
| 1 Jan 2026 | 1,187,703 | 28.9 |
| 23 Sep 2026 | 1,512,853 | 36.8 |

The table holds households at the 2025 count throughout and leaves out systems registered and later decommissioned, so earlier rates are slight underestimates. The plausible US equivalent is arithmetic, not a forecast: at 36.8 per 1,000, the 132.7 million US households would have about **4.9 million** systems. How many US households have a balcony or other outdoor space that could hold one is a separate question, answered in [how many US households could use balcony solar](https://balco.nyc/us-balcony-solar-potential).

Every German figure here is a floor. HTW Berlin, a university of applied sciences that researches plug-in solar, estimated in February 2025 that 1.5 to 4 million devices were on the grid, when the register held a little over 862,000. It is a wide range, derived from HTW’s 2022 market research rather than a count; that 2022 study, based on a survey of sellers, found only 10 to 20% of devices registered at the time, when owners also had to notify the grid operator. We found no measurement of the gap since registration was simplified, so we used registered figures only.

The US has no national register to measure against. State laws require notice to the utility in some cases (Maryland and Virginia before installing, Maine within 30 days above 420 W) and none in others, so an American count, if anyone compiles one, will be assembled from utility notices, state by state.

## What carries over to the US, and what does not

Germany shows what happens when the paperwork is removed and electricity is expensive: registered systems reached one for every 27 households within four years, then the count leveled off while the systems grew. It does not show the same thing would happen under American wiring, prices and law. The differences, side by side:

|  | Germany | United States |
|---|---|---|
| Household voltage | 230 V | 120 V |
| Inverter limit, as current | 800 VA ≈ 3.5 A, 22% of a 16 A circuit | 1,200 W in eight of nine signed laws = 10 A, 67% of a 15 A circuit |
| Registration | One national register, five facts | No register; utility notice in some states |
| Surplus power | Unpaid by default | Unpaid under every signed law that addresses it |
| Right to install | Tenants and condo owners may demand permission, nationwide since Oct 2024 | Four states; in force only in Vermont |
| Average household price | 40.55 euro cents/kWh (second half of 2025) | 17.9 ¢/kWh (12 months to June 2026) |

The current is the difference that matters most for safety. The same wattage draws about twice the current at 120 V: an 800 W system is 6.7 A in the US against 3.5 A in Germany, and the common US cap of 1,200 W puts nearly three times Germany’s current onto a smaller circuit. German experience with 800 VA therefore describes a smaller load than the one US laws allow; the circuit arithmetic is in [is plug-in solar safe?](https://balco.nyc/is-plug-in-solar-safe)

Price is the difference that matters most for demand. Both price figures are averages that include fixed charges. At the European Central Bank’s reference rate on 23 September 2026, $1.1411 per euro, Germany’s figure is about 46 US cents: roughly 2.6 times the US average, above the average in every US state (Hawaii’s 42.75¢ included, in balco.nyc’s state data), and above the 34¢ Con Edison marginal rate balco.nyc uses for New York City ([why that rate](https://balco.nyc/electricity-rate)). The German boom happened at prices few American households pay; the closest parallels are the high-price states, not the average. What an 800 W system would produce and save at your address is what [the calculator](https://balco.nyc/) estimates.

## Common questions

**How many balcony solar systems are there in Germany?**

Germany's official register, the Marktstammdatenregister, listed 1,512,855 plug-in solar systems in operation on 23 September 2026, with about 1.07 GW of inverter capacity and 1.65 GW of panels, by balco.nyc's compilation. That is about 37 for every 1,000 households. It is a floor: HTW Berlin estimated in February 2025 that 1.5 to 4 million devices were on the grid when about 862,000 were registered.

**Is balcony solar still growing in Germany?**

The number of new systems has leveled off. About 450,000 were registered in each of 2024 and 2025, and registrations from January to August 2026 were 11% below the same months of 2025. The systems are getting bigger instead: new systems in 2026 average about 1,390 W of panels, against 775 W in 2023.

**What is Germany's balcony solar law?**

Since 16 May 2024, section 8(5a) of Germany's Renewable Energy Sources Act lets a plug-in solar device of up to 2 kW of panels and 800 VA of inverter output, giving its surplus to the grid unpaid, be connected without any notice to the grid operator beyond an entry in the national register. It may run on the existing meter until a two-way meter is fitted. Since 17 October 2024, tenants and condominium owners have a claim to permission to install one. This is a summary, not legal advice.

**Can German renters install balcony solar without their landlord's permission?**

No. Section 554 of the German Civil Code, amended in October 2024, gives tenants a right to demand the landlord's permission, which the landlord can refuse only where the installation cannot reasonably be expected of them after weighing the tenant's interests. Lease terms that take the right away are void. The US has nothing comparable nationally; among the states only Vermont's right to install is in force as of September 2026.

**Why is the German limit 800 W when US laws allow 1,200 W?**

The numbers are not comparable in watts alone. German homes run at 230 V, so 800 VA is about 3.5 A, 22% of a typical 16 A circuit. US outlets run at 120 V, so 1,200 W is 10 A, two-thirds of a 15 A circuit: nearly three times the current on a smaller circuit, which is why German safety experience does not transfer directly.

**If the US matched Germany, how many plug-in solar systems would it have?**

At Germany's rate of 36.8 registered systems per 1,000 households, the 132.7 million US households counted by the Census Bureau in 2024 would have about 4.9 million systems. That is a scale marker, not a forecast: the US has cheaper electricity on average, more owner-occupied houses and, in most states, no plug-in law in force.
