# How much does the building across the street cost a balcony panel?

URL: https://balco.nyc/how-balcony-shading-is-modeled  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

Anything from nothing to more than four-fifths of its output, and one angle decides which. balco.nyc ran its own shade code over 1,152 street geometries and found that the loss follows how high the top of the building opposite stands above your balcony: for a south-facing 800 W panel in New York City, 20° up costs about 18% of the year’s output, 30° about 41% and 45° about 64%. From a third floor across a 20 m street, a six-to-ten-story building costs 377 of an open view’s 604 kWh a year, about $128 at Con Edison’s 34¢ marginal rate.

## What the building opposite costs, floor by floor

balco.nyc ran the calculator’s own shade code, unchanged, over **1,152 street geometries**: six floors (1st, 2nd, 3rd, 5th, 8th and 12th), the calculator’s four building heights and four distances, four directions (south, east, west, north) and three cities: Jacksonville (30.3°N), New York City (40.7°N) and Minneapolis (45.0°N), the largest cities in Florida, New York and Minnesota. A second run swept the obstruction angle from 0° to 80° in 1° steps. Each run’s twelve monthly shade factors were weighted by that city’s PVWatts output for the same direction, month by month, as the calculator applies them, to give one annual factor.

Here is the result for a south-facing 800 W panel hung vertically on a railing in New York City, 20 m (about 65 feet) from the building across the street. Each cell gives the share of open-view output kept, then the kWh a year after the 0.95 railing factor (an open view makes 604), then the angle from the railing up to the top of the building opposite.

| Your floor (panel height) | 1 to 2 floors opposite (7 m) | 3 to 5 floors (13 m) | 6 to 10 floors (25 m) | 11 floors or more (43 m) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1st (1.0 m) | 0.86 · 521 · 17° | 0.56 · 339 · 31° | 0.29 · 173 · 50° | 0.16 · 98 · 65° |
| 2nd (4.0 m) | 0.94 · 565 · 8° | 0.76 · 458 · 24° | 0.35 · 211 · 46° | 0.18 · 111 · 63° |
| 3rd (7.1 m) | 1.00 · 604 | 0.86 · 522 · 16° | 0.38 · 227 · 42° | 0.19 · 116 · 61° |
| 5th (13.2 m) | 1.00 · 604 | 1.00 · 604 | 0.58 · 349 · 31° | 0.22 · 136 · 56° |
| 8th (22.3 m) | 1.00 · 604 | 1.00 · 604 | 0.94 · 569 · 8° | 0.35 · 213 · 46° |
| 12th (34.5 m) | 1.00 · 604 | 1.00 · 604 | 1.00 · 604 | 0.78 · 473 · 23° |

Three things stand out. **A building no taller than your balcony costs nothing**: the model counts only what rises above you, which is why the lower-left of the table is all 1.00. **Floors matter because they shrink the rise**: from the 3rd floor to the 8th, the same six-to-ten-story building goes from costing 62% of the year’s output to 6%. And **cells with the same angle carry nearly the same loss**, whichever floor and building produced them: the 1st floor opposite three to five stories and the 5th floor opposite six to ten both sit near 31° and keep 0.56 and 0.58, the small gap being the half-degree between them. Section 3 explains why.

Two notes on method. Inside New York City the calculator uses the real buildings around you, not this wall (section 2); the wall puts floors, directions and cities on equal terms. And the model’s own one-line annual figure, weighted by New York’s monthly sunshine, reads high under heavy shade (0.47 rather than 0.38 for the bold cell) because it underweights the winter months a south railing depends on; every figure here uses the PVWatts weighting.

## How balco.nyc models shade

PVWatts, the production model from NLR (formerly NREL) behind every estimate, assumes nothing stands in front of the panel. The shade model answers one question on top of it: of the light PVWatts assumed, how much reaches this balcony? It works in four steps.

- **A skyline.** The horizon around the balcony is stored in 360 one-degree compass bins, each holding the highest obstruction angle in that direction. In New York City it is built from the city’s building footprints and roof heights for the buildings within 200 m (up to 500 of them), with the balcony placed on the wall you pin, at your floor’s share of the building’s recorded height. Elsewhere there is no national equivalent, so your description becomes a street canyon: a continuous wall parallel to your facade. Looking out at an angle φ from straight ahead, it rises to β(φ) = atan(max(0, H − h) × cos φ / D), where H is the building’s height, D its distance and h = (floor − 1) × 3.05 m + 1.0 m the height of your balcony.

- **A sun sweep.** On the 15th of each month, every 10 minutes from sunrise to sunset, the sun’s position is computed and its light split into beam (60%) and diffuse (40%).

- **Beam and diffuse, separately.** Beam counts only when the sun stands above the skyline in its own compass bin. Diffuse counts in proportion to the sky the panel can still see, treating the sky as uniformly bright. For the described wall, that open share works out to 1 − sin β, where β is the wall’s angle straight out; the code reproduces it to within 0.01.

- **A monthly ratio.** Each month’s factor is the light received divided by the light assumed, never below 0.10, and the calculator multiplies each month of PVWatts output by its own factor.

The ratio is why **an open view scores 1.00 at every orientation**, north included. PVWatts is told which way the panel faces, so it has already priced the hours when the sun is behind the facade; those hours add almost nothing to either side of the ratio. An earlier version of the site’s model charged them as shade, scoring an unobstructed east-facing balcony 0.54 and a north-facing one 0.32 with no building in sight. That was fixed on 31 August 2026; the test suite now asserts 1.00 for an open view in every direction, and every open-view run behind this page returned 1.00.

## The rule: one angle predicts the loss

Behind that pattern is an exact rule, not an approximation. In the model, floor, building height and distance matter only through one number: the angle from your railing up to the top of the building straight across, β = atan((H − h) / D). Scale the rise and the distance together and nothing changes. A 1st-floor balcony 20 m from a 13 m building and one 40 m from a 25 m building both look up at 31°, and both keep 0.562 of their output, to three decimals. You can skip the trigonometry and use the rise divided by the distance.

| Angle to the top | Rise ÷ distance | South, Jacksonville | South, New York | South, Minneapolis | East or west, New York | North, New York | Open sky, 1 − sin β |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10° | 0.18 | 0.92 | 0.92 | 0.92 | 0.87 | 0.83 | 0.83 |
| 15° | 0.27 | 0.88 | 0.88 | 0.88 | 0.80 | 0.75 | 0.74 |
| 20° | 0.36 | 0.83 | 0.82 | 0.80 | 0.71 | 0.66 | 0.66 |
| 25° | 0.47 | 0.78 | 0.74 | 0.66 | 0.63 | 0.59 | 0.58 |
| 30° | 0.58 | 0.72 | 0.59 | 0.57 | 0.54 | 0.51 | 0.50 |
| 35° | 0.70 | 0.63 | 0.51 | 0.47 | 0.47 | 0.44 | 0.43 |
| 40° | 0.84 | 0.47 | 0.41 | 0.41 | 0.39 | 0.37 | 0.36 |
| 45° | 1.00 | 0.39 | 0.36 | 0.32 | 0.32 | 0.30 | 0.29 |
| 50° | 1.19 | 0.31 | 0.29 | 0.26 | 0.25 | 0.24 | 0.23 |
| 60° | 1.73 | 0.20 | 0.20 | 0.18 | 0.14 | 0.14 | 0.13 |

Share of open-view output kept. East and west never differ by more than 0.01; east, west and north change by at most 0.04 between the three cities.

Two shapes are in that table. **Facing north, the factor tracks the open-sky column almost exactly.** In the model, 95% of the light a north-facing vertical panel in New York is assumed to receive is diffuse, so it loses whatever share of the sky the building fills: about 1.7 points per degree at first, slowing as the wall climbs. **Facing south, the panel holds up better at first.** With the wall at 20°, 94% of its beam still arrives, so it loses mostly diffuse light, about one point per degree. Then the curve breaks where the wall passes the winter sun. The model’s noon sun on 15 December stands 36.4° up in Jacksonville, 26.0° in New York and 21.7° in Minneapolis. Beyond that angle each extra degree removes direct sun from more of the winter, and the factor falls by two to three points a degree, in steps, one for each pair of months whose noon sun the wall overtakes.

As a rule for New York: a building 20° above your railing (a rise of about a third of the distance) costs a south balcony about a fifth of its output; 30° (a rise of just over half) about two-fifths; 45° (a rise equal to the distance) about two-thirds. Facing east, west or north, 1 − sin β is a close, slightly low estimate of the share you keep.

## Direction and latitude: north loses the largest share and the fewest kWh

The usual intuition is that a north-facing balcony has little to lose to the building opposite, because it lives on diffuse light. That is half right. At every angle north keeps the *smallest share*: a vertical panel counts the low sky straight ahead most heavily, and that is the part a building fills first. South keeps the largest, because much of its beam comes from above the roofline. In kilowatt-hours the order reverses, because north has far less to lose. New York City, 20 m across the street, share kept and kWh a year lost:

| Balcony | Angle | South (open: 604 kWh) | East (446) | West (421) | North (167) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3rd floor, 3–5 floors opposite | 16° | 0.86 (−82) | 0.77 (−102) | 0.77 (−96) | 0.72 (−46) |
| 5th floor, 6–10 floors opposite | 31° | 0.58 (−255) | 0.53 (−208) | 0.54 (−195) | 0.50 (−83) |
| 3rd floor, 6–10 floors opposite | 42° | 0.38 (−377) | 0.36 (−286) | 0.36 (−269) | 0.34 (−110) |
| 3rd floor, 11+ floors opposite | 61° | 0.19 (−487) | 0.13 (−386) | 0.13 (−365) | 0.14 (−144) |

That puts a number on a common argument about apartments. An unobstructed north balcony can out-produce a boxed-in south one, but only at the heavy end: in New York the building opposite has to stand about 53° above a south railing (a rise 1.3 times the distance) before an open north view makes more, and about 25° before an open east or west view does.

**Latitude matters only for the south-facing column.** The same street takes nearly the same bite out of an east, west or north balcony in all three cities, because their light arrives low or diffuse everywhere. For south, a lower winter sun lets a given building bite earlier: at 30° a south balcony keeps 0.72 in Jacksonville, 0.59 in New York and 0.57 in Minneapolis. (In kWh, the weather PVWatts simulates muddies this: an open south railing makes 612 kWh in Jacksonville, 604 in New York and 730 in Minneapolis.)

## Which months take the loss

Because the calculator applies shade month by month, it can also say when the building costs you. For a south-facing New York balcony 20 m from the building opposite, the monthly factors are:

| Month | 16° (3rd floor, 3–5 opposite) | 31° (5th floor, 6–10) | 42° (3rd floor, 6–10) | 61° (3rd floor, 11+) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jan | 0.87 | 0.15 | 0.10 | 0.10 |
| Feb | 0.90 | 0.74 | 0.11 | 0.10 |
| Mar | 0.89 | 0.80 | 0.73 | 0.10 |
| Apr | 0.86 | 0.75 | 0.67 | 0.25 |
| May | 0.82 | 0.68 | 0.59 | 0.46 |
| Jun | 0.80 | 0.65 | 0.54 | 0.39 |
| Jul | 0.81 | 0.66 | 0.56 | 0.42 |
| Aug | 0.85 | 0.72 | 0.64 | 0.52 |
| Sep | 0.88 | 0.78 | 0.72 | 0.10 |
| Oct | 0.90 | 0.79 | 0.12 | 0.10 |
| Nov | 0.88 | 0.28 | 0.10 | 0.10 |
| Dec | 0.84 | 0.14 | 0.10 | 0.10 |
| Share of the year’s loss, Oct–Feb | 46% | 69% | 72% | 56% |

Under light shade the loss is spread through the year and even leans slightly toward summer, when diffuse light is a bigger part of what a vertical south panel receives. Once the building passes the winter sun, the dark months arrive together: at 42°, October through February sit between 0.10 and 0.12 while March and September keep more than 0.7. Those five months make half of an open south railing’s year in New York, and **72% of this balcony’s loss**. Latitude moves the edges: the same geometry leaves three months at 0.11 or lower in Jacksonville (November to January) and five in Minneapolis (October to February), where March also falls to 0.66.

Facing east, west or north, the monthly factors barely move (0.73 to 0.80 for an east balcony at 16°), so the loss follows the output, which for those directions peaks in summer. One average factor applied to a whole year would overstate a shaded south balcony, whose worst months are its most productive; [how to calculate balcony solar output](https://balco.nyc/calculate-balcony-solar-output) shows the monthly arithmetic. And 0.10 is a floor, not a measurement: no month may fall below it, so read those entries as “almost nothing.”

## What the model leaves out

Several things close to a balcony never reach the skyline:

- **Trees.** The lowest category is “1 to 2 floors, or trees”, modeled as a solid 7 m wall all year. Real crowns are partly transparent: in a US Forest Service study a sugar maple cut the sunlight on a south wall in its shade by about 80% in leaf and nearly 40% when bare. For a south balcony, whose loss is mostly in winter, a bare street tree costs much less than the model assumes.

- **The slab above and the walls beside you.** The balcony overhead, side partitions and the walls of a recessed balcony cut the sky next to the panel; the model covers only the railing clipping the panel’s lower edge, with a flat 0.95 factor. In New York City it skips your own building entirely, so its wings and courtyards are invisible.

- **Gaps and corners.** The described wall has no cross streets or gaps, so a described estimate errs low, and it cannot place a tower on the diagonal.

- **Reflections.** Buildings are treated as black. A sunlit, light-colored facade sends some light back, and a north-facing balcony looks at the sunny side of the building opposite, so the north figures above are probably the most pessimistic. The standard ground-reflection term assumes open ground to the horizon; the shade factor simply scales it with everything else.

- **Snow.** None, on the panel or on the ground. A vertical panel sheds snow quickly but not instantly, and a snowy street reflects more light than the fixed 0.20 ground reflectance the calculator gives PVWatts.

- **Sky and weather.** The model’s sky is uniformly bright; real skies are brighter around the sun and near the horizon, the part a building blocks first. Its 60/40 beam-to-diffuse split is a Northeast figure used everywhere, and a cloudier winter would likely soften a south balcony’s winter loss a little.

- **Part of a panel in shadow.** Shade is computed at one point, so the panel is either in sun or not. A shadow edge across a panel costs more than its area, because cells are wired in series; a 2025 study validated against field measurements found that coarser models overestimated the monthly energy of a partly shaded string by up to 54%.

None of these figures has been compared with metered balconies. Like everything else the calculator produces, they are modeled, not measured.

## How to describe your view in the calculator

Outside New York City the calculator asks two questions about what stands across from your balcony, and turns the answers into the wall described in section 2:

| What stands opposite | Modeled height | How far away | Modeled distance |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nothing, an open view | 0 m | Very close: an alley, courtyard or light well | 8 m |
| 1 to 2 floors, or trees | 7 m | Across a street | 20 m |
| 3 to 5 floors | 13 m | Across a wide road or parking lot | 40 m |
| 6 to 10 floors | 25 m | Far away | 80 m |
| 11 floors or more | 43 m |  |  |

The bands are wide, so a few habits make the answer better:

- **Describe what is straight out.** The modeled wall is highest dead ahead and lower toward the sides. If a tower stands off to one side, describe the building ahead and expect somewhat less.

- **Only what rises above you counts.** A building no taller than your balcony gives the same result as “Nothing, an open view.” To estimate your angle, count the floors opposite above yours, allow about 3 m each, divide by the distance and use the table in section 3.

- **Measure facade to facade,** not curb to curb.

- **Run the neighboring band.** A six-story building is modeled at 25 m, mid-band. Near an edge, run the adjacent band too and read the pair as a range.

- **Remember trees are solid.** Describe a tree by its height, knowing it is modeled as a wall all year.

In New York City these questions do not appear: you pin your balcony on a 3D model of the block, and the calculator uses the real buildings instead. [Does my balcony get enough sun?](https://balco.nyc/balcony-sunlight) covers the sun’s path and winter, [the methodology](https://balco.nyc/methodology) documents every constant, and [the calculator](https://balco.nyc/) runs your own address.

## Common questions

**How much does a building across the street reduce balcony solar output?**

It depends almost entirely on one angle: how high the top of the building stands above your balcony, seen from the railing. In balco.nyc's shade model a south-facing panel in New York City loses about 18% of its annual output to a building 20 degrees up, about 41% at 30 degrees and about 64% at 45 degrees. From a third floor across a 20 m street, a six-to-ten-story building costs about 377 of an open view's 604 kWh a year.

**How do I work out the obstruction angle from my balcony?**

Subtract your balcony's height from the height of the building opposite, divide by the distance between the two facades, and take the arctangent. A rise of about a third of the distance is 20 degrees, just over half is 30 degrees, and a rise equal to the distance is 45 degrees. Counting floors works: allow about 3 m for each floor of the building opposite that stands above yours.

**Does a north-facing balcony lose less to the building opposite?**

In kilowatt-hours, yes; as a share of its output, no. In balco.nyc's model a north-facing vertical panel lives almost entirely on diffuse light, and a building straight ahead blocks the part of the sky such a panel counts most, so it keeps roughly 1 minus the sine of the obstruction angle: about 66% at 20 degrees, against 82% for a south-facing panel in New York City. But an open north panel there makes only about 167 kWh a year, so at a 42-degree obstruction it loses about 110 kWh while a south one loses about 377.

**Why does shade hit a south-facing balcony hardest in winter?**

Because the winter sun is low. Once the building opposite rises above the mid-December noon sun, about 26 degrees in New York City, 36 in Jacksonville and 22 in Minneapolis, the balcony loses its direct sun for weeks around the solstice. In balco.nyc's model a New York third floor facing a six-to-ten-story building 20 m away keeps at most 12% of its output in each month from October to February, and those months hold 72% of its annual loss.

**Why does an unshaded north-facing balcony get a shade factor of 1.00?**

Because the shade factor multiplies PVWatts output, and PVWatts already accounts for which way the panel faces. The factor answers only how much of the light PVWatts assumed actually reaches the balcony, so with nothing in the way it is 1.00 in every direction. Charging a north balcony for the hours the sun is behind it would count orientation twice.

**Does the balco.nyc shade model account for trees, reflections and snow?**

No. Trees are modeled as solid walls all year, though a bare deciduous tree lets much of the winter light through; buildings are treated as non-reflective, which probably makes the model pessimistic for north-facing balconies that face a sunlit facade; and snow is modeled neither on the panel nor on the ground. The balcony slab above, side walls and a shadow falling across only part of a panel are also left out.

**How far away does a building need to be before it stops mattering?**

Distance matters only through the angle it creates. In balco.nyc's model a third-floor south-facing balcony in New York City keeps 90% of its output with a six-to-ten-story building 80 m away and 76% with an 11-plus-story tower at that distance, against 38% and 19% when the same buildings stand 20 m away.

## Sources

- [NLR (formerly NREL) — PVWatts V8 API](https://developer.nlr.gov/docs/solar/pvwatts/v8/): the tilt and azimuth inputs, and the monthly AC output (ac_monthly) used to weight each geometry’s twelve shade factors into an annual one.
- [NYC Office of Technology and Innovation — building footprints (NYC Open Data)](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/BUILDING/5zhs-2jue): the footprint outlines the New York City shade model draws for every building within 200 m of an address.
- [City of New York — building footprints metadata](https://github.com/CityOfNewYork/nyc-geo-metadata/blob/master/Metadata/Metadata_BuildingFootprints.md): that each footprint carries its roof height above ground and its ground elevation, and that a zero or null roof height means none was available.
- [NYC Department of City Planning — Primary Land Use Tax Lot Output (PLUTO)](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/Primary-Land-Use-Tax-Lot-Output-PLUTO-/64uk-42ks): tax-lot records, including number of floors, used for the building you pin in New York City.
- [Sandia PV Performance Modeling Collaborative — isotropic sky diffuse model](https://pvpmc.sandia.gov/modeling-guide/1-weather-design-inputs/plane-of-array-poa-irradiance/calculating-poa-irradiance/poa-sky-diffuse/isotropic-sky-diffuse-model/): the uniform-sky assumption and the (1 + cos tilt) / 2 sky view the shade model uses for diffuse light.
- [Sandia PV Performance Modeling Collaborative — POA sky diffuse](https://pvpmc.sandia.gov/modeling-guide/1-weather-design-inputs/plane-of-array-poa-irradiance/calculating-poa-irradiance/poa-sky-diffuse/): that sky diffuse light has isotropic, circumsolar and horizon-brightening components, of which the model uses only the first.
- [Sandia PV Performance Modeling Collaborative — POA ground reflected](https://pvpmc.sandia.gov/modeling-guide/1-weather-design-inputs/plane-of-array-poa-irradiance/calculating-poa-irradiance/poa-ground-reflected/): the standard ground-reflection model’s assumption of open ground visible to the horizon, with no buildings.
- [NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory — Solar Calculator](https://gml.noaa.gov/grad/solcalc/): reference solar positions; the site’s simplified NOAA sun-position code gives the mid-December noon elevations quoted (36.4°, 26.0°, 21.7°).
- [Heisler, “Effects of individual trees on the solar radiation climate of small buildings,” Urban Ecology 9 (1986), US Forest Service](https://research.fs.usda.gov/treesearch/34772): a sugar maple reduced irradiance in its shade on a south-facing wall by about 80% in leaf and nearly 40% leafless.
- [Tian, Loonen, Valckenborg and Hensen, “High-resolution hierarchical PV system performance modeling in urban environments” (arXiv, 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.13424): that coarse-resolution models under realistic partial shading overestimated a string’s monthly energy yield by up to 54%.
- [US Census Bureau — Vintage 2025 subcounty population estimates](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/popest/datasets/2020-2025/cities/totals/sub-est2025.csv): Jacksonville, New York City and Minneapolis as the largest cities in Florida, New York and Minnesota, the three reference points modeled.

# How do I put a solar panel on my balcony?

URL: https://balco.nyc/install-balcony-solar  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

A balcony solar setup is two or three panels clamped or ballasted on your railing, wired to a small microinverter whose cord plugs into an ordinary 120-volt outlet. The physical work is an afternoon. In New York, hold off: plug-in solar stays outside the rules until the SUNNY Act is signed and takes effect ninety days later. Spend the wait getting written building permission, checking your outlet, circuit and railing, and choosing a certified kit.

## What the installation actually is

A balcony solar system is short and simple compared to a rooftop array. One to three rigid panels are fixed to your railing or stood on the balcony floor. Their DC leads run a metre or so into a microinverter, usually a sealed brick that mounts behind or beneath the panels. The microinverter has a single AC cord ending in a standard plug. That plug goes into an outdoor outlet.

Nothing is drilled into the building. Nothing goes on the roof. Nobody opens your service panel. The whole thing can be taken down and carried out in a lift.

The microinverter is the part that matters. It converts panel DC into AC matched to the grid’s voltage, frequency and phase, so the power it makes flows into your apartment’s wiring and is consumed by whatever is running at that moment — the fridge, the router, the standby loads. It is not stored.

It also does the safety-critical job: **anti-islanding**. When grid power disappears, the inverter detects the loss and stops producing within two seconds, the limit set by IEEE 1547, the interconnection standard inverters are certified against. This is why a plug-in system cannot energize wiring that a utility worker or a firefighter believes is dead — and also why, having no battery, it gives you nothing at all during a blackout. People are regularly surprised by that. It is a direct consequence of the safety design, not a defect.

UL 1741 is the long-standing US standard covering grid-interactive inverter behavior, including anti-islanding. UL 3700, published in December 2025 with certification launched in January 2026, is newer and narrower: it covers the complete plug-in photovoltaic system as a product, not just the inverter inside it.

## Why the installation itself waits

The SUNNY Act (S8512C / A9111C) passed the New York Senate in April 2026 and the Assembly in late May 2026. As of today it has not been signed. Governor Hochul has until the end of 2026 to act, and the bill takes effect on the ninetieth day after it becomes law — so the earliest realistic date on which a compliant device is squarely inside the rules is some months after a signature, not the day of one.

The Act defines a *portable solar generation device* as a photovoltaic system supplying a maximum aggregate continuous AC inverter nameplate output of no more than 1,200 watts to the grid. It must be listed or certified by an accredited nationally recognised testing laboratory as a complete plug-in photovoltaic system, must include a mechanism preventing it from energizing the building’s wiring or the grid during an outage, and must be installed in accordance with the New York State fire prevention and building code and the manufacturer’s instructions. Compliant devices are exempted from interconnection and net-metering requirements. Full detail is on the [SUNNY Act page](https://balco.nyc/sunny-act).

> **The SUNNY Act removes the utility barrier. It does not grant you the right to install anything.**

There is a second, practical reason to wait. The Act directs the State Fire Prevention and Building Code Council to update the code for these devices. Those installation rules — the ones a New York City inspector or an insurer would eventually cite — do not exist yet. Installing now means guessing at requirements that are about to be written down, and possibly having to redo the mounting when they are.

None of this stops you preparing. Permission, site checks and product selection are the slow parts anyway, and none of them require a panel on your railing.

## Permission is the long pole, not the wiring

In a New York City apartment building, the electrical work is trivial and the approvals are not. Start here, because a refusal ends the project before you have spent anything.

- **Renters.** You need your landlord’s permission, in writing. The SUNNY Act contains no tenant protections — nothing in it prevents a landlord from saying no. New Jersey’s law, signed on 1 September 2026 and in effect from 1 March 2027, does protect tenants who pay their own electric bill and bars homeowners’ and condo associations from enforcing bans on exterior placement. New York’s bill does not.

- **Co-op and condo residents.** Expect the board, and expect an alteration agreement. Boards commonly ask for a certificate of insurance, a description of the mounting method, and an undertaking to restore the balcony. Some will want a licensed engineer’s letter on the attachment.

- **Landmarked buildings and historic districts.** The Landmarks Preservation Commission reviews exterior work on designated buildings. LPC has broadened the range of solar installations eligible for staff-level review, but visibility from a public thoroughfare remains the deciding factor, and a panel hung on a street-facing railing is about as visible as it gets.

When you ask, ask specifically. A vague request to “put up solar” invites a vague refusal. Name the product, the mounting method, whether anything is drilled, the total weight, how it is removed, and who carries the liability. Offer to place it where it is not visible from the street. Get the answer in writing and keep it.

## Check your balcony before you buy anything

Five things decide whether a given balcony can host a system at all. Work through them before spending money, because two of them are common deal-breakers in New York City apartments.

| Check | What you are looking for | Who can answer |
|---|---|---|
| Outdoor outlet | An existing receptacle rated for a wet location, with a proper in-use cover. Many NYC balconies have none at all. | Look. If there is none, a licensed electrician plus building approval. |
| The circuit behind it | Which breaker feeds that outlet, its rating (usually 15 or 20 amps), and what else is on it. | Map it yourself by switching breakers; an electrician if the panel is unlabelled or old. |
| Railing structure | A guard solidly anchored to the structure, with a load path that can take an off-centre pull. Glass panels and slender balusters often cannot take a clamp. | Managing agent or super for the construction; an engineer for anything uncertain. |
| Egress | Panels, brackets and cable entirely clear of any fire escape, egress path, or window used for escape. | NYC Fire Code, Chapter 10. If in doubt, the answer is no. |
| Sun | Which way the balcony faces, how high you are, and what blocks the sky. | The calculator, and an hour of watching where the shade falls. |

> **A solar panel must never obstruct a fire escape, a means of egress, or access to either. New York City’s Fire Code requires these to be continuously maintained free of obstructions, and that applies to hardware and cables as much as to furniture and plants.**

## The electrical risks, specifically

Plug-in solar is unusual because a cord-and-plug connection bypasses the safeguards that cover a conventional PV installation — no permit review, no inspection, no utility sign-off. The hazards are well understood and they are avoidable, but only if you know what they are.

- **Buy a certified complete system, not assembled parts.** A UL 1741 inverter bolted to panels you bought separately is not a certified plug-in system. The SUNNY Act asks for listing of the complete system, which is what UL 3700 is for. When UL Solutions tested plug-in solar products already on the US market, it reported that none of them met the UL 3700 requirements — so the certification mark is a real filter, not a formality.

- **Anti-islanding is not optional.** Any device you consider must shut down when the grid does. This protects utility crews and firefighters working on what they reasonably believe is a dead circuit.

- **Live prongs.** A panel in sunlight is generating whether or not it is plugged in, so the blades of an ordinary plug on a solar cord can be live when it is pulled. Anti-islanding should shut the inverter down, but it is allowed up to two seconds and is not evaluated as shock protection. UL 3700 addresses this by covering systems with a dedicated plug-in PV plug and receptacle rather than a household plug; [the live-plug problem is explained here](https://balco.nyc/is-plug-in-solar-safe).

- **Backfeeding masks the breaker.** A breaker measures only the net current flowing through it. If solar is feeding a circuit while appliances draw from it, the breaker sees the difference, not the total. The wiring between the solar and the loads can then carry more current than the breaker ever detects — heating conductors without tripping anything. Overcurrent protection is one of the three risk categories UL identified for these systems, alongside touch safety and ground faults.

- **Never an extension cord, a power strip or a multi-outlet adapter.** These are built to carry power one way to a load. They add cord length and connections on the source side, and their own fuse or breaker cannot see the real current on the circuit either. Use the manufacturer’s cord, straight into a properly rated wall receptacle.

- **One system per circuit, and know what shares it.** A balcony outlet that also feeds a bedroom running a portable air conditioner is not a good host.

Call a licensed electrician if there is no outdoor outlet, if you cannot identify the breaker, if the receptacle has no ground or trips repeatedly, or if your building’s wiring is old enough that you are guessing. This is a small job for an electrician and an expensive one to get wrong yourself.

Note also that NEC Article 705 was written for permanently installed, hard-wired PV and does not cleanly address cord-and-plug systems. That gap is part of why New York’s fire code update matters, and part of why the honest answer to some detailed questions right now is that the rules are not settled.

## Mounting, wind, and things falling off buildings

A solar panel is a flat, rigid sail. On a high floor in New York, wind pressure and the gusting that comes off neighbouring towers are the governing load — not the panel’s weight. This is the part of a balcony install that is genuinely worth being conservative about, because a failure does not hurt you, it hurts whoever is on the sidewalk.

- **Two mounting approaches.** Clamped or hooked to the railing, or ballasted flat on the balcony floor at an angle. Ballasting avoids attaching anything to the guard, but adds concentrated weight — ask the managing agent about the balcony’s live-load capacity rather than estimating it.

- **Use a secondary tether.** A separate cable or strap from the panel frame to a solid anchor, independent of the primary brackets, so a loosened clamp does not become a falling object. Stainless or otherwise corrosion-resistant hardware only.

- **Prefer mounting inside the railing.** Hanging a panel on the outside face puts a hard object over the sidewalk, and many buildings prohibit exterior-face mounting outright.

- **Do not drill the building envelope.** Anything that penetrates a wall, parapet or waterproofing membrane is a different category of work with different approvals, and a water-infiltration claim is the fastest way to lose a board’s goodwill.

- **Route the cable properly.** Not pinched under a door, not through a window that closes on it, not draped where it can chafe. Use the manufacturer’s routing and any supplied strain relief.

- **Re-check it seasonally.** Bracket torque, tether integrity, cable condition, and the state of the connectors. Twice a year is reasonable; after any severe wind event is sensible.

If your railing is glass, if the guard is visibly aged, or if you cannot establish what the brackets would be bearing on, get an engineer to look at it. That cost may well exceed the value of the electricity, which is a legitimate reason to decide against the whole thing.

## Whether it is worth it for your apartment

Preparation is also the point at which to decide honestly whether to proceed. A typical 800 W setup in New York City produces roughly **400 to 900 kWh a year**. That is a wide band because location dominates: a high-floor, south-facing balcony produces about **three times** what a low-floor, north-facing one does. Con Edison’s SC-1 all-in marginal rate is about **$0.34/kWh**, so the value of that output is what you avoid buying, not a credit — the SUNNY Act exempts these devices from net metering.

Kits for a typical 800 W system run about **$850** budget, **$1,200** mid-range and **$1,600** premium. Add anything your building requires on top: an electrician for an outdoor receptacle, an engineer’s letter for the board, a certificate of insurance. The [cost and payback page](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-cost) works the arithmetic through.

Run your own numbers on the [calculator](https://balco.nyc/), and read [how we get them](https://balco.nyc/methodology). Then consider the cases where the sensible answer is no. A north-facing balcony on a low floor, hemmed in by an adjacent building, with no outdoor outlet and a board that will require an alteration agreement, is a project where the costs are real and immediate and the savings are small and slow. There is no shame in concluding that this does not work for your apartment. It works very well for some, and poorly for others, and the difference is mostly the direction your balcony faces.

## Common questions

**Can I install a balcony solar panel in New York City right now?**

Not yet. New York's SUNNY Act, which would exempt plug-in solar devices up to 1,200 watts of AC inverter output from interconnection and net-metering requirements, passed both legislative chambers in 2026 but was still awaiting Governor Hochul's signature as of September 2026, and it takes effect on the ninetieth day after it becomes law. Until then, installation should wait. You can usefully spend that time getting written building permission, checking your outlet and railing, and choosing a certified kit.

**Do I need an electrician to install balcony solar?**

A certified plug-in kit is designed to connect to an existing outdoor outlet without an electrician. You do need a licensed electrician if your balcony has no weather-rated receptacle, if you cannot identify which breaker feeds it, or if the outlet trips repeatedly, lacks a ground, or looks damaged. In a New York City apartment building, adding an outdoor receptacle is also usually a building alteration requiring the landlord's or board's approval.

**Will balcony solar power my apartment during a blackout?**

No. Grid-tied microinverters must have anti-islanding protection, which shuts the inverter down within two seconds when grid power disappears. This exists so the system cannot energize wiring that a utility worker or firefighter believes is dead. A standard plug-in solar kit has no battery, so it produces nothing at all during an outage.

**Can I plug a balcony solar panel into an extension cord or power strip?**

No. Cords, strips and adapters are built to carry power one way to a load, and they add connections and a fuse or breaker that cannot measure the true current on a circuit once solar is feeding into it. A certified system should plug directly into a properly rated, weather-protected wall receptacle using the manufacturer's own cord. Anything else risks overheating wiring without tripping any protective device.

**Does the SUNNY Act mean my landlord or co-op board has to allow balcony solar?**

No. The SUNNY Act removes the utility-side barrier by exempting compliant devices from interconnection and net-metering requirements; it does not create a right to install one. New York renters still need their landlord's permission, co-op and condo residents still need board approval, and buildings that are individual landmarks or sit in historic districts may need Landmarks Preservation Commission review.

**Can I put a solar panel on my fire escape?**

No. The New York City Fire Code requires fire escapes, and access to them, to be continuously maintained free of obstructions, and that applies to panels, brackets and cables just as it does to furniture and plants. The same rule covers any required means of egress, including a window used as an escape route. A balcony that doubles as a fire escape balcony is not a viable site for solar.

## Sources

- [NY State Senate Bill 2025-S8512C (SUNNY Act)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/S8512/amendment/C): the definition of a portable solar generation device, the 1,200 W AC limit, certification and fire-code conditions, and the ninetieth-day effective date.
- [New York legislature passes SUNNY Act plug-in solar legislation](https://pv-magazine-usa.com/2026/06/01/new-york-legislature-passes-sunny-act-plug-in-solar-legislation/): the absence of renter and HOA protections in the New York bill, and the contrasting New Jersey bill.
- [UL Solutions debuts a testing and certification framework for plug-in solar](https://www.ul.com/news/ul-solutions-debuts-testing-and-certification-framework-safer-plug-solar-across-united-states): UL 3700, published December 2025, covering the complete plug-in system rather than the inverter alone.
- [Safety considerations for plug-in photovoltaic systems](https://www.ul.com/insights/safety-considerations-plug-photovoltaic-pipv-systems): the three risk categories: overcurrent protection, touch safety and ground-fault protection.
- [UL Solutions flags safety risks in US plug-in solar](https://www.pv-tech.org/us-plug-in-solar-questions-remain-over-safety-certifications-and-regulation/): cord-and-plug connections bypassing code review, and UL's finding that tested products did not meet UL 3700.
- [Balcony PV enters the code conversation](https://iaeimagazine.org/columns/certification-insights/balcony-pv-enters-the-code-conversation/): NEC Article 705 was written for hard-wired PV and does not cleanly cover cord-and-plug systems.
- [NYC Fire Code 2022, Chapter 10 — Means of Egress](https://up.codes/viewer/new_york_city/nyc-fire-code-2022/chapter/10/means-of-egress): the requirement that means of egress be continuously maintained free of obstructions.
- [NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission — technical resources](https://www.nyc.gov/site/lpc/applications/technical-resources.page): LPC review of exterior work on designated buildings and in historic districts.

# Is balcony solar worth it? Payback in every state

URL: https://balco.nyc/is-balcony-solar-worth-it  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

On an unshaded south-facing railing, usually yes: balco.nyc’s PVWatts runs for the largest city in every state put payback on a $1,200 mid-range 800 W kit between 4.8 years in California and 13.9 in Washington, with the median state at 9.9. In New York City, at Con Edison’s 34¢ marginal rate, it is 5.5 years. The price of electricity explains most of the gap between states, but for your own balcony direction and shade matter more: a north-facing railing, or a low floor facing a taller building across the street, can push payback past 20 years.

## The answer, state by state

balco.nyc ran NREL’s PVWatts model for the largest city in every state and the District of Columbia, with the calculator’s own parameters: an 800 W system hung vertically on a railing, multiplied by 0.95, the site’s allowance for the railing and mounting hardware shading the bottom of the panel. Each city’s output was valued at its state’s average residential electricity price from the U.S. Energy Information Administration, over the twelve months to June 2026, and run through the calculator’s payback loop: electricity prices rising 3% a year, the panels losing 0.5% of their output a year, nominal dollars with no discounting, and a 25-year cap. Two assumptions flatter every figure in this section, and later sections take them away: every kWh is used at home, and nothing across the street casts a shadow.

On those terms, a south-facing railing pays back a $1,200 kit in a median of **9.9 years**. The fastest state is California at 4.8 years and the slowest is Washington at 13.9. Direction matters as much as the state does:

| Railing faces | Median output, kWh/yr | Median payback: $850 / $1,200 / $1,600 kit | States paying back within 10 years: $850 / $1,200 / $1,600 |
|---|---|---|---|
| South | 658 | 7.2 / 9.9 / 12.7 yrs | 50 / 28 / 12 of 51 |
| East or west (average of the two) | 489 | 9.5 / 12.9 / 16.4 yrs | 32 / 11 / 3 of 51 |
| North | 200 | 20.4 / 25+ / 25+ yrs | 1 / 0 / 0 of 51 |

balco.nyc’s computation from its published PVWatts runs and EIA prices, for 50 states and DC. “25+” means the kit has not paid for itself after 25 years.

As shares: with the mid-range kit, 55% of states pay back a south-facing railing within ten years, 22% an east- or west-facing one, and none a north-facing one. With a north railing and the mid-range kit, 32 states do not pay back within 25 years at all. The kit price moves the answer a long way: at $850 a south railing pays back inside ten years in every state except Washington (10.3 years).

New York City gets its own line because balco.nyc values a kWh there at Con Edison’s all-in marginal rate of 34¢, not the statewide average of 28.0¢, which covers every utility in the state. At that rate the same 604 kWh south railing saves about $205 a year and pays back a $1,200 kit in **5.5 years** (4.0 on the budget kit, 7.2 on the premium). Only California and Hawaii are faster. Facing east or west it takes 7.5 years, and facing north 17.2. [Why New York City uses a different rate](https://balco.nyc/electricity-rate).

## Price explains the spread, not sunshine

The obvious guess is that balcony solar pays best where it is sunniest. The data say otherwise. Across the 51, balco.nyc regressed the logarithm of payback (south railing, mid-range kit) on the logarithm of the electricity price, and separately on the logarithm of output. Price gives an r² of **0.87**; output gives **0.02**. In plain terms, the price of electricity accounts for 87% of the state-to-state variation in payback and the amount of sunshine for 2%. It is the same calculation the [state-by-state table](https://balco.nyc/states) runs.

Two things produce that result. Prices vary far more than sunshine does: from 12.3¢ in North Dakota to 42.8¢ in Hawaii, a factor of 3.5, while south-railing output runs from 510 kWh in Honolulu to 819 kWh in Albuquerque, a factor of 1.6. And the two pull against each other. Sunnier states tend to have cheaper electricity (the correlation between them is −0.25), so Albuquerque’s extra output is worth only 15.3¢ a kWh, and output on its own predicts almost nothing. Honolulu is the extreme case. At 21°N the summer sun passes almost overhead, so a vertical south panel there makes the least of any city, and an east- or west-facing one actually makes more (539 kWh). Hawaii still ranks second because its electricity costs more than twice the US average of 17.9¢.

|  | State (city modeled) | Average price | South railing, kWh/yr | Year-one saving | Payback, $1,200 kit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fastest | California (Los Angeles) | 32.9¢ | 720 | $237 | 4.8 yrs |
| Hawaii (Honolulu) | 42.8¢ | 510 | $218 | 5.2 yrs |
| Massachusetts (Boston) | 30.4¢ | 673 | $204 | 5.5 yrs |
| Maine (Portland) | 29.0¢ | 692 | $201 | 5.6 yrs |
| Rhode Island (Providence) | 29.0¢ | 670 | $194 | 5.8 yrs |
| Slowest | Arkansas (Little Rock) | 13.3¢ | 613 | $82 | 12.7 yrs |
| Oregon (Portland) | 15.5¢ | 526 | $81 | 12.7 yrs |
| Tennessee (Nashville) | 13.5¢ | 602 | $81 | 12.7 yrs |
| Louisiana (New Orleans) | 13.0¢ | 605 | $79 | 13.1 yrs |
| Washington (Seattle) | 14.0¢ | 524 | $73 | 13.9 yrs |

Run the other way, the same arithmetic gives a rule of thumb. For a railing producing the median 658 kWh, a $1,200 kit pays back in ten years at about **16¢/kWh**, in seven years at about 24¢, and in five years at about 35¢. An east- or west-facing railing needs about 22¢ to reach ten years. A north-facing one would need about 54¢, which no state averages.

## If you cannot use every kWh

Every figure so far assumes the panel’s whole output replaces electricity you would otherwise buy. That holds only while something in the home is drawing at least as much power as the panel is making. Anything beyond that flows out to the grid, and under most plug-in laws it earns nothing. Of the nine signed state plug-in laws and the two bills awaiting a governor (California’s and New York’s), seven exclude these devices from net metering or say outright that exported power is not paid for. Vermont’s act says exports “shall not be compensated”. The other four do not say, and none provides a credit. balco.nyc therefore treats surplus as worth nothing.

How much of a balcony system’s output a US household actually uses has not been measured, as far as we could find. The nearest reference is German. The consumer agency Verbraucherzentrale NRW estimates that a single 400 W module on an unshaded south balcony makes about 280 kWh a year and cuts the household’s purchases by about 200 kWh, so roughly 70% is used at home. An 800 W system doubles the midday output without doubling the midday demand, so in the same household it would use a smaller share. What decides it is what runs in daylight: a refrigerator, a router and standby loads run all day, and air conditioning helps in summer. Treat 80% and 60% as a bracket, not a measurement:

| South railing, $1,200 kit | All output used | 80% used | 60% used |
|---|---|---|---|
| California (32.9¢) | $237/yr · 4.8 yrs | $190/yr · 6.0 yrs | $142/yr · 7.8 yrs |
| Illinois (18.5¢) | $114/yr · 9.4 yrs | $91/yr · 11.5 yrs | $69/yr · 14.7 yrs |
| Texas (15.9¢) | $92/yr · 11.5 yrs | $73/yr · 13.9 yrs | $55/yr · 17.7 yrs |
| New York City (34¢) | $205/yr · 5.5 yrs | $164/yr · 6.8 yrs | $123/yr · 8.8 yrs |

The three states are chosen to span the range: a high price, a middling one and a low one. Losing a fifth of the output adds 1.2 years in California and 2.4 in Texas. Losing two-fifths adds 3.0 and 6.2. The longer the payback to begin with, the more years each unused kWh costs. A household that is out all day with little left running should read its answer one row down in the [decision table](https://balco.nyc#decision).

## The building across the street

The state figures are for a balcony with nothing in front of it. To show what an ordinary urban obstruction does, balco.nyc ran the calculator’s shade model on a scenario most city dwellers can picture. The balcony faces south on the 3rd floor, about 7 m above the street. Across a 20 m street stands a building of 6 to 10 floors, which the calculator treats as 25 m tall. From the railing, the top of that building sits about 42° above the horizon straight ahead. The midday sun stays below that line for three months around the winter solstice in Los Angeles and Houston, and for five months in Chicago. Those months carry a large share of a vertical south panel’s year, because it faces the low winter sun almost head-on: 36% of annual output in Los Angeles and Houston comes from November to January, and 48% in Chicago from October to February.

| 3rd floor, 6–10 floors opposite, 20 m away | Open view, kWh/yr | With the building, kWh/yr | Share kept | Payback, $1,200 kit: open → shaded | Shaded, $850 kit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Los Angeles (32.9¢) | 720 | 306 | 42% | 4.8 → 10.6 yrs | 7.8 yrs |
| Chicago (18.5¢) | 616 | 239 | 39% | 9.4 → 21.0 yrs | 15.9 yrs |
| Houston (15.9¢) | 576 | 248 | 43% | 11.5 → 23.0 yrs | 17.5 yrs |
| New York City (34¢) | 604 | 227 | 38% | 5.5 → 13.3 yrs | 9.9 yrs |

balco.nyc’s computation: the calculator’s street-canyon horizon and monthly shade integration, applied to each city’s PVWatts monthly output, then the 0.95 railing factor. In the darkest months the panel gets almost nothing but diffuse light, and the model applies its floor of 10% of unshaded output.

Move the same balcony up to the 5th floor and the model keeps 58% to 72% of the open-view output. On the 8th floor it keeps about 94% in all four cities. Shade on this scale does more damage than any other adjustment in this article except facing north. It roughly doubles payback in all four cities, or worse, and it turns Los Angeles, the fastest city in the table, into one slower than the median state. Combine it with 60% self-consumption and a shaded 3rd-floor balcony does not pay back a mid-range kit within 25 years in Chicago or Houston, and takes 16.4 years in Los Angeles.

Outside New York City, the calculator asks what stands across from your balcony and how far away it is, then builds this kind of horizon. It treats the building opposite as an unbroken wall with no gaps or cross streets, so a described estimate tends to overstate shade, not understate it. In New York City it uses the actual surrounding buildings. [How floor height and obstruction decide output](https://balco.nyc/balcony-sunlight).

## What “worth it” leaves out

A payback period answers one question: if you can install this, and use what it makes, how long until it has paid for itself? Several things come before that question.

- **Whether it is allowed where you live.** As of 23 September 2026, balco.nyc’s state table lists nine states with a signed plug-in solar law. Five are in force (Colorado, Maine, Maryland, Utah and Vermont) and four are not yet in effect (Connecticut, New Hampshire, New Jersey and Virginia). California’s SB 868 has passed both houses and was presented to the Governor on 31 August; it awaits his decision. New York’s SUNNY Act has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature. Of the rest, seven (counting DC) have a bill pending, 18 have seen one fail, and 15 have none that we could find. Without a law in force, the utility’s interconnection rules apply, which usually means getting approval before connecting anything that feeds power into a home circuit. Of the five fastest-payback states above, only Maine has a law in force. This summarizes state laws and is not legal advice. [Each state’s page](https://balco.nyc/states) has its bills, dates and sources.

- **Permission.** Only four of the nine signed laws (Colorado, New Jersey, Vermont and Virginia) limit a landlord’s or association’s power to refuse. New York’s bill grants no right to install. For a renter, the payback clock starts when the landlord says yes.

- **A certified system to buy.** UL 3700, UL’s safety requirements for plug-in PV equipment and complete systems, was published in December 2025, and certification opened in January 2026. The first components certified to it, microinverters, were announced in July 2026. As of September 2026 no complete system has been certified to it. When UL Solutions tested plug-in products already on sale, none of them complied. Several laws, New York’s among them, require listing of the complete system, so in those states a compliant kit may not yet exist at any price.

- **The price you actually pay per kWh.** The EIA figures used here are averages: total residential revenue divided by total kWh sold. They include fixed monthly charges, which a panel cannot reduce, so they overstate what an avoided kWh saves. For example, a $15 fixed charge spread over 900 kWh a month adds about 1.7¢ to the average. Tiered and time-of-use rates can push your real figure either way, and a state average covers every utility in the state. The better number is your own bill: the total, minus fixed charges, divided by the kWh billed. [How to read it](https://balco.nyc/electricity-rate).

- **Costs that are not the kit.** The kit prices are for hardware only. If your balcony has no outdoor outlet, adding one is an electrician’s job, and Maine requires a licensed electrician and a dedicated circuit for any plug-in system over 420 W. There is no federal tax credit to offset the cost, because the residential clean energy credit (IRC 25D) ended for expenditures after 31 December 2025. [What that means for a kit bought now](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-tax-credit). All paybacks here are in nominal dollars. Discounting future savings would make every one of them longer. [The full cost picture](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-cost).

## The decision in one table

Read your situation from the first column. Paybacks are for an 800 W kit, from balco.nyc’s runs above, and assume every kWh is used at home unless the row says otherwise.

| Your balcony and your electricity | Verdict on the numbers | What the numbers say |
|---|---|---|
| South, south-east or south-west; open view or high floor; electricity 24¢/kWh or more (the nine dearest states, and New York City at 34¢) | Worth it | 4.8 to 7.7 years on a $1,200 kit; 3.5 to 5.6 on $850 |
| Same balcony; electricity 16–24¢ (14 states and DC) | Reasonable, if the kit is cheap | 6.9 to 10.5 years on $1,200; 5.0 to 7.7 on $850 |
| Same balcony; electricity under 16¢ (27 states) | Marginal | 8.7 to 13.9 years on $1,200; 6.3 to 10.3 on $850 |
| East- or west-facing, open view | Worth it only where power is dear | Within ten years on $1,200 in 11 states, all above 23¢; median 12.9 years |
| North-facing | Not on the numbers | Best case Hawaii, 11.5 years on $1,200; more than 25 years in 32 states |
| Low floor, taller building across the street | Usually not | 3rd floor, 6–10 floors opposite at 20 m: 10.6 years in Los Angeles, 21 in Chicago, 23 in Houston |
| Home empty in daylight, little left running | One row down | At 60% used, paybacks run roughly 50% to 60% longer |
| No law in force, no permission, or no certified complete system you can buy | Not yet | Whatever the payback, it starts only when you can install |

The table uses one city per state and a state-average price. Output varies within a state, and so do prices from one utility to the next. [The calculator](https://balco.nyc/) runs your address, your direction, what stands opposite and your own rate. If you want to know which of these widely repeated claims survive the arithmetic, [we checked them](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-myths).

## Common questions

**Is balcony solar worth it?**

For an unshaded south-facing railing, usually. balco.nyc's PVWatts runs for the largest city in each state put payback on a $1,200 mid-range 800 W kit between 4.8 years (California) and 13.9 years (Washington), with a median of 9.9 years, assuming all the power is used at home, electricity prices rising 3% a year and 0.5% annual panel degradation. East- or west-facing railings take a median of 12.9 years, north-facing ones more than 25 in most states, and heavy shade from a building across the street can roughly double any of these figures.

**How long does a balcony solar panel take to pay for itself?**

For an 800 W system on an unshaded south-facing railing, the median US state takes 7.2 years on an $850 kit, 9.9 years on a $1,200 kit and 12.7 years on a $1,600 kit, according to balco.nyc's calculations from NREL PVWatts output and EIA average electricity prices. In New York City, valued at Con Edison's 34-cent marginal rate, a $1,200 kit pays back in about 5.5 years.

**Does balcony solar make sense where electricity is cheap?**

Less so. Across the 50 states and DC, the electricity price explains 87% of the variation in balcony solar payback and the amount of sunshine only 2%. Where average residential electricity is under 16 cents per kWh, an unshaded south-facing 800 W system takes about 9 to 14 years to pay back a $1,200 kit, and 6 to 10 years on an $850 one.

**Is a north-facing balcony worth solar panels?**

Not on the numbers alone. An unshaded north-facing vertical 800 W panel makes a median of about 200 kWh a year across US states' largest cities, roughly 30% of a south-facing one. On a $1,200 kit that means more than 25 years to pay back in 32 states; the best case, Hawaii, is 11.5 years, and only because its electricity costs about 43 cents per kWh.

**Do I get paid for balcony solar power I send to the grid?**

Under most state plug-in laws, no. Of the nine signed state plug-in solar laws and the two bills awaiting a governor as of September 2026, seven exclude these devices from net metering or say exported power is not compensated, and the other four do not say. If only 60% of an 800 W system's output is used at home, payback runs roughly 50% to 60% longer, for example from 9.4 to 14.7 years in Illinois on a $1,200 kit.

**How much does shade change balcony solar payback?**

Enough to roughly double it. In balco.nyc's shade model, a south-facing 3rd-floor balcony facing a 6-to-10-floor building across a 20-meter street keeps only about 38% to 43% of its unshaded output, because the building blocks the low winter sun a vertical panel depends on. That stretches payback on a $1,200 kit from 4.8 to 10.6 years in Los Angeles and from 9.4 to 21 years in Chicago. The same balcony on the 8th floor keeps about 94%.

- [U.S. EIA — Form EIA-861M monthly sales and revenue by state](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/data/eia861m/): residential revenue and sales by state; balco.nyc’s average prices are revenue divided by sales over the twelve months to June 2026, so they include fixed charges.
- [Con Edison — historical average full-service electric rates](https://www.coned.com/-/media/files/coned/documents/save-energy-money/using-private-generation/historical-average-full-service-electric-rates.pdf): the SC-1 residential series behind the 34¢ marginal rate used for New York City.
- [Vermont Legislature — Act 149 (S.202) as enacted](https://legislature.vermont.gov/Documents/2026/Docs/ACTS/ACT149/ACT149%20As%20Enacted.pdf): plug-in devices are not eligible for net metering, and exported generation “shall not be compensated”.
- [Utah Legislature — H.B. 340 Solar Power Amendments, enrolled copy](https://le.utah.gov/Session/2025/bills/enrolled/HB0340.pdf): a portable solar generation device is exempt from interconnection requirements and not subject to net metering program requirements.
- [Maine Legislature — LD 1730 (SP 676), enacted text](https://legislature.maine.gov/legis/bills/getPDF.asp?paper=SP0676&item=5&snum=132): systems over 420 W and up to 1,200 W must be installed by a licensed electrician on a dedicated circuit, and may not be used for net energy billing.

- [Electrek — the first US microinverter certified to UL 3700](https://electrek.co/2026/07/20/us-first-ul-3700-balcony-solar-microinverter-hoymiles/): the first UL 3700 certification of a component, a microinverter, in July 2026, not of a complete system.
