---

# Is plug-in solar safe? The circuit arithmetic and the evidence

URL: https://balco.nyc/is-plug-in-solar-safe  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

It can be, but not automatically, and the reason is arithmetic rather than paperwork. balco.nyc’s worst-case calculation: a 1,200 W plug-in inverter on a shared 15 A, 120 V circuit can let part of that circuit’s wire carry 25 A — 67% over its rating — without the breaker ever tripping. That case needs full sun, heavy loads and an unlucky outlet at the same moment, which is rare, and a dedicated circuit removes it. Germany, with about 1.3 million registered systems at a smaller 800 VA limit, has reassuring modeling but no systematic incident data.

## The breaker cannot see what the inverter adds

A household branch circuit assumes that power arrives from one end. The breaker measures the current leaving the panel, and the wire is sized to carry whatever the breaker allows: under the National Electrical Code, 14 AWG copper may be protected at no more than 15 A and 12 AWG at no more than 20 A, matching those wires’ ratings in the 60 °C column that applies to NM-B house cable.

A plug-in inverter injects current at an outlet partway along the circuit. Anything plugged in beyond that outlet can then draw from both sources at once: up to the breaker’s rating from the panel, plus the inverter’s output. The breaker measures only its own share, so it does not trip — the mechanism UL Solutions’ white paper on plug-in PV illustrates with a 600 VA unit. Here is balco.nyc’s arithmetic for the sizes US laws allow, at 120 V (heat rises with the square of current):

| Circuit (breaker / wire) | Inverter | Inverter current | Worst-case current in the wire | Over the wire’s rating | Heat vs. at rating |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 15 A / 14 AWG | 400 W | 3.3 A | 18.3 A | +22% | 1.5× |
| 15 A / 14 AWG | 800 W | 6.7 A | 21.7 A | +44% | 2.1× |
| 15 A / 14 AWG | 1,200 W | 10.0 A | 25.0 A | +67% | 2.8× |
| 20 A / 12 AWG | 400 W | 3.3 A | 23.3 A | +17% | 1.4× |
| 20 A / 12 AWG | 800 W | 6.7 A | 26.7 A | +33% | 1.8× |
| 20 A / 12 AWG | 1,200 W | 10.0 A | 30.0 A | +50% | 2.3× |

Read the table as a ceiling, not an expectation. It needs three things at once: the inverter near full output, its outlet between the panel and the loads rather than at the end of the run, and those loads drawing the breaker’s full rating. On the last outlet of a circuit, or alone on a dedicated one, no wire carries more than the larger of the two currents. Concretely: two 1,500 W space heaters on one 15 A circuit draw 25 A and trip the breaker. Add a 1,200 W inverter at full output on an outlet between them and the panel, and the breaker sees exactly 15 A and holds while the cable to the heaters carries 25 A.

An overload is not ignition. The same 14 AWG copper is rated 25 A in the ampacity table’s 90 °C column, and UL Solutions frames the risk as fire or shock through damaged conductors, insulation and connected equipment. What the extra current spends is the code’s margin, which the continuous-load convention narrows: continuous loads are held to 80% of a circuit’s rating, and the NEC’s interconnection rules count inverter output at 125%. If the 80–100% gap is the only spare capacity, it is 3 A — **360 W** — on a 15 A circuit and 4 A (480 W) on a 20 A one. Only one row fits: 400 W on 20 A.

Full output is also uncommon. balco.nyc ran NREL’s PVWatts V8 hour by hour for New York City with the calculator’s settings (800 W of panel, DC/AC ratio 1.1, the site’s mount-loss factors of 0.95 vertical and 0.99 at 35° applied). A vertical south-facing railing system ran at 90% or more of its inverter’s rating for about **5 hours a year**, and at 75% or more for 57; tilted to 35°, for 22 and 273 hours. More panel behind the same inverter means far more hours at the ceiling (section 4).

> **Not electrical advice.** This is worst-case arithmetic. Whether a given circuit can host a given system is for a licensed electrician applying the NEC as your jurisdiction has adopted it.

## The panel, the 120% rule and the 1,200 W number

The panel has the same problem at a larger scale, and there the NEC has a rule, written for hard-wired solar. Section 705.12 allows a source on a panel’s busbar if 125% of its output current plus the main breaker’s rating stays within the busbar’s rating — or within 120% of it, the “120% rule,” when the source and the main breaker sit at opposite ends of the busbar. For a 120 V plug-in source, balco.nyc’s arithmetic:

| Panel (busbar / main) | Room under the 120% rule | Largest inverter current | Largest inverter at 120 V | 1,200 W device (counted as 12.5 A) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 60 A / 60 A | 12 A | 9.6 A | 1,152 W | Over by 0.5 A |
| 100 A / 100 A | 20 A | 16 A | 1,920 W | Fits |
| 200 A / 200 A | 40 A | 32 A | 3,840 W | Fits |

At the panel, then, 1,200 W binds only on a small one. But a plug-in enters the busbar wherever its branch breaker sits, and the stricter 100% version of the rule leaves no room on a panel whose main breaker matches its busbar. UL Solutions says the 120% permission does not apply to branch-circuit wiring, where section 1’s arithmetic lives, and notes that the 2026 NEC, like every earlier edition, does not recognize plug-in PV.

**Why 1,200 W?** The rationale is not stated in the laws. Utah’s HB 340, the first, sets 1,200 W on a standard 120 V outlet with no stated reason. New York’s SUNNY Act, which has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature, uses the same figure, and neither its text nor its sponsor memo explains it. Colorado’s legislative declaration is silent on its 1,920 W. The arithmetic shows where each number sits:

- **1,200 W** is 10 A at 120 V: two-thirds of a 15 A circuit’s rating.

- **Germany’s 800 VA** at 230 V is about 3.5 A: 22% of the 16 A circuit HTW Berlin modeled.

- **Maine’s 420 W** do-it-yourself tier is 3.5 A, almost exactly the German current; the law does not say that is why.

- **Colorado’s 1,920 W** is 16 A: 80% of a 20 A circuit, and the 120%-rule limit of a 100 A panel. The statute does not say which, if either, was intended.

The common US cap puts nearly three times Germany’s current on a household circuit. That does not make it unsafe by itself, but it means the German record describes a smaller overload.

## Blackouts, live plugs and GFCIs

**Anti-islanding protects the grid.** A microinverter follows the utility’s voltage and frequency and cannot create a supply of its own; UL 1741 and IEEE 1547 require it to stop energizing its output within two seconds of losing the grid. That is why a plug-in system shuts down in a blackout and cannot feed a line a utility crew believes is dead — and why, without a battery, it gives no backup power. Maine requires inverters that shut off 0.2 seconds after a disruption.

**A live plug is a different hazard.** On a plug-in solar cord the source sits behind the plug, so in sunlight the blades are connected to a generator — the reason a homemade cord with plugs on both ends is called a “suicide cord.” Pulling the plug looks to the inverter like losing the grid, so it should stop, and advocates’ testimony to the Vermont legislature relies on that. UL Solutions does not accept it as sufficient: anti-islanding is a grid function allowed up to two seconds, never evaluated as shock protection that must survive a component or software fault. Its proposed fixes are a uniquely shaped plug and receptacle with no exposed live parts, or an inverter output separately evaluated as touch-safe.

The standards reflect that. UL 3700, the Outline of Investigation for plug-in PV equipment that UL issued on 11 December 2025 (an outline, not yet a consensus standard), covers equipment with a plug-in PV plug for a permanently installed plug-in PV receptacle, and requires receptacles, GFCIs and overcurrent devices in the circuit to be listed for current in both directions. Germany’s DIN VDE V 0126-95 allows an ordinary household plug only with covered contacts, a disconnect in the plug or protective devices in the inverter.

**GFCIs were not designed for backfeed.** Outdoor receptacles at US homes need GFCI protection, and GFCIs are evaluated for one-way current. In UL Solutions’ tests with an inverter backfeeding the circuit, GFCI circuit breakers averaged 32.8 to 36.7 milliseconds to clear a simulated body fault, beyond the standard’s 28.6 ms limit, because the inverter kept feeding the fault until anti-islanding cut in. GFCI receptacles, which open both conductors, stayed within the limit.

## What Germany’s record does and does not show

Germany is the evidence everyone cites. Since the Solarpaket I amendments took effect on 16 May 2024, a *Steckersolargerät* may have up to 800 VA of inverter output and 2,000 W of panels, and must be registered in the Bundesnetzagentur’s Marktstammdatenregister. The first product standard, DIN VDE V 0126-95, followed in December 2025. By April 2026 the register held about 1.31 million devices.

**There is no systematic incident data.** We found no German register, insurer series or fire-service statistic that counts fires or shocks attributable to plug-in solar; the official register records installations, not incidents. The PV fire figure most often quoted — Fraunhofer ISE’s 2013 count of 120 fires caused by PV systems over 20 years, among 1.3 million installations — predates the balcony boom and concerns conventional systems. The advocates’ Vermont testimony says four million German systems are in use with no significant incidents reported. It cites no dataset, and “none reported” is not “none” when nothing is set up to collect reports.

**What exists is modeling.** A February 2025 HTW Berlin report tested the 800 W limit on a 16 A German circuit. In a deliberately extreme case — cable in insulation, already loaded to 1.13 times its rating around the clock — an 800 W device pushed part of the circuit to 21.6 A, 135% of rating, for up to 16 hours a year, and the modeled conductor to 104 °C for a few minutes: above its 70 °C operating temperature, below the ignition point of common building materials, and enough to age insulation faster. With 2,000 W of panel behind the inverter, full output lasted about 1,000 hours a year. With load profiles from 74 real households, the device made no significant difference to conductor temperature or to the modeled number of fires.

Three reasons not to import that conclusion whole. The current is smaller: 3.5 A, against 10 A for a 1,200 W US device on a circuit rated lower. European residual-current devices open both conductors, which UL’s tests found keeps shock protection intact under backfeed; a US GFCI circuit breaker does not. And Germany’s grid-standards forum, VDE FNN, still advises that an electrician first check whether an existing circuit is adequately sized and protected for feed-in, to avoid overload and fire.

## What the US laws require

Every enacted US plug-in law makes the same basic trade: the utility loses the right to demand approval, fees or extra equipment, and the device must be listed by a nationally recognized testing laboratory and must stop energizing the building and the grid in an outage. Beyond that they diverge. The table comes from balco.nyc’s [state tracker](https://balco.nyc/states), built from the legislatures’ bill pages. It is not legal advice, and details vary by utility.

| State | Status | Cap | Certification | Meter, circuit and notice rules |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Utah | In force since May 2025 | 1,200 W | UL or equivalent; must meet the NEC | No utility approval or fees |
| Maine | In force July 2026 | 420 W; up to 1,200 W with conditions | UL 3700 or comparable, or configured per the NEC; off within 0.2 s | Above 420 W: licensed electrician, dedicated single-outlet circuit, notice within 30 days |
| Vermont | In force July 2026 | 1,200 W per meter | UL 3700 or equivalent; IEEE 1547-2018 | Smart meter required; “temporarily but securely attached” |
| Connecticut | From 1 October 2026 | 1,200 W | UL or equivalent; UL 1741; IEEE 1547; NEC | One device per meter |
| Colorado | In force August 2026 | 1,920 W | Listed by a recognized laboratory | One device per wall outlet per address; utility may require notice |
| New York (SUNNY Act) | Passed both chambers; awaits the Governor's signature | 1,200 W AC | Listed as a complete plug-in system | Notify the utility within 30 days |

Three things stand out. The caps are per meter, per address or per outlet, not per circuit: they stop a household from stacking devices but say nothing about what else shares the circuit a device lands on. Maine is the exception; above 420 W it requires exactly the dedicated circuit that makes section 1’s worst case impossible. Several laws require compliance with the NEC, which does not yet recognize plug-in PV, so “meets the NEC” is not yet a well-defined test. And under the standard written for these hazards, UL 3700, components have been listed but no complete system had been as of September 2026; [what UL 3700 covers and where certification stands](https://balco.nyc/ul-3700-plug-in-solar-certification) has the detail.

Maryland and Virginia also require notice to the utility before installation, and Colorado, Maryland and Virginia exempt devices of 391 W or less from code or listing provisions that would require rewiring; New Jersey draws that line at 400 W. [Every law side by side](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-laws-compared) has the rest.

## A practical checklist

None of this replaces a licensed electrician, the NEC as adopted where you live, or the product’s instructions; the [installation guide](https://balco.nyc/install-balcony-solar) has more detail.

- **A dedicated circuit if you can get one.** With nothing else on the circuit, no wire can carry breaker current plus inverter current. It is the first mitigation UL Solutions lists and what Maine requires above 420 W. If the outlet is shared, find out what else is on that breaker and keep heaters, air conditioners and hair dryers off it while the system is producing.

- **An outdoor-rated, GFCI-protected receptacle** with an in-use cover. Ordinary GFCIs are evaluated for one-way current, so follow the system’s instructions on whether the protection must be listed for backfeed. No outdoor outlet means an electrician and, in an apartment, the building’s approval.

- **The manufacturer’s cord, straight into the wall.** No extension cords, power strips or adapters. The same masking arithmetic applies inside a power strip, and every added plug is another set of blades never evaluated as a generator’s output.

- **One system per circuit, within your state’s cap.** Two inverters on one circuit add their currents to the worst case.

- **A complete listed system, unmodified.** A listed inverter paired with separately bought panels is not a listed plug-in system.

- **Secure mounting, sized for wind.** A panel is a sail: use the system’s brackets and a secondary tether, mount inside the railing where you can, and re-check after storms.

- **Never on a fire escape or in an egress path.** New York City’s Fire Code requires means of egress and fire escapes to be kept free of obstructions; panels, brackets and cables count.

Call an electrician first if you cannot identify the breaker, if the receptacle has no ground or trips repeatedly, or if the wiring is old enough that you are guessing.

## Common questions

**Is balcony solar safe?**

It can be, but not automatically. A plug-in system listed by a recognized testing laboratory, on a suitable circuit, is designed to be safe, but the hazards are specific: undetected circuit overload, live plug blades and interference with GFCI protection. balco.nyc's worst-case arithmetic shows a 1,200 W inverter on a shared 15 A circuit can let part of the wire carry 25 A without tripping the breaker. That needs full sun, heavy loads and an unlucky outlet at once, which is rare, and a dedicated circuit removes it.

**Can plug-in solar overload a circuit without tripping the breaker?**

Yes, in a worst case. The breaker measures only current coming from the panel, so if loads beyond the inverter's outlet draw the breaker's full rating plus the inverter's output, the wire between them carries both. By balco.nyc's arithmetic, on a 15 A, 120 V circuit that is 18.3 A with a 400 W inverter, 21.7 A with 800 W and 25 A with 1,200 W, or 22% to 67% over the wire's rating. UL Solutions identifies this as one of the three main risks of plug-in PV.

**Does plug-in solar work during a blackout?**

No. UL 1741 and IEEE 1547 require grid-interactive inverters to stop energizing their output within two seconds of losing the grid, so a plug-in system shuts down in an outage. This anti-islanding function protects utility crews working on lines they believe are dead. Without a battery, the system provides no backup power.

**Are the prongs on a plug-in solar cord live when it is unplugged?**

They can be, which is one reason certification matters. A microinverter should stop when unplugged because it loses the grid, but UL Solutions says that grid function, which is allowed up to two seconds and is not evaluated as shock protection, is not enough on its own. UL 3700 and Germany's DIN VDE V 0126-95 add protection such as a dedicated receptacle design, covered contacts or protective devices in the inverter.

**Has balcony solar caused fires in Germany?**

Nobody can say precisely, because Germany has no systematic incident register for plug-in solar; its official register records about 1.31 million installations, not incidents. The strongest evidence is modeling: a 2025 HTW Berlin report found that with real household loads an 800 W device did not significantly raise wiring temperatures or the modeled number of fires, though a deliberately extreme case aged insulation faster. A 1,200 W US device puts nearly three times as much current on a circuit.

**Why do US plug-in solar laws cap systems at 1,200 watts?**

The laws do not say. Utah's HB 340, the first, allows up to 1,200 W on a standard 120 V outlet without a stated rationale, and later laws and bills, including New York's SUNNY Act, which has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature, use the figure without explaining it. At 120 V, 1,200 W is 10 A, two-thirds of a 15 A circuit's rating, compared with about 3.5 A for Germany's 800 VA limit at 230 V.

**Can I plug a balcony solar system into an extension cord or power strip?**

No. A power strip has the same blind spot as a wall breaker, so loads plugged into it can draw the strip's rating plus the inverter's output through its internal wiring, and every extra plug adds blades never evaluated as the output of a generator. Use the manufacturer's cord directly in a properly rated, GFCI-protected outdoor receptacle, and ask an electrician if there is none.

## Sources

- [UL Solutions — Interactions of Plug-In PV with Protection of Existing Power Systems (white paper, filed as Maine legislative testimony)](https://legislature.maine.gov/testimony/resources/EUT20260106Soltan134125472587136094.pdf): the undetected-overload mechanism and 600 VA example; that the 705.12(B) 120% permission does not apply to branch-circuit wiring; the 80% continuous convention; the two-second anti-islanding allowance and why it is not touch protection; the GFCI test results (32.8–36.7 ms against 28.6 ms); dedicated-circuit and unique-receptacle mitigations; European devices opening both conductors.
- [UL Standards & Engagement — UL 3700, Outline of Investigation for Interactive Plug-In PV (PIPV) Equipment and Systems](https://www.shopulstandards.com/ProductDetail.aspx?UniqueKey=49440): edition 1 published 11 December 2025; scope covers a PIPV plug for a permanently installed PIPV receptacle and requires circuit components to be listed for bidirectional current.

# Getting balcony solar past an NYC co-op or condo board

URL: https://balco.nyc/nyc-coop-condo-board-balcony-solar  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

Yes, your board can stop you, and in New York City about one home in five has a board to ask. balco.nyc’s count of the city’s PLUTO tax-lot file puts 724,425 of 3.74 million homes (19.4%) in co-ops or individually owned condos, and one in three in Manhattan. No New York law gives a shareholder or unit owner a right to a railing panel, so the job is a request a board can approve: a removable device, nothing drilled, insurance and an indemnity, and a promise to take it down when the facade needs work.

## One New York home in five answers to a board

Whose permission you need depends on how your building is owned, and New York City publishes enough data to count it. balco.nyc summed residential units by building class in PLUTO, the Department of City Planning’s tax-lot file (version 26v2, the dataset the calculator uses for building heights). Co-ops are the classes the Department of Finance defines as cooperatives: C6 and C8 walk-ups, D4 and D0 elevator buildings, R9 (a co-op inside a condominium) and A8 (land co-ops such as Breezy Point). Condos are the R classes. PLUTO reports each condominium as one record with all its apartments added together.

That raw count overstates condos, because many newer rental towers are legally condominiums with a handful of tax lots, often one residential unit holding hundreds of apartments owned by a landlord. balco.nyc matched each PLUTO condo to the Department of Finance’s list of condominium unit lots and treated any condo with fewer unit lots than a quarter of its apartments as a rental. That moves 149,017 apartments in 1,102 condominiums out of the board column. Moving the cut to a half or three-quarters changes the total by under 8,500.

| Borough | All homes | Co-op | Owned condo | Board-run properties | Share with a board | Condo-structured rentals |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Manhattan | 958,956 | 197,566 | 122,702 | 6,243 | 33.4% | 62,076 |
| Brooklyn | 1,115,989 | 83,405 | 67,351 | 7,291 | 13.5% | 42,505 |
| Queens | 890,313 | 123,044 | 44,412 | 2,280 | 18.8% | 23,400 |
| Bronx | 591,146 | 56,266 | 16,962 | 664 | 12.4% | 20,079 |
| Staten Island | 180,241 | 1,937 | 10,780 | 246 | 7.1% | 957 |
| New York City | 3,736,645 | 462,218 | 262,207 | 16,724 | 19.4% | 149,017 |

Residential units from PLUTO 26v2, counted by balco.nyc. “Properties” are tax lots, and one lot can hold many buildings: Co-op City’s 15,372 apartments sit on two.

So **724,425 homes, 19.4% of the city’s 3.74 million**, are in buildings where a board of shareholders or unit owners, not a landlord or the occupant, decides what goes on a railing. Nearly two thirds of them are co-ops. The rest of the city splits into condo-structured rentals (4.0%), one- and two-family houses (21.9%), and rental buildings and everything else (54.7%, a group that also holds three-family houses and small mixed-use buildings, many of them owner-occupied).

Two checks. The 2023 Housing and Vacancy Survey, as reported by the City Comptroller, counted 450,000 occupied co-op apartments and 318,000 in condominiums, 22% of occupied homes: close to PLUTO’s co-op count, with the condo figure between balco.nyc’s two condo counts (262,207 owned, 411,224 in every condo-structured building). And building classes are only labels. One Roosevelt Island lot of 8,018 apartments, which holds rental buildings as well as co-ops, is classed as a co-op; leaving it out gives 19.2%.

## What the board is deciding, and why no law overrides it

No statute helps a New York City shareholder or unit owner here. The state’s solar-rights law covers rooftop systems and homeowners’ associations ([the statute-by-statute reading](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-condo-hoa)), and the [SUNNY Act](https://balco.nyc/sunny-act), which has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature, would remove the utility’s veto and says nothing about boards, landlords or leases. What governs is your building’s own documents.

- **Co-op.** The corporation owns the building; you hold shares and a proprietary lease, which typically bars installing equipment or making alterations without the corporation’s consent. The NYC Bar’s model co-op alteration agreement opens by reciting exactly that. The Attorney General’s guide to co-op boards points shareholders to the offering plan, the board or the managing agent for copies of the lease, bylaws and house rules.

- **Condo.** New York’s Condominium Act lets a unit include a “balcony, terrace and patio” but lists main walls and fire escapes among the common elements, so your declaration decides which side of the line your balcony falls on. The wall, and often the railing, belongs to everyone. The NYC Bar’s 2026 model condo agreement forbids changes to common elements unless the board approves them in its “sole and absolute discretion”.

- **A new building still run by its sponsor.** The City Bar’s notes to that condo form say sponsor-controlled boards commonly restrict renovations until the building has a permanent certificate of occupancy. In a co-op, the Attorney General generally requires the sponsor to give up control once it has sold more than half the shares, or five years after closing, whichever comes first.

- **Renting inside a co-op or condo.** You need the apartment owner’s consent and then the board’s, because the owner is bound by the lease or condominium documents and would sign any alteration agreement. [Renters’ options](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-renters) and [the rent-stabilized and NYCHA guide](https://balco.nyc/nyc-rent-stabilized-nycha-balcony-solar) cover the landlord side.

Two approvals sit outside the board: the utility, which is the part the SUNNY Act addresses ([what Con Edison requires](https://balco.nyc/con-edison-plug-in-solar)), and, in a designated building or historic district, the [Landmarks Preservation Commission](https://balco.nyc/nyc-landmarks-balcony-solar).

## What an alteration agreement asks for

The closest thing New York City has to a standard is a pair of model forms from the New York City Bar Association’s Cooperative and Condominium Law Committee: a co-op agreement last updated in 2010, and a condo agreement, approved by both the City and State bar associations, that the City Bar published in 2026. The Bar calls them a starting point and many buildings use their own, but clause by clause they show what a board will ask:

| Clause | What the model forms say | What it means for a railing panel |
|---|---|---|
| Plans | Detailed plans and specifications, prepared by a licensed architect or engineer if the board requires, reviewed by the board’s designated engineer, whose changes you must make. | For a removable device, a data sheet, a mounting drawing and photos may do. Ask before paying for stamped drawings. |
| Deposits and fees | Blanks for a security deposit, a managing agent’s processing fee, and a review deposit that pays the board’s lawyer and engineer. | The one cost that can exceed the kit. Ask for a waiver or a cap. |
| Insurance | Co-op model: liability cover of at least $1,000,000, which may be part of a homeowner’s policy or umbrella, naming the corporation and its agents. Condo model: amounts to be set with the building’s insurer. | Ask your unit-owner insurer for a certificate naming the board, and whether the policy covers a device outside the unit. |
| Indemnity | You, and any contractor, defend and indemnify the building against claims arising from the work. | A falling panel is the claim the board is pricing. The indemnity is only as good as the insurance behind it. |
| Permits | You obtain whatever the Department of Buildings, the Fire Department or the Landmarks Preservation Commission requires, and the board’s engineer decides what is required. | A new outdoor outlet means a licensed electrician. A designated building may need Landmarks approval. |
| Exterior walls | Co-op model: no penetration of any exterior wall. Condo model: none without the board’s approval, at its discretion. | Clamp; do not drill. Route the cable through an existing opening. |
| Upkeep and removal | You maintain the work and restore it after any building repair. The co-op model lets the corporation remove air conditioners, terrace plantings and similar installations for repairs, at the shareholder’s expense. | Expect to take the panel down for facade inspections and repairs, at your cost. |
| Sale | A buyer must take on the agreement before the co-op registers the transfer or the condo waives its right of first refusal. | Take the panel down before selling, or tell buyers it comes with obligations. |

Neither form was written with a plug-in device in mind; both assume construction, with contractors, working hours and debris. A panel with no contractor and nothing built can reasonably ask for a shorter process than a kitchen renovation.

## Why the facade makes boards cautious

In a building over six stories, a railing panel lands in an expensive compliance program. The city’s Facade Inspection & Safety Program (FISP, still widely called Local Law 11) requires the exterior walls and appurtenances of those buildings to be examined every five years by an inspector the owner hires. The rule’s list of appurtenances includes railings, window air conditioners and “any equipment attached to or protruding from the facade”. It also requires balcony guards and railings to be checked for whether their parts are positively secured against movement; any that are not are filed as unsafe.

An unsafe filing is the building’s problem, not yours. The owner must start repairs at once, put up whatever the public needs, such as sidewalk sheds, fences or netting, and correct the condition within 90 days or on a timetable the inspector sets, with monthly penalties if it stays uncorrected. That is the arithmetic behind the conditions boards reach for first: mount on the inside of the railing, never the street side; add a secondary tether; and take the panel down, at your cost, whenever the inspector or the facade contractor needs the railing. The inspection cycle, the fire-escape rule (nothing may obstruct one) and what an inspector looks for are on [the facade and fire-escape rules page](https://balco.nyc/nyc-fire-escape-facade-rules).

## What a board can refuse, and what a court will review

The leading New York case on board power is itself an alteration dispute. In *Levandusky v One Fifth Avenue Apartment Corp.* (75 NY2d 530, decided 5 April 1990), a shareholder moved a two-inch steam riser during a kitchen renovation, despite a lease clause requiring the corporation’s prior written consent, and the board issued a stop-work order; the dispute also covered three air conditioners that the Landmarks Preservation Commission had cited. The Court of Appeals held that “so long as the board acts for the purposes of the cooperative, within the scope of its authority and in good faith, courts will not substitute their judgment for the board’s.” A challenger must show that the decision has no legitimate relationship to the building’s welfare, deliberately singles someone out, was made without considering the relevant facts, or exceeds the board’s authority. New York courts give condo boards the same deference. Where a proprietary lease promises that consent to alterations will not be unreasonably withheld, the test becomes reasonableness, but in 2018 the Appellate Division upheld a refusal under such a clause (*Perrault v Village Dunes Apt. Corp.*) as legitimately related to the co-op’s welfare.

Most refusals a board is likely to give would survive that review:

- anything on the street side of the railing, or hanging over a sidewalk, yard or neighbor’s terrace;

- anything that drills into the facade, parapet, balcony slab or waterproofing;

- a device installed before the SUNNY Act takes effect, while New York still requires utility approval to connect one, or one without a listing for the complete system. As of September 2026 no complete plug-in system is listed to [UL 3700](https://balco.nyc/ul-3700-plug-in-solar-certification), so a board that waits for one is not being arbitrary;

- a railing the board’s engineer cannot vouch for, or any placement near a fire escape;

- a building-wide rule about what may be visible from the street, applied evenly.

The refusals most open to challenge fit *Levandusky*’s exceptions: treating you differently from a neighbor whose identical installation was approved, or a decision driven by a director’s private interest. In 2023 the Appellate Division let a shareholder’s claim proceed against two board members he alleged had blocked his penthouse renovation at 860 Fifth Avenue because of its effect on their own apartment (*Tahari v 860 Fifth Ave. Corp.*). Filed in 2018, the case was back before that court in October 2025. Set against a panel worth at most about $205 a year (section 6), the realistic remedy is persuasion, not a lawsuit.

## The request packet

Start with what the panel is worth, because that sets how much process is worth paying for. balco.nyc’s PVWatts runs for New York City put an unshaded 800 W vertical railing system, after the site’s 0.95 railing factor, at 635.7 × 0.95 = **604 kWh** a year facing south, 446 facing east, 421 west and 167 north. At Con Edison’s 34¢ marginal rate that is about **$205**, $152, $143 and $57 a year. Those are ceilings: no shade from the buildings opposite, and every kWh used in the apartment as it is made ([why that matters](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-net-metering)). A mid-range kit costs about $1,200; a review deposit that rivals it changes the decision, so ask about fees first. [The calculator](https://balco.nyc/) gives the figure for your own railing.

- **Your documents, read first.** The proprietary lease and house rules, or the declaration, bylaws and rules. Look for clauses on alterations, the exterior, window air conditioners and terraces, and for whether consent may not be unreasonably withheld.

- **One page on the device.** Product, the certification listing for the complete system, panel size and weight, inverter output (the SUNNY Act caps it at 1,200 W), and the anti-islanding function that stops it within two seconds of a grid outage.

- **A mounting drawing and photos.** Inside face of the railing, clamped not drilled, a secondary tether to a solid anchor, and the cable through an existing opening. If there is a fire escape, show the panel clear of it.

- **The outlet.** Which existing outdoor receptacle it uses and what else is on that circuit. If there is none, adding one is electrical work: in New York City that means a licensed electrician and, for most work, a Department of Buildings permit, and it becomes an ordinary alteration of its own.

- **An insurance certificate.** From your unit-owner policy, naming the corporation or board and its agents, at the limit your building’s form sets ($1,000,000 in the City Bar’s co-op model).

- **Signed undertakings.** An indemnity; removal on request for facade inspection or repair, before a sale, and if the building later adopts a rule against the devices; restoration of the railing at your cost.

- **Two specific asks.** Approval conditional on the SUNNY Act taking effect and on a listed device, and a waiver or cap on review fees for work that involves no construction.

Consider asking for a policy rather than an exception, as buildings already have for the other appliance hung on a facade, the window air conditioner. A house rule for plug-in panels (placement, a mounting standard, insurance, removal) lets the board’s engineer review one design once and makes the next request routine. The Attorney General’s co-op guide notes that a request backed by many shareholders carries more weight, and that an organized group can seek to elect new directors. Put the request in writing, and get the answer and any conditions in writing too.

> **Not legal advice.** This page describes model forms, a court standard and city rules as of 23 September 2026. Your lease or declaration and your building’s own forms decide your case, and a lawyer who handles co-op and condo matters can read them with you.

## Common questions

**Can my co-op board stop me installing balcony solar in New York City?**

Yes. A co-op's proprietary lease typically requires the corporation's consent before equipment is installed or anything is altered, and no New York law gives a shareholder a right to a railing-mounted panel. The SUNNY Act, which has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature, removes only the utility barrier. Courts review a refusal under the business judgment rule from Levandusky v One Fifth Avenue Apartment Corp. (1990) and defer to it if the board acted in good faith, within its authority and for the building's purposes. This is not legal advice.

**Does a New York City condo owner need board approval for a balcony solar panel?**

Almost always. New York's Condominium Act lets a unit include a balcony, but main walls and fire escapes are common elements, and a panel clamped to a railing on the facade affects property the owners hold in common. Condo bylaws and alteration agreements generally forbid changes to common elements or penetrations of exterior walls without the board's consent; the NYC Bar's 2026 model condo agreement leaves that to the board's sole and absolute discretion.

**How many New York City homes are in co-ops or condos?**

balco.nyc's count of the city's PLUTO tax-lot file (version 26v2, August 2026) finds 462,218 co-op apartments and 262,207 individually owned condo units: 724,425 homes, or 19.4% of 3.74 million. Another 149,017 apartments are in rental buildings legally structured as condominiums. In Manhattan the co-op and owned-condo share is 33.4%. The 2023 Housing and Vacancy Survey, as reported by the City Comptroller, counted 450,000 occupied co-op apartments and 318,000 in condominiums.

**What does a co-op or condo alteration agreement ask for?**

The NYC Bar's model forms ask for plans and specifications (by a licensed architect or engineer if the board requires), review by the board's engineer, security and review deposits, liability insurance naming the building (at least $1,000,000 in the co-op model), an indemnity, any government permits the work needs, no penetration of exterior walls, and a commitment to maintain the work and restore it after building repairs. A buyer of the apartment must take the agreement on.

**Can I sue my co-op or condo board if it refuses balcony solar?**

You can, but New York courts defer to boards under the business judgment rule. A challenger must show the decision has no legitimate relationship to the building's welfare, singles them out, was made without considering the relevant facts, or exceeds the board's authority. Litigation is also slow and costly next to the stakes: balco.nyc's PVWatts runs put an unshaded south-facing 800 W railing system in New York City at about 604 kWh a year, worth about $205 at Con Edison's marginal rate.

**I rent an apartment in a co-op or condo. Whose permission do I need for balcony solar?**

Both the apartment owner's and the board's. The owner is bound by the proprietary lease or condominium documents and would sign any alteration agreement, so the request goes through them. Neither the SUNNY Act nor any other New York law requires either of them to agree.

## Sources

- [NYC Open Data (Department of City Planning) — Primary Land Use Tax Lot Output (PLUTO)](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/Primary-Land-Use-Tax-Lot-Output-PLUTO-/64uk-42ks): version 26v2; residential units, building class and condominium number for every tax lot, which balco.nyc grouped by borough and class through the Socrata API on 23 September 2026.

- [New York City Bar Association — Notes to New Form of Condominium Alteration Agreement](https://www.nycbar.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/20221592-Notes-for-City-Bar-2025-Condo-Alt-Agmt_FINAL.pdf): approval by the City and State bar associations, the aim of an industry standard, sponsor-controlled boards restricting renovations before a permanent certificate of occupancy, insurance set with the building’s insurer, and assignment to a purchaser.

Corp., 75 NY2d 530 (1990)](https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/archives/levandusky_one.htm): the steam riser and air conditioners, the business judgment standard, and the four grounds on which a board decision can be reviewed.
- [Smith, Buss & Jacobs LLP — Are Boards Always Protected by the “Business Judgment” Rule? (2019)](https://www.sbjlaw.com/blogs/are-boards-always-protected-by-the-business-judgment-rule/): the rule applied to co-op and condo boards, and Perrault v Village Dunes Apt. Corp. (2d Dept 2018) on leases requiring that consent not be unreasonably withheld.

- [FindLaw — Tahari v 860 Fifth Ave. Corp., Appellate Division, First Department (9 October 2025)](https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/ny-supreme-court-appellate-division/117812552.html): the same 2018 action (index no. 654702/18) before the Appellate Division again in October 2025.

# Fire escapes, egress and façade rules for balcony solar in NYC

URL: https://balco.nyc/nyc-fire-escape-facade-rules  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

A fire escape is not a balcony, and nothing may be mounted on it: the Fire Code, the Housing Maintenance Code and the Multiple Dwelling Law all forbid obstructing one, and balco.nyc’s search of HPD’s violation records finds six citations for solar panels on fire escapes, half of them since January 2025. A true balcony is a different question. balco.nyc’s count of the city’s PLUTO tax-lot data puts 1.15 million homes, 30.8% of New York City’s 3.74 million, in buildings over six floors, where the Façade Inspection & Safety Program (Local Law 11) has every balcony railing examined every five years.

## A fire escape is not a balcony

New Yorkers call the platform outside a fire-escape window a balcony, and so does the law. The Housing Maintenance Code defines a fire escape as “a combination of outside balconies and stairs providing an unobstructed means of egress” (§27-2004). The last three words are the point: a fire escape is an exit that happens to be outdoors. Three separate laws say nothing may be placed on it.

| Rule | What it requires | Applies to |
|---|---|---|
| NYC Fire Code FC 1027.7 (2022 edition) | Fire escapes, “and access thereto”, kept in operational condition and “continuously maintained free from obstructions and impediments” | All buildings; enforced by the FDNY |
| Housing Maintenance Code §27-2007(c) | No tenant “or any other person” may place any encumbrance before or upon a fire escape, or obstruct access to it | Dwellings; enforced by HPD |
| Multiple Dwelling Law §53(8)(c) | No person may place “any encumbrance of any kind” before or upon any fire escape | Multiple dwellings (state law) |

HPD’s inspectors already apply those words to solar panels. balco.nyc searched the free-text description of every violation in HPD’s open Housing Maintenance Code Violations dataset for “solar” and found **six citations for panels on fire escapes**. Five were written as class B orders to “remove the encumbrance obstructing egress from fire escapes” (the Bronx in 2015, Brooklyn in 2019, the Bronx in 2022 and May 2026, Brooklyn in July 2026). The sixth, in the Bronx in January 2025, was class C, immediately hazardous, for solar panels “attached to 3rd sty balcony of fire escape”. Half of the six date from 2025 or later, and the two from 2026 were still open on 23 September. HPD has also written four class C violations since 2015 for rooftop arrays blocking the route from the roof bulkhead to a fire escape or the gooseneck ladder. A text search misses any panel an inspector described in other words, so six is a floor, not a count.

Nothing in the [SUNNY Act](https://balco.nyc/sunny-act) changes this. The bill has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature. Its text requires a device to be installed in accordance with the state fire prevention and building code and never mentions fire escapes or egress. The caption under the illustration on balco.nyc’s home page, “never mount panels on a fire escape or block another exit route”, describes the law as it stands.

## What counts as an obstruction

None of the three texts sets a size, a weight or a time limit, and “any encumbrance of any kind” includes a flowerpot. Flowerpots are in fact much of the enforcement. balco.nyc pulled all **5,503** fire-escape encumbrance violations (HPD order 539) issued in 2025, at 2,892 buildings, and counted what the inspectors wrote down. One violation often names several things, so the rows overlap:

| What the 2025 violation names | Violations | Share of 5,503 |
|---|---|---|
| Household items or storage | 2,073 | 38% |
| Plants or flowerpots | 2,015 | 37% |
| Air conditioners (680 of them described as protruding) | 1,060 | 19% |
| Bicycles, grills, furniture, wires, antennas or dishes | 149 | 3% |
| None of the above named | 555 | 10% |

All 5,503 were class B, which HPD gives an owner 30 days to correct. Brooklyn had 1,999 of them, the Bronx 1,659, Manhattan 1,034, Queens 656 and Staten Island 155. The counts are keyword matches on HPD’s own wording, done by balco.nyc, not an HPD classification.

The Fire Code adds detail that maps directly onto a solar install:

- **The window is part of the fire escape.** The code protects the access as well as the platform. FC 1027.7.3 bars an air conditioner from a window that gives access to a fire escape unless another window in the same room also does, and HPD writes up units that stick out onto the platform. A panel hung outside that window, or a cord that stops it opening fully, raises the same objection.

- **The drop ladder needs its path.** FC 1027.7.4 says a drop ladder’s operation may not be obstructed by awnings, furniture, heaters, parked cars “or other obstructions”. Nothing may sit where the ladder comes down, in a yard or on a lower terrace.

- **The roof route counts.** The four rooftop class C citations were for arrays in the way of the path from the bulkhead to fire escapes or the gooseneck ladder.

- **A balcony can be egress without looking like a fire escape.** The Housing Maintenance Code describes fire towers entered through a “communicating balcony”, and some balconies connect to a stair, a neighbor’s balcony or a drop ladder. If yours does, treat it as a fire escape and ask the managing agent before anything else.

## Two rulebooks, two sets of buildings

The fire-escape rules apply to any building that has one. The Façade Inspection & Safety Program (FISP) applies only above six stories. To see how the city’s housing splits across that line, balco.nyc counted every tax lot with residential units and more than six floors in the city’s PLUTO file (version 26v2), and set the result beside DOB’s own façade filings for Cycle 9, the last complete cycle (February 2020 to February 2025). The FISP columns include commercial buildings; the PLUTO columns are residential only.

| Borough | Residential lots over six floors | Homes in them | Share of the borough’s homes | Buildings filing a Cycle 9 FISP report | First report “unsafe” |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Manhattan | 5,254 | 589,987 | 61.5% | 7,969 | 23.9% |
| Bronx | 1,160 | 187,251 | 31.7% | 1,680 | 27.3% |
| Brooklyn | 1,827 | 224,471 | 20.1% | 1,893 | 29.5% |
| Queens | 998 | 141,837 | 15.9% | 1,769 | 21.9% |
| Staten Island | 34 | 6,765 | 3.8% | 94 | 34.0% |
| New York City | 9,273 | 1,150,311 | 30.8% | 13,405 | 24.9% |

So **30.8% of the city’s 3,736,645 homes** are in buildings whose façades, balcony railings included, a licensed inspector must examine every five years. In Manhattan it is 61.5%. Another 917,711 homes (24.6%) are in five- and six-floor buildings just under the line.

In practice the two rulebooks barely overlap. Matching the 2,862 tax lots HPD cited for fire-escape encumbrances in 2025 against PLUTO, balco.nyc finds that **2,816 (98.4%) have six floors or fewer**, 1,837 of them five or six. Only 41 are over six floors. HPD inspects mostly in response to complaints, so this shows where citations land, not where every fire escape is. The practical reading holds anyway: in a walk-up the fire escape is the constraint, and above six floors the façade program is.

The count has known gaps. PLUTO gives one floor count per tax lot, for its tallest building, and leaves out above-ground basements, while the rule also reaches six stories over a cellar that stands more than halfway out of the ground. Another 1,867 residential lots have no floor count at all. DOB describes the program as overseeing about 16,000 buildings in Cycle 9; its filings list 16,538 building records.

## What a Local Law 11 façade inspector checks on a balcony

The program began as Local Law 10 of 1980, after falling terra cotta killed a Barnard student on West 115th Street in 1979, and was widened by Local Law 11 of 1998, the name most people still use. Under 1 RCNY §103-04, the owner of a building over six stories must have a Qualified Exterior Wall Inspector (QEWI), an architect or engineer qualified by DOB, examine every exterior wall and appurtenance once in each five-year cycle. Cycle 10 began on 21 February 2025. The deadline depends on the last digit of the tax block: 4, 5, 6 or 9 by February 2027; 0, 7 or 8 by February 2028; 1, 2 or 3 by February 2029.

Three parts of the rule decide what an attached panel means:

- **What gets inspected.** The rule’s list of appurtenances names railings, guard rails, balcony enclosures, window air conditioners, flower boxes and satellite dishes, and ends with “any equipment attached to or protruding from the facade”. It does not mention solar panels, and balco.nyc found no DOB guidance on plug-in panels. A panel clamped to a balcony railing is at least hardware on an inspected appurtenance. Whether the QEWI records it as an appurtenance in its own right is the inspector’s judgment.

- **The railing standard.** Guards and railings, balconies included, must be checked to confirm that balusters, intermediate rails and panel fillers are “positively secured against movement”, and any that is not is classified unsafe. A panel’s wind load runs through exactly those connections.

- **One condition is enough.** A single unsafe condition classifies the whole building as unsafe until an amended report certifies the repair. The owner must start repairs at once, put up sidewalk sheds, fences or netting where needed to protect the public, and correct the condition within 90 days unless DOB allows longer.

That is the background a board hears a solar request against. Of the 13,405 buildings that filed in Cycle 9, **24.9%** filed their first report as unsafe and another 42.7% as SWARMP (safe with a repair and maintenance program). Two in three needed work before anyone clamped anything to a railing. The filings do not say which conditions were railings.

Whether a clamp-on panel needs a DOB permit is also unsettled. DOB’s rule on work that can skip a permit (1 RCNY §101-14, Table 3) says installing appurtenances such as satellite dishes, awnings, flagpoles and larger signs “to the exterior wall or at perimeters of balconies, terraces, or rooftops” does need one, except at one- and two-family homes. Solar panels are not on that list, and balco.nyc found no DOB statement either way. The closest listed item needs a permit, which is a reason to ask the building’s architect or engineer rather than assume. What to put in front of a board is on [the co-op and condo board guide](https://balco.nyc/nyc-coop-condo-board-balcony-solar).

## Wind and falling objects: what the rules do and do not say

balco.nyc found no New York City rule that says how an object on an occupied balcony must be fastened. The code’s explicit wind rule, Building Code §3303.4.5.1, requires material on an exposed floor or roof to be “secured or otherwise safeguarded to prevent dislodgement by wind”. But it sits in Chapter 33, which governs construction and demolition operations, not a finished balcony, and citing it for a balcony panel would overstate the law.

What does apply is broader. The owner must keep the building and every part of it in a safe condition (Administrative Code §28-301), which is why a board carries the risk and not only the resident. And DOB’s weather advisories spell out what it expects before a storm. The one issued on 29 December 2025, with wind gusts forecast up to 45 mph, told property owners to bring in potted plants and lawn furniture, anchor grills, and “remove aerial antennas and satellite television dishes”.

A satellite dish is the nearest household analogue to a railing panel, and DOB’s storm advice for it is removal. A panel you will not take down for every advisory has to be mounted so that it never needs to be: inside the railing, on the manufacturer’s brackets, with a tether independent of them. The mounting detail is in [how to install balcony solar](https://balco.nyc/install-balcony-solar), and the electrical risks are in [is plug-in solar safe](https://balco.nyc/is-plug-in-solar-safe).

## Four questions before you ask the building

- **Is it a fire escape, or part of one?** A stair, a ladder, an opening in the floor, a drop ladder below or a link to other platforms means yes. The answer is then no, and the rest of this list does not matter.

- **Does the plan touch a fire-escape window?** The panel, its bracket and its cord must stay clear of any window that gives access to a fire escape, including a neighbor’s.

- **Is the building over six floors?** Then the railing is on a five-year inspection cycle. Offer to mount inside the railing without drilling, give the board the product’s weight and mounting instructions, and commit to removing the panel for the inspection and for any façade work.

- **Who else has a say?** Landmarked buildings add the Landmarks Preservation Commission ([landmarks and balcony solar](https://balco.nyc/nyc-landmarks-balcony-solar)). Rent-stabilized tenants and NYCHA residents have their own constraints ([rent stabilization and NYCHA](https://balco.nyc/nyc-rent-stabilized-nycha-balcony-solar)). The utility side is on [Con Edison and plug-in solar](https://balco.nyc/con-edison-plug-in-solar).

This page summarizes city and state rules as written on 23 September 2026. It is not legal advice, and the building’s own architect or engineer, and the agencies named here, decide individual cases.

## Common questions

**Can I put a solar panel on my fire escape in New York City?**

No. The NYC Fire Code (FC 1027.7) requires fire escapes and access to them to be kept free of obstructions, and the Housing Maintenance Code (section 27-2007) and the Multiple Dwelling Law (section 53) forbid placing any encumbrance on one. HPD enforces this against solar panels: balco.nyc found six HPD violations since 2015 citing solar panels on fire escapes, including one in the Bronx in January 2025 classed as immediately hazardous. The platform of a fire escape is legally a balcony, but it is an exit route, not usable space.

**What counts as obstructing a fire escape in NYC?**

Anything placed on the platform, stairs or ladder, or in front of the window that gives access to it; the laws set no minimum size. In 2025 HPD issued 5,503 fire-escape encumbrance violations at 2,892 buildings. By balco.nyc's keyword count, 37% named plants or flowerpots, 38% household items or storage and 19% air conditioners, mostly units protruding onto the platform. The Fire Code also bars anything that stops a drop ladder from reaching the ground.

**Does Local Law 11 (FISP) apply to a solar panel on a balcony railing?**

It applies to the railing, in any building over six stories. The Facade Inspection & Safety Program rule, 1 RCNY 103-04, requires a Qualified Exterior Wall Inspector to examine every appurtenance every five years, lists railings and 'any equipment attached to or protruding from the facade', and classes any railing whose parts are not positively secured against movement as unsafe. Solar panels are not named in the rule and DOB has issued no guidance on plug-in panels, so how an inspector records one is a judgment call.

**How many New York City homes are in buildings subject to facade inspections?**

About 1.15 million, or 30.8% of the city's 3.74 million homes, by balco.nyc's count of residential tax lots with more than six floors in the city's PLUTO data (version 26v2). The share is 61.5% in Manhattan, 31.7% in the Bronx, 20.1% in Brooklyn, 15.9% in Queens and 3.8% on Staten Island. The count slightly understates coverage, because the rule also reaches some six-story buildings over a raised cellar.

**Do I need a Department of Buildings permit to attach a solar panel to a balcony railing?**

It is not settled. DOB's rule on permit-exempt work, 1 RCNY 101-14, says installing appurtenances such as satellite dishes, awnings and flagpoles at the perimeter of a balcony requires a permit in buildings other than one- and two-family homes, but it does not mention solar panels, and balco.nyc found no DOB statement on clamp-on plug-in panels. Ask the building's architect or engineer before assuming no permit is needed.

**Does the SUNNY Act allow solar panels on fire escapes?**

No. New York's SUNNY Act (S8512C / A9111C) has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature. It would exempt small plug-in systems from utility interconnection rules and requires them to be installed in accordance with the fire prevention and building code. It says nothing about fire escapes or egress and gives no right to install, so the Fire Code and Housing Maintenance Code prohibitions still apply.

# Balcony solar in an NYC landmark or historic district: does LPC approval apply?

URL: https://balco.nyc/nyc-landmarks-balcony-solar  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

Almost certainly yes, if the panel attaches to the building: the Landmarks Law requires a Landmarks Preservation Commission permit for any addition to a designated building’s exterior, even work that needs no Buildings Department permit. LPC has written no rule for balcony panels — its solar criteria cover only roofs — so a street-facing railing panel would go to a public hearing. balco.nyc’s count of the city’s PLUTO tax-lot data puts 253,715 homes, 6.8% of New York City’s residential units, in historic districts or on individual landmark lots, and 17.2% of Manhattan’s.

## The short answer, and how many homes it reaches

If the panel attaches to the outside of a designated building — clamped, strapped or bolted to a balcony railing — the Landmarks Law almost certainly requires a Landmarks Preservation Commission (LPC) permit before it goes up. The law defines “minor work” as any “addition to” the parts of a building that needs no Buildings Department permit, and makes it unlawful to do such work without an LPC permit (Administrative Code §§25-302 and 25-310). LPC’s own permit page says the same in plain terms: exterior work needs its permit even when the Buildings Department requires none.

LPC has written nothing about balcony or plug-in panels. Its solar criteria (§2-21 of its rules, Title 63 of the Rules of the City of New York) cover roofs and rooftop structures, and no staff-level rule covers equipment on a street-facing facade. On the rules as written, a front-balcony panel goes to the full Commission at a public hearing.

balco.nyc counted who this affects, using the city’s PLUTO tax-lot data (release 26v2, August 2026). **253,715 homes on 30,344 tax lots — 6.8% of New York City’s 3,736,645 residential units — are in a historic district or on an individual landmark lot.** In Manhattan it is 17.2%, about one home in six, and a third of the borough’s residential lots.

| Borough | Residential lots regulated | Homes regulated | Share of the borough’s homes | Share of its residential lots |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Manhattan | 10,777 | 164,582 | 17.2% | 33.2% |
| Brooklyn | 14,930 | 62,688 | 5.6% | 6.0% |
| Queens | 3,555 | 15,592 | 1.8% | 1.2% |
| Bronx | 813 | 10,173 | 1.7% | 1.1% |
| Staten Island | 269 | 680 | 0.4% | 0.2% |
| New York City | 30,344 | 253,715 | 6.8% | 4.0% |

How balco.nyc counted: a lot is included if PLUTO’s histdist field names a historic district or its landmark field records an individual landmark; “homes” is PLUTO’s unitsres. Lots with only an interior landmark (26 lots, 364 units) are excluded, since that designation does not reach the facade. So are two Roosevelt Island lots (8,383 units) that PLUTO flags because the Octagon and the Chapel of the Good Shepherd stand on them; the apartment towers around them are not designated. Historic districts hold 90% of the total.

## The five historic districts with the most homes

From the same count, these are the five historic districts, as PLUTO names them, with the most residential units:

|  | Historic district | Borough | Homes | Residential lots |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Upper West Side/Central Park West | Manhattan | 28,602 | 1,675 |
| 2 | Greenwich Village | Manhattan | 21,219 | 1,709 |
| 3 | Upper East Side | Manhattan | 10,117 | 814 |
| 4 | Brooklyn Heights | Brooklyn | 9,519 | 1,179 |
| 5 | Riverside–West End Extension II | Manhattan | 8,652 | 290 |

LPC designated Riverside–West End in three parts. Taken together, the district and its two extensions hold 18,772 homes and would rank third. Next on the list are Jackson Heights in Queens (8,062) and Park Slope in Brooklyn (7,356).

Most regulated homes are in apartment buildings, not rowhouses. Three in four regulated residential lots (73%) hold one to five homes, but **81% of regulated homes are in buildings of six or more units**, where a board or landlord stands between the resident and LPC. The individual landmarks include two public-housing developments, Williamsburg Houses and Harlem River Houses; NYCHA residents face their own rules, covered in [the rent-stabilized and NYCHA guide](https://balco.nyc/nyc-rent-stabilized-nycha-balcony-solar).

## What LPC’s solar rules cover, and what they leave out

LPC’s rules define “mechanical equipment” to include “solar and wind power equipment” (63 RCNY §2-21(b)), so a solar panel is regulated like a condenser or a generator. Amendments adopted on 11 July 2023, in effect since August 2023, widened what staff can approve without a hearing. The criteria in §2-21(g)(3), unchanged in the current compilation (effective 25 July 2024), allow:

- **Flat roofs:** arrays that are “minimally visible” over any facade if placed to minimize visibility, and more visible over a rear or side facade only when seen through a gap of 25 feet or less between buildings.

- **Pergolas, bulkheads and other rooftop structures:** panels parallel and close to the surface, black-on-black if visible.

- **Sloped roofs:** panels visible over the street front only where other locations lack sun, in a small black-on-black footprint, off slate or tile, and not on an individual landmark.

“Minimally visible” is defined by numbers. Seen from any public thoroughfare, the equipment may project no more than 12 inches into the line of sight if it is under 60 feet up, rising to 36 inches above 100 feet, or it must not “call attention to itself.” A panel on the outside of a street-facing railing is in full view, so it cannot meet the first test.

The words balcony and railing do not appear in any of those criteria. The nearest rule is §2-21(e), for wall-mounted HVAC “and other mechanical equipment” on *secondary* facades, meaning rear or side walls that do not face a street. Staff will approve such equipment if it is minimally visible, or more visible when it is seen next to utilitarian features such as fire escapes, sits in the least visible spot, attaches reversibly and has a neutral finish. Apart from window and through-wall air conditioners, there is no matching provision for a primary facade, meaning one that faces a street. LPC’s April 2024 solar fact sheet encourages proposals outside the rules to seek a public hearing.

Nothing pending changes this. The amendments LPC calendared in July 2026 would add a rule for new metal balconies on rear facades and touch §2-21 only for louvers. balco.nyc also checked LPC’s permit-application dataset (351,502 records, updated 21 September 2026). Of 524 solar applications since the current work-type categories began in April 2023, 424 were tagged “flat roof”, 102 “sloped roof” and 2 “other”. **No record in the dataset carries a work type naming a balcony or a railing.**

## Is a removable railing panel an “alteration”?

Removability does not take it outside LPC’s reach. LPC’s solar fact sheet itself calls mechanical equipment temporary and reversible in nature, and regulates it anyway; its rules even provide permits for temporary signs and artwork that stay up a year or less (§2-05). Reversibility is a criterion for approval, not an exemption. The law’s test is whether something is added to the building, and a clamp on the railing adds something.

Which permit applies depends on the Buildings Department. If the installation needs no DOB permit, it is minor work and needs a Permit for Minor Work (§25-310). If it does need one, LPC issues a Certificate of No Effect when the work does not harm protected features (§25-306), or the full Commission decides on a Certificate of Appropriateness (§25-307). Whether DOB wants its own permit is a separate question, covered in [the facade and fire-escape guide](https://balco.nyc/nyc-fire-escape-facade-rules).

Only two LPC exemptions come close. Seasonal window air conditioners that sit within the window frame need none (§2-21(c)(1)), and its Permit Guidebook exempts temporary signs that do not physically attach to the building or can easily be moved. Neither mentions solar. A panel standing on the balcony floor, attached to nothing, falls in a gap LPC has not addressed. Ask LPC before buying (its permits page gives 212-669-7817) and get the answer in writing.

| Where the panel goes | Nearest LPC rule | Likely route |
|---|---|---|
| Street-facing balcony railing | None: no staff rule for equipment on a primary facade | Public hearing; Certificate of Appropriateness if approved |
| Rear balcony, not visible from a street or park | §2-21(e), by analogy | Probably staff level (PMW or CNE); LPC’s call |
| Rear balcony seen through a gap or beside a fire escape | §2-21(e)(1) | Possibly staff level, if in the least visible spot with a neutral finish |
| Roof or setback terrace | §2-21(g)(3), flat-roof criteria | Staff level if minimally visible |
| Freestanding on the balcony floor, attached to nothing | None | Unaddressed; ask LPC in writing |

The easy route and the sunny side are not always the same wall. Manhattan’s grid is rotated about 29° from true north (see [does my balcony get enough sun](https://balco.nyc/balcony-sunlight)), so buildings on a cross street face roughly 29° or 209°. balco.nyc’s PVWatts runs for an 800 W vertical railing system in New York City, after the 5% railing loss, give 604 kWh a year facing 180°, 562 facing 225°, 265 facing 45° and 167 facing 0°. So the rear wall of a building on the south side of a cross street, facing about 209°, sits between 562 and 604 kWh: roughly $191–$205 a year at Con Edison’s 34¢ marginal rate. On the north side the rear faces about 29° and sits between 167 and 265 kWh, $57–$90, and the sunny wall is the street front LPC protects most. These are unshaded ceilings.

## How to ask LPC, and how long it takes

Every application goes through Portico, LPC’s online permit portal ([portico.lpc.nyc.gov](https://portico.lpc.nyc.gov/)). There is no fee to submit an application. The owner must sign it, and LPC’s rules spell out who counts as the owner (63 RCNY §2-01):

- **Co-op:** the president or another appropriate officer of the co-op board. The managing agent’s signature is not sufficient.

- **Condo:** an officer of the condominium association for common areas, which often include balconies. A unit owner signs only for work on their own unit (see [condo and co-op rules](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-condo-hoa)).

- **Rental:** the landlord (see [renters and landlords](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-renters)).

LPC has published no checklist for a balcony panel. Adapted from its rooftop solar fact sheet, a complete application would include photographs of the facade, balcony and street; the panel’s product cut sheet; a dimensioned drawing of how the panel, clamps and safety tether attach and where the cable runs; a mock-up photographed from the sidewalk at LPC’s 6-foot eye level; and a statement of how the panel comes off without damaging the railing.

A building expecting several requests can apply for a master plan (§2-02). It sets one approved design, and each later installation that conforms to it gets a staff-level permit.

By law, LPC must act within 20 working days for a Permit for Minor Work, 30 for a Certificate of No Effect and 90 for a Certificate of Appropriateness, counted from when the application is complete. Actual times are shorter. balco.nyc measured the gap between the received and issue dates LPC records for applications received in 2024 and 2025:

| Outcome | Applications | Median days, received to issued |
|---|---|---|
| Permit for Minor Work (staff) | 3,663 | 15 |
| Certificate of No Effect (staff) | 7,955 | 17 |
| Approved at a public hearing (status update letter) | 428 | 109 |
| Solar-only applications, April 2023 to September 2026 (CNE) | 438 | 8 |

Solar has become routine on roofs. Of 470 applications since April 2023 whose only listed work was solar, 438 (93%) ended in a staff-level Certificate of No Effect. Brooklyn filed 372 of the 524 solar applications, Manhattan 62. None of that predicts how a railing panel would fare; the dataset has no category for one.

## What LPC approval means for the board, and what it doesn’t

The order is fixed: **the board or landlord comes first**, because LPC will not take an application without the owner’s signature. An LPC permit is then necessary but not sufficient. It says the work is acceptable for the landmark. It does not oblige the building to allow it. In New York a board’s decision made in good faith, within its authority and for the building’s purposes will generally stand, as [the co-op and condo board guide](https://balco.nyc/nyc-coop-condo-board-balcony-solar) explains. The reverse also holds: board consent without an LPC permit still leaves a Landmarks Law violation.

That is why boards in historic districts ask about LPC early. LPC’s enforcement is aimed at the property owner, and it holds the current owner responsible even for work a prior owner did without permits. The usual sequence is a warning letter, then a summons heard at the Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings. An unpermitted panel is the building’s violation to cure, and a permit removes that risk: often the most useful thing a resident can bring to a skeptical board.

LPC approval also does not make plug-in solar legal to connect. New York’s [SUNNY Act](https://balco.nyc/sunny-act) has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature. Its text does not mention landmarks, historic districts, landlords or boards, so it neither overrides LPC nor gives anyone a right to install. See [Con Edison and plug-in solar](https://balco.nyc/con-edison-plug-in-solar) for the utility side and [how to install balcony solar](https://balco.nyc/install-balcony-solar) for the physical checks.

> **Not legal advice.** This page reads the Landmarks Law, LPC’s rules and its published data as of 23 September 2026. LPC has not ruled on a plug-in balcony panel, so how it would treat yours is a judgment its staff or Commission makes case by case. Check your building’s status on LPC’s [Discover NYC Landmarks map](https://experience.arcgis.com/experience/fa1bcaad31374a88839da3f0166e640a/) and ask LPC before you buy.

## Common questions

**Do I need LPC approval to put a solar panel on my balcony in an NYC historic district?**

If the panel attaches to the building, almost certainly yes. The Landmarks Law requires an LPC permit for any addition to the exterior of a designated building, including work that needs no Buildings Department permit (Administrative Code sections 25-302 and 25-310). LPC has not ruled on plug-in balcony panels specifically, so ask it in writing before buying. This is not legal advice.

**Does the Landmarks Preservation Commission have rules for balcony or plug-in solar panels?**

No. As of September 2026, LPC's staff-level solar criteria (63 RCNY section 2-21(g)(3)) cover flat roofs, sloped roofs and rooftop structures only. The closest provision is section 2-21(e), for wall-mounted mechanical equipment on rear and side facades. No rule lets staff approve equipment on a street-facing facade, so a front-balcony panel would go to a public hearing.

**How many New York City homes are in historic districts or landmarks?**

balco.nyc's count of the city's PLUTO tax-lot data (release 26v2) puts 253,715 residential units on 30,344 tax lots in historic districts or on individual landmark lots: 6.8% of the city's 3,736,645 units. Manhattan has 164,582 of them, 17.2% of its homes. Historic districts account for 90% of the total.

**How long does LPC take to approve solar panels?**

For rooftop solar, usually days. In LPC's permit data, applications since April 2023 whose only work was solar got a staff-level Certificate of No Effect in 93% of cases, with a median of 8 days from receipt to issue. Proposals that go to a public hearing took a median of 109 days to approval in 2024-2025. The legal limits, counted from a complete application, are 20, 30 and 90 working days for the three permit types.

**Can I apply to LPC myself if I live in a co-op or a rental?**

No. LPC's rules (63 RCNY section 2-01) require the owner's signature: an officer of the co-op board (a managing agent's signature is not enough), an officer of the condo association for common areas, which often include balconies, or the landlord for a rental. A condo owner signs only for work on their own unit. In practice the board or landlord has to agree before LPC will review the application.

**Does the SUNNY Act override landmark rules in New York?**

No. The SUNNY Act has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature. Its text does not mention landmarks, historic districts, landlords or boards. It deals with utility interconnection for compliant plug-in devices, not with building permission, so LPC permits and the building's consent would still be required.

**Can I avoid LPC review with a freestanding panel that is not attached to anything?**

Possibly, but LPC has not said. The law covers additions to a building, and LPC exempts seasonal window air conditioners and unattached, movable signs, but no exemption mentions solar. A panel standing on a balcony floor falls in an unaddressed gap. Call LPC (212-669-7817), describe it exactly, and get the answer in writing.

## Sources

- [NYC Administrative Code — Title 25, Chapter 3: Landmarks Preservation and Historic Districts](https://codelibrary.amlegal.com/codes/newyorkcity/latest/NYCadmin/0-0-0-133896): the Landmarks Law: definitions of “minor work”, “exterior architectural feature” and “ordinary repairs and maintenance” (§25-302); Certificate of No Effect (§25-306), Certificate of Appropriateness (§25-307) and Permit for Minor Work (§25-310). LPC’s own site links to this edition.
- [NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission — Rules (63 RCNY), compilation effective 25 July 2024](https://www.nyc.gov/assets/lpc/downloads/pdf/Rules/Rules_of_the_NYC_Landmarks_Preservation_Commission.pdf): §2-01 (who must sign), §2-02 (master plans), §2-05 (temporary installations), §2-21(b) (“mechanical equipment” includes solar; “minimally visible”), §2-21(c)(1) (window air conditioners), §2-21(e) (wall-mounted equipment on secondary facades) and §2-21(g)(3) (solar panels).
- [LPC — Fact Sheet: Installing Solar Panels (April 2024)](https://www.nyc.gov/assets/lpc/downloads/pdf/pubs/Solar%20Panels.pdf): solar treated as mechanical equipment and described as temporary and reversible; application materials (photos, drawings, cut sheets, mock-ups at 6-foot eye level); proposals outside the rules encouraged to seek a public hearing.

- [LPC — Permits and Making Alterations](https://www.nyc.gov/site/lpc/about/permits-and-making-alterations.page): most exterior changes to front and rear facades in historic districts need LPC review; ordinary repairs do not; the Commission’s number for questions about whether a permit is needed.
- [LPC — Apply on Portico](https://www.nyc.gov/site/lpc/applications/apply.page): Portico as the only filing route; statutory deadlines of 30, 20 and 90 working days for CNE, PMW and CofA.
- [LPC — Permit Guidebook (2025 edition)](https://www.nyc.gov/assets/lpc/downloads/pdf/LPC-Permit-Guidebook.pdf): owner attestation in co-op and condo buildings; review times; the signage exemption for signs not physically attached and easily moved.
- [LPC — Proposed Amendments to LPC Rules, calendared July 2026](https://www.nyc.gov/assets/lpc/downloads/pdf/Rules/LPC_Proposed_Rules_Amendments_07132026.pdf): the pending package: a new rule for rear metal balconies and a §2-21 change limited to louvers; nothing on solar at balconies.
- [LPC — LPC Approves New Rules Streamlining Procedures (11 July 2023)](https://www.nyc.gov/site/lpc/about/pr2023/lpc-approves-new-rules-streamlining-procedures.page): the 2023 amendments broadening the solar installations eligible for staff-level review.
- [LPC — Violations](https://www.nyc.gov/site/lpc/violations/violations.page): enforcement against owners, including for work by prior owners; warning letter, summons and OATH hearing.
- [NYC Open Data — Primary Land Use Tax Lot Output (PLUTO), release 26v2](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/Primary-Land-Use-Tax-Lot-Output-PLUTO-/64uk-42ks): the histdist, landmark and unitsres fields behind balco.nyc’s count of regulated homes by borough and district (queried 23 September 2026).
- [NYC Open Data — LPC Permit Application Information](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Housing-Development/LPC-Permit-Application-Information/dpm2-m9mq): 351,502 LPC permit records (updated 21 September 2026) behind balco.nyc’s counts of solar applications, work types and review times.
- [NYC Open Data — LPC Designated and Calendared Buildings and Sites](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Housing-Development/Designated-and-Calendared-Buildings-and-Sites/ncre-qhxs): used to confirm which structures on the two Roosevelt Island lots are designated, and to identify large landmark lots such as Williamsburg Houses and Harlem River Houses.
