# Rent-stabilized and NYCHA apartments: can you install balcony solar?

URL: https://balco.nyc/nyc-rent-stabilized-nycha-balcony-solar  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

Only with permission. Neither the Rent Stabilization Code nor NYCHA’s rules gives a tenant a right to attach a panel outside the apartment, and the SUNNY Act, which has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature, would not change that. The second question is who pays the electric bill: balco.nyc’s count of the 2023 Housing and Vacancy Survey finds 84.5% of rent-stabilized households pay for their own electricity but only 10.5% of public-housing households do, so in most NYCHA apartments a panel would cut the Authority’s bill, not the resident’s. Where a stabilized tenant pays Con Edison, an 800 W south railing panel is worth about $205 a year with an open view and $77 on a 3rd floor facing a 6-to-10-floor building across the street, against a median stabilized rent of $1,500 a month.

## Two questions: who says yes, and whose meter

A plug-in panel in a regulated apartment raises two separate questions. The first is permission. A rent-stabilized tenant needs the landlord’s; a public-housing resident needs NYCHA’s. Neither the Rent Stabilization Code nor NYCHA’s published rules gives a tenant a right to hang equipment outside the apartment, and New York’s [SUNNY Act](https://balco.nyc/sunny-act) would not create one.

The second question is whose electric bill the panel lowers. A plug-in panel feeds the apartment’s circuits, so it only slows the meter those circuits run through. If the electricity is included in the rent, that meter belongs to the landlord or to NYCHA, and so does the saving.

To size the second question, balco.nyc counted the public-use microdata of the **2023 New York City Housing and Vacancy Survey** (HVS), the triennial Census Bureau survey, sponsored by the city’s housing department, that classifies every rental by regulation status. It asks every household which utilities it pays. The estimates below are weighted, with 90% margins of error from the survey’s 80 replicate weights:

| Households, 2023 | Occupied units | Pay for their own electricity | Electricity included in rent |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rent-stabilized | 960,700 (±19,300) | 812,100 — 84.5% (±1.0 pt) | 148,700 (±9,900) |
| Public housing (NYCHA) | 167,700 (±2,400) | 17,600 — 10.5% (±1.8 pt) | 150,100 (±3,500) |
| Market-rate renters, for comparison | 1,118,500 (±26,900) | 80.4% (±1.7 pt) | 219,500 (±20,200) |

So a typical stabilized tenant is in the same position as any renter with a Con Edison account: with the landlord’s yes, the panel’s output comes off the tenant’s own bill. A typical NYCHA resident is not: nine public-housing households in ten have no electric bill for a panel to reduce. Two limits on the count: the survey asks which utilities a household pays, not whom it pays, so a tenant billed by the landlord through a submeter counts as paying; and the Census Bureau imputed the answer for 7.7% of stabilized households and 2.8% of public-housing ones.

## Rent stabilization: the lease decides, and the Code keeps it

The Rent Stabilization Code regulates rents, renewals and evictions. balco.nyc found nothing in it that gives a stabilized tenant a right to fix equipment to a railing, window or facade, and nothing that singles such equipment out. The question sits in the lease. Read the clauses on alterations and installations, and any on windows, fire escapes and the outside of the building: if they require the owner’s consent, you need it before anything goes on the railing.

Two provisions of the Code shape what happens next.

- **Renewals keep the old terms.** Under 9 NYCRR §2522.5(f)(1), a renewal lease must be “on the same terms and conditions as the expired lease,” unless the owner shows a change is needed to comply with a specific law or regulation, or DHCR approves it. A no-alterations clause in your lease will be in the renewal. By the same rule, an owner generally cannot add a new ban at renewal because you asked.

- **A violation must be cured, not just alleged.** Under §2524.3(a), an owner may seek possession on the ground that a tenant is violating “a substantial obligation” of the tenancy only after the tenant fails to cure it within 10 days of written notice (15 if the notice is mailed). Taking an unapproved panel down within that period would cure it. If a case did reach court, New York’s RPAPL §753(4) requires a 30-day stay of the warrant, “during which time the respondent may correct such breach.”

Whether a given clause is a “substantial obligation” is for a court to decide. Damage is the part removal does not undo. The same section also covers a tenant who has willfully violated an obligation “inflicting serious and substantial injury upon the owner.” A clamp that comes off clean is one thing; holes drilled in a facade or railing are another. The proportionate course is to ask first and install only on a written yes.

## A panel saves whoever pays the meter

For the 148,700 stabilized households whose rent includes electricity, the arithmetic changes completely. DHCR calls these “electrical inclusion” buildings, where the owner pays for electricity. A panel there lowers the reading on the owner’s meter; the tenant’s regulated rent does not move.

DHCR applies the same logic to air conditioners, in the other direction. Its Fact Sheet #27 lets an owner in an electrical-inclusion building charge a monthly surcharge for each air conditioner, because the owner pays for the power it uses. Since 21 November 2022 (Chapter 619 of the Laws of 2022), an owner may not charge it for a tenant-installed unit when the tenant pays for the electricity. The money follows the meter.

Two practical notes:

- **Submetered buildings.** Some owners bill each apartment from its own submeter. That requires authorization from the Public Service Commission, and residents’ rates are capped so they never pay more than the utility would charge. A panel lowers the submeter reading, so the saving is the tenant’s, valued at the submetered rate rather than necessarily at Con Edison’s.

- **Not sure which you are?** If a Con Edison bill arrives in your name, you pay for your electricity. If the owner or a billing company charges you from your apartment’s own meter, you are submetered and the saving is still yours. If electricity never appears on any bill, it is included in the rent.

## What a south-facing panel is worth to a stabilized tenant

For a stabilized tenant who pays Con Edison, a kilowatt-hour made and used at home is worth the all-in marginal rate of about [34¢](https://balco.nyc/electricity-rate). balco.nyc’s PVWatts run for New York City puts an 800 W system hanging vertically on a south-facing railing at 635.7 kWh a year before the railing loss; the site multiplies that by 0.95 for the railing and hardware, giving **604 kWh**, or **$205 a year** at $0.34.

That is the open-view figure, and stabilized apartments are mostly low. The same HVS microdata put **67.6%** (±1.5 pt) of stabilized households on the 4th floor or below, where the building across the street matters most. balco.nyc ran the calculator’s own shade model for one common case: a 3rd-floor balcony (7.1 m up) facing a building of 6 to 10 floors, which the calculator treats as 25 m, across a 20 m street. Straight ahead, that building’s roofline sits 41.8° above the horizon. The model keeps 38% of the output: **227 kWh, or $77 a year**.

| South railing, 800 W, New York City | kWh/yr | Per year | Per month | Share of a $1,500 rent | Payback, $1,200 kit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open view | 604 | $205 | $17.11 | 1.1% | 5.5 years |
| 3rd floor, 3–5 floors opposite at 20 m | 522 | $177 | $14.79 | 1.0% | 6.3 years |
| 6th floor, 6–10 floors opposite at 20 m | 463 | $158 | $13.13 | 0.9% | 7.1 years |
| 3rd floor, 6–10 floors opposite at 20 m | 227 | $77 | $6.43 | 0.4% | 13.3 years |

balco.nyc’s computation: PVWatts V8 monthly output for New York City × 0.95 railing factor × the calculator’s monthly shade factors, valued at $0.34/kWh. Payback uses the calculator’s loop: prices rising 3% a year, output falling 0.5% a year, nominal dollars. Rent share is against the HVS 2023 median stabilized rent of $1,500 a month ($18,000 a year).

Set against rent, the saving is small: about 1% of a median stabilized rent with an open view, 0.4% in the shaded case. Set against how long stabilized tenants stay, it looks better. Half of stabilized households had moved in by 2015, and 45.7% (±1.5 pt) had been in place since 2013 or earlier, against a median move-in year of 2020 for market-rate renters. A 5.5-year payback fits inside a typical stabilized tenancy; 13.3 years may not, though a plug-in kit leaves with you.

Two assumptions flatter these numbers. Every kWh is assumed to be used in the apartment; anything exported earns nothing (see [how much of the output a household actually uses](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-net-metering)). And the figures are modeled, not metered. The full chain is in [how to calculate balcony solar output](https://balco.nyc/calculate-balcony-solar-output).

## NYCHA: house rules, master meters and the Authority’s own solar

NYCHA’s 2025 Fact Sheet counts 177,565 apartments in 335 developments: 152,926 public-housing apartments in 1,882 residential buildings, and 24,639 in 92 developments converted under PACT/RAD, which private partners now manage. The Fact Sheet does not say how many have balconies. The HVS does not ask (it leaves balconies out of its room count), and NYCHA’s house-rules summary mentions balconies only to ban smoking on them.

**The rules.** Neither NYCHA’s *Highlights of House Rules, Lease, Law and NYCHA Policy* (form 040.821, revised September 2024) nor its December 2024 Resident Handbook mentions solar. The nearest rules are strict. The handbook bars residents from installing “a satellite dish or any other antenna that might be attached to window frames, window guards, or the brickwork on the exterior of the building.” Roofs are restricted areas. A resident who wants an air conditioner, freezer, dishwasher or washing machine must first sign an Appliance Agreement (form 150.110). And NYCHA “may start a proceeding to terminate tenancy” when a tenant breaches its rules. The practical reading: nothing goes on a balcony or out of a window without written approval from the development’s property management office. In a PACT development, ask the PACT partner’s management.

**The meters.** NYCHA’s Admissions and Continued Occupancy Plan says “most NYCHA buildings are master metered” and that residents in them “do not pay utility bills and they do not receive a utility allowance.” That matches balco.nyc’s HVS count of 150,100 public-housing households with electricity included. For them a panel would trim NYCHA’s bill, and NYCHA buys its electricity under its own “rates and regulations,” in the words of its solar program, so there is no reason to expect Con Edison’s residential 34¢ to describe that saving either.

The exception is the roughly 17,600 public-housing households that pay for their own electricity, in NYCHA’s individually metered developments. They pay Con Edison directly and get a utility allowance, deducted from rent, that NYCHA sets from estimated usage rather than from the actual bill. For them a panel’s saving would be theirs: $205 a year unshaded is about 2.8% of a year’s rent at the average public-housing rent of $621 a month. Public-housing households also live higher: 57.5% (±3.1 pt) are on the 5th floor or above, against 31.4% of stabilized households.

**NYCHA’s own solar.** Under its ACCESSolar program, NYCHA leases roofs to developers for community solar. The arrays “generate power using their own meters (not behind a NYCHA meter),” and credits go to subscribers’ electric bills. Because of the rates and regulations under which it buys electricity, NYCHA says it cannot purchase the power, and acts only as host. As of May 2025, 6.8 MW had been built and 12.5 MW more was in design or construction, against a Sustainability Agenda goal of 30 MW by 2026. The April 2026 agenda lists “Complete NYCHA’s 30-megawatt solar goal” among its targets for the next five years. The same limit applies as to a balcony panel: a community-solar credit reduces an electric bill, so among NYCHA residents it reaches those who pay their own, a group the program names, not the nine in ten whose electricity comes with the rent.

## What the SUNNY Act changes, and how to ask

New York’s SUNNY Act (S8512C / A9111C) has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature. It would stop utilities requiring approval or charging fees for certified plug-in devices of up to 1,200 W, starting 90 days after it is signed. Its text says nothing about landlords, tenants or leases, so it would give a stabilized tenant or a NYCHA resident no right to install. Until it is signed and in force, a plug-in panel in New York City still needs [Con Edison’s approval](https://balco.nyc/con-edison-plug-in-solar) to connect.

The request itself is the one described in [the national guide for renters](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-renters), which has a checklist and a letter. What changes in a New York regulated building:

- **Say who pays the meter.** If electricity is included in your rent, the owner or NYCHA gets the saving. Say so in the request; it is theirs to weigh.

- **Keep off the fire escape and out of the brick.** No panel, bracket or cable on or across a fire escape, and nothing drilled into the facade: see [fire escapes and facade rules](https://balco.nyc/nyc-fire-escape-facade-rules). In a historic district or landmark, [Landmarks review](https://balco.nyc/nyc-landmarks-balcony-solar) may apply. If you rent from a unit owner or sponsor in a co-op or condo, [the board’s rules](https://balco.nyc/nyc-coop-condo-board-balcony-solar) can apply on top of the lease.

- **Get the yes in writing**, signed by the owner or managing agent, or by NYCHA property management, and keep it with your lease. Managing agents change; a letter does not.

> **Not legal advice.** This page summarizes the Rent Stabilization Code, New York statute and NYCHA’s published rules as of 23 September 2026. Your lease, any written consent and the facts of your building decide your case.

Before asking at all, check the number. Run your address through [the calculator](https://balco.nyc/): a low-floor balcony across a narrow street from a taller building may be worth $77 a year, which is worth knowing before you ask anyone.

## Common questions

**Can my landlord stop me from putting a solar panel on my rent-stabilized apartment's balcony?**

Yes. The Rent Stabilization Code gives a stabilized tenant no right to attach equipment to a railing, window or facade, so the lease and the landlord decide; if the lease requires consent for alterations, you need it. Under the Code a renewal lease keeps the same terms as the old one. New York's SUNNY Act, which has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature, has no landlord or tenant provision.

**Could installing balcony solar without permission get a rent-stabilized tenant evicted?**

Not without a chance to fix it. Under 9 NYCRR 2524.3(a) an owner must first give written notice to cure a violation of a substantial lease obligation within 10 days (15 if mailed), and removing the panel cures it; if a case reaches court, RPAPL 753(4) requires a 30-day stay to correct the breach. Damage to the building is treated more seriously. This is not legal advice.

**Can NYCHA residents install balcony solar panels?**

Only with NYCHA's written approval. NYCHA's rules do not mention solar, but they bar satellite dishes and antennas attached to window frames, window guards or exterior brickwork, require an Appliance Agreement for major appliances, and allow NYCHA to start termination proceedings for rule breaches. In most NYCHA buildings electricity is included in the rent, so a panel would lower NYCHA's bill, not the resident's.

**Will a balcony solar panel lower my bill if electricity is included in my rent?**

No. A plug-in panel only slows the meter its circuit runs through, so if the owner pays for electricity the saving goes to the owner. balco.nyc's count of the 2023 NYC Housing and Vacancy Survey finds about 148,700 rent-stabilized households and 150,100 public-housing households with electricity included in the rent. In a PSC-authorized submetered building the tenant does keep the saving.

**How much would a balcony solar panel save a rent-stabilized tenant in NYC?**

If the tenant pays Con Edison, balco.nyc's model puts an 800 W south-facing railing system at 604 kWh a year with an open view, about $205 at Con Edison's 34-cent marginal rate, or roughly 1.1% of a year's rent at the $1,500 monthly median. On a 3rd floor facing a 6-to-10-floor building across a 20-meter street it falls to 227 kWh, about $77 a year.

**How many rent-stabilized tenants pay their own electric bill?**

About 812,100 of 960,700 occupied rent-stabilized apartments, or 84.5% (plus or minus 1.0 point), by balco.nyc's weighted count of the 2023 NYC Housing and Vacancy Survey microdata. Among public-housing households the share is 10.5%, about 17,600, because most NYCHA buildings are master-metered.

**Does NYCHA's rooftop solar lower residents' electric bills?**

Only for residents with their own electric bill. NYCHA's ACCESSolar program hosts community solar on its roofs, metered separately from NYCHA, with credits going to subscribers' bills; NYCHA names residents who pay their own utility bills as a target group. As of May 2025, 6.8 MW was built and 12.5 MW more was in design or construction toward a 30 MW goal.

# A portable power station with solar, or plug-in balcony solar?

URL: https://balco.nyc/portable-solar-vs-plug-in-solar  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

On the numbers, plug-in solar wins. balco.nyc’s hour-by-hour model of an 800 W south-facing railing in New York City finds that a plug-in system can displace up to 604 kWh a year, about $205 at Con Edison’s 34¢, while the same panels charging a 1 kWh power station that you empty every night deliver about 294 kWh ($100), because the battery is full on 263 days of the year and the rest of the sun is wasted. What the power station buys instead is independence: it never connects to the grid, so there is nothing for the utility to approve, and it keeps working in a blackout, when a plug-in system switches itself off.

## Two setups that share only the panels

Both setups start with the same panels on the same railing. They differ in where the power goes next.

- **Plug-in, or grid-tied:** panel → microinverter → wall outlet. The microinverter turns the panels’ direct current into alternating current synchronized with the grid and feeds it into the apartment’s wiring, where whatever is switched on uses it first. What the apartment is not using at that moment flows out to the grid, [generally unpaid](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-net-metering).

- **Off-grid:** panel → power station → the appliances you plug into it. A power station is a battery with a solar charge controller, an inverter and its own outlets. It never touches the building’s wiring, and once the battery is full the rest of the day’s sun goes uncollected.

|  | Plug-in balcony solar | Panels and a power station |
|---|---|---|
| Utility approval | Needed, unless a state plug-in law in force exempts it | None; there is no connection to approve |
| In a blackout | Shuts itself off within two seconds | Runs on its battery; the panels refill it by day |
| Output you can use | What the apartment draws while the sun is up | What the battery holds, plus whatever runs from it while the sun is up |
| Surplus | Exported, usually unpaid | Lost once the battery is full |
| Safety standard | Inverter: UL 1741. Complete system: the UL 3700 outline, to which no complete system was listed as of September 2026 | UL 2743, the standard for portable power packs |

Some batteries sold for balconies include an inverter that feeds a wall socket. However they are marketed, those run in parallel with the grid, so they need a plug-in law that covers them or the utility’s approval; they are covered in [adding a battery to balcony solar](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-battery). This page is about a power station that stays off the grid.

## What each setup needs legally

**Off-grid needs no utility approval, because nothing connects to the utility.** Interconnection rules govern generators that run in parallel with the grid. New York’s Standardized Interconnection Requirements (effective 9 February 2026) exempt generators and storage “neither designed to operate, nor operating, in parallel” with the utility’s system; Texas’s rule covers “the interconnection and parallel operation” of on-site generation. A power station charged by its own panels and powering only what is plugged into it does neither.

**Grid-tied needs a plug-in law or the utility’s approval.** As of 23 September 2026, five states have plug-in solar laws in force (Utah, Maine, Colorado, Maryland and Vermont) and four more have signed laws that start by March 2027 ([compared provision by provision](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-laws-compared); every state is on [the states page](https://balco.nyc/states)). Elsewhere, a panel feeding an outlet falls under the utility’s interconnection process. For the three places modeled below:

- **[New York](https://balco.nyc/states/new-york):** the [SUNNY Act](https://balco.nyc/sunny-act) (S8512C / A9111C), which would exempt devices of up to 1,200 W AC from interconnection, has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature. Until it is signed and in effect, the interconnection requirements apply.

- **[Maryland](https://balco.nyc/states/maryland):** a plug-in law has been in force since 1 July 2026. The utility cannot require approval or a fee for a certified device of up to 1,200 W, but must be notified before installation.

- **[Texas](https://balco.nyc/states/texas):** no plug-in solar bill has been filed, by balco.nyc’s search of the legislature’s records, so the Public Utility Commission’s interconnection rule applies.

Three things apply either way. A landlord, co-op board or association can refuse panels on a railing however they are wired (see [renters](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-renters) and [condos and HOAs](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-condo-hoa)), and in New York City panels and cables must stay off fire escapes. A power station’s output must never be connected to a wall outlet, which turns a plug into a live generator lead ([is plug-in solar safe?](https://balco.nyc/is-plug-in-solar-safe)). And UL notes that installation codes treat a portable battery installed in a stationary situation as stationary energy storage, which must be listed to UL 9540. This is not legal advice; details vary by state and utility.

## What each does in a blackout

A plug-in system goes dark when the grid does. UL 1741 and IEEE 1547 require its inverter to stop energizing its output within two seconds of losing the grid, so it cannot feed a line a utility crew believes is dead. Without a battery it gives no backup power at all.

A power station keeps running whatever is plugged into it until the battery is empty, and the panels refill it each day. In balco.nyc’s hourly model of an 800 W south-facing railing in New York City (section 4), the panels average **2.33 kWh a day in January and 1.07 in June**; a vertical panel meets the low winter sun almost head-on. The worst seven-day stretch of the modeled year averages 0.66 kWh a day, about 0.56 kWh at the outlets after storage losses. In Houston in July, the month Hurricane Beryl left 2.6 million Texas customers without power in 2024, the same railing averages 0.88 kWh a day, about 0.75 at the outlets. That keeps phones, a router, a laptop and LED lights going, not air conditioning.

How much that is worth depends on where you live. The EIA reports that US customers averaged 11 hours without power in 2024, nearly twice the previous decade’s average, mostly from hurricanes and other major events; outside such events, outages routinely total about two hours a year. For most households backup is insurance against a rare long outage, and the payback figures below give it no value. For anyone who depends on powered medical equipment it may be the main reason to own one.

## How much of the output you actually get to use

A plug-in panel’s output saves money only when the apartment is using power at the same moment. A power station’s saves money only if the battery has room for it and you then use what it holds. The second limit is tighter.

**How balco.nyc modeled it.** We ran PVWatts V8, the National Laboratory of the Rockies’ model that the calculator uses, hour by hour for an 800 W vertical south-facing railing in New York City, Baltimore and Houston with the calculator’s parameters; the runs reproduce the site’s state data exactly, and every hour is multiplied by the 0.95 railing factor. The plug-in system gets the AC output (604 kWh a year in New York); the power station, which needs no microinverter, gets the DC output (632 kWh). Energy passing through the station loses 15%: 85% is the round-trip efficiency the laboratory’s Annual Technology Baseline adopts for a home lithium-iron-phosphate battery. We found no government or standards-body measurement of portable power stations’ round-trip efficiency; one reviewer’s bench tests found AC output alone ranging from under 70% to over 90% of rated capacity, so brackets show a weaker unit at 75%. Whatever the station cannot supply is bought from the utility. Capacity fade and the station’s standby draw are ignored, which flatters it.

| New York City, 800 W south-facing railing | kWh used a year | Worth at 34¢ |
|---|---|---|
| Plug-in, every kWh used at home (the ceiling) | 604 | $205 |
| Plug-in, apartment drawing a steady 150 W, empty in the daytime | 364 | $124 |
| 1 kWh power station, used after dark and emptied every night | 294 (273) | $100 ($93) |
| 2 kWh power station, used after dark and emptied every night | 447 (406) | $152 ($138) |
| 1 kWh power station, a steady 100 W running from it day and night | 433 (398) | $147 ($135) |
| 2 kWh power station, a steady 100 W running from it day and night | 505 (457) | $172 ($156) |
| Either power station, with 0.5 kWh a day of use moved onto it | 181 | $62 |

balco.nyc’s computation. Brackets assume 75% efficiency. The 150 W row is from [how much of the output an apartment uses](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-net-metering).

**A 1 kWh station is too small for this railing.** The panels make more than it can hold on 263 days of the year, and 286 of their 632 kWh, 45%, is never collected; in January they make 2.33 kWh a day. A 2 kWh station fills on 111 days and loses 105 kWh.

**Daytime use matters as much as size.** Energy used while the sun is up need not be stored, so a steady 100 W lets even a 1 kWh station deliver 433 kWh. But 100 W around the clock is 2.4 kWh a day, about an eighth of an average New York household’s use, and it has to be appliances you can move from the wall to the station. And what you move is the ceiling: half a kilowatt-hour a day caps either station at about 181 kWh a year.

The fair comparison is with the second plug-in row. An apartment empty all day and drawing a steady 150 W uses 364 of the plug-in system’s 604 kWh; on the same hourly data, one drawing 200 W uses 433 and one drawing 300 W uses 524. A 2 kWh station emptied every night beats the first two. On energy alone, a power station worked hard can match a plug-in system in a small, efficient apartment. The money is another matter.

## Cost and payback in New York, Maryland and Texas

**Costs.** The plug-in system is the $1,200 mid-range 800 W kit balco.nyc uses throughout. The off-grid setup is charged the same $1,200 for panels and mounting, plus $550 for a 1 kWh station or $900 for a 2 kWh one: median selling prices of about $0.55 and $0.44 per watt-hour for units of those sizes in an August 2026 survey of 114 models by a review site. Charging it the full kit price, microinverter included, flatters the plug-in side by the price of a microinverter. New York City is valued at Con Edison’s all-in marginal rate; Maryland and Texas at EIA state averages for the 12 months to June 2026, which include fixed charges and so overstate what an avoided kWh saves. Payback is simple: cost over the first year’s saving, with no price rises or panel degradation. (The calculator’s loop, with prices rising 3% a year, gives 5.5 years for the New York plug-in kit.)

| Setup (cost) | New York City, 34¢ | Maryland (Baltimore), 20.75¢ | Texas (Houston), 15.9¢ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plug-in, every kWh used ($1,200) | 604 kWh · $205/yr · 5.8 yrs | 673 kWh · $140/yr · 8.6 yrs | 575 kWh · $91/yr · 13.1 yrs |
| 1 kWh station, used after dark ($1,200 + $550) | 294 kWh · $100/yr · 17.5 yrs | 307 kWh · $64/yr · 27.5 yrs | 294 kWh · $47/yr · 37.5 yrs |
| 2 kWh station, used after dark ($1,200 + $900) | 447 kWh · $152/yr · 13.8 yrs | 487 kWh · $101/yr · 20.8 yrs | 422 kWh · $67/yr · 31.3 yrs |
| 2 kWh station, steady 100 W day and night ($1,200 + $900) | 505 kWh · $172/yr · 12.2 yrs | 557 kWh · $115/yr · 18.2 yrs | 479 kWh · $76/yr · 27.6 yrs |

balco.nyc’s computation: hourly PVWatts V8, 0.95 railing factor, 85% station efficiency, simple payback. The Texas plug-in row assumes the utility approves the connection.

In every city and setup the plug-in system pays back two to three times as fast, and where power is cheap the gap in years is widest: in Texas every power-station setup takes more than 27 years.

**Battery wear.** Used after dark, every kWh passes through the battery: a 1 kWh station in New York goes through about 319 full cycles a year, a 2 kWh station about 243. Sandia National Laboratories’ multi-year test of commercial cells found lithium-iron-phosphate cells lasting 2,500 to 9,000 equivalent full cycles before falling to 80% of capacity, depending on conditions (mostly extrapolated, since the cells had not yet reached 80%), against 200 to 2,500 for NMC cells. At the low end, the two stations reach 80% in about 8 and 10 years, before either pays back in New York; the laboratory’s cost baseline assumes a home battery lasts 15 years, long enough for the 2 kWh setup but not the 1 kWh one. In Maryland and Texas the paybacks run past both. These are tests of cells, not whole power stations; a manufacturer’s cycle rating for a complete unit is its own claim.

**Where it does work: you want the station anyway.** If you would buy a power station for outages regardless, count only the panels. Still charging them the full $1,200, a 2 kWh station used after dark pays the panels back in 7.9 years in New York City, 11.9 in Maryland and 17.9 in Texas; with a steady 100 W load, 7.0, 10.4 and 15.8.

## Which one fits which apartment

- **A plug-in law is in force and the building agrees:** plug-in solar gives about twice the usable energy of a 1 kWh station for less money, provided the apartment uses a fair share of the output while the sun is up. See [payback in every state](https://balco.nyc/is-balcony-solar-worth-it).

- **No law in force and no realistic route to utility approval:** the power station needs nobody’s sign-off but the building’s. In New York that holds until the SUNNY Act is signed and takes effect. Expect about half the plug-in system’s energy from a 1 kWh station used after dark, more from a 2 kWh one or from running loads through it all day.

- **Outages are the concern:** only the power station helps. A battery that feeds a wall socket is still grid-tied, and needs a plug-in law that covers it or the utility’s approval.

- **Choosing a size:** in New York City the second kilowatt-hour of capacity adds 153 kWh a year of use after dark, worth about $52, for about $350 more.

These figures are for an unshaded south-facing railing; east, west and north railings, and balconies facing taller buildings, produce less (see [output by direction](https://balco.nyc/800w-balcony-solar-output) and [sunlight and shading](https://balco.nyc/balcony-sunlight)). [The calculator](https://balco.nyc/) runs your own address, direction and surroundings, and [the methodology](https://balco.nyc/methodology) explains the model.

## Common questions

**Do I need utility approval to charge a portable power station with solar panels?**

No. Utility interconnection rules cover generators that operate in parallel with the grid, and a power station charged by its own panels and powering only what is plugged into it never connects to the grid. New York's interconnection requirements, for example, say systems neither designed nor operating in parallel with the utility are not subject to them. A landlord, co-op board or association can still refuse panels on a railing, and this is not legal advice.

**Does plug-in balcony solar work during a power outage?**

No. UL 1741 and IEEE 1547 require a grid-tied inverter to stop energizing its output within two seconds of losing the grid, so a plug-in balcony system shuts down in a blackout. That protects utility crews working on lines they believe are dead. A power station charged by solar panels keeps running whatever is plugged into it until its battery is empty, and the panels refill it by day.

**Which saves more money, a solar power station or plug-in balcony solar?**

Plug-in solar, in every case balco.nyc modeled. For an 800 W south-facing railing in New York City, a plug-in system can displace up to 604 kWh a year, worth about $205 at Con Edison's 34-cent marginal rate, against 294 kWh ($100) through a 1 kWh power station emptied every night and 447 kWh ($152) through a 2 kWh one. Simple payback is 5.8 years for the plug-in kit against 13.8 to 17.5 years for the power stations used after dark.

**How big a power station does an 800 W balcony solar panel need?**

Bigger than 1 kWh to make use of it. In balco.nyc's hourly New York City model, an 800 W south-facing railing produces 2.33 kWh a day in January, so a 1 kWh station fills on 263 days of the year and 45% of the panels' output is never collected. A 2 kWh station fills on 111 days. In New York the second kilowatt-hour of capacity adds about 153 kWh a year of use after dark, worth about $52.

**Can I plug a power station into a wall outlet to power my apartment?**

No. Connecting a power station's output to a wall outlet backfeeds the building's wiring and can leave the prongs of a plug live, a shock hazard. Batteries sold for balconies that do feed a wall socket through a grid-tied inverter run in parallel with the grid, so they need a state plug-in law that covers them or the utility's approval. Wiring a battery into a home's electrical panel is stationary energy storage, which installation codes require to be listed to UL 9540.

**How long does a power station battery last?**

It depends on chemistry and use. Sandia National Laboratories' multi-year test of commercial cells found lithium-iron-phosphate cells lasting 2,500 to 9,000 equivalent full cycles before falling to 80% of capacity, depending on conditions, against 200 to 2,500 for NMC cells. A 1 kWh station charged by an 800 W railing in New York City and emptied every night goes through about 319 cycles a year, so it would reach 80% in about 8 years at the low end of that range.

## Sources

- [National Laboratory of the Rockies — PVWatts V8 API](https://developer.nlr.gov/docs/solar/pvwatts/v8/): the hourly AC and DC output behind balco.nyc’s power-station and plug-in comparisons for New York City, Baltimore and Houston; the runs used the calculator’s parameters and reproduce the site’s state data.
- [National Laboratory of the Rockies — Annual Technology Baseline 2025: residential battery storage](https://atb.nlr.gov/electricity/2025/residential_battery_storage): 85% as the representative round-trip efficiency for a lithium-iron-phosphate home battery, a 15-year lifetime and about one cycle a day.
- [Preger et al., “Degradation of Commercial Lithium-Ion Cells as a Function of Chemistry and Cycling Conditions,” Sandia National Laboratories, J. Electrochem. Soc. (2020)](https://www.osti.gov/biblio/1650174): LFP cells lasting 2,500 to 9,000 equivalent full cycles to 80% capacity (mostly extrapolated), against 250 to 1,500 for NCA and 200 to 2,500 for NMC.
- [GearLab — how we tested power stations](https://www.outdoorgearlab.com/topics/camping-and-hiking/best-power-station/how-we-test): a reviewer’s bench test of AC output against claimed capacity, ranging from under 70% to over 90%; the basis for the 75% sensitivity case. Not a standards test.
- [Solar Waypoint — Portable Power Station Price Index 2026](https://www.solarwaypoint.com/portable-power-station-price-index/): median selling prices of about $0.55/Wh for 950–1,100 Wh units and $0.44/Wh for 1,601–3,200 Wh units across 114 models (28 August 2026), used for the $550 and $900 station prices. An affiliate review site, cited only for prices.
- [New York State Public Service Commission — Standardized Interconnection Requirements (effective 9 February 2026)](https://dps.ny.gov/nys-standardized-interconnection-requirements): generators and storage neither designed to operate nor operating in parallel with the utility’s system are not subject to the requirements.
- [Public Utility Commission of Texas — 16 TAC §25.211, Interconnection of On-Site Distributed Generation](https://www.puc.texas.gov/agency/rulesnlaws/subrules/electric/25.211/25.211.pdf): the rule governs the interconnection and parallel operation of on-site generation.
- [Maryland Public Service Commission — balcony solar](https://psc.maryland.gov/regulated-utilities/electricity/renewable-energy/balcony-solar/): up to 1,200 W, no utility approval or fee, notice to the utility before installation, certification by a nationally recognized testing laboratory.
- [New York State Senate — S8512C (SUNNY Act)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/S8512/amendment/C): exemption from interconnection and net-metering requirements for devices up to 1,200 W AC and the outage shut-off requirement; passage of both chambers on 28 May 2026.
- [UL Solutions — Interactions of Plug-In PV with Protection of Existing Power Systems (testimony to the Maine Legislature)](https://legislature.maine.gov/testimony/resources/EUT20260106Soltan134125472587136094.pdf): a grid-interactive inverter must cease to energize its output within two seconds of losing the grid under UL 1741 and IEEE 1547.
- [UL Solutions — Q&A: portable power packs](https://www.ul.com/thecodeauthority/knowledgecenter/qa-portable-power-packs): UL 2743 covers portable power packs intended for use when grid power is unavailable; a portable battery installed in a stationary situation falls under stationary storage rules requiring UL 9540.
- [EIA — Hurricanes in 2024 led to the most hours without power in the United States in 10 years](https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=66744): 11 hours of interruptions per customer in 2024, about two hours a year outside major events, and 2.6 million Texas customers without power after Hurricane Beryl.
- [EIA — Form EIA-861M monthly sales and revenue](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/data/eia861m/): the data behind balco.nyc’s Maryland (20.75¢) and Texas (15.9¢) average residential prices, 12 months to June 2026.
- [EIA — 2024 Average Monthly Bill, Residential (Table 5A)](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/sales_revenue_price/pdf/table_5A.pdf): New York average residential consumption of about 571 kWh a month, the basis for comparing a 2.4 kWh-a-day load with household use.
- [Con Edison — historical average full-service electric rates](https://www.coned.com/-/media/files/coned/documents/save-energy-money/using-private-generation/historical-average-full-service-electric-rates.pdf): the SC-1 series behind the 34¢ marginal rate used for New York City.

# Is plug-in solar legal in New York?

URL: https://balco.nyc/sunny-act  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

Not yet — but the barrier is one signature away. New York requires utility approval for any device that pushes power back into a household circuit, and no utility currently grants it for plug-in solar. The SUNNY Act removes that requirement for compliant devices up to 1,200 W. It has passed both chambers of the Legislature and is waiting on the Governor. This page tracks where it stands, what it will change, and — the part most coverage skips — what it deliberately will not change.

## Where the bill stands

> **As of September 23, 2026: passed, unsigned.** The Solar Up Now New York Act passed the State Senate unanimously in April 2026, and its final version cleared both chambers on 28 May 2026 (the Assembly vote was 89–47). It awaits the Governor’s signature: the legislature’s records show it has not yet been delivered to Governor Hochul, and her time to decide starts only when it is. The bill stays alive until the 2025–26 session ends on 31 December 2026. If signed, it takes effect 90 days later.

The bill is S8512C in the Senate and A9111C in the Assembly — the “C” amendment is the version that passed, which matters if you are reading the text rather than the summaries. It was sponsored by Senator Liz Krueger and Assemblymember Emily Gallagher.

Nothing about your legal position changes until it is signed. If you are reading this after the Governor has acted, the date above tells you how stale this page is; we review it whenever the bill's status moves.

## What the Act changes

Today, New York treats a plug-in solar device the same way it treats a rooftop array: it is a generator connected to the grid, so it needs an interconnection agreement with your utility. That process is designed for permanent installations with an electrician, a permit and a meter change. For an appliance you hang on a railing and plug into an outlet, it is a wall.

The SUNNY Act removes that wall for small devices. Specifically, it:

- exempts compliant plug-in solar of up to 1,200 W AC output from interconnection and net-metering requirements;

- bars utilities from requiring you to obtain approval to use one;

- bars utilities from charging a fee tied to using one.

What it does not do is pay you. These devices are not net-metered, so power you generate and do not use is not credited — it simply flows to your neighbours. The economics come entirely from offsetting what you would otherwise buy, which is why the value depends so heavily on Con Edison's rate rather than on any incentive.

## What it does not change

> **The Act removes the utility barrier only. It grants no right to install anything.**

This is the most consistently misreported part of the bill, and for most New Yorkers it is the part that decides whether they can actually do this. Roughly two thirds of New York City households rent, and a large share of the rest are in co-ops or condos. In all of those cases the balcony railing, the facade and the window frame are not yours to modify unilaterally.

After the Act is signed you will still need, depending on your building:

- **Renting:** your landlord's permission, and a lease that does not prohibit attaching things to the railing or facade.

- **Co-op:** board approval, usually under the house rules covering alterations and anything visible from the street.

- **Condo:** board approval, since a balcony is typically a limited common element rather than your own property.

- **Landmarked or historic district buildings:** potentially Landmarks Preservation Commission review for anything that changes the appearance of a facade.

None of that is affected by the SUNNY Act. If you want one of these, the conversation with your building is the real work, and it can start now.

## The limits that apply

| Requirement | What it means in practice |
|---|---|
| 1,200 W AC inverter output | The cap is on the inverter, not the panels. A system with more panel wattage is fine so long as the inverter's AC output stays at or under the cap. A typical balcony setup is 400–800 W, comfortably inside it. |
| Accredited-lab certification | The device must be certified by a laboratory such as UL. Imported kits sold without a recognised certification will not qualify, however cheap they are. |
| State fire code compliance | Applies to the device and to how it is mounted. Balcony fire-egress rules still apply: a panel must not block a fire escape or an egress path. |
| 90 days after signing | The Act is not in force the day it is signed. Count 90 days forward from the signature. |

## When you could actually install

Take the two dates together. The Governor has until the end of 2026 to act, and the Act takes effect 90 days after she does. A signature in late 2026 puts the earliest lawful residential installation in **early 2027**. A signature earlier than that pulls the date forward by the same amount; a veto resets the clock to the next legislative session.

That gap is not dead time. Getting building permission, working out which railing actually faces the sun, and choosing a certified kit are all things you can do before the law changes — and the first of those is usually the slowest.

## How New York compares

New York is not first. Utah passed the first plug-in solar law in 2025, carving out an exemption for systems up to 1.2 kW. By September 2026 eight more states had signed comparable laws: Maine, Virginia, Colorado, Maryland, Connecticut, New Hampshire, Vermont and, on 1 September, New Jersey. That makes nine. New York would be the tenth unless California gets there first: its SB 868 has also passed both houses and awaits Governor Newsom’s decision, due by 30 September 2026. Five are already in force (Utah, Maine, Colorado, Maryland and Vermont); Connecticut’s takes effect on 1 October 2026, Virginia’s and New Hampshire’s on 1 January 2027, and New Jersey’s on 1 March 2027. Most use the same 1,200 W threshold New York has chosen; Colorado allows 1,920 W.

Several go further than New York on permission. New Jersey bars landlords from stopping tenants who pay their own electric bill, stops homeowners’ associations enforcing bans on exterior placement, and stops towns banning the devices; Vermont lets tenants proceed after ten days’ notice; Virginia bars larger landlords from prohibiting them. Reporting on which states have *signed* versus merely *passed* a bill, and on when each law takes effect, is inconsistent, so treat any list you read — including this one — as needing a date and a check against the state’s own legislature page. balco.nyc keeps a [sourced, dated table of every state](https://balco.nyc/states).

Germany is the usual reference point for what happens next: *Balkonkraftwerk* installations there are counted in the millions, following rule changes that made registration trivial. Germany also granted tenants a right to install, which is the step New York has explicitly not taken.

The practical consequence of the state-by-state patchwork is that compliance does not travel. A kit sold as legal in one state is not automatically legal here, and the certification requirement is where most imported hardware fails.

## What to do now

If you are trying to work out whether this is worth pursuing for your apartment, the binding constraint is almost never the law — it is whether your balcony gets enough sun. A high-floor south-facing railing can produce roughly three times what a low-floor north-facing one does, and in a city this dense the buildings across the street matter as much as the direction you face — [which is the question worth answering first](https://balco.nyc/balcony-sunlight). If the sun is there, the next two are [what a kit costs and how long it takes to pay back](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-cost) and [what installing one actually involves](https://balco.nyc/install-balcony-solar).

[Run your address through the calculator](https://balco.nyc/) to see what an 800 W system would produce where you actually live, modelled against the real shadows of your block. If the answer is small, the legal question is moot for you. If it is large, start the conversation with your landlord or board now, because that is the part with the longest lead time.

## Common questions

**Is plug-in solar legal in New York right now?**

Not yet. New York requires utility approval for any device that pushes power back into a household circuit, and Con Edison does not currently grant it for plug-in solar. The SUNNY Act removes that requirement, but it has not been signed. Until it is, installing a plug-in solar device in New York means operating outside your utility's interconnection rules.

**What is the SUNNY Act?**

The Solar Up Now New York Act (S8512C / A9111C) exempts compliant plug-in solar devices of up to 1,200 watts AC inverter output from New York's interconnection and net-metering requirements, and bars utilities from requiring approval or charging a fee for them. It was sponsored by Senator Liz Krueger and Assemblymember Emily Gallagher.

**Has the Governor signed the SUNNY Act?**

As of September 4, 2026, no. The bill passed the Senate unanimously in April 2026 and the Assembly in late May 2026, and is awaiting Governor Hochul's signature. She has until the end of 2026 to sign or veto it.

**When could I actually install a balcony solar panel in New York?**

The Act takes effect 90 days after it is signed. If it is signed in late 2026, the realistic opening for a legal residential installation is early 2027.

**Does the SUNNY Act give me the right to install a panel on my balcony?**

No. This is the most commonly misunderstood part of the bill. The Act removes the utility barrier only. It does not override a lease, a co-op's house rules, a condo board's bylaws, or a landlord's decision. If you rent, or live in a co-op or condo, you will still need permission from whoever controls the facade or railing.

**What size system does the SUNNY Act allow?**

Up to 1,200 watts of AC inverter output. The device must comply with New York's fire code and be certified by an accredited testing laboratory such as UL. The panel wattage can exceed 1,200W as long as the inverter's AC output does not.

**Is balcony solar legal anywhere else in the US?**

Yes. Utah passed the first plug-in solar law in 2025, and by September 2026 Maine, Virginia, Colorado, Maryland, Connecticut, New Hampshire, Vermont and New Jersey had signed comparable laws, nine states in all; five are already in force. New York and California have each passed a bill that awaits its governor. The rules differ by state, so a device that is compliant in one is not automatically compliant in another.

## Sources

- [NY State Senate — Bill S8512](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/S8512): the bill text and its status history — the primary source for anything on this page.
- [Senate unanimously passes the SUNNY Act](https://www.nysenate.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2026/liz-krueger/senate-unanimously-passes-sunny-act): April 2026 passage.
- [SUNNY Act passes the NYS Legislature](https://www.nysenate.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2026/liz-krueger/sunny-act-passes-nys-legislature-bringing-plug-solar-one): passage of both chambers.
- [New York legislature passes SUNNY Act plug-in solar legislation](https://pv-magazine-usa.com/2026/06/01/new-york-legislature-passes-sunny-act-plug-in-solar-legislation/): the 1,200 W cap and certification requirement.
- [New Yorkers can soon hang solar panels from their windows, if Gov. Hochul approves](https://gothamist.com/news/new-yorkers-can-soon-hang-solar-panels-from-their-windows-if-gov-hochul-approves): NYC context.
- [Balcony solar plug-in power awaits Hochul's signature](https://www.newyorkalmanack.com/2026/07/balcony-solar-plug-in-power-hochul/): status through July 2026.
- [Where does balcony solar stand in your state?](https://www.canarymedia.com/articles/solar/states-passing-balcony-solar-laws): state-by-state tracker — which states have signed and which are still pending.
- [New Jersey Legislature — S2368 (P.L.2026, c.82)](https://www.njleg.state.nj.us/bill-search/2026/S2368): New Jersey’s plug-in solar law: signed 1 September 2026, effective 1 March 2027, with tenant, association and municipal protections.
- [Vermont Legislature — S.202 (Act 149)](https://legislature.vermont.gov/bill/status/2026/S.202): Vermont’s plug-in solar law, in force from 1 July 2026, including the tenant-notice provision.
- [Virginia LIS — HB 395 (Chapter 1052)](https://lis.virginia.gov/bill-details/20261/HB395): Virginia’s plug-in solar law, effective 1 January 2027, including the landlord provision.
- [California Legislative Information — SB 868](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB868): California’s plug-in solar bill, passed by both houses and presented to the Governor on 31 August 2026.

# UL 3700 and whole-system certification for plug-in solar, explained

URL: https://balco.nyc/ul-3700-plug-in-solar-certification  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

UL 3700 is the first US safety document written for a plug-in solar system as a whole, with panel, microinverter, cord and plug evaluated together. As of 23 September 2026 no complete plug-in system is listed to it. Only components, mainly microinverters, carry UL 3700 claims. balco.nyc read the certification clause in all nine signed state laws: only 2, Maine and Vermont, ask for a listing of the whole system, and they hold 0.6% of US residents. New York’s SUNNY Act, which has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature, would require a “complete plug-in photovoltaic system” listing that no product holds.

## What UL 3700 is, and what it is not

UL 3700’s full name is the *Outline of Investigation for Interactive Plug-In PV (PIPV) Equipment and Systems*. Edition 1 is dated 11 December 2025 and is sold through the standards store of UL Standards & Engagement (ULSE), labeled a UL LLC outline. UL Solutions opened certification against it on 8 January 2026.

The word “outline” matters. ULSE’s glossary defines an outline of investigation as a certification document owned by UL LLC, not a consensus document and not developed through ULSE’s standards process. It is a certifier’s document for a category too new for a full standard: a normal first step, and what Maine, Vermont and New Jersey cite, but not an established national standard.

Its scope, as ULSE publishes it, is plug-in PV equipment and systems that connect by a plug-in PV cord and plug to a permanently installed receptacle meant for that purpose; Intertek, which also certifies to UL 3700, calls it a dedicated plug-in PV receptacle. The DC side is capped at 64 V open-circuit under the outline’s test conditions, and rooftop, building-integrated and hard-wired PV are excluded. The aim is the hazards that only exist once panel, microinverter, cord and household circuit are combined: current the breaker cannot see, plug blades that stay live, interference with ground-fault protection, and current flowing backward through devices built for one direction.

The case for it is a finding UL Solutions has made public. Its vice president of principal engineering, Ken Boyce, told PV Tech in August 2026 that the company bought plug-in products on the open market, tested them against UL 3700, and none complied. Whether that matters for your purchase depends on your state; balco.nyc’s compilation of every signed law’s certification wording is in section 4.

## UL 1741, IEEE 1547, NRTL and “listed”: the vocabulary

Four documents come up, and they answer different questions:

| Document | What it evaluates | What it does not tell you |
|---|---|---|
| UL 3700 (outline, 2025) | Plug-in PV equipment, or a complete plug-in system with its cord, plug and protection | Anything not submitted to it: a microinverter evaluated to it is not a system evaluated to it |
| UL 1741 (ed. 3, ANSI) | Inverters and other grid-interconnection equipment; used with IEEE 1547 and 1547.1 for grid-connected units | The panels, the cord and plug, or the circuit it feeds |
| IEEE 1547-2018 | How a generator interconnects with the grid, including islanding | Fire and shock safety of the product |
| UL 61730 | The PV module (panel) | Everything downstream of the panel |

Islanding is why utilities care: a generator that keeps energizing a line after the grid fails can shock a worker who believes it is dead. Most state laws add their own anti-islanding clause; Maine’s requires inverters that shut off 0.2 seconds after power is disrupted.

The legal vocabulary comes from federal workplace-safety rules. A **nationally recognized testing laboratory (NRTL)**, under 29 CFR 1910.7, is an OSHA-recognized organization that tests for safety, lists or labels equipment, inspects production and is independent of the manufacturers it tests. OSHA’s current list has 21, including UL LLC, CSA Group, Intertek and both TÜV organizations. Every law below accepts an equivalent NRTL, not only UL, except Colorado’s 2027 sales rule, which says “UL labeled and listed”.

- **Listed** (29 CFR 1910.399): named in a list published by an NRTL that inspects production, as meeting recognized standards or tested safe for use in a specified manner. **Labeled**: carrying that NRTL’s mark.

- **Certified** is not defined there. UL uses “Certified (Listed)” interchangeably for end products; the state laws mix “certified”, “listed or certified” and “labeled and listed” without distinguishing them.

- **Recognized component** (the backward “UR” mark): a part evaluated for use inside a larger certified product. UL says it is not a certification of a standalone product.

## Why a listed inverter and listed panels are not a listed plug-in system

A listing covers the product submitted, in the configuration tested, for a specified use. A microinverter listed to UL 1741 has been evaluated for its own safety and its behavior on the grid. A panel listed to UL 61730 has been evaluated for shock and fire safety as a panel. Neither was tested with the other, with the kit’s cord and plug, or feeding a shared 15 A kitchen circuit. Put them in one box and you have two listings, not one.

The hazards UL 3700 targets belong to the combination. An inverter feeding a circuit at one outlet while appliances draw at others can push more current through part of the wire than the breaker sees; balco.nyc’s worst case is [25 A on a 15 A circuit](https://balco.nyc/is-plug-in-solar-safe). No test of the inverter alone can find that. Live plug blades and GFCI interaction also depend on how the parts are connected.

The market shows the distinction. Bright Saver, a nonprofit that sells plug-in kits at cost, describes the microinverter in its kit as UL 3700 compliant. The same page says it cannot ship to New York, Maine or Vermont because their laws require “whole-system certification, which no system on the market has achieved yet.” In New York the law in question is the SUNNY Act’s text, which is not yet law. The kit ships to the rest of the continental US, which is how the market reads the other statutes: where a law names no system standard, a kit of listed components is sold as compliant. No regulator or court has tested that reading.

## What each state law asks for: balco.nyc’s compilation

balco.nyc read the certification clause in the enacted text of all nine signed plug-in solar laws, and in the New York and California bills, as of 23 September 2026. Quotation marks show statutory wording; the last column is our reading, not legal advice.

| State | Status | What the text requires | What it means in practice |
|---|---|---|---|
| Utah | In force since 7 May 2025 | “Certified by Underwriters Laboratories or an equivalent nationally recognized testing laboratory.” | No standard named. Kits of listed components are sold as compliant; whether “the device” means the whole kit is unsettled. |
| Maryland | In force since 1 July 2026 | “Certified by Underwriters Laboratory or an equivalent” NRTL | As Utah. The customer also gives the utility a certification of safety features and capacity. |
| Colorado | In force since 12 Aug 2026 | The system “and associated equipment” is “labeled and listed” by an NRTL; from 2027, no sales over 391 W unless “UL labeled and listed” | No standard named. “System” leans toward a system listing; the 2027 rule names UL, not any NRTL. |
| Connecticut | From 1 Oct 2026 | UL or equivalent NRTL, and “meets the requirements set forth in Underwriters Laboratories Standard Number 1741”; IEEE 1547; NEC | The one standard named is the inverter standard, which a listed microinverter already meets. |
| New Hampshire | From 1 Jan 2027 | NRTL certification to nationally recognized safety standards | No standard named. The building-code section waits until the state certifies a national plug-in standard exists. |
| Virginia | From 1 Jan 2027 | “Certified by a nationally recognized testing laboratory, as described in 29 C.F.R. § 1910.7, or an equivalent” NRTL | As Utah. Tenants must show the landlord documentation that the device qualifies. |
| New Jersey | From 1 Mar 2027 | Listed or certified to UL 3700, or a comparable standard or combination of standards, by an NRTL | Names UL 3700, but combination of standards leaves open whether stacked component listings count. |
| Maine | In force since 29 July 2026 | System “listed or certified in accordance with UL 3700” or a comparable NRTL standard, or “configured in accordance with the National Electrical Code” | System-level listing. The NEC route is unclear: the 2026 NEC has no plug-in PV provisions. |
| Vermont | In force since 1 July 2026 | “Complies with UL 3700 for plug-in photovoltaic systems by UL Solutions or an equivalent certification”; IEEE 1547-2018 | System-level listing. No complete system has one. |
| New York (bill) | Passed both chambers; not yet delivered to the Governor | “Listed or certified by an accredited nationally recognized testing laboratory as a complete plug-in photovoltaic system to a standard” | The strictest wording. No standard named, but the complete system must be listed. |
| California (bill) | With the Governor since 31 Aug 2026 | “Certified as a plug-in photovoltaic system” by UL or an equivalent NRTL, plus a certified anti-backfeed feature | System-level. From 2030 it would ban sales of plug-in devices that do not qualify. |

**The count.** Of the nine signed laws, three name UL 3700: Maine, Vermont and New Jersey. Only **two, Maine and Vermont, ask for UL 3700 or an equivalent listing of the system itself**, with no route through a combination of other standards. Five name no standard (Utah, Maryland, Colorado, Virginia, New Hampshire), and Connecticut names only the inverter standard. That is six of nine whose wording a kit of separately listed parts can plausibly meet, two that require a system listing, and New Jersey in between.

**Weighted by population** (Census Bureau 2025 estimates), Maine (1,414,874) and Vermont (644,663) hold 2,059,537 people: **0.6%** of the 341.8 million US residents, and 5.0% of the 41.4 million in states with a signed law. If New York (20,002,427) and California (39,355,309) enact their bills, a system-level requirement would cover 61,417,273 people: **18.0%** of US residents and 61% of everyone under one of these eleven texts. The missing product would go from a two-small-state problem to the main constraint for most people these laws cover.

The laws differ on much more than certification; [the provision-by-provision comparison](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-laws-compared) has the rest.

## Where certification stands in September 2026

**No complete plug-in system is listed to UL 3700 as of 23 September 2026.** In late August, PV Tech reported that UL Solutions was still working toward its first UL 3700 certification. On 23 September, Bright Saver’s kit page still said no system on the market had achieved whole-system certification.

What exists are equipment-level claims for microinverters. On 15 July 2026 APsystems said its EZ1 plug-in microinverter was certified to UL 3700 by CSA Group, an NRTL on OSHA’s list. The same day Hoymiles launched its HiFlow Pro as the first UL 3700-compliant plug-in microinverter in the US; the coverage named no certifying lab. Neither claim is a listing of a complete system with panels, cabling and mounting, which is what Maine, Vermont and New York’s bill describe.

Two limits: balco.nyc could not search UL’s Product iQ directory, which requires an account, and has not searched every NRTL’s listings. If a complete system is listed after the review date above, the certifier’s directory is the authority, not this page.

For New York the timing is the point. The SUNNY Act has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature. If signed, it takes effect 90 days later, and its interconnection exemption would cover only devices listed as complete plug-in systems; on today’s market, none. It grants no right to install, so renters and co-op residents still need permission ([what the Act does and does not change](https://balco.nyc/sunny-act)).

## How to check a listing, and what “UL certified” can mean

A seller’s “UL certified” is a claim about some part of the product, to some standard. Four checks make it verifiable:

- **Find the mark and file number on each part**: the inverter’s nameplate and the panel’s label, not the box or the product page.

- **Look it up with the certifier.** UL’s Product iQ is free with an account and searches by file number, category code or model; CSA Group’s product listing is public. By the federal definition, a listed product is one that appears in such a list.

- **Read what the listing covers**: which standard, which model numbers, and whether it is the kit as sold or one part of it.

- **Get it in writing and keep it.** Ask the seller which lab listed which product, to which standard, under which file number. Maryland has you give the utility a certification of safety features, and Virginia tenants must show their landlord documentation.

| The claim | What it can mean | What it does not establish |
|---|---|---|
| “UL certified” or “UL listed” | Some part is listed by UL | Which part, to which standard |
| “UL 1741”, “UL 1741 SB”, “IEEE 1547” | The inverter’s safety and grid behavior | Anything about panels, cord, plug or circuit |
| “UL 3700 compliant” | The maker’s own statement | A listing by any NRTL |
| A microinverter certified to UL 3700 | That equipment was evaluated to the outline | That the complete system was |
| “ETL listed”, “CSA certified” | Listed by another NRTL, which most of the laws accept as equivalent | Which standard, until you look it up |
| Backward “UR” mark | A recognized component for factory assembly | Suitability as a standalone product |

> **Not legal advice.** Whether a kit satisfies a statute is for that state’s regulators, code officials and courts, and can vary by utility and building. Check the enacted text linked from your [state page](https://balco.nyc/states); a plug-in law binds the utility, not your landlord, board or insurer, unless it says so.

## Common questions

**What is UL 3700?**

UL 3700 is the Outline of Investigation for Interactive Plug-In PV (PIPV) Equipment and Systems, edition 1, dated 11 December 2025. It is a UL LLC certification document rather than a consensus standard, and UL Solutions began certifying to it on 8 January 2026. It evaluates plug-in solar equipment or a complete plug-in system, including the cord, plug, receptacle arrangement and ground-fault and overcurrent behavior, rather than the panel or inverter alone.

**Is any balcony solar kit certified to UL 3700?**

Not as a complete system, as of 23 September 2026. Some microinverters carry UL 3700 claims: APsystems says its EZ1 was certified by CSA Group in July 2026, and Hoymiles launched its HiFlow Pro as UL 3700-compliant. But no complete kit with panels, cabling and mounting is listed to UL 3700. PV Tech reported in August 2026 that UL Solutions was still working toward its first UL 3700 certification, and Bright Saver says no system on the market has achieved whole-system certification.

**If my kit has a UL 1741 microinverter and UL-listed panels, is it UL certified?**

Its parts are, but the kit as a whole is not. A listing covers the product submitted, in the configuration tested. UL 1741 covers the inverter's safety and grid behavior, and UL 61730 covers the panel. Neither tests the combination with the cord, plug and household circuit, which is where plug-in hazards such as unseen overcurrent arise. Whether separately listed parts satisfy a particular state law depends on that law's wording.

**Which states require UL 3700 for plug-in solar?**

Of the nine states with signed plug-in solar laws as of 23 September 2026, Maine, Vermont and New Jersey name UL 3700. Maine and Vermont ask for UL 3700 or an equivalent listing of the system itself. Maine also allows a system configured to the state-adopted electrical code. New Jersey also accepts a comparable standard or combination of standards. Utah, Maryland, Colorado, Virginia and New Hampshire require NRTL certification without naming a standard, and Connecticut names UL 1741.

**Does New York's SUNNY Act require UL 3700?**

It does not name UL 3700, but it is stricter. The bill requires a device listed or certified by an accredited nationally recognized testing laboratory as a complete plug-in photovoltaic system. As of 23 September 2026 no complete system holds such a listing. The SUNNY Act has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature; if signed, it takes effect 90 days later and grants no right to install.

**What is an NRTL?**

A nationally recognized testing laboratory is defined in federal rule 29 CFR 1910.7. It is an organization recognized by OSHA that tests equipment for safety, lists or labels it, inspects production and is independent of the manufacturers it tests. OSHA's list has 21, including UL LLC, CSA Group, Intertek and TÜV SÜD. State plug-in laws that say UL generally accept an equivalent NRTL as well.

**How can I check whether a plug-in solar product is really listed?**

Find the certification mark and file number on the nameplate of each part, then look it up in the certifier's own directory: UL's Product iQ (free with an account) or CSA Group's public product listing, for example. Check which standard the listing is to and whether it covers the complete kit or one component. A claim of being UL 3700 compliant is the maker's own statement, not a listing.
