# How many US homes could use balcony solar, and how much could they make?

URL: https://balco.nyc/us-balcony-solar-potential  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

About 34.7 million US households, 68 million people, live in buildings of two or more units. balco.nyc’s estimate from Census Bureau surveys puts 22.5 million of them with a porch, deck, balcony or patio, and 8 million to 14 million with outdoor space where a railing panel is plausible, facing a usable direction. An unshaded 800 W panel there makes about 580 kWh a year; if 5% installed one, the total would be 230 to 410 million kWh, under 0.03% of what American homes use.

## The estimate in five steps

No US survey counts balconies, so balco.nyc built the number from two Census Bureau surveys and its own solar runs. The American Community Survey (ACS) counts households by building size. The American Housing Survey (AHS), run for the Department of Housing and Urban Development, reports which homes have outdoor space and how tall their buildings are. balco.nyc’s PVWatts runs for the largest city in every state give what a panel there would make. Each step narrows the count:

| Step | US households | Where the number comes from |
|---|---|---|
| All occupied homes, 2024 | 132.7 million | ACS 2024 1-year, table B25032 |
| …in a building with two or more units | 34.7 million (26.2%) | ACS B25032 |
| …with a porch, deck, balcony or patio | 22.5 million | AHS 2023 share by building size, applied to the ACS counts |
| …of which above the ground floor | 12.8 million | AHS 2023 stories in structure, units spread evenly over the floors |
| …facing south, south-east, south-west, east or west | 8.0 to 14.1 million | 5 of the 8 compass directions, assuming facades face every way equally |

balco.nyc’s computation, state by state. The low end of the last row starts from the above-ground count; the high end from every porch, deck, balcony or patio.

So the answer is **roughly 8 million to 14 million households**, 23% to 40% of those in apartment buildings. It is a ceiling on what is physically possible, not a forecast. It does not ask whether the household may install a panel (86% of them rent), whether there is an outdoor outlet, whether a plug-in law applies, or whether the building across the street blocks the sun. Each of those removes more.

## How many Americans live in apartments

The ACS 2024 1-year estimates, the newest released, count 132,737,146 occupied homes in the United States; **34,742,315 (26.2%)** are in buildings of two or more units, from a two-family house to a tower. In people (table B25033), that is 68.3 million Americans, 20.6% of the 331.7 million living in households, and 46.5 million of them are in buildings of five or more units. Counting vacant units too (table B25024), there are 39.6 million homes in multi-unit buildings.

| Building size | Households, 2024 | Renting |
|---|---|---|
| 2 to 4 units | 9,689,275 | 81.9% |
| 5 to 9 units | 5,725,714 | 87.9% |
| 10 to 19 units | 5,484,624 | 89.7% |
| 20 to 49 units | 4,920,407 | 86.9% |
| 50 or more units | 8,922,295 | 87.1% |
| All buildings of 2+ units | 34,742,315 | 86.2% |

US Census Bureau, ACS 2024 1-year, table B25032. Margins of error on these national counts are under 1%.

Two things follow. Apartment households are overwhelmingly renters: 29.9 million of 34.7 million, and 65% of all US renter households. For them a panel is the landlord’s decision first ([can renters install balcony solar?](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-renters)). And the biggest group lives in the smallest buildings: 9.7 million households in duplexes, triple-deckers and small walk-ups, more than the 8.9 million in buildings of 50 or more units.

## How many apartments have a balcony

No federal survey counts balconies on their own. The AHS asks about a “porch, deck, balcony, or patio” as one item, in its 2023 table *Rooms, Size, and Amenities*, and counts one if it is attached to the unit or free-standing, open or enclosed, and at least 4 by 4 feet. That makes it an upper bound: a ground-floor patio or an enclosed porch counts, and neither is a railing facing open sky.

| Building size | Porch, deck, balcony or patio: US | New York State | Above the ground floor (US, estimated) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 to 4 units | 73% | 55% | 44% |
| 5 to 9 units | 70% | 34% | 52% |
| 10 to 19 units | 69% | 35% | 59% |
| 20 to 49 units | 59% | 15% | 64% |
| 50 or more units | 51% | 21% | 75% |

Shares of occupied units, AHS 2023 Table Creator. The last column is balco.nyc’s estimate from the AHS count of stories per building. Margins of error at 90% confidence: about ±2 points for the US shares, ±4 to ±10 for New York’s.

The share falls as buildings get taller, and owners report outdoor space more often than renters (61% against 49% in buildings of 50+ units). Place matters even more. New York is the outlier among the states the AHS reports: about a third of its apartment households have any outdoor space, against two-thirds nationally. Where the AHS publishes a state figure for a building size (all five sizes for New York, Illinois and Massachusetts; four for Ohio and Pennsylvania), balco.nyc used it; elsewhere, the national rate with those five states removed, 62% to 76% by building size. The survey withholds this detail for California, Texas and Florida, so their counts rest on that rate. The result is **22.5 million households**, 65% of apartment households, the same share the AHS reports nationally.

The AHS does not record which floor a unit is on, only how many stories its building has. If units are spread evenly across floors (buildings of four to six stories counted as five, seven or more as ten), 44% of homes in two- to four-unit buildings are above the ground floor, rising to 75% in buildings of 50+ units. Assuming outdoor space is as common upstairs as down, that leaves **12.8 million**. This is the least certain step (section 7).

## What one balcony could make

Nothing records which way American balconies face, so balco.nyc assumed facades face every way equally and counted five of eight compass directions as usable: south, south-east, south-west, east and west. That is the 5/8. The three left out earn it: a vertical north-facing railing makes about 29% of a south-facing one in the median state, north-east or north-west about 45% ([output by direction](https://balco.nyc/800w-balcony-solar-output)).

For output, balco.nyc averaged its PVWatts runs for those five directions in each state’s largest city, for an 800 W system hung vertically, and multiplied by 0.95, the site’s allowance for the railing shading the bottom of the panel. Weighted by where the balconies are, one panel makes **579 kWh a year**, from 441 kWh in Anchorage to 725 kWh in Las Vegas; in New York City, 520 kWh (604 facing south, 421 facing west).

That is about 9% of an apartment’s electricity: the EIA’s 2020 Residential Energy Consumption Survey puts average use at 6,093 kWh a year in buildings of five or more units and 6,665 kWh in two- to four-unit buildings. At each state’s EIA average residential price (20.4¢ weighted by where the balconies are), it is worth about **$119 a year** if every kWh is used at home. Those averages include fixed charges, so they somewhat overstate what a kWh not bought is worth, and exported surplus earns nothing under most plug-in laws ([self-consumption](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-net-metering)).

All of this assumes an open view. balco.nyc’s shade model keeps only 38% to 43% of a south railing’s output on a third floor facing a six- to ten-story building 20 m away ([is balcony solar worth it?](https://balco.nyc/is-balcony-solar-worth-it)). A national count cannot see what stands opposite each balcony; the calculator can, given an address.

## If 1% or 5% took it up

Take-up cannot be measured yet, so here are two round scenarios applied to the 8.0 to 14.1 million households, each with one 800 W panel, unshaded and fully used at home:

| Households adopting | Households | Panels | Electricity a year | Worth, at state-average prices |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1% | 80,000 – 141,000 | 64 – 113 MW | 46 – 81 million kWh | $10 – $17 million |
| 5% | 401,000 – 703,000 | 321 – 563 MW | 232 – 407 million kWh | $48 – $84 million |

balco.nyc’s computation: households × each state’s five-direction PVWatts output × 0.95 × the state’s EIA average price. Shade would lower the last two columns.

Nationally these are small numbers. The top of the 5% range is under 0.03% of the 1,483 billion kWh American homes bought in 2024 (EIA: 143.1 million residential customers averaging 863 kWh a month), or the annual use of 38,000 to 67,000 apartments. The case for balcony solar is made household by household, not on the grid. As a market, 5% adoption at the site’s $1,200 mid-range kit price is $0.5 billion to $0.8 billion of kits, bought once: arithmetic on these assumptions, not a forecast.

The obvious benchmark is Germany. Its register of generators, the Marktstammdatenregister kept by the Bundesnetzagentur, listed **1,512,855** plug-in systems in operation when balco.nyc queried it on 23 September 2026, and the Bundesnetzagentur says about 430,000 were registered in 2025 alone. The US 5% scenario is 0.9 to 1.6 years of German registrations at that pace, and Germany’s registered total equals 11% to 19% of the whole US pool above. The comparison is of scale only: German systems also sit on houses and gardens, German rules allow up to 2,000 W of panels behind an 800 VA inverter, and the register counts only what owners register. [What Germany’s numbers show](https://balco.nyc/germany-balcony-solar).

## Where the potential is, and where it is legal

Five states hold 44% of apartment households and ten hold just over 60%. New York has the highest share of any state, 51.2% of its households (only the District of Columbia is higher, at 67.7%), but its low rate of outdoor space puts California, Texas and Florida ahead of it in plausible balconies:

| State | Apartment households | Share of state’s households | Plausible for a railing panel | kWh/yr per panel | Plug-in law, 23 Sep 2026 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| California | 4,369,726 | 31.7% | 1.12 – 1.92 million | 653 | Passed, awaiting the Governor |
| New York | 4,007,157 | 51.2% | 0.45 – 0.83 million | 520 | Passed, awaiting the Governor |
| Texas | 2,908,158 | 25.4% | 0.76 – 1.27 million | 551 | No bill found |
| Florida | 2,510,189 | 27.5% | 0.65 – 1.10 million | 567 | No bill found |
| Illinois | 1,646,905 | 32.3% | 0.34 – 0.62 million | 535 | Bill pending |
| New Jersey | 1,299,775 | 36.7% | 0.32 – 0.58 million | 549 | Signed; in force 1 Mar 2027 |
| Massachusetts | 1,198,494 | 42.4% | 0.22 – 0.44 million | 574 | Bill pending |
| Pennsylvania | 1,113,895 | 20.8% | 0.22 – 0.41 million | 567 | Bill pending |
| Ohio | 1,056,109 | 21.4% | 0.23 – 0.43 million | 552 | Bill pending |
| Washington | 903,714 | 28.5% | 0.24 – 0.39 million | 453 | Bill died |

balco.nyc’s computation. Apartment households: buildings of 2+ units (ACS 2024, B25032). Output: average of five railing directions for the state’s largest city, unshaded, after the 0.95 railing factor. Law status: balco.nyc’s state tracker.

Where it is legal is a much smaller map:

| Plug-in law, 23 Sep 2026 | Where | Apartment households | Share of US | Plausible for a railing panel |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| In force | Colorado, Maine, Maryland, Utah, Vermont | 1,726,863 | 5.0% | 445,000 – 760,000 |
| Signed, not yet in force | Connecticut (1 Oct 2026), New Hampshire and Virginia (1 Jan 2027), New Jersey (1 Mar 2027) | 2,727,857 | 7.9% | 683,000 – 1,211,000 |
| Passed, awaiting a governor | California, New York | 8,376,883 | 24.1% | 1,565,000 – 2,746,000 |
| Bill pending, bill died, or none found | 39 other states and DC | 21,910,712 | 63.1% | 5,327,000 – 9,351,000 |

About one apartment household in twenty lives where a plug-in law is in force; nearly one in four lives in the two states waiting on a governor. California’s SB 868 was presented to Governor Newsom on 31 August and, as of 23 September 2026, awaits his decision, due by 30 September; New York’s SUNNY Act has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature, and it grants no right to install. A law is not permission either: most of these households rent, and of the five in-force states only Vermont limits a landlord’s power to refuse today (Colorado’s limit starts on 1 January 2027). See the [provision-by-provision comparison](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-laws-compared) and each [state page](https://balco.nyc/states). This is a summary of statutes, not legal advice.

## Every assumption, and which way it cuts

The estimate rests on assumptions that can be stated, and most of them push it up rather than down:

- **Outdoor space is a combined item.** The AHS does not separate balconies from porches, decks and patios, so 22.5 million overstates balconies.

- **The ground-floor step is a model.** Ground-floor units probably have patios more often than upper floors have balconies, and the AHS counts a basement as a story, so 12.8 million is likely high. Against that, some ground-floor patios have a fence or railing a panel could hang on. Assuming different heights for the tallest buildings moves the count by about 2%.

- **Direction is assumed uniform.** If balconies favor the sunny side, more than 5/8 are usable; if they face the street, it depends on the grid.

- **State detail is thin.** Forty-five states and DC, including California, Texas and Florida, use the national rate without New York, Illinois, Massachusetts, Ohio and Pennsylvania. AHS shares from 2023 are applied to ACS counts from 2024.

- **Output is a ceiling.** One city per state, an 800 W panel hung vertically, no shade, every kWh used at home.

- **Not counted:** landlord, condo or co-op permission; an outdoor outlet; state law; a certified kit (as of September 2026 no complete plug-in system is certified to UL 3700, although components are). Houses and townhouses are left out; most have a roof or yard instead.

The honest reading: the US has several million apartment balconies where a plug-in panel is physically plausible, each able to make roughly 440 to 725 kWh a year on an open view, worth $63 (Washington) to $233 (Hawaii) at state-average prices, $96 in the median state. How many get one depends on law, landlords and shade, not on the count of balconies. For a single balcony, the calculator replaces every assumption here with your address, your direction and what stands across the street.

## Common questions

**How many Americans live in apartments?**

The Census Bureau's 2024 American Community Survey counts 34.7 million households, 26.2% of the 132.7 million in the US, in buildings with two or more units. That is 68.3 million people, 20.6% of Americans living in households, and 46.5 million of them live in buildings with five or more units. About 86% of these apartment households rent.

**How many US apartments have a balcony?**

No federal survey counts balconies separately. The 2023 American Housing Survey asks about a 'porch, deck, balcony, or patio' as one item, and about 65% of households in multi-unit buildings report one, falling from 73% in two- to four-unit buildings to 51% in buildings of 50 or more units. balco.nyc's estimate is 22.5 million households, an upper bound on balconies because ground-floor patios count too. New York is far lower: about a third of its apartment households report any outdoor space.

**How many US homes could use balcony solar?**

balco.nyc estimates 8.0 to 14.1 million apartment households have outdoor space where a railing panel is physically plausible and that faces south, south-east, south-west, east or west. The low end counts only outdoor space above the ground floor; the high end counts every porch, deck, balcony or patio. The figure ignores permission, outlets, shade and state law, each of which lowers it.

**How much electricity could balcony solar produce in the US?**

An unshaded 800 W panel hung on a railing facing a usable direction makes about 579 kWh a year on average, by balco.nyc's PVWatts runs weighted by where the balconies are, or about 9% of what an apartment uses. If 5% of the plausible 8 to 14 million households installed one, the total would be 232 to 407 million kWh a year, under 0.03% of US residential electricity use. Shade would lower it.

**How many apartment households live in states where plug-in solar is legal?**

As of 23 September 2026, 1.73 million, or 5.0% of US apartment households, live in the five states with a plug-in solar law in force: Colorado, Maine, Maryland, Utah and Vermont. Another 7.9% live in Connecticut, New Hampshire, New Jersey and Virginia, whose laws are signed but not yet in force, and 24.1% in California and New York, where bills have passed and await the governor. A law in force is not a right to install for renters in most of these states.

**How does the US compare with Germany on balcony solar?**

Germany's national generator register, the Marktstammdatenregister, listed 1,512,855 plug-in solar systems in operation on 23 September 2026, and the Bundesnetzagentur says about 430,000 were registered in 2025 alone. If 5% of plausible US apartment balconies got a panel, that would be 401,000 to 703,000 systems, about 0.9 to 1.6 years of German registrations at the 2025 pace. The comparison is of scale only, since German systems also sit on houses and gardens.

## Sources

Balkonkraftwerk)” and status “In Betrieb”, it returned 1,512,855 units when balco.nyc queried it on 23 September 2026.

# What is balcony solar?

URL: https://balco.nyc/what-is-balcony-solar  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

Balcony solar, also called plug-in solar, is a small photovoltaic system — usually one to four panels on a balcony railing, facade or window — connected to a microinverter that plugs into an ordinary wall outlet. The power flows into your apartment’s circuits and is used by whatever is switched on. It is not off-grid: it shuts down in a blackout. Output is typically capped at 800–1,200 watts AC. Several US states allow it; New York does not yet.

## What a balcony solar system actually is

A balcony solar kit is a complete, self-contained generator small enough to be carried up in a lift and installed without an electrician. Four parts, and no more than four:

- **Panels.** Usually one to four rigid or semi-flexible modules, hung from a railing, clamped to a parapet, bolted to a facade or mounted outside a window.

- **A microinverter.** A weatherproof box, roughly the size of a hardback book, that converts the panels’ DC output into grid-frequency AC and limits how much it delivers.

- **A cable and plug.** A single AC lead ending in a standard household plug, or in a locking connector on systems designed for a dedicated socket.

- **Mounting hardware.** Rail hooks, ballasted feet or brackets. Usually the part that decides whether a given balcony is workable at all.

What it is *not* is worth stating as plainly. It is not a rooftop array made small, and it is not a camping power station. Those three things behave very differently:

|  | Balcony solar | Rooftop solar | Portable panel and battery |
|---|---|---|---|
| How it connects | A plug into an existing outlet | Hardwired to the electrical panel by a licensed contractor, under a utility interconnection agreement | Not connected to the building at all — it charges a battery you plug appliances into |
| Who installs it | The resident, in an afternoon | A contractor, over days, with permits and inspection | The resident, in minutes |
| Scale | Hundreds of watts to about 1.2 kW AC | Several kilowatts | Whatever the battery can hold |
| Works in a blackout | No — it shuts off automatically | No, unless paired with a battery and transfer switch | Yes; that is the whole point of it |
| Surplus sold back | Where legal, generally earns nothing | Credited under net metering rules | Nothing to sell — it never touches the grid |

## How the electricity gets into your apartment

The microinverter is the whole trick. It is a *grid-following* device: it reads the voltage and frequency already present at the outlet, locks onto that 60 Hz waveform, and pushes current out in phase with it. It cannot create a supply of its own. It can only add to one that is already there.

Once that current is on the branch circuit, ordinary physics takes over. Electricity flows to the nearest load, so a fridge on the same circuit draws from the inverter before it draws from the street. Your meter simply records less coming in. There is no switching, no controller, and nothing for you to operate.

If the grid goes down, the inverter loses its reference waveform and stops within about two seconds. This is called anti-islanding, and it is a safety requirement, not a defect: it stops your panels from energizing a line that a utility crew believes is dead. The practical consequence for you is that **balcony solar gives you no backup power whatsoever**. In a blackout it is inert.

Most state laws cap a plug-in system at 1,200 watts, though none balco.nyc has read says why. At 120 volts that is ten amps, and it is not trivial: the breaker protecting a branch circuit only sees the current drawn from the panel, so a device feeding ten amps in at an outlet can let loads further along the circuit draw more through part of the wiring than the breaker allows. That is why the laws insist on certified equipment and why an electrician’s look at the circuit is worth having; [the circuit arithmetic is worked here](https://balco.nyc/is-plug-in-solar-safe). Certification standards for this equipment cover anti-islanding behavior, voltage and frequency trip limits, and the safety of a plug that is energized from both ends.

## Where the savings come from

A balcony system saves money in exactly one way: by displacing electricity you would otherwise have bought. There is no second mechanism.

In Con Edison territory the number that matters is the all-in marginal rate — supply, delivery and surcharges together — which balco.nyc models at **$0.34/kWh**. Every kilowatt-hour your panels produce *and you consume at that moment* is worth that much. Every kilowatt-hour produced while the apartment is empty flows out to the grid and, in the states that have legalised these devices, generally earns nothing at all.

That makes self-consumption the dominant variable, and it is a behavioral one rather than a technical one. A refrigerator, a router, a standby television and a hot-water recirculation pump run through the middle of the day whether or not you are home, and they absorb a real share of a small system’s output. Beyond that baseload, the value depends on who is in the flat at noon.

For sizing, balco.nyc models a typical 800 W NYC system at roughly **400–900 kWh a year**. That is a wide band on purpose. A high-floor, south-facing balcony produces about **three times** what a low-floor, north-facing one does, and the difference between those two cases is far larger than the difference between a budget kit and a premium one.

> **One thing balcony solar can never touch: Con Edison’s fixed monthly customer charge, about $20, is billed whether you use any electricity or not. It is excluded from the $0.34/kWh marginal rate, and no amount of generation reduces it.**

Kit costs for a typical 800 W NYC setup run about **$850 budget, $1,200 mid-range, $1,600 premium**. To see the yield and payback for a specific address, floor and facing direction rather than a typical one, use the [calculator](https://balco.nyc/), or read the [cost and payback breakdown](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-cost).

## Whether it is legal where you live

**Plug-in solar is not yet legal in New York.** The obstacle is not a fire code or a building rule — it is that New York requires anyone connecting a generator to the grid to sign an interconnection agreement with their utility, and no tariff recognises a device you plug into a wall socket. There is no compliant path to install one today.

The bill that would change this is the SUNNY Act (S8512C / A9111C). It would exempt compliant devices producing up to **1,200 W of AC inverter output** from interconnection and net-metering requirements, and bar utilities from charging fees for them. It passed the Senate unanimously in April 2026 and the Assembly in late May 2026. It now awaits Governor Hochul’s signature; she has until the end of 2026 to act, and it would take effect 90 days after signing.

What the SUNNY Act does not do is as important as what it does. **It removes the utility barrier only. It grants no right to install anything.** A renter still needs the landlord’s permission, and a co-op or condo resident still needs the board’s. The [SUNNY Act page](https://balco.nyc/sunny-act) covers the text, the timeline and what would still stand in your way.

Elsewhere the picture has moved quickly. Utah passed the first plug-in solar law in 2025, and by September 2026 Maine, Virginia, Colorado, Maryland, Connecticut, New Hampshire, Vermont and New Jersey had signed comparable laws — nine states, most using the same 1,200 W threshold. New York, whose SUNNY Act has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature, and California, whose SB 868 awaits Governor Newsom, could be next. [The rules in every state](https://balco.nyc/states) are listed with their bills and dates.

## Germany, the case everyone points to

Balcony solar is not a new idea being tried out. It is a mature German consumer product, sold in supermarkets, that the United States is now importing along with its regulatory shape.

- German rules cap the inverter’s **AC output at 800 watts** while allowing considerably more panel capacity behind it — the inverter simply clips the peak, which raises output in dim conditions without ever exceeding the limit.

- Since the 2024 Solarpaket I reforms, an owner registers the system in the Bundesnetzagentur’s Marktstammdatenregister online, in minutes. No grid-operator approval is involved.

- More than **1.3 million** systems were recorded as operating in that register by mid-2026, with roughly 430,000 added during 2025 alone.

- Since October 2024, German law treats a balcony system as a privileged modification: landlords and owners’ associations can no longer refuse a reasonable request without documented grounds.

Two cautions before reading German experience across. German households run on 230 V circuits, which changes the current a given wattage draws. And Germany paired legalisation with a tenant’s right to install — the step New York has explicitly not taken.

## What balcony solar is bad at

It is a modest device and it is worth being clear about its ceiling.

- **It is at the mercy of your balcony.** Orientation, floor height and the buildings across the street matter more than any equipment choice. In dense Manhattan and downtown Brooklyn, a neighbouring tower can take most of a winter’s production.

- **It gives you no resilience.** Anti-islanding means it goes dark exactly when you might want it most. Backup requires a battery, which is a separate purchase and a separate decision.

- **Surplus is wasted.** Without export compensation, generation that exceeds what your flat is drawing is simply given away.

- **Mounting is a real engineering question in a tall building.** Wind loading on a panel at the fortieth floor is not the same as on a German ground-floor balcony, and the NYC Building Code requires railing components to be designed for wind where the load is significant. This is the point at which many NYC balconies turn out not to work.

- **There is no federal tax credit.** The residential clean-energy credit under Section 25D expired for systems placed in service after 31 December 2025. Balcony solar is bought at full price.

- **Permission is the usual sticking point.** Even after legalisation, a co-op board that objects to the look of a panel from the street can end the conversation.

## How this site estimates output for a specific balcony

Anything you read about balcony solar in general — including everything above — describes a category. What decides whether it is worth it for you is one particular balcony, on one particular floor, facing one particular direction, with particular buildings in front of it.

balco.nyc estimates that case by running an 8,760-hour annual simulation in **NREL’s PVWatts V8**, positioned using **NYC PLUTO** building data, with a custom 3D shadow model of neighbouring buildings within **200 metres**, and emissions converted using the **EPA eGRID2023 NYCW** factor.

The stated accuracy is **±15%**, or ±20% on the client-side fallback path. That figure describes the modelled band, and nothing more.

> **These estimates are modelled, not metered. No installed NYC system has been measured against them, because none can legally be installed yet. Treat the output as a well-constructed simulation, not as a measurement.**

The full method, its inputs and its known weaknesses are set out on the [methodology page](https://balco.nyc/methodology).

## Common questions

**What is balcony solar?**

Balcony solar, also called plug-in solar, is a small photovoltaic system of roughly one to four panels mounted on a balcony railing, facade or window and connected to a microinverter that plugs into a standard household outlet. The electricity it generates flows into the apartment's circuits and is consumed by whatever appliances are running. Systems are typically limited to between 800 and 1,200 watts of AC output.

**How does balcony solar work?**

The panels feed a microinverter that reads the voltage and frequency already present at the wall outlet and pushes matching AC current onto that circuit. Appliances draw from this nearby source before drawing from the grid, so the meter records less imported electricity. Because the inverter needs an existing grid signal to synchronize with, it shuts down automatically within about two seconds if the power goes out.

**Is balcony solar legal in New York?**

No. As of September 2026, New York still requires an interconnection agreement with the utility for any grid-connected generator, and no tariff covers a device plugged into an outlet. The SUNNY Act (S8512C / A9111C) would exempt compliant systems up to 1,200 W AC; it passed both chambers in 2026 and awaits Governor Hochul's signature, taking effect 90 days after she signs.

**Does balcony solar work during a power outage?**

No. Grid-following microinverters require an existing grid waveform to synchronize with, and safety rules require them to stop energizing the circuit within about two seconds of an outage so that utility crews are not exposed to a live line. Balcony solar therefore provides no backup power at all. Blackout resilience requires a separate battery system.

**Will I still need my landlord's or co-op board's permission?**

Yes. The SUNNY Act, if signed, would remove the utility's ability to require an interconnection agreement or charge fees, but it grants no right to install anything on a building. Renters would still need landlord approval and co-op or condo residents would still need board approval. Germany added a tenant's right to install in 2024; New York's bill does not include one.

**How much does a balcony solar kit cost, and how much does it produce in New York City?**

A typical 800 W setup costs roughly $850 for a budget kit, $1,200 mid-range, or $1,600 premium, before mounting complications. balco.nyc models annual production for such a system in New York City at roughly 400 to 900 kWh, with a high-floor south-facing balcony producing about three times what a low-floor north-facing one does. These are modelled estimates with a stated accuracy of plus or minus 15%, not metered results.

- [New York legislature passes SUNNY Act plug-in solar legislation](https://pv-magazine-usa.com/2026/06/01/new-york-legislature-passes-sunny-act-plug-in-solar-legislation/): Assembly passage, certification and fire-code conditions, anti-islanding requirement.

# What is PVWatts, and what do its defaults get wrong for a balcony?

URL: https://balco.nyc/what-is-pvwatts  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

PVWatts is the free solar calculator from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR, the lab formerly called NREL): it simulates a panel hour by hour through a typical weather year. It can model a balcony, but its defaults describe a rooftop array, and balco.nyc’s PVWatts runs show that left at those defaults it overstates a vertical, south-facing 800 W railing panel by about 72% in New York City (1,037 kWh a year against 604), 70% in Chicago and 82% in Phoenix, before any shade from the buildings opposite. Roughly 85% of that gap is a single setting: tilt.

## What PVWatts is, and how accurate NLR says it is

PVWatts is a free web calculator and API published by the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR), the Department of Energy lab in Golden, Colorado that was called the National Renewable Energy Laboratory until the Department renamed it on 1 December 2025. Most people still search for it as “NREL PVWatts”. It is the same tool, now at pvwatts.nlr.gov, with its API at developer.nlr.gov; the old nrel.gov addresses no longer resolve.

What it does is narrow and well documented. For a location, it takes a typical meteorological year (TMY) of weather from the National Solar Radiation Database — one year of hourly data chosen to represent a multi-year period — and simulates all 8,760 hours: where the sun is, how much light reaches a panel at the tilt and azimuth you enter, how much reflects off the glass, how hot the cells run, the DC output, the inverter’s conversion, and finally a flat percentage for other losses. Version 8, the current one, reads the NSRDB’s tmy-2020 files.

It asks for six inputs: system size, module type, array type, system losses, tilt and azimuth. Optional ones cover the DC-to-AC ratio, inverter efficiency and ground coverage ratio, and since V8, albedo, bifacial modules and a month-by-month irradiance loss for soiling or snow. Reset to its defaults on 23 September 2026, the calculator reads: 4 kW, standard module, fixed open rack, 20° tilt, due south, 14.08% losses, DC-to-AC ratio 1.2, 96% inverter efficiency, ground coverage ratio 0.4.

On accuracy, NLR is candid. Its Version 5 manual puts the possible error at up to ±10% on annual totals and ±30% on monthly totals for typical weather, and says a particular year can depart from the long-term average by up to ±20% annually and ±40% monthly. The calculator’s current cautions page repeats those bands and calls its results accurate to within 10 to 12% of long-term performance. No Version 8 manual exists yet; the API documentation says one is forthcoming, so the 2014 manual remains the most detailed reference.

> **Those bands assume the inputs describe the system.** The same cautions page warns that results can be overly optimistic with the default losses when nearby buildings or trees shade the modules. On a balcony the inputs are the problem, not the model.

## From PVWatts’ defaults to a balcony, one setting at a time

To measure how far the defaults sit from a balcony, balco.nyc ran PVWatts V8 through its public API on 23 September 2026 for an 800 W (0.8 kW), due-south system in New York City, Chicago and Phoenix. Each run starts from the calculator’s defaults and changes only what its row names, until it reaches the parameters balco.nyc’s own calculator sends. The last step is balco.nyc’s 5% railing loss, which PVWatts has no input for. Figures are kWh a year, with the change from the row above.

| Step | New York City | Chicago | Phoenix |
|---|---|---|---|
| PVWatts defaults: open rack, 20° tilt, standard module, DC/AC 1.2 | 1,037 | 1,050 | 1,416 |
| Tilt 90°, vertical on a railing | 669 (−35.4%) | 684 (−34.8%) | 857 (−39.5%) |
| Premium module instead of standard | 663 (−0.9%) | 678 (−1.0%) | 853 (−0.5%) |
| Micro-inverter: DC/AC 1.1, 96.5% efficiency | 667 (+0.5%) | 681 (+0.5%) | 856 (+0.4%) |
| Monthly urban soiling, 3% in winter to 7% in summer | 635 (−4.7%) | 648 (−4.8%) | 819 (−4.4%) |
| Albedo fixed at 0.20 and losses at 14% (balco.nyc’s PVWatts parameters) | 636 (+0.1%) | 649 (+0.1%) | 819 (+0.1%) |
| Railing loss ×0.95, applied by balco.nyc outside PVWatts | 604 (−5.0%) | 616 (−5.0%) | 778 (−5.0%) |
| Defaults overstate the balcony panel by | 72% | 70% | 82% |

The New York arithmetic: 1,036.8 kWh at the defaults against 635.7 × 0.95 = 603.9 kWh for the balcony, a ratio of 1.72. Put the other way, a vertical south-facing panel makes about 58% of the default estimate in New York and Chicago and 55% in Phoenix. In yield terms, the defaults imply 1,296 kWh per kW in New York; the balcony gets 755 (the [kWh formula](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-kwh-formula) shows how that per-kW figure is used).

Tilt is nearly the whole story. Moving the panel from 20° to vertical removes 367 of the 433 kWh gap in New York, 85% of it; the share is 84% in Chicago and 88% in Phoenix, where the summer sun stands higher and meets a vertical face at a more glancing angle. Soiling and the railing account for about 7% each. Everything else nets to about 1%.

None of this means PVWatts is wrong. Told the panel is vertical, it models a vertical panel; its defaults simply describe a tilted rooftop array. The final PVWatts figures in the table are the same runs behind balco.nyc’s [state pages](https://balco.nyc/states), which publish them for the largest city in every state.

## The settings that barely move a vertical panel, and not the way you would expect

Two steps that a reader might expect to help do not, and it is worth being exact about what PVWatts’ documentation does and does not explain.

**Premium module.** PVWatts’ module-type help lists the premium module at about 21% efficiency and −0.35%/°C, against 19% and −0.37%/°C for standard, both behind anti-reflective glass. The slightly better temperature coefficient should, if anything, add output. Instead the premium setting produced 0.9% less for the vertical New York panel, and 0.5% less at 20°. The documentation does not say why, and it is not fully consistent: its technical-reference page still quotes the Version 5 coefficient of −0.47%/°C for standard modules. We report the result as measured and have not traced its cause. The calculator itself cautions that it does not distinguish better-performing modules from worse ones; module type is a modeling label, not a quality dial.

**Open rack versus roof mount.** The documented difference is temperature: PVWatts assumes an open-rack array runs cooler (installed nominal operating cell temperature 45 °C, against 50 °C for roof mount), which should favor open rack. At 20° the two land within 0.1% in New York. At 90°, open rack was 1.0% *lower*, and its plane-of-array irradiance was 1.6% lower too, which a temperature model cannot cause. balco.nyc re-ran the vertical New York panel with the ground coverage ratio at its minimum, 0.01: the irradiance matched roof mount again and open rack came out 0.5% *ahead* (680 against 677 kWh); at 0.9 it fell to 616 kWh. So in V8 the ratio affects fixed open-rack arrays, although the help page says it applies only to one-axis tracking. PVWatts defines the ratio by the spacing between rows of modules; a balcony has one row. The effect is small and runs against the balcony, so balco.nyc, which leaves the ratio at its default, errs low by about 1.6% here.

**Inverter and soiling.** The micro-inverter step adds about 0.5%, which is what the efficiency change alone predicts (96.5 ÷ 96 = 1.005), so the lower DC-to-AC ratio does almost nothing for a vertical panel. The monthly soiling profile, averaging 5% across the year, costs 4.4 to 4.8%. Replacing the weather file’s albedo with a fixed 0.20 changes almost nothing.

## A vertical panel is a winter panel

The annual total hides a change of shape. The table compares New York City at the defaults (20° tilt) with the same 800 W system at 90°: only the tilt differs, and both are before soiling and railing losses. From balco.nyc’s PVWatts V8 runs, kWh per month.

| Month | 20° tilt | Vertical | Vertical as % of 20° |
|---|---|---|---|
| Jan | 63.1 | 75.2 | 119% |
| Feb | 72.9 | 71.6 | 98% |
| Mar | 89.2 | 67.5 | 76% |
| Apr | 100.3 | 50.5 | 50% |
| May | 109.4 | 40.7 | 37% |
| Jun | 110.7 | 34.7 | 31% |
| Jul | 113.6 | 39.3 | 35% |
| Aug | 104.1 | 44.6 | 43% |
| Sep | 92.3 | 59.4 | 64% |
| Oct | 74.5 | 64.9 | 87% |
| Nov | 55.8 | 60.8 | 109% |
| Dec | 50.8 | 60.4 | 119% |
| Year | 1,037 | 669 | 65% |

From November through January the vertical panel makes more than the tilted one, 19% more in December and January, because the low winter sun meets a vertical face closer to head-on. In June it makes 31% as much. Over the six months from October to March the two are almost level, 400 against 406 kWh; the whole annual gap opens in spring and summer. December to February is **31% of the vertical panel’s year** and 18% of the tilted panel’s. Chicago and Phoenix show the same pattern, with the vertical panel ahead in November, December and January in both.

This matters for any monthly figure: a bill offset, a comparison with winter usage, or a July check on whether the panel is working. A vertical panel producing a third of a rooftop array’s output in June is behaving as modeled.

## What PVWatts does not model on a balcony

PVWatts simulates an unobstructed array and values its output simply. On a balcony, five things it leaves out can matter as much as every setting above.

- **The buildings opposite.** PVWatts does not model shading by nearby objects, and its default 14% loss includes just 3% for shading. In a street canyon obstruction is often the [largest single variable](https://balco.nyc/balcony-sunlight). balco.nyc adds a horizon model: from 3D building footprints for a New York balcony, and elsewhere from a description of what stands opposite and how far away. In balco.nyc’s fallback table, a low floor in a dense canyon keeps 45% of the unshaded output and a top floor with an open view keeps 97%.

- **The railing and hardware.** Rails, clamps and the balcony edge can clip the bottom of a panel. PVWatts assumes nothing does. balco.nyc applies a flat 5% at 90° (3% at 70°, 2% at 60°, 1% at 35°), an assumption rather than a measurement.

- **The balcony above.** A slab overhead cuts off part of the sky a vertical panel would otherwise see and, depending on how far it projects, some direct sun. Neither PVWatts nor balco.nyc models it; the [methodology](https://balco.nyc/methodology) lists it as a known limitation.

- **Self-consumption.** PVWatts values output at an annual average retail rate and, by its own description, effectively assumes net metering. Surplus from a plug-in panel is usually uncompensated unless a specific state law or utility credits it. balco.nyc assumes every kWh is used in the home and that surplus earns nothing. If your daytime base load is below the panel’s midday output, some production goes unpaid, and neither tool can see your load.

- **What a kWh is worth.** One average rate is not the number a panel displaces. In New York City balco.nyc uses Con Edison’s all-in marginal rate of about 34¢/kWh ([why that rate](https://balco.nyc/electricity-rate)); elsewhere it uses the EIA state average, which includes fixed charges and can overstate what a saved kWh is worth, and lets you enter your own rate.

## How to use PVWatts for a balcony yourself

PVWatts is free and needs no account. These are the settings balco.nyc sends it for a railing panel:

| Input | Enter | Why |
|---|---|---|
| DC system size | 0.8 for 800 W of panels | The panels’ combined nameplate rating, in kW |
| Module type | Premium | balco.nyc’s setting; Standard gave about 1% more in these runs |
| Array type | Fixed (open rack) | Air on both faces of the panel |
| System losses | 14% | PVWatts’ default; see the note below |
| Tilt | 90 | Vertical; 60 or 70 for an angled bracket |
| Azimuth | The direction your facade faces, clockwise from true north | S 180, SW 225, W 270, E 90. A Manhattan building facing the avenue faces about 209° or 29°, not 180° |
| DC to AC size ratio | 1.1 | A micro-inverter matched to one or two panels |
| Inverter efficiency | 96.5 | Micro-inverter |
| Ground coverage ratio | 0.4 (default), or 0.01 | 0.01 removes rows of panels a balcony does not have: +1.6% in the New York run |
| Albedo | 0.20, or leave “from weather file” | About 0.1% either way |
| Monthly irradiance loss (soiling) | 3, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 7, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3 | January to December; an urban profile averaging 5% |

Then multiply the annual kWh by 0.95 for the railing, and by your own estimate of what the buildings opposite take away. Facing direction matters about as much as tilt: with these settings, balco.nyc’s New York runs give 604 kWh a year facing south, 446 facing east, 421 facing west and 167 facing north, after the railing loss and before shade.

One note on losses. PVWatts builds its 14% from ten categories that include 2% for soiling and 3% for shading, and its soiling help suggests adjusting the total if you also enter monthly soiling. balco.nyc keeps 14% and treats the bundle as covering longer wiring runs and availability instead. If you prefer PVWatts’ suggestion, set soiling to zero in its loss calculator: the total drops to 12.3% and output rises about 2%.

balco.nyc does all of this for any US address, and adds the two things PVWatts cannot: shade and price. It calls PVWatts V8 for your exact coordinates with these parameters, applies the railing factor, builds a horizon from the buildings around a New York balcony (or from your description elsewhere), and values the output at a rate for your location. [Run it for your balcony](https://balco.nyc/), or read [how the calculation works](https://balco.nyc/calculate-balcony-solar-output) and [what an 800 W kit produces](https://balco.nyc/800w-balcony-solar-output).

## Common questions

**What is PVWatts?**

PVWatts is a free solar production calculator and API from the National Laboratory of the Rockies, formerly the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL). It simulates a photovoltaic system hour by hour through a typical meteorological year of weather data from the National Solar Radiation Database, using six basic inputs: system size, module type, array type, system losses, tilt and azimuth.

**Is PVWatts accurate?**

For the system you describe, NLR's PVWatts documentation puts the possible error at up to ±10% on annual totals and ±30% on monthly totals for typical weather, and says a particular year can depart from the long-term average by up to ±20%. Those bands assume the inputs are right. PVWatts does not model shade from nearby buildings, and its default settings describe a tilted rooftop array, not a vertical balcony panel.

**How much do PVWatts' defaults overstate a balcony solar panel?**

In balco.nyc's PVWatts V8 runs for a south-facing 800 W system, the default settings overstate a vertical railing panel by about 72% in New York City, 70% in Chicago and 82% in Phoenix. That compares the defaults with balco.nyc's balcony parameters plus a 5% railing loss, before any shade from nearby buildings. The tilt setting accounts for roughly 85% of the gap.

**Can PVWatts model a vertical balcony panel?**

Yes. Enter a tilt of 90 degrees and the azimuth your facade faces, measured clockwise from true north. For an 800 W south-facing panel in New York City, balco.nyc's runs show this cuts the annual estimate from about 1,037 kWh at the defaults to about 669 kWh, before soiling, railing and shade losses.

**Is NREL PVWatts the same as NLR PVWatts?**

Yes. The Department of Energy renamed the National Renewable Energy Laboratory the National Laboratory of the Rockies on 1 December 2025. PVWatts is the same tool, now at pvwatts.nlr.gov, with its API at developer.nlr.gov; the old nrel.gov addresses no longer resolve.

**Does PVWatts account for shade from nearby buildings?**

No. PVWatts does not model shading by nearby objects; its default 14% system loss includes only 3% for shading, and NLR warns that results can be overly optimistic when buildings or trees shade the array. On a city balcony shade is often the largest factor, so it has to be estimated separately. balco.nyc adds a horizon model for this.

**Why does a vertical balcony panel produce so much less than PVWatts' default?**

Mostly because of tilt. PVWatts' default is a panel tilted 20 degrees, which faces the high summer sun; a vertical panel meets it at a glancing angle. In balco.nyc's New York runs the vertical panel makes 31% as much as the 20-degree panel in June but 19% more in December and January, and the two are almost level from October to March.

## Sources

- [U.S. Department of Energy — Energy Department renames NREL “National Lab of the Rockies”](https://www.energy.gov/cmei/articles/energy-department-renames-nrel-national-lab-rockies): the Department’s own announcement of the rename.
- [NLR — PVWatts Calculator (Version 8)](https://pvwatts.nlr.gov/): the web calculator; its default inputs were read from the calculator’s reset-to-defaults response on 23 September 2026 (4 kW, standard, open rack, 20°, 180°, 14.08%, DC/AC 1.2, 96%, GCR 0.4).
- [NLR Developer Network — PVWatts V8 API](https://developer.nlr.gov/docs/solar/pvwatts/v8/): the API and parameters used for balco.nyc’s runs, the NSRDB tmy-2020 weather data, and the statement that a technical report on Version 8 is forthcoming.
- [Dobos, PVWatts Version 5 Manual, NREL/TP-6A20-62641 (2014)](https://pvwatts.nlr.gov/downloads/pvwattsv5.pdf): error of up to ±10% annual and ±30% monthly for typical weather, and up to ±20%/±40% for a particular year; the hourly simulation sequence.

- [PVWatts help — Get Started](https://pvwatts.nlr.gov/docs/en/help_start.php): the six required inputs, the optional advanced inputs, and valuation at an annual average retail electricity rate.
- [PVWatts help — Solar Resource Data](https://pvwatts.nlr.gov/docs/en/help_resource.php): hourly typical meteorological year data from the NSRDB, representing a multi-year period.

- [PVWatts help — Module Type](https://pvwatts.nlr.gov/docs/en/help_module_type.php): standard (19%, −0.37%/°C) and premium (21%, −0.35%/°C) modules, both with anti-reflective glass.
- [PVWatts help — Technical Reference](https://pvwatts.nlr.gov/docs/en/help_reference.php): the calculation sequence, and the older −0.47%/°C standard-module coefficient that conflicts with the module-type page.
- [PVWatts help — Array Type](https://pvwatts.nlr.gov/docs/en/help_system_array_type.php): cell-temperature assumptions (INOCT 45 °C open rack, 50 °C roof mount) and that PVWatts does not model shading by nearby objects.
- [PVWatts help — Ground Coverage Ratio](https://pvwatts.nlr.gov/docs/en/help_system_gcr.php): the ratio’s definition by row spacing, its 0.4 default, and the statement that it applies only to one-axis tracking.
- [PVWatts help — Monthly Irradiance Loss](https://pvwatts.nlr.gov/docs/en/help_system_soiling.php): monthly soiling input, and the suggestion to adjust system losses if soiling is entered monthly.

# Solar panels behind a window: how much do they lose?

URL: https://balco.nyc/window-solar-panels  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

A solar panel behind a window loses about half its output through ordinary double glazing and about two-thirds through low-e glass. balco.nyc’s calculation for a south-facing window in New York City puts an 800 W-equivalent panel that would make 604 kWh a year on an open railing at 307 kWh behind clear double glazing and 206 kWh behind low-e glass, and Chicago, Los Angeles and Houston come out in the same proportions. For the 100–200 W panels people actually stand in windows, that is 24 to 89 kWh a year, worth about $4 to $29 at state average prices.

## The short answer, in four cities

Glass, sunlight angles and the window frame each take a share, and the shares multiply. balco.nyc started from its own unshaded PVWatts runs for a vertical, south-facing 800 W panel in the four largest US cities (the runs behind [the output-by-state guide](https://balco.nyc/800w-balcony-solar-output)) and applied three factors: how much of the light silicon can use passes through the glass head-on (section 2), how much more is lost because sunlight rarely arrives head-on, and how much sky the frame and wall leave a panel inside the room (section 3). The outdoor baseline carries the calculator’s 0.95 railing factor; behind a window, a 0.80 frame factor takes its place. In New York the chain runs: 635.7 kWh (PVWatts, before any railing loss) × 0.712 (clear double glazing, head-on) × 0.848 (angles) × 0.80 (frame and reveal) ≈ **307 kWh**.

| South-facing, 800 W equivalent, unshaded | Average price | Outdoors on a railing | Behind clear double glazing | Behind low-e double glazing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| New York City | 27.96¢ | 604 kWh · $169 | 307 kWh · $86 | 206 kWh · $58 |
| Chicago | 18.54¢ | 616 kWh · $114 | 312 kWh · $58 | 209 kWh · $39 |
| Los Angeles | 32.89¢ | 720 kWh · $237 | 357 kWh · $117 | 239 kWh · $79 |
| Houston | 15.90¢ | 576 kWh · $92 | 285 kWh · $45 | 191 kWh · $30 |

Behind clear double glazing a panel keeps **49–51%** of its open-railing output in all four cities; behind the low-e glass we modeled, **33–34%**. The dollar figures use the EIA’s average residential price for each state over the 12 months to June 2026, an average that includes fixed charges. At Con Edison’s 34¢ [marginal rate](https://balco.nyc/electricity-rate), the New York window figures become $104 and $70.

“800 W equivalent” is a unit for comparison: at the calculator’s 19% module efficiency, 800 W of panels covers about 4.2 square meters, more south-facing glass than most apartments have. Section 4 scales the numbers to panels that fit.

## Why low-e glass costs so much: the near-infrared

None of the numbers in a window’s specifications is the one a solar panel cares about. The **solar heat gain coefficient** (SHGC) counts all the solar heat that ends up indoors, including energy the glass absorbs and re-radiates inward, so it is not a transmittance at all. **Visible transmittance** is weighted to the human eye. **Solar transmittance** averages over the whole solar spectrum out to 2,500 nm, but a silicon cell’s response fades out a little beyond 1,100 nm.

The difference matters because of where silicon does its work. Weighting the standard spectrum for sunlight on a vertical surface (ASTM G197) by a generic silicon cell’s quantum efficiency, balco.nyc finds that **about half of the cell’s current comes from near-infrared light between 700 and 1,200 nm** (50%, or 55% with an idealized cell). That is the band a spectrally selective low-e coating exists to turn away: a Department of Energy technology alert defines such glazings as ones that “sharply cut off or reduce solar transmission beyond the visible range.”

So we computed the number that matters directly. From the measured spectral transmittance and reflectance of glass products in Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory’s glazing database, published with LBNL’s pyWinCalc code, we built each double-glazed unit wavelength by wavelength, allowing for light bouncing between the panes, and weighted it by that silicon response:

| Glazing, light arriving head-on | Visible transmittance | Solar transmittance | PV-weighted transmittance (used here) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Single clear pane, 3 mm (older windows) | 0.90 | 0.83 | 0.84 |
| Clear double glazing | 0.81 | 0.70 | 0.71 |
| Double glazing, pyrolytic (“hard-coat”) low-e | 0.75 | 0.57 | 0.64 |
| Double glazing, sputtered silver low-e | 0.65 | 0.39 | 0.48 |

For clear glass, solar transmittance is a fair stand-in. For low-e it understates what a panel receives, because much of what the coating blocks lies beyond silicon’s reach anyway, while visible transmittance overstates it. The two coatings differ for a reason the same DOE document gives: pyrolytic coatings transmit fairly evenly across the spectrum, while sputtered silver ones cut off sharply past the visible. The low-e column in section 1 uses the sputtered unit.

Low-e is the norm: by 2017, LBNL reported, 80% of US residential window sales included it. And our example is a mid-range coating. ENERGY STAR’s current criteria require an SHGC of 0.40 or less in its North-Central zone and 0.23 or less in the South-Central and Southern zones. Because SHGC includes all the solar energy that passes straight through, a window rated 0.23 transmits well under the 39% our low-e unit does, and a panel behind it would lose more than our low-e column shows.

## Angles, frames and a smaller piece of sky

Glass reflects more as light strikes it more obliquely, and a double-glazed unit has four surfaces to reflect from. LBNL’s WINDOW 5 results for a clear double-glazed unit, distributed with the Department of Energy’s EnergyPlus, give its solar transmittance as 0.727 head-on, 0.703 at 40° from square, 0.601 at 60°, 0.458 at 70° and 0.220 at 80°, and 0.624 for diffuse light arriving from the whole sky — 86% of the head-on value. balco.nyc applied that curve hour by hour to PVWatts’ direct and diffuse light on a south wall, weighting each hour by output. Over the year a south window keeps **85% of its head-on transmittance in New York**, 84% in Chicago and 82% in Los Angeles and Houston. We used the same curve for the low-e glass; coated glass behaves broadly, not exactly, alike.

The seasons help. In New York a south window keeps 94–95% of its head-on transmittance in December and January, when the low sun meets the glass almost square, and 70% in June, when the high sun glances off it. A vertical south panel makes most of its electricity in winter, so the window takes least when there is most to take. East and west windows in New York scored slightly better on this term, 0.87–0.88, on smaller totals.

Then there is the frame. Outdoors on a railing, a panel sees half the sky dome. Inside, it sees the sky through a hole in a wall whose sides, head and sill block the edges of the sky and, for much of the day, part of the direct sun. We modeled three placements against each city’s hourly sun and weather:

- a 200 W-size panel (0.7 × 1.3 m) inside a 0.8 × 1.4 m pane, 15 cm behind the outer edge of the opening, keeps 81% of its view outdoors and 74–80% of its direct sun: **0.77–0.80** overall;

- a 100 W-size panel (0.54 × 1.0 m) in a 0.6 × 1.1 m opening set 25 cm back, as in a thick masonry wall: 0.52–0.56;

- the same panel behind a 1.2 × 1.5 m picture window, 10 cm back: 0.97–0.98.

The tables use **0.80**: an assumption about a middling window, not a measurement. A real window can cost a tenth of that loss or more than twice it.

Two common things make it worse. A sash bar or the meeting rail of a double-hung window crossing the panel casts a thin shadow that costs far more than its area, because a panel’s cells are wired in series and a string cannot carry more current than its most shaded cell. And an insect screen outside the glass takes a large bite: EnergyPlus’s reference fiberglass screens, 0.38–0.41 mm strands at 1.55–1.67 mm spacing, are only 55–60% open to light arriving head-on.

## What “window solar” is, and what a real panel makes

“Window solar” means three different things, and only two go in a window you already have:

- **A portable panel and a power station.** The common setup: a small panel, often folding, that stands on the sill or hangs on suction cups, cabled to a portable power station — a battery with a built-in inverter and its own outlets.

- **Pocket chargers.** Small suction-cup panels with a built-in battery for a phone.

- **Photovoltaic glass.** A different product altogether: the window itself generates, and it is installed as the glazing rather than placed behind it. See-through designs trade efficiency for transparency. A 2017 lab device at the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (now the National Laboratory of the Rockies), a window that tints itself in sunlight, reached 11.3% efficiency tinted and 68% visible transmittance clear over 20 switching cycles; the Department of Energy calls unproven durability its greatest barrier.

For the first kind, here is what balco.nyc’s factors give for a 100 W and a 200 W panel behind a south-facing window, using the 0.80 frame factor:

| City | 100 W, clear double | 100 W, low-e double | 200 W, clear double | 200 W, low-e double |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| New York City | 38 kWh · $11 | 26 kWh · $7 | 77 kWh · $21 | 51 kWh · $14 |
| Chicago | 39 kWh · $7 | 26 kWh · $5 | 78 kWh · $14 | 52 kWh · $10 |
| Los Angeles | 45 kWh · $15 | 30 kWh · $10 | 89 kWh · $29 | 60 kWh · $20 |
| Houston | 36 kWh · $6 | 24 kWh · $4 | 71 kWh · $11 | 48 kWh · $8 |

The same 200 W panel on an open railing would make 144–180 kWh in these cities. Behind a single clear pane, the clear-glass figures rise by about 18%.

These are ceilings: they assume every kilowatt-hour displaces one you would have bought. A power station loses some of what it stores in charging and in its inverter, and once it is full the panel’s output goes nowhere; we have modeled neither. How a power-station setup compares with a plug-in kit is the subject of [portable solar vs plug-in solar](https://balco.nyc/portable-solar-vs-plug-in-solar).

## Permission: off-grid or grid-tied

How the panel is wired decides who has a say, not where it sits. A panel charging a portable power station, with your devices plugged into the station’s own outlets, never connects to the building’s wiring. Utility interconnection rules cover generators running in parallel with the grid — New York’s Standardized Interconnection Requirements are written for generators “connected in parallel with utility distribution systems” — so this setup needs no utility application and no plug-in solar law.

A plug-in microinverter behind a window is different. It feeds power into your circuits while the grid is live, which makes it a small grid-tied generator exactly as on a balcony; moving it indoors changes where the panel is, not what it is electrically. It needs your utility’s interconnection approval or a state plug-in solar law that waives it, and [those laws differ provision by provision](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-laws-compared). New York has no such law in force: the SUNNY Act has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature, and it grants no right to install.

A landlord’s say is separate: anything screwed into the frame or hung outside the glass is a matter for the lease ([the renters guide](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-renters) covers asking). This is general information, not legal advice, and the rules vary by state and utility.

## Heat behind the glass

Most of the light a panel absorbs becomes heat, and all of it does once the battery it charges is full. Behind glass, in still air, the panel cannot shed that heat as it would on a breezy railing. PVWatts’ temperature model assumes an open rack outdoors, and we found no published measurement of panel temperatures behind residential windows, so we cannot say what the heat costs in output.

Two cautions do have sources. The U.S. Fire Administration says not to put lithium-ion batteries in direct sunlight and not to charge them above 105°F (40°C): the panel belongs in the window, the power station does not. And glass makers warn that indoor blinds and drapes close to a pane raise the glass’s temperature and with it the risk of thermal stress cracking, with tinted and spectrally selective glass more susceptible than clear. A dark panel pressed against the glass looks like the same situation, though we found no test of it. Leaving a few centimeters of air costs a little sky (section 3) and is the more cautious choice. For a plug-in inverter behind a window, the circuit arithmetic in [is plug-in solar safe?](https://balco.nyc/is-plug-in-solar-safe) applies unchanged.

## Common questions

**Do solar panels work through a window?**

Yes, at reduced output. balco.nyc's calculation for a south-facing window in New York, Chicago, Los Angeles and Houston finds a panel behind clear double glazing makes about half of what it would on an open railing, and about a third behind a mid-range low-e window, once the glass, the angle of the sunlight and the window frame are all counted.

**Why do low-e windows cut solar panel output so much?**

About half of a silicon cell's current comes from near-infrared light between 700 and 1,200 nm, and that is the band spectrally selective low-e coatings are designed to reflect. Computed from LBNL spectral data and weighted for silicon, a sputtered low-e double-glazed unit passes 0.48 of the useful light head-on, against 0.71 for clear double glazing.

**How much does a 100 W solar panel make behind a window?**

Behind a south-facing window in the four largest US cities, balco.nyc's figures put a 100 W panel at 36 to 45 kWh a year behind clear double glazing and 24 to 30 kWh behind low-e glass, worth roughly $4 to $15 a year at state average electricity prices. Those are ceilings: they assume every kWh is used and ignore the power station's own losses.

**Can I use a window's SHGC or visible transmittance to estimate solar panel output?**

Neither is right. The solar heat gain coefficient includes heat the glass absorbs and re-radiates indoors, and visible transmittance is weighted to the human eye. Solar transmittance is a fair stand-in for clear glass; for low-e glass the transmittance that matters to silicon lies between the solar and the visible figures, 0.48 in balco.nyc's mid-range low-e example.

**Does a solar panel in a window need utility approval?**

Not if it only charges a portable power station whose own outlets you plug devices into: it never connects to the grid, and interconnection rules cover generators running in parallel with it. A plug-in microinverter behind a window is grid-tied and needs the utility's approval or a state plug-in solar law, just as on a balcony. This is general information, not legal advice.

**Is it safe to leave a solar panel against a window?**

Keep the battery out of the sun: the U.S. Fire Administration says not to put lithium-ion batteries in direct sunlight or charge them above 105 degrees F. Glass makers warn that blinds and similar objects close to a pane raise its temperature and the risk of thermal stress cracking, especially on tinted or low-e glass, so leaving an air gap behind the glass is the cautious choice.

**Are transparent solar windows the same thing as window solar panels?**

No. Photovoltaic glass replaces the window's glazing and generates power itself; it is installed as part of the window, not placed behind it. See-through designs give up efficiency for transparency: a switchable lab device at the National Renewable Energy Laboratory, now the National Laboratory of the Rockies, reached 11.3% efficiency in its tinted state in 2017, and the Department of Energy calls unproven durability its greatest barrier.

## Sources

- [National Laboratory of the Rockies — PVWatts V8 API documentation](https://developer.nlr.gov/docs/solar/pvwatts/v8/): the model behind the outdoor baseline and the hourly direct (dn), diffuse and plane-of-array irradiance used to weight the window’s angle and frame losses; balco.nyc’s runs use the calculator’s parameters for New York, Chicago, Los Angeles and Houston.
- [Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory — pyWinCalc](https://github.com/LBNL-ETA/pyWinCalc): LBNL’s window-calculation code, whose example data supply the spectral transmittance and reflectance of generic clear 3 mm glass (NFRC ID 102), a pyrolytic low-e (NFRC ID 9923) and a sputtered low-e (NFRC ID 1042) from LBNL’s glazing database, the ASTM G197 spectrum for a vertical surface and a generic silicon quantum-efficiency curve, from which balco.nyc computed the visible, solar and PV-weighted transmittances.
- [EnergyPlus — Window5DataFile.dat (LBNL WINDOW 5 output, DoubleClear)](https://github.com/NatLabRockies/EnergyPlus/blob/develop/datasets/Window5DataFile.dat): solar transmittance of a clear double-glazed unit (two 3 mm panes, 12.7 mm air gap) by angle of incidence: 0.727 at 0°, 0.703 at 40°, 0.601 at 60°, 0.458 at 70°, 0.220 at 80°, and 0.624 hemispherical.
- [EnergyPlus — WindowScreenMaterials.idf](https://github.com/NatLabRockies/EnergyPlus/blob/develop/datasets/WindowScreenMaterials.idf): strand diameter and spacing of the reference fiberglass insect screens, from which their 55–60% open area at normal incidence follows.
- [U.S. Department of Energy, Federal Energy Management Program — Federal Technology Alert: Spectrally Selective Glazings (LBNL, 1998)](https://eta-publications.lbl.gov/sites/default/files/femp-spec-sel-low-e.pdf): the definition of spectrally selective glazing as cutting off transmission beyond the visible range, that selective coatings reflect infrared while transmitting daylight, and that pyrolytic low-e coatings transmit fairly evenly across the solar spectrum.
- [Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory — Energy-Efficient Windows Save Billions (April 2017)](https://bies.lbl.gov/news/energy-efficient-windows-save): that 80% of residential window sales in the US incorporate low-e coatings.
- [ENERGY STAR — Residential Windows, Doors and Skylights, Version 7.0 specification](https://www.energystar.gov/sites/default/files/ES_Residential_WDS_V7_Final%20Specification%202022.pdf): the SHGC limits of 0.40 (North-Central) and 0.23 (South-Central and Southern), and the definition of SHGC as the solar heat gain entering the space relative to incident solar radiation.
- [PVEducation — Spectral response](https://www.pveducation.org/pvcdrom/solar-cell-operation/spectral-response): how a silicon cell’s response falls away at long wavelengths near its 1.12 eV band gap.
- [PVEducation — Mismatch for cells connected in series](https://www.pveducation.org/pvcdrom/modules-and-arrays/mismatch-for-cells-connected-in-series): that the current of series-connected cells cannot exceed that of the poorest cell, which is why a thin frame shadow costs more than its area.
- [Wheeler et al., Switchable photovoltaic windows enabled by reversible photothermal complex dissociation from methylammonium lead iodide, Nature Communications (2017), NLR](https://docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy18osti/68407.pdf): 11.3% efficiency in the tinted state, 68% visible transmittance in the clear state, and about 20 switching cycles.
- [U.S. Department of Energy — Switchable Photovoltaic Windows](https://www.energy.gov/cmei/buildings/articles/switchable-photovoltaic-windows): that the switchable PV window is a research project and that unproven durability is the greatest barrier to deployment.
- [New York State Department of Public Service — Standardized Interconnection Requirements](https://dps.ny.gov/distributed-generation-information): that New York’s interconnection requirements cover distributed generators and storage connected in parallel with utility distribution systems.
- [U.S. Fire Administration — Battery fire safety](https://www.usfa.fema.gov/prevention/home-fires/prevent-fires/batteries/): not to put lithium-ion batteries in direct sunlight, and not to charge them below 32°F or above 105°F (40°C).
- [Vitro Architectural Glass — Managing thermal stress breakage](https://glassed.vitroglazings.com/topics/managing-thermal-stress-breakage): that indoor shading close to the glass raises its temperature, and that tinted and spectrally selective glass is more susceptible to thermal stress breakage than clear.
- [U.S. Energy Information Administration — Form EIA-861M monthly sales and revenue](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/data/eia861m/): average residential prices for the 12 months to June 2026: New York 27.96¢, Illinois 18.54¢, California 32.89¢, Texas 15.90¢ per kWh.
